News.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle appears in court over child sex abuse material
News.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has appeared in court after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.

Markle was arrested on a federal complaint alleging he held images that show child sex abuse, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said.

The 82-year-old was arrested in Florida after the FBI searched two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for almost 20 years.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, the US Department of Justice (DoJ) said. Markle has previously denied allegations of possessing images of child sex abuse, calling them "sick lies".

Markle's court hearing lasted for 30 minutes, and the charges were laid out against him by federal prosecutor Courtenay Derry, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

He was brought into court a wheelchair, escorted by two US Marshals. Markle was wearing black trousers and a black t-shirt.

The court ordered Markle to submit to home detention at his assisted living facility in Florida and electronic monitoring.

No plea was taken during the hearing, and an arraignment date in California will be determined in due course, a joint statement from the DoJ and the US Attorney's Office Central California said.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex have not commented on Markle's arrest.

FBI director Kash Patel said authorities "moved quickly" when arresting Markle.

"Mr Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," Patel said.

He added that the FBI would "use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids â any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide".

Markle was arrested after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in LA registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

News.title: With Stephen Miller pick as new chief of staff, Trump readies for a battle
News.content:
In the aftermath of the Republican Party's sweeping defeat in Tuesday's midterm elections, Donald Trump said he would be willing to work with the newly ascendent Democrats in Congress.

On Friday, however, he elevated Stephen Miller, his bare-knuckled political operative and longtime adviser, to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff.

Far from an olive branch to Congress, Miller's promotion could be a sign that the president is girding for political battle by installing a partisan firebrand in the top White House job.

"The mission now is more clear than ever: Fight with all of our soul to support our president and defend this magnificent republic," Miller posted on X, adding that he was "honored beyond words" to be Trump's pick for the job.

One of the most powerful positions in Washington, the chief of staff is gatekeeper to the president, agenda-setter in the White House and chief negotiator with Congress and other outside political interests.

"Stephen Miller's been with me since the beginning," Trump said in comments to reporters after announcing the move on his Truth Social website. "He gets it."

News.title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
News.content:
Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".

"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.

She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.

In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".

On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.

The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."

Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

News.title: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event
News.content:
We live in a complex, electrically powered world - but the more connected everything becomes the more catastrophic it is when that fails.

In the drive towards efficiency over the last five decades, we've lost backup systems, says Lord Harris.

An example of this is the new communication system being adopted by the emergency services, which will replace radio comms with mobile phone network technology, says Lord Harris, "so if the mobile phone goes down it will also impact on emergency services communications".

However, the government insists "moving emergency services onto modern 4G and 5G technologies" is "resilient and reliable".

Government enthusiasm for resilience is nothing new. Oliver Dowden, the then deputy prime minister, launched the last Conservative government's disaster planning initiative in May 2024. The launch was somewhat overshadowed by Sunak announcing an election on the same day but, two years on, calls for at least three days of resilience have only grown stronger.

At the beginning of researching this article I spoke to an engineer about the UK's TV and radio transmission masts, their lonely isolation from the rest of the digital landscape sounded like a failing. It now feels like an argument in their favour.

The current urgency for disaster planning is coming at an interesting moment for technology we used to rely on. The UK's copper wire landline system - which would work even in a power cut - will be switched off on 31 January 2027. The future of FM radio is also under government review.

The response from the government was that while copper landlines had been a useful fallback during power cuts, they were now unreliable and difficult to repair.

As I ended my call with Kemp, I asked him if his report had helped improve our readiness for a Black Sky. He paused.

"If anything, we've gone backwards," he said. "Switching off the public switch telephone network, I think shows that there has been really no thought at all about how you communicate when you've no longer got power."

While writing this piece last Saturday I had to break off for an hour because my street was suddenly plunged into darkness. We had a power cut.

I found my emergency torch, but the batteries had leaked. My candles had been pushed to the back of a cupboard and I had no idea where I had put my wind-up radio with its emergency torch.

It felt like an omen.

News.title: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed
News.content:
"I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again."

That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled.

Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show.

Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me."

The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after the BBC's Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act.

The men involved have denied all the allegations against them.

As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation.

None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review.

News.title: Parliament restoration delays 'frustrating', says Commons Speaker
News.content:
The Speaker of the House of Commons has expressed "frustration" with the lack of progress on restoration to protect the Palace of Westminster.

Sir Lindsay Hoyle told the BBC the current process for approving essential renovations to Parliament amounted to "putting ourselves in handcuffs", and said more time was spent "doing surveys" than getting repairs under way.

The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for the ailing building's restoration, which could cost up to Â£40bn and take 61 years.

It said every additional year of delay cost taxpayers Â£420m, while its chairman warned the Palace could be left vulnerable to a devastating fire like that which engulfed the Notre Dame.

Sir Lindsay said his "biggest frustration" with the Victorian building's restoration was that "we're not getting on with the work".

"We spend more time doing surveys," he told BBC Radio 4's The Week in Westminster. "Instead of doing surveys, why don't we start repairing the building?"

The Speaker criticised current legislation which means the main renovations cannot begin until Parliament has approved the entire project's scope and funding.

"It's very frustrating when the Act of Parliament prevents you carrying out the major repairs that you need to. Talk about putting ourselves in handcuffs."

He added: "What we have to do is renovate and repair the problems areas."

News.title: Gladiator II stuntman sues over injuries from on-set explosion
News.content:
"The Claimant, playing a dead soldier, was lying on the port side of a ship which had been lit up by gas powered flame bars to simulate it being on fire," according to documents he filed at London's High Court.

"He was positioned only a few feet away from the gas line. Without warning, there was a gas explosion that caught the Claimant and blew him forwards.

"He saw 20 foot tall flames and felt immense heat. His costume caught fire. He was immediately aware that strips of skin had peeled from his arms.

"He panicked and ran, falling over a few times before escaping the flames. Bottles of water were thrown on him by colleagues, he was undressed and clingfilm was applied to his burns."

The legal claim said he suffered "flash burns" to 15% of his body, plus injuries to both knees and his right wrist, and was flown by helicopter to hospital in Marrakesh.

"He remained in excruciating pain. Treatment there was limited," Sarsfield's claim said. He was repatriated to the UK four days later, where his wounds were "treated appropriately" in hospital.

"Formerly a man of considerable physical prowess, the Claimant suffered considerable physical de-conditioning," with limitations to his mobility, and also suffered psychological symptoms, his claim said.

It added: "He has sustained significant scarring that is permanent and which is hypersensitive. He needs to keep out of the sun."

August Street Films' legal defence said "no admissions are made as to the alleged injuries sustained by the Claimant".

The company is a subsidiary of film studio Paramount, which said several people were hurt in the accident.

A Paramount spokesperson said in 2023: "While filming a planned stunt sequence on the set of the Gladiator sequel, an accident occurred during which several crew members experienced non-life-threatening injuries.

"The safety and full medical services teams on-site were able to act quickly so that those who were impacted immediately received necessary care. They are all in stable condition and continue to receive treatment.

"The well-being of the cast and crew is of the utmost importance to us, and we have strict health and safety procedures in place on all our productions. We will continue monitoring the situation and taking all necessary precautions as we resume production."

Sarsfield, August Street Films and Paramount declined to comment further.

News.title: Whole Australia team knew of sandpaper use, Khawaja says
News.content:
Khawaja, who scored 6,229 runs in 88 Tests, said that discussions about tampering with the ball began during the second Test of the series against South Africa.

That match, played at Port Elizabeth - now Gqeberha - led to what Khawaja said was the "discovery of sandpaper as an effective agent" after "open" discussions held in the dressing room at St George's Park.

"At this point Smith essentially threw his hands in the air and said he didn't want to know," Khawaja wrote.

Australia were rumbled in the third Test when television cameras clearly showed Bancroft using sandpaper on the ball to help generate reverse swing.

Khawaja was also shocked not to be asked to provide any evidence during Cricket Australia's investigation.

"In an ideal world, I don't want to do this. I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth," he said.

"The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."

While Smith, Warner and Bancroft - all batters - were punished, there was never an explanation of how bowlers Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon did not notice a change in the state of the ball.

In a 2021 interview with the Guardian, Bancroft was asked if the bowlers knew and replied: "It's pretty probably self-explanatory."

Days after Bancroft's interview was published, the quartet released their statement which said: "We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

"And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Llong and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage.

"We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo. It has gone on too long and it is time to move on."

News.title: Met Police boss 'wouldn't be surprised' if more allegations made about Brand
News.content:
During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.

Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.

Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Bayles and another member of Brand's staff had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did.

Shortly after, he sexually assaulted her.

She had complained to her manager, who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.

In recent years, Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.

In a statement, Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.

"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."

Bayles said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".

He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

Bayles said this was why he decided to stop working with Brand in 2010 and had not had any contact with him since. He added that during his time with Brand, no complaints were made about the entertainer's behaviour.

"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

News.title: Manhunt after boy injured by sword, sparking Gloucester school lockdowns
News.content:
Police described both suspects as white males. One is aged in his late teens to early 20s, of a medium to large build, and about 6ft tall. He was wearing white sliders at the time of the incident.

The other suspect is described as being about 5ft 5ins tall, of slim build and wearing black clothing.

St Peter's High School pupil Jimmy said the situation was "really scary" and he was still in shock.

After getting into the Tuffley school for the day, he said his friends came in and told him something had happened near his home.

He said the school's alarm then went off and the computer he was on displayed a message saying "This is a lockdown".

"The computers are not accessible at all and we've all had to turn the lights off, lock the doors, turn all the blinds down, and we've had to get on the ground," he said.

"At the time I was scared. My heart was racing," he added.

Jimmy said pupils were locked in their classrooms for two to three hours.

"[When police cars arrived] I thought this is getting serious, I'm getting worried, I don't know what's going on," he said.

The 15-year-old said he was able to message his mother when the school let students use their phones after about an hour.

"When I was able to eventually get out, she was giving me a bunch of hugs," he said.

"What I am is shocked. I'm surprised that this happened," he added.

Jimmy said the school had previously run lockdown drills but a real event had never happened before.

News.title: Man, 41, and boy, 16, arrested after car damaged by gunshots
News.content:
Two people have been arrested after armed police responded to an incident in which a car was hit by gunshots.

South Wales Police said a vehicle on the A48 in Morriston, Swansea, sustained damage "consistent with a firearms discharge" on Friday.

A 41-year-old man from Llansamlet, Swansea, had been arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm with intent to endanger life, while a 16-year-old boy, also from Llansamlet, had been arrested on suspicion of affray.

The force said officers were still investigating and that it had been declared a critical incident.

Residents have been told to avoid the area and events, including a local firework display, have been cancelled.

Video circulating online shows police officers next to a stationary car that appears to have been struck by a shotgun blast on Clase Road near an Asda superstore.

A National Police Air Service helicopter was circling the area but has since returned to base.

South Wales Police said the incident was ongoing, with road closures in place.

Ch Supt Stephen Jones said: "A policing presence will be visible in the area whilst this investigation is ongoing."

"It is important that people avoid the area so we can effectively deal with this incident and return the area to normality."

The local football club, Morriston Town AFC, cancelled a planned firework display on Friday.

"Unfortunately, the police have advised due to an issue ongoing, the event has to be cancelled. With immediate effect," it said in a social media post, advising people to stay at home.

News.title: One of the year's most prolific meteor showers to light up the night sky this weekend
News.content:
The Leonid meteor shower is set to dazzle sky gazers across the UK throughout November.

The celestial spectacle takes place from now until 30 November with the peak taking place on the night of 17 November.

There could be the chance to spot up to 10-15 meteors per hour.

The shower is made up of dust particles from the Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which leaves a trail of debris as it follows its path around the Sun.

These particles enter the Earth's atmosphere at up to 44 miles (71km) per second - meaning these streaks of light are the fastest meteors in the sky.

News.title: Skepta: 'I'm what it looks like if you give an immigrant child a chance'
News.content:
And while Skepta's been focused on the message, he has also been deliberate about how he's delivering it.

"It took six years to make this because it's important to make sure we're not tone deaf," he says.

He learned the value of that when, in 2024, he had to take down artwork for his single Gas Me Up (Diligent), following allegations that it referenced the Holocaust.

The image showed a group of men with shaved heads, one featuring a tattoo reading "Gas Me Up".

It had been a reference to skinhead culture, but Skepta acknowledged how without that context people could find it offensive and promised to be more mindful going forward.

Determined not to miss the mark this time around, he says: "I feel like we've delivered a classic."

Early reviews are mixed as to whether critics agree, however. While Complex said The Fork and Knife was "top-tier" and worth the wait, external, The Observer said it was well-intentioned but questioned whether it was "over-egged", external.

At a time when he thinks standards have been slipping though, striving for a classic is more important than ever.

"I don't think there's been a good grime album for a long time," Skepta says.

"And I'm here to set levels."

In September, Digga D called out the viral 'UK Poo' trend, which saw a wave of tracks blowing up on TikTok defined by what he described as "foolishness".

"I can't sit on here and be like 'I'm happy with how the UK scene is right now'," the rapper told 1Xtra's DJ Target. "Because I'm not."

Turns out Skepta isn't happy either.

Drawing on his idols, and even featuring some of them like Suggs, he says he is "here to make rap sophisticated again".

As BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first UK rap chart show, he's hopeful more grime artists will be inspired to sharpen their pen game.

"Rap is a sport and it's very hard for visibility when we're being compared to people who have major machines behind them," he says.

"So this rap chart is going to give all the newcomers and a lot of people who are producing in their bedroom a chance to be seen and heard."

News.title: Man, 35, charged with murder of Carrie Mullane
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder by police investigating the disappearance and suspected murder of Carrie Mullane (Noonan).

Mullane, who is 39, has been missing since she arrived in Enniskillen from Limerick on 10 October 2026.

The 35-year-old man is also charged with preventing the lawful burial of a corpse.

He is due to appear via video link before Dungannon Magistrates' Court on 7 November.

Earlier on Friday, police carried out a number of searches in County Fermanagh, including Lough Erne.

A small boat and a camper van were recovered and taken away for examination.

News.title: Dutch launch shows smugglers are adapting, says MP
News.content:
Dover MP Mike Tapp says smugglers will keep adapting after it was discovered that a boat stopped in the Channel with 38 migrants on board had launched from the Netherlands.

Prosecutors have confirmed the vessel that was found floating with no engine near Cadzand on Saturday had entered the water from Dutch territory.

This year crossings have already been attempted along a wider stretch of coast from Belgium to Normandy.

The UK government said that overall crossings were down significantly this year.

"As launch disruptions grow, the criminal gangs will adapt and a part of that will be finding new launch locations and methods," said Tapp.

"That means our operational efforts must also be agile.

"We have seen a significant reduction in crossings this year, but we still have a long way to go."

News.title: 'Misleading' student loans information left out examples of higher-salary repayments
News.content:
Several universities in England have only been using below-average salaries in examples of student loan repayments on their websites, the BBC has found.

Treasury Committee chair Dame Meg Hillier, who led a recent inquiry into student loans, said some information about repayments was "misleading", including one instance where they were compared to the "cost of a daily coffee".

She also said the Department for Education (DfE) must include higher-salary examples on its own website, too.

The DfE said it would review the information it provides, while universities said their websites referred to government information and would be reviewed where necessary.

Student loan repayments are tied to earnings, so the more you earn, the more you repay every month - and graduates generally go on to earn more than non-graduates.

Current and prospective students in England take out Plan 5 loans to pay for their tuition fees and living costs. They repay 9% of anything they earn over Â£25,000 for 40 years, or until the loan is paid off.

The BBC looked at publicly available information on more than 110 university websites in England and found cases of inaccurate information about the salary at which they start repaying and the length of time they repay for.

It also found that 12 universities only gave students worked examples of repayments based on earnings that are less than the UK average, which is Â£39,039.

News.title: Delhi air pollution tracker: Why is winter haze so bad in India’s capital?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Delhi’s air quality fell into the "very poor" category this week, days before the Hindu festival of Diwali was expected to make it worse.

The Central Pollution Control Board classes readings of 301 to 400 as "very poor" and beyond 400 as "severe".

The deterioration in air quality came after the Indian capital saw the lowest average AQI for October in eight years, at 166, and north-westerly winds carrying smoke from crop burning in neighbouring states returned after a storm.

The Commission for Air Quality Management, which coordinates pollution control across the National Capital Region, invokes Stage II of the Graded Response Action Plan on Monday. Stage II involves the use of measures such as more mechanical sweeping and water sprinkling to control road dust, higher parking charges to discourage private vehicle use, restrictions on the use of coal and firewood in open eateries and restaurants, stricter rules on diesel generators, and more inspections of construction and demolition sites. The commission also asked governments and municipal bodies to consider staggered working hours for public offices.

The Delhi state government's Winter Action Plan also came into force this week. It bars vehicles that don’t meet Bharat Stage VI, India's latest vehicle emissions standard, from entering the capital until 31 January, with authorities turning back 1,539 such vehicles at Delhi's borders and issuing fines of more than 6.8 million rupees (£58,000) on the first day.

The air pollution is expected to worsen over the weekend as many people celebrating Diwali burst fireworks, as they do almost every year.

The Supreme Court ruled earlier this week that people celebrating Diwali could use certified green fireworks, carrying QR codes for buyers and authorities to verify the manufacturer, in Delhi and its neighbouring areas on 7 and 8 November between 6am and 7am and between 8pm and 10pm local time, but not within 300 metres of hospitals, care homes, schools, or other silence zones.

The order requires police to patrol designated sales areas, carry out random QR-code checks and seize illegal fireworks.

Wind and particle map

Past week and forecast

Why is Delhi's winter air pollution so bad?

The most harmful air pollutant is PM2.5, fine particulate matter measuring less than 2.5 micrometres across that can penetrate deep into the lungs.

The largest single source of winter PM2.5 in Delhi, at 27 per cent, is particles that form in the air from gaseous emissions, known as secondary particulate matter, according to a January 2026 report by the Indian government’s commission on air quality. Transport makes up about 23 per cent of the particulate matter, burning of crop residue, waste and other biomass 20 per cent, dust 15 per cent and industry 9 per cent.

Cold weather keeps the pollutants close to the ground, with temperatures and winds at their lowest and the layer of air near the surface in which pollutants can spread at its thinnest.

Farmers still burn crop residue because it is a cheap and fast way to clear fields, despite government schemes to manage stubble. Biomass burning also includes municipal and residential waste.

What are the health impacts of air pollution?

Air pollution kills millions of people a year, mostly through heart disease and stroke.

The World Health Organisation estimated that outdoor air pollution caused 4.2 million premature deaths globally in 2019, of which 68 per cent were from heart disease and stroke, 14 per cent from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 14 per cent from acute infections of the lower airways and 4 per cent from lung cancer.

A study published in 2024 in The Lancet Planetary Health estimated that 3.8 million deaths in India between 2009 and 2019 were linked to air pollution.

Long-term exposure to PM2.5 raises the risk of respiratory infections, heart diseases and lung cancer. Emerging evidence also links exposure to pregnancy and birth outcomes, fertility and type 2 diabetes, although those links are less firmly established.

People who are ill, children, older people, and the poor are more susceptible to the worst effects. The WHO describes air pollution as "one of the greatest environmental risks to child health".

What can you do to protect yourself from air pollution?

Sensitive groups like children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, should avoid all outdoor activity once the air quality index passes 100, and everyone should avoid outdoor exercise once it passes 150, the Swiss air quality monitor IQAir advises.

Above 200, sensitive groups should stay indoors and restrict their activities. Above 300, everyone should avoid exercise and stay indoors, IQAir says. At these levels it also advises keeping windows closed and running an air purifier indoors.

News.title: Hugo Keenan scores hat-trick as Ireland seal emphatic victory over Argentina
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick as Ireland preserved their unbeaten home record against Argentina with a comfortable 42-12 bonus-point victory in the Nations Championship.

The Pumas had famously stunned Andy Farrell’s 2025 British and Irish Lions squad on their previous visit to the Aviva Stadium, yet they entered the match having lost all 11 of their past meetings with Ireland in Dublin.

Felipe Contepomi’s side took an early lead when Mateo Carreras caught a cross-field kick from Tomas Albornoz over diminutive scrum-half Craig Casey to touch down in the left corner.

However, full-back Keenan crossed the line either side of a try by captain Dan Sheehan, allowing the hosts to establish a 21-5 advantage by half-time.

Sam Prendergast registered his maiden international try alongside five successful conversions, before Keenan’s third score and a powerful finish from Ronan Kelleher sealed a resounding win for the home team.

Carreras managed a late consolation try for Argentina, but the visitors' attempt to cause a surprise was hampered by yellow cards for Justo Piccardo and Efrain Elias, alongside an early head injury to skipper Julian Montoya.

This outcome was Ireland’s third victory from four Nations Championship matches, following summer successes against Australia and Japan and a defeat to New Zealand.

With head coach Farrell accepting that his side must improve to compete at next year’s World Cup, the opening fixture of the autumn provided an opportunity to assess several squad options.

Argentina’s 10th-minute score further subdued a flat crowd which was significantly below capacity.

However, Ireland swiftly hit back. Casey initially won a turnover penalty and then started a flowing team move from right to left which culminated with Mack Hansen sending Keenan racing across the try line.

open image in gallery Ireland’s win was a third from four matches in the Nations Championship after summer successes against Australia and Japan were followed by defeat against New Zealand ( Getty )

Hooker Sheehan – captaining his country in the absence of the injured Caelan Doris – crashed over 10 minutes later after Nick Timoney was held up following a lineout maul.

Argentina lost hooker Montoya before falling further behind when Keenan collected another Hansen pass to dance past three defenders and powerfully pirouette over.

While the Pumas have a wretched record away to Ireland, they have won three of four World Cup meetings between the nations.

Their hopes of securing a landmark success on Irish soil were hampered further by centre Piccardo being sent to the sin bin in the 35th minute for not retreating following a penalty.

Sheehan was then denied his second try when he was forced into touch just before grounding in an incident which led to him and Montoya’s replacement Leonel Oviedo each departing for head injury assessments.

Fly-half Prendergast secured Ireland’s bonus point within two minutes of the restart, spotting a gap between Marcos Kremer and Juan Martin Gonzalez to superbly race away and dot down.

Keenan was unable to prevent Pumas wing Carreras scoring his second before completing his treble following quick hands from forwards Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and Ryan Baird.

Replacement hooker Kelleher then bulldozed over in the aftermath of Elias being sent to the bin for a high tackle on Keenan, with Ciaran Frawley converting.

Ireland prop Sam Illo – on for his home debut – became the third player shown a yellow card before Farrell’s men cruised through the closing stages ahead of upcoming appointments with Fiji and world champions South Africa.

News.title: China confirms discussions underway on historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Beijing has confirmed for the first time that it is discussing a historic meeting between Chinese leader Xi Jinping, US president Donald Trump and Russian president Vladimir Putin.

Mao Ning, a spokesperson for the Chinese foreign ministry, said at a press briefing this week in Beijing that China “is in communication with relevant parties regarding a meeting between the three heads of state.”

Nothing is set, but the three-leader gathering would take place this month on the sidelines of a regional summit in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.

If it happens, it would be historic, but experts say the three leaders are unlikely to discuss anything substantive because their interests are at odds.

But they would gather for a photo, with China carefully choreographing the meeting, experts say.

open image in gallery Chinese President Xi Jinping walks by honor guard during a welcoming ceremony for Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema ( Reuters )

“I think it will happen. The question is the format and the content,” said Sun Yun, director of the China program at the Stimson Centre. “China wants the image but not the costs.”

Beijing is hosting this year’s leaders summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a 21-member grouping that includes the US and Russia.

Mr Trump is expected to travel to Shenzhen to meet the Chinese leader for the third time this year, maintaining a fragile trade truce that is set to expire in January.

In a sign that tensions persist, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, in a Friday video call with Chinese vice premier He Lifeng, urged Beijing to take “concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and critical minerals,” according to a statement from Greer's office.

open image in gallery Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting with members of the Security Council in Moscow, ( Reuters )

China's official news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday that both sides had in-depth and constructive exchanges in the call, and that China expressed concerns about Washington’s restrictive economic and trade measures against Beijing.

While he’s in China, Trump has said he would be interested in meeting Xi and Putin to discuss nuclear arms controls, though Putin is focused on talking about the war in Ukraine without Kyiv at the table.

“Putin has the most to gain from a leaders’ trilateral, and the Russians are clearly behind the push for a meeting, which would be a diplomatic coup,” said Danny Russel, a former senior State Department official who served in former president Barack Obama’s administration.

Mr Trump, with his “crush on authoritarian strongmen," would love the meeting, though he clearly has been warned by his advisers to steer clear of Ukraine as a topic of the discussions, said Mr Russel, who is now a distinguished fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

open image in gallery Donald Trump speaks to reporters after arriving in West Palm Beach, Florida, on 6 November 2026 ( Getty )

Sun of the Stimson Centre said Russia would likely use the summit to nudge China and the US closer to Moscow's positions on Ukraine, while “China will have to manage Russian manipulation.”

China also would not engage in talks on arms controls or discussions about Ukraine or Iran, other than its diplomatic refrain that peace is important and wars should end, Sun said.

Beijing's biggest challenge may be the perception. The summit “should not be equated to three great powers dividing up the world,” she said.

The meeting may amount to no more than a photo opportunity that would allow Putin to be seen next to U.S. and Chinese leaders, said Craig Singleton, senior director of the China program at the Foundation for Defence of Democracies.

“But these photo opportunities have diminishing diplomatic returns,” Mr Singleton said. “The spectacle may be historic without producing anything particularly consequential.”

News.title: Andy Farrell wants more from Ireland despite big win over Argentina
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Andy Farrell challenged Ireland to be more ruthless after they swept aside Argentina with a 42-12 bonus-point victory in the Nations Championship in Dublin.

Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick as the hosts ran in six tries but head coach Farrell felt his side missed opportunities to inflict even greater damage on the Pumas.

Further tries from captain Dan Sheehan, fly-half Sam Prendergast and replacement hooker Ronan Kelleher completed a dominant display against opposition hampered by ill-discipline and a string of costly errors.

Andy Farrell challenged Ireland to be more ruthless after they swept aside Argentina with a 42-12 bonus-point victory in the Nations Championship in Dublin.

Ireland’s emphatic win was a third from four matches in the competition after summer successes against Australia and Japan were followed by defeat against New Zealand.

“Obviously, the scoreline is a good one because not many teams do that to Argentina,” said Farrell. “They’re a very good side and a dangerous side.

“We saw that certainly at times, we fought hard to scramble back, so the 12 points (conceded) is very pleasing.

“The 42, six tries, I thought some outstanding stuff, some really clinical stuff.

“But I think the story of the game is we missed a chance to be ruthless.

open image in gallery Ireland’s Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick (Brain Lawless/PA) ( PA Wire )

“Having said that, the opportunities that we did have in the right parts of the field showed the dominance as far as field position and territory.

“So for a hit out, first up international game (of the season), a big one at that, it’s a good day.”

Mateo Carreras crossed twice for Argentina, including a 10th-minute opener.

But their hopes of an upset were undermined by yellow cards for Justo Piccardo and Efrain Elias and an early head injury to captain Julian Montoya.

Farrell praised “immense” full-back Keenan following his first home Test since March last year and was also impressed with wings Mack Hansen and Robert Baloucoune.

“I thought the back three was outstanding,” said Farrell.

“Hugo Keenan, it’s 22 months since he played here. He didn’t even remember what side of the pitch we warmed up on, which is a bit of an insult! But, wow, he was immense, wasn’t he?

“Same with Mack and Rob. The pace that he (Baloucoune) put on to the ball, he was a threat every time he got his hands on the ball, offloading the ball, good in the air, so delighted with the back three.”

Ireland have a host of injury concerns ahead of next weekend’s meeting with Fiji.

Sheehan was forced off for a head injury assessment but Farrell said the hooker “seems fine”. Baloucoune, Hansen, Sean Jansen and Josh van der Flier also picked up knocks.

open image in gallery Argentina’s Mateo Carreras (left) scored both his side’s tries (Brian Lawless/PA) ( PA Wire )

Argentina stunned Farrell’s 2025 British and Irish Lions squad on their last visit to the Aviva Stadium but have now lost all 12 of their meetings with Ireland in Dublin.

Pumas head coach Felipe Contepomi admitted individual mistakes proved costly.

“I’m very proud for the effort and what they tried to do and just going hard from the start of the game,” he said.

“But then we know there were a lot of individual errors which we need to get better because when you start summing up all those errors at this level against a team that is very cohesive, that is one of the three best teams in the world for the last 10 years, it makes it really hard.”

News.title: ‘We’re in a very fragile moment’: Sheryl Crow on the US midterms, Kid Rock and the next James Bond
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Dividing people, telling people who they should be, who they shouldn’t be, what they should believe, who they should hate,” observes Sheryl Crow of the Trump administration. “We’ve seen this in history, and we’re in a very fragile moment. I’m hoping [the midterms] reveal a desire through our votes to see this change and [to hold people] accountable.”

The American rock star was speaking to me ahead of the US midterm elections, an event that turns out to be a bloodbath for the Republicans who lose control of Congress to the Democrats, and with several states turning blue after years in the red. Crow has been a vocal critic of her country’s president over the years, and in September told her followers that “voting is our best and only option”. After our conversation, when the results make it clear that America wants change, she celebrates with a short statement to Instagram: “America voted for hope and equality for all. That’s what I call patriotism.”

It’s a suitably hopeful moment to speak with one of our greatest living songwriters, whose music frequently melds her signature sunny pop optimism with a harder rock edge, one that spurs you into picking yourself up, dusting yourself off and getting the hell on with it. Thirty years since she reminded us that “Everyday Is a Winding Road” and “A Change Would Do You Good”, she’s still at it – better than ever, in fact – with a new collection of songs about hope, resilience and putting up a fight.

“This music is definitely me working through what we’re all working through, I think, which is this feeling of: why do I feel so alone, and who are we at this moment in our humanity?” Crow says. “It’s really a testimony to the value of human connection.”

Her new project is titled Pick You Up, and it is appropriately uplifting, but also thoughtful and reflective about our uncertain times. She shies away from calling it an album, having initially announced that her 2019 record Threads, featuring duets with Neil Young and Stevie Nicks, would be her last. She then surprised everyone in 2024 with Evolution, having been inspired to write about the dark direction she thought humanity was taking.

Regardless of what you call Pick You Up, though, it contains some of her best songwriting, including the stunning opener “Freight Train”, which was fuelled by childhood memories of hearing the train whistle as it passed through her hometown of Kennett, Missouri, at night. “It’s really interesting getting older,” she tells me (clarifying, with a laugh, “I’m not going to say getting old,”) “because you spend quite a lot of time in reflection.”

It’s hard to believe she’s 64, but Crow has quite the extraordinary life to reflect back on. The nine-time Grammy winner started out as a music teacher, singing in cover bands at weekends, before a local producer helped her make a name for herself writing advertising jingles (she once said she made $40,000 for a jingle she wrote for McDonald’s). She gatecrashed auditions for Michael Jackson’s first solo world tour and, a month later, found herself singing backup to thousands of fans each night for over a year – something she described in a previous interview with The Independent as “a crash course in the music industry”.

open image in gallery A young Sheryl Crow performing with Michael Jackson in 1988 ( WireImage )

By the mid-Nineties, her debut album Tuesday Night Music Club had produced Crow’s first hit, “All I Wanna Do” and earned her three Grammy nominations, including for Best New Artist. Yet she’s on record as stating that her contemporaries in the decade’s male-dominated alt-rock scene shunned her. Instead, she found herself being championed by an old guard that included the Rolling Stones, Johnny Cash, Prince and Don Henley. Bob Dylan once gave her advice on overcoming writer’s block, while Stevie Nicks and Emmylou Harris contributed backing vocals to her fourth album, C’mon C’mon.

Now the same age as many of her mentors were when they were handing her advice, Crow recalls a conversation she had with Robert Plant, where the Led Zeppelin rocker told her he believed he was writing some of his best work but feared it wouldn’t be heard “because we’re not in the young demographic”. She doesn’t exactly disagree, but she’s found that idea liberating while writing her latest works: “There’s a joy of going in and not thinking like, ‘Is this going to be a hit?’” she explains. “These songs felt very immediate and inspired by the most interesting conversations in my life – conversations I’ve had with my kids in the kitchen.”

Crow, who relocated from LA to Nashville in 2007, has two sons – Wyatt, 19, and Levi, 16 – both of whom she adopted as a single parent. She says the things they asked about are “not things that would ever have crossed my mind when I was their age. They’re grown-up issues, and they’re complicated”. It’s fascinating to be a singer, she says, “but it’s more fascinating to be a mom.”

She and her sons have talked about the manosphere, those dark spots on the internet where men are told that the bulk of the problems they face – from mental health to low income, employment or their inability to get a girlfriend – are the fault of women and, more specifically, women’s empowerment.

“It’s a pretty powerful and successful device for propaganda, to figure out a way to get into every young male’s phone through algorithms to disseminate some of the most hateful rhetoric towards women that I’ve ever heard,” Crow says. “It’s important for me to say as a mom, ‘It’s not OK. It shouldn’t be normalised.’” Those conversations were what in part inspired her new song, “Freedom Bus”, a dreamy protest song on which she sings: “Whoever said freedom was free/ There ain’t no freedom without history/ And folks who died for you and me/ So don’t be an asshole, let everyone be.”

open image in gallery ‘Let everyone be’: Crow performing during the 19th ACM Honors at The Pinnacle in Nashville, August 2026 ( Getty )

The manosphere, she believes, is just another way of keeping us divided, and only benefits those in power. “We can’t be fools about this, we really do have to step back and look at who we’re becoming,” she says. She recalls driving home to see her parents and seeing a billboard with a picture of Trump’s face and one of his favoured slogans near their house: “They’re not after me, they’re after you, and I just happen to be standing in their way.”

“That thing sat in the middle of a field in a pretty rural area,” Crow says. “If you’re trying to get into the minds of people who are living their everyday lives, it’s pretty powerful to tell them that somebody who doesn’t agree with you is coming for your freedom.” The rows over transgender rights, gun control, women’s bodies… “all that crap is just tactics of fear,” she continues. “At a certain point, I’m hoping that we will be a little more analytical about the way we're being taken for fools.” What would be best, she believes, is to “set the phone down and start having conversations”.

It's pretty powerful to tell them that somebody who doesn't agree with you is coming for your freedom

You can’t win ’em all, though. Crow isn’t afraid of tough subjects, and there’s only a slight grimace as I ask about her relationship with controversial singer Kid Rock, with whom she has collaborated in the past and once described as a friend. The “All Summer Long” star – real name Robert Ritchie – happens to be one of Trump’s most vocal musical supporters. Crow has called him out previously for a vulgar remark he made about Taylor Swift in 2019, but also spoke of him somewhat fondly in a July interview with Bill Maher, during a conversation about getting along with people who share different beliefs to your own.

open image in gallery Kid Rock and Crow performing together in 2011 ( Getty )

“I don’t really see Bobby very much… I know he has a new Christian record out,” she says, carefully. “There are a lot of things about Christianity that I really hold dear, and one of those things is to not judge. Look around, help your community the best you can. The blessing is always in the blessing. So wherever he or anybody else is in their life, I am not going to be judgmental about that, and I’m always open to dialogue.” Like country star Miranda Lambert, with whom she collaborated on a brilliant cover of Loretta Lynn’s “Coalminer’s Daughter”, Crow prefers to take Dolly Parton’s lead instead of sewing more division when it comes to politics.

“I think she made her viewpoints very clear without ever wielding hate or shaming, gaslighting or any of those things that seem to be the norm,” Crow says of the late queen of country, who died in August this year. “She makes me wake up and think, ‘Am I leaving the world a better place than how I found it?’ Because she was able to do that and still be successful and be a badass woman who could outwit or out-sing any man on the planet.” She cracks a grin. “There, I said it! So that’s kind of where I stand with people who are in my life, who choose hateful rhetoric over disseminating that Christian love.”

She’s encouraged by younger artists like Olivia Rodrigo, who threw the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival in Irvine, California, in August to celebrate women across the spectrum of music, from Chappell Roan to Stevie Nicks, rapper Doechii and rock band Garbage. Rodrigo was inspired by Sarah McLachlan’s Lilith Fair event – at which Crow performed – in the late Nineties, and used the proceeds raised to go towards charities benefiting women and girls. “Oh my gosh, I love her,” Crow says of the younger star, with whom she has performed with on a few occasions. She presented Rodrigo with a Woman of the Year prize at the Billboard Women in Music Awards in 2022; Rodrigo joined her for a duet of “If It Makes You Happy” when Crow was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame a year later.

open image in gallery Crow and Olivia Rodrigo performing at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame ceremony in 2023 ( Getty )

“I texted her about her doing the festival and said, I can feel you approach the world from that perspective of like, ‘I want to be a good person,’” Crow says. “The fact she invited all these [charities to the festival] to educate the community about the ways they could lift each other up – that’s so powerful. It speaks volumes about her.” She gets excited talking about Rodrigo’s music, too: “Her songwriting is so clever, she’s such a good writer. There are certain people I listen to and go, ‘Gosh, now I want to go home and write… they inspire me.’ And Olivia is one of them.”

There are certain people who inspire me to write... Olivia Rodrigo is one of them

Crow namechecks Rodrigo again when I ask who she’d pick to do the 007 song (“she’s so versatile, she’d be amazing”). She famously recorded “Tomorrow Never Dies” for the film of the same name, starring Pierce Brosnan, in 1997, and was nominated for the Golden Globe for Best Original Song (losing to Celine Dion’s then omnipresent Titanic theme, “My Heart Will Go On”, by James Horner and Will Jennings). And what about the man himself… who should play Bond next? Crow is an avid fan of British television, and singles out frontrunner Jack Lowden, the star of Apple TV’s thriller series Slow Horses. “He’s just brilliant,” she says. “He’s so versatile and so likeable… I just feel like he’d be so great. Slow Horses is my favourite TV show, it blows my mind.”

open image in gallery Crow: ‘Lowden would be so great as James Bond’ ( AFP/Getty )

A lot has changed across the entertainment industry since Crow’s early days of fame, but she’s taking it in her stride, as usual. “It’s so different now with streaming – I was lucky because I would have songs that were big enough that, even if you didn’t like me, you got exposed to me [on the radio],” she says. “All the stuff on the radio became the soundtrack to your life, but now it’s different, and there is liberation in that because I’m not competing with my last success.” At the same time, she believes that the decision-making has been placed directly in the hands of music fans: “Emmylou Harris always said, ‘It’s my vote.’ Like if I buy your record, I’m voting for you, right?”

Similarly, she’s thrilled that young artists are managing to fill arenas and stadiums again: “That gives me hope because AI can never perform live… people go to concerts because they want the human contact, they want it in their molecules,” she says. “I think our [collective] loneliness is driving us to go stand in a place with strangers and watch people play music that they love.” It takes her right back to her childhood, lying in bed and hearing the freight train, and realising that “every kid in the world” was going through the same thing – trying to sleep and being distracted by the sound of a train or a car passing by.

“There’s something beautiful about us going through the same experiences, the same emotions – from fear to longing to disappointment,” she says. “We don’t go through life alone. We may be in separate beds and separate houses, but we’re not alone. We are connected.”

‘Pick You Up’ by Sheryl Crow is out now

News.title: Golf GTI at 50: a fitting celebration, but perhaps the end of an era
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Seeing as we’re almost at the end of 2026, I thought I’d best get a few words in before it’s too late about the Volkswagen Golf GTI, deservedly celebrating its half-century with a special 50th anniversary edition.

The famous GTI has been around for so long that I confess I had taken it for granted rather too easily, forgetting both the remarkable story of its origins and the sad fact that I don’t think this pure-petrol-not-even-a-mild-hybrid car will be around to celebrate its 100th birthday. Then again, neither will I.

In due course, depending on politics and the periodic revisions to the zero emissions vehicle mandate, passenger vehicles such as this propelled solely by fossil fuels will pass into history, and finding a petrol station in which to fill up will become as frustrating as locating an NHS dentist. So there’s a slight tinge of sadness as well as nostalgia that comes as standard on what must be the last generation of the conventional Golf GTIs.

open image in gallery The Volkswagen Golf GTI Edition 50 comes with a lightweight performance pack including slightly lowered suspension, stiffer springs

Certainly I cannot see how anything quite like the original, 1976 Golf could be invented again in today’s world. It was the product of a samizdat project involving a cell of six highly motivated petrolheads at VW HQ, who took it upon themselves to take a standard three-door front-wheel-drive basic Golf and transform it into a practical sports car, at a time when safety and emissions regulations were threatening to take the fun out of driving (plus ça change). They extracted 100 brake horsepower out of the old 1.6-litre engine using fuel injection, uprated brakes and other bits, and, with their German sense of humour, replaced the old gear knob with an actual golf ball.

With some cosmetic touches such as red highlights and tartan seats apparently inspired by contemporary London punk fashion, a star was born and by the 1990s every manufacturer from Peugeot to Proton was paying tribute. Today, only a few rivals persist, the mechanically similar cousins from Audi, Skoda and Cupra (the latter also offering useful estate variants), plus the premium offerings from Mercedes-Benz and BMW, the Honda Civic Type R having come off sale last year.

THE SPEC Volkswagen Golf GTI Edition 50 Price: £52,113 (starts at £48,075) Engine capacity: 2.0l petrol, 4-cyl, 7sp auto Power output (hp): 325 Top speed (mph): 168 0 to 60 (seconds): 5.3 Fuel economy (mpg): 37.1 CO2 emissions (WLTP, g/km): 173

The good news is that the current range of GTIs is the best yet. In the spirit of the original, the Edition 50 pushes things a little further, with power outputs of 265 horsepower for the standard GTI, 300 for the GTI Clubsport and 325 for the Edition 50. They’re all only five door jobs now, with no manual gearshifts, and the engine is turbocharged, but the power still goes through the front wheels, and with more grip control than you’d have any right to expect.

open image in gallery There are many special drive modes and settings on offer

The Edition 50 comes with a lightweight performance pack including slightly lowered suspension, stiffer springs, an Akrapovič titanium exhaust and striking 19-inch forged alloy wheels with pleasingly razor-like edges to the spokes. Pub bores, which of course I’m not, will be attracted to the prospect of discussing the many special drive modes and settings are also on offer, including a bespoke one for the Nürburgring.

Despite its sporting credentials, the Golf is a smooth and calm machine in everyday use. Following revisions a couple of years ago, the touchscreen and haptic heating controls work much better, as does the dual-clutch seven-speed automatic gearbox that was once (a few generations back) the car’s most irritating flaw. As with every Golf GTI the Edition 50 badging is tastefully applied, and the lovely moss-green pain of my example perfectly finished.

open image in gallery Despite its sporting credentials, the Golf is a smooth and calm machine in everyday use

So 2.5 million GTIs on from the original this is in almost all respects the best GTI ever, and as a default choice for people who can’t waste time on this sort of thing, an excellent option. (No one can really make full use of the GTI’s faster four-wheel drive sibling, the Golf R).

My real quibble, or, more accurately, shock was the price – some £52,113 for my fully-specced example. In 1976 you could personally import an early left-hand drive GTI for about £4,000, and not much more when the official imports arrived three years later. That’s only £28,126 in today’s money. I know the modern car costs billions to develop, is vastly safer and more luxurious, not to mention bigger and faster, but maybe we’ve lost something on the road from 1976.
