News.title: I shopped like a man for a week and it completely changed my weekly household budget
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When the “girl math” trend blew up on TikTok, I couldn’t help but feel frustrated. Yes, sometimes returning clothes feels like you’ve made money, even when you haven’t. But the large majority of women I know aren’t fooling themselves about their finances. Instead, they’re counting every penny to make ends meet during a cost of living crisis that has hit women the hardest and caused the gender financial wellbeing gap in Britain to widen even further, with women more likely to have lower wages and childcare responsibilities, and less likely to have savings or money for fun than men.

On top of this, we’re also contending with the Pink Tax: when products and services marketed towards women cost more than men’s comparable products, despite serving the same purpose with the same quality, if not better. For example, browsing for black Calvin Klein thongs on Amazon, I came across a three-pack for £36. Meanwhile, men’s boxers, which use far more material and contain 5 per cent more cotton, cost just £25.97.

Often, it’s assumed that Pink Tax only covers female-specific items: tampons, sanitary pads, and HRT, for example. These non-optional extras shouldn’t be ignored – on average, women spend £2,418 a year on female-specific costs, with nearly a quarter of women now cutting back on food or household bills to afford personal care products, new research from Clearspring has found.

However, gendered pricing covers a far wider range of products than this, as the practice sits in a grey area and is yet to be made illegal for retail businesses in the UK. So brands are able to sidestep the Equality Act by adding a scent, changing a colour, or slightly altering packaging to claim that the same product is distinct.

As each pay-cheque is spread even more thinly than the last, this sneakiness begins to enrage me with even more persistent force. After the thongs, I noticed that a men’s basic white cotton T-shirt (£5) is half the price of the women’s one (£10) in Tesco, until the latter version was finally reduced to the same amount as the men’s in the sale – bargain!

It’s a truth universally acknowledged that all of your toiletry products will run out at once. Ordinarily, a trip to buy shampoo, deodorant, sanitary products, razors and shower gel fills me with dread; In 2026, a trip to Boots or Superdrug can set me back about £30 for the basics. That is just under what I allow myself to spend on a weekly food shop, while my boyfriend has the capacity to spend around double that on his food.

Toiletries are one of the worst product areas for Pink Tax, with women paying nearly 40 per cent extra for their lower-cost essentials on average, Co-operative Bank has found. So on my next trip for toiletries, I bought men’s products from the brands I ordinarily shop from and saved £6. Add on what I didn’t spend on sanitary products (by using the supply at work – a luxury not all women have, with one in 10 now in period poverty) that rose to £11: easily enough for some extra food items in my shop.

While a bathroom re-stock isn’t a weekly activity, these price inflations happen all over the place, from clothes and cosmetics to even children’s toys. Over on TikTok, one woman was brave enough to get a haircut in her boyfriend’s barber shop to save some cash. The outcome was surprisingly perfect and cost her £7, rather than £40.

open image in gallery Toiletries are one of the worst product categories for gender-based pricing ( Getty/iStock )

While swerving the Pink Tax is semi-possible on items that aren’t sanitary products or HRT, surely brands should not be slyly attempting to shaft female shoppers – many of whom are already paid less, have suffered the “motherhood penalty”, or have fallen into the gender pension gap.

MPs in the UK have previously attempted to challenge this practice, with Liberal Democrat Christine Jardine introducing her Gender-based Pricing (Prohibition) Bill in the House of Commons in 2019. The government responded, saying that charging different prices didn’t automatically indicate discrimination and the bill failed to advance by the deadline in 2021, despite cross-party support for Jardine’s proposal from both Labour and Conservative MPs. Five years on, the situation is largely the same.

In the wake of Jardine’s initial debate, supermarkets like Tesco committed to making women’s razors the same price as men’s. After a Change.org campaign, Boots also reviewed the prices of certain cosmetic products. However, without policy over gendered pricing, there is no consistency across the high street, and prices can slowly creep back up as brands introduce new lines.

“I think there are bigger issues that we have to deal with, which is general societal misogyny, which we see everywhere,” Jardine says.

“We need to address through small, individual things, like Pink Tax on women’s products – and be aware of it more widely. Medical misogyny, the manosphere: we’re seeing all sorts of problems. Deodorant and haircut prices are a symptom of the fact that there is still a deep-rooted everyday misogyny which we have to overcome.”

“The pink tax exists purely for profit,” echoes the equality for girls charity Plan International. “Businesses think that women are willing to pay more for some products than men. So, they market these products differently to women,” the charity concludes, recommending legislative and policy pressure to provoke corporate responsibility. But, until then, where you can as a consumer, shopping like a man is the best thing you can do to save yourself money — and avoid being mugged off.

News.title: Michael Carrick, Sir Alex Ferguson and Man United’s seemingly impossible question
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Even as he risks being consigned to Manchester United history, Michael Carrick was talking about Manchester United’s history. They are celebrating one of their managers and, whether or not Aston Villa are defeated on Sunday, it is not him. Friday marked the 40th anniversary of Sir Alex Ferguson’s appointment. There is a dinner this weekend to honour the great Scot.

There is also the chance Sunday marks Carrick’s last game at the helm. Ferguson has been in charge for two-thirds of the last four decades and end his tenure of his own volition, retiring after 26-and-a-half years. Carrick could become the seventh man sacked since then, without even including the interim appointment Ralf Rangnick. He is already the fifth of Ferguson’s former players to have served as caretaker manager.

Ferguson has been the inspiration for them all. He remains the benchmark, the gold standard, but also the anomaly. A banner at Old Trafford, commemorating Ferguson, reads: “The impossible dream”. For much of the last 13 years, following him has seemed similarly impossible.

“Well, it's not impossible,” Carrick countered. “Anything's possible. You've got to build, you've got to be realistic. You've got to put things in perspective as well, the recent history that we've had and where we want to get to, but it's not going to happen in a blink of an eye. It's not going to happen overnight. Success does take time, and we don't like having to spend time, but it does take a period of time to build.”

That is true. That said, the inconvenient details are that it seemed to happen overnight when Carrick had an immediate impact upon his return to Old Trafford in January and that results show regression this season.

United enter the weekend in 17th place in the Premier League, in a 14th consecutive campaign without a title challenge. In all competitions, they have a lone win in their last 10 matches. Matheus Cunha’s dramatic decider against Roma on Tuesday prompted suggestions it was Carrick’s Mark Robins moment; there is a parallel of sorts because, a couple of weeks after Robins scored against Nottingham Forest in January 1990, Ferguson’s United were 17th.

Then he was more than three years into his reign. Now Carrick is only three months into his first season after being appointed. If several of his predecessors think there was a brutality to their sacking, others can feel the United powerbrokers afforded them too much time. But the broader trend is that managers tend to be afforded less time now.

“The game's certainly changed, no doubt,” Carrick reflected. “It always does. It evolved, and it had evolved to the stage probably after Sir Matt [Busby] in the years after that, to then Sir Alex.”

open image in gallery Sir Alex Ferguson and Sir Matt Busby remain the only managers to have brought sustained success to Manchester United ( PA Archive )

The mention of Busby underlines the heights United have touched under two great empire-builders of managers, but rarely under anyone else. Busby took up the job in 1945 so only one managerial appointment United have made in the last eight decades, and only two in the last 12, have been definitively superb; a handful of others, whether Tommy Doherty, Ron Atkinson or Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, may be termed qualified successes, but no more. Should Carrick go with United in the lower reaches of the table, he would not even belong in that bracket.

But the past is United’s constant companion. “There's always different things to compare, but always we've got to live in the present as well,” said Carrick; it is worth noting he is less openly nostalgic than his friend Solskjaer but it is evident neither had the track record to manage United. Their playing days were a factor.

There is forever the hope Ferguson’s magic has rubbed off on someone, anyone. Carrick is a very different character to his former manager: less fiery, less cutting in his comments, less of a dictator and more of a diplomat.

open image in gallery Carrick played under Ferguson at United for seven seasons and admitted he talks to him now more than ever ( PA Archive )

But as a midfielder, he was a favourite of Ferguson’s. “I'm probably closer to him now and speak more to him now than I did when I was playing,” Carrick said. “I think the relationships change over time and that's only natural. Ever since I came here, the impact he had on me as an individual was immense. Not necessarily directly as in talking all the time and advice all the time. Personally, it was more of the influence that he had and the habits that you try and pick up from him, as did everyone around the football club over that period of time. Then you move on and evolve a little bit into a friendship, really, which is really nice.”

His friend casts a long shadow. Carrick won five Premier Leagues and appeared in three Champions League finals, all under Ferguson, though he played on under David Moyes, Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho. The 84-year-old collected silverware in a way that others of his generation collected stamps. He made it appear natural.

“There's a lot of winning, a lot of trophies and a lot of success,” said Carrick. “It's difficult to bring success. It was difficult then. It's difficult now. It just shows you how tough it is to have sustained success. Again, we’ve got to live in the moment.” But the moment is troubled and United can forever live in the past. As the celebrations of Ferguson show, it is often a preferable place.

News.title: Ireland send out ominous warning with second-gear walloping of Argentina
News.content:
Is it time to fire up the emerald green bandwagon? Not quite yet. But this was not a bad start to Ireland’s autumn; a 42-12 walloping of Los Pumas with Andy Farrell’s team still nowhere near their best. That should be highly encouraging for those of an Irish persuasion.

A year out from the World Cups of 2015, 2019 and 2023, Ireland had enjoyed banner seasons, eyeing up global glory. They never made it past the quarter-finals.

The build-up this time has been tougher going – the Aviva, unusually for this time of year – was not even full for this Nations Championship encounter. But perhaps Ireland will be better for it. They had far too much on a crisp Friday night in Dublin for an Argentina team who were missing a few of their stars, notably Bath’s Santiago Carreras and Lyon prop Thomas Gallo, but still packing 750 caps’ worth of Test experience in their starting XV.

Farrell was missing a few big names himself. Caelan Doris and Jack Conan were out injured, with the Englishman opting to hand Sean Jansen and Nick Timoney starts in the back row. Farrell also chose to start Craig Casey rather than Jamison Gibson-Park – arguably their best player of the last 18 months – at scrum-half, with Sam Prendergast starting again at 10 given Jack Crowley’s absence.

All in all there was a slightly experimental feel to proceedings, making Argentina potentially dangerous visitors. But Ireland had far too much in reserve. Hugo Keenan grabbed a hat-trick and took the player of the match award. Robert Baloucoune was consistently excellent. Mack Hansen’s return on the wing was hugely welcome. Tominey stood out in the back row.

Farrell said he was delighted with the result, if not the entire performance, making special mention of the likes of Keenan, Hansen, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, all of whom were returning from long injury lay-offs.

“The game’s never going to be perfect. But if you look at the bigger picture, to win 42-12 against a really good side in Argentina, I don’t think too many teams have done that,” Farrell said. “You have to be pleased.”

Asked whether he was happier with the 42 points scored or the meagre 12 conceded, Farrell added that it was probably the latter: “We want to be known for our defence. It shows our mentality.”

Los Pumas scored the first try of the game, Mateo Carreras getting the jump on Casey in the corner to field a Tomás Albornoz crossfield kick.

News.title: ‘Air Caluori’ puts on show as England A offer exciting glimpse into future
News.content:
England A 59 Argentina XV 24

Noah Caluori and Luke Northmore both scored twice as England A produced an emphatic victory over Argentina XV at the Rec.

On a night when England’s back line showcased plenty of attacking flair and free-flowing rugby, the hosts ran in nine tries to shrug off a dogged Argentina outfit.

Bath’s Max Ojomoh shone bright on his own turf and combined effortlessly with Northmore in a midfield partnership which showed plenty of promise for the future.

A young and inexperienced touring Argentina side hung tough in a see-sawing first half which yielded seven tries, but England found another gear after the break, with Jack Kenningham and Jamie Blamire among those on the scoresheet.

The hosts enjoyed a dream start when Caluori dotted down inside the opening two minutes, setting the tone for a helter-skelter first half.

News.title: Tuchel: Bellingham and I were up and down – now we are in a good place
News.content:
Jobe never wanted to be a carbon copy of his brother. He wanted to write his own story. The club, too, has resisted direct comparisons. They just wanted Jobe, not the younger brother of a world-class star. Now the brothers will be reunited in the England squad. For Jude, it is a dream come true. He previously said: “We’ve played together on the streets for so long. Playing for England alongside my brother would be the greatest dream of my life. That would mean more to me than any trophy.”

Dortmund have never fought harder for a player in recent years than Bellingham. The club’s executives first met him in person in the summer of 2020, when Jude signed. Jobe accompanied his brother to Germany. From that moment on, the club monitored every step of his development: his progress through the youth ranks at Birmingham City, the family club of the Bellinghams, and the evolution of his positioning on the pitch. After all, as a child, Jobe was still playing as a centre-forward. Over time, however, he gradually moved into deeper roles.

In May 2025, BVB decided to make their move. Word had reached Dortmund that Eintracht Frankfurt were interested and had already invited Bellingham to their training facilities. The pressure was on. Dortmund responded by pulling out all the stops. President Hans-Joachim Watzke, the man who shaped the club for more than two decades and led it to the top of German football, stepped in. He flew to England and met Bellingham face to face. It was a secret mission. Watzke was determined not to attract any attention that could jeopardise negotiations.

The problem: Sunderland, Bellingham’s former club, had secured promotion to the Premier League only a day earlier. Hundreds of supporters were gathered outside the hotel where Watzke and Bellingham were due to meet. To avoid being recognised, Watzke put on sunglasses and a cap before making his way through the crowd. He brought two gifts with him. Firstly, a BVB shirt with Jobe’s name on the back. Secondly, a handwritten note from Kovac expressing his desire to work with the midfielder. A few days later, Watzke received a phone call. It was Jobe. His decision had been made. He was joining Dortmund.

News.title: A tech editor’s guide to finding genuine Black Friday discounts
News.content:
The Black Friday shopping season is here. The world’s biggest technology brands, including Amazon, Samsung, Apple and Sony, are all expected to drop their prices, with British retailers such as John Lewis, Currys and Argos throwing their hats in the ring as we speed towards the new year.

While you might already have your eye on a gadget or two in the hope they drop in price during the sales, it’s important to shop wisely – and, crucially, manage expectations.

As Telegraph Recommended’s tech editor, who has been covering the Black Friday sales for well over a decade, I have picked up a number of must-know tips.

Whether that’s buying last year’s iPhone for less than the latest model, or accepting the sad truth that game consoles won’t be discounted ahead of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch, here’s everything you need to know – including early discounts.

Apple

News.title: White House postpones tech boss meeting after AI crash
News.content:
The White House has postponed a meeting of Silicon Valley tech bosses including Meta chief Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia boss Jensen Huang following Thursday’s stock market sell-off.

Donald Trump’s administration was scheduled to convene a session on Friday with an industry panel known as the “President’s Council ​of ⁠Advisers on Science and Technology”, which advises Mr Trump on tech matters.

However, the meeting was cancelled by the White House and is yet to be rescheduled. Thursday’s tech rout, which saw the Nasdaq 100 fall the most in six years, wiped more than $1 trillion off the Magnificent 7.

The tech ​panel also includes top Silicon Valley bosses such as AMD’s ‌Lisa Su and Marc ​Andreessen, co-foudner of Andreessen ​Horowitz.

The move comes after the President reaffirmed his commitment to the buildout of data centres, saying that “only foolish leadership will say “NO” to the riches they bring.”

Tech shares fell sharply on Thursday over fears the Democratic “blue wave” will halt the construction of data centres, which have fuelled the AI boom

It comes as US stocks staged a small rebound, with the Nasdaq Composite up 1.77pc.

Meta shares were up 2.5pc on Friday following a 4pc fall on Thursday, while Nvidia rebounded 3.6pc after a drop of 9.3pc a day earlier.

News.title: Cheap version of game-changing HIV preventive drug granted approval by US authorities
News.content:
Millions of people in low and middle income countries are set to get access to a game-changing HIV prevention drug within weeks, after US health authorities green lit a cheap form of the product.

Earlier this week the US Food and Drug Administration granted tentative approval to a generic form of the drug lenacapavir, made by Indian manufacturer Dr Reddy’s Laboratories.

Under an agreement hammered out between drug manufacturers and philanthropic donors in 2025 120 low and middle income countries across Africa, Asia, the Middle East and the Caribbean, will get access to the generic drug, at just $40 per patient per year – compared to the US list price of $28,000.

Lenacapavir, a long-acting injection administered twice a year, was hailed as the scientific breakthrough of 2024 and a potential turning point in the fight against HIV. Clinical trials have shown it provides almost 100 per cent protection against catching the HIV virus for six months and it is more effective and convenient than taking daily pre-exposure prophylactic (PrEP) pills.

Last year, Gilead Sciences, which developed lenacapavir, signed royalty-free, non-exclusive voluntary licencing agreements with six generic manufacturers to enable the production and supply of a generic. Dr. Reddy’s is the first to get FDA approval and it is hoped the first batches will be ready by the end of the year.

Jessica Burry, HIV technical officer at Unitaid, which in conjunction with the Clinton Health Access Initiative and Wits RHI supported Dr Reddy’s in its bid to manufacture the generic, said it normally takes 10 years for a generic form of a drug to be launched.

“So we’re celebrating this milestone,” she said. “There’s a lot of demand in the countries where we’re working and we think having an affordable generic could make a real difference.”

Standard PrEP involves daily pills which some people find difficult to stick to.

News.title: The perilous road to parenthood: Mongolia’s fight to make childbirth safer

As the 4x4 raced south, bouncing across Mongolia’s rocky valley roads and dusty forest steppes, an obstetrician was doing her best to ease Otgonbayar Odbayar’s pain and panic.

Hours earlier, the reindeer herder’s waters had broken. But Otgonbayar was six weeks early – and almost 250 miles away from the doctors who could provide the caesarean she knew she needed.

She contacted the nearest clinic, kicking off a relay of calls that spanned the length of Khuvsgul, a region bordering Russia. Soon, a plan came back through the chain: one health team would collect the 26-year-old and sprint south, while doctors from the provincial hospital in Murun would hurtle north. They’d meet in the middle.

Otgonbayar Odbayar with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But Otgonbayar’s three-hour journey was touch and go. “Halfway through, her contractions got very intense and very close together,” said Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh, the obstetrician who collected her. “She was in a lot of pain. We put her on an IV and were driving so fast.”

They made it to the small clinic in Tugul a little after 11pm, but then faced an excruciating 90 minute wait for the team from Murun, who had further to travel on Mongolia’s rutted roads. Dr Tsogbadrakh didn’t have a Plan B: the baby was in breech position, and the scar from Otgonbayar’s previous c-section still hadn’t fully healed.

Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“When [the doctors] arrived, I felt relief,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh. “If we had waited only 30 more minutes to start surgery, no one could tell what would have happened.”

Yet Otgonbayar’s ordeal is now the exception in Mongolia, underscoring just how far the vast country has come in its three-decade drive to tackle the childbirth risks posed by geography.

In 1990, 200 women died for every 100,000 births, but that ratio plunged to 47 by 2015 – making Mongolia one of only nine countries to hit global targets to reduce maternal mortality by 75 per cent over the 25-year period, according to analysis in the Lancet.

Strides have slowed but continued, and the rate now hovers at around 37. By contrast, other countries with a similar maternal mortality ratio in 1990, including Algeria, Brazil, the Philippines and Kiribati, still see more than 70 deaths per 100,000 births, according to Our World in Data.

In a country as vast and sparse as Mongolia – which is more than six times the size of the UK, but home to just 3.5 million people – health gains have been reliant “on overcoming the distance between women and the care they need”, said the health minister Batshugar Enkhbayar.

That has meant introducing telemedicine initiatives to bring specialist advice to remote clinics, waiting homes where pregnant women can stay in the final weeks before delivery, and better trained staff to spot risks before they become acute. In the last year, the country has also started to trial portable ultrasounds.

Northern Mongolia near the Russian border Credit : Simon Townsley

“We cannot always eliminate that distance,” said Mr Enkhbayar, “so we have to plan around it.”

The Telegraph spent a week in Mongolia to find out what this looks like in practice, driving hundreds of miles to meet pregnant women and new mothers in provincial hospitals, village clinics and remote herder communities.

There are also lessons for other countries: the latest data shows that globally, 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023 – one death every two minutes. In the UK, around 250 women died in childbirth between 2022 and 2024, equal to more than one expectant mother a week.

Obstetrician Otgongerel Uvgii with Otgonbayar Odbayar following her recent birth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But in low and middle income countries, the vast majority of fatalities are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as preeclampsia, which are all entirely preventable. Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives.

And, when a mother survives childbirth – like Otgonbayar eventually did – her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At 2:10am on October 4, the doctors safely delivered Otgonbayar’s third child, a little boy weighing 2.3kg. The family hadn’t yet decided on a name when we visited the stuffy maternity room a day later – but they were already thinking about his future.

“It was very scary and painful, everything was going wrong,” said Otgonbayar, swaddling her newborn in a pink Peppa Pig blanket. “But I feel lucky now. I’m just so glad I’ve been able to meet my baby.

“He doesn’t look like me, [he looks] exactly like his father,” she added, smiling. “I hope in the future he grows to be a good person, and to be healthy.”

Almost 150 miles south in Murun, two expectant mothers are staying in the waiting home that Otgonbayar had planned to use. It’s a simple space: six single beds line the walls of the light and airy room, and there’s a basic kitchen next door.

More than 300 of these facilities are dotted across the country, attached to village clinics and provincial hospitals. Women can stay for free, for as long as they need – in Murun, 147 expectant mothers used the waiting home between January and September, for an average of eight days.

Dr Nyam-Ulzii Odkhuu, one of eight gynaecologists at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Giving birth is actually very difficult here – just imagine the road they have to take and the distances they have to travel, just to give birth to their babies,” said Dr Nyam-Ulzii Odkhuu, one of eight gynaecologists at Murun provincial hospital. “So it’s important to have maternity waiting homes, especially in Khuvsgul, as we have so many remote villages. It’s a necessity.”

The idea is not a new one. In the 1970s and 1980s, an ad-hoc system saw some towns and villages set up specific gers – Mongolia’s traditional, circular tents – so pregnant women from remote herder families could be close to a clinic before their due date.

But then the Soviet Union fell. Although not officially part of the USSR, Mongolia was considered almost a “satellite state” – a socialist nation that was heavily dependent on Russia. When the bloc broke apart, Mongolia faced a “violent economic crisis” and social turmoil that researchers have called the “lost decade”.

Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh and midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal making house calls on horseback Credit : Simon Townsley

In this climate the pregnancy gers almost disappeared, fertility rates dropped and the maternal mortality ratio rose, said Dr Buyanjargal Yadamsuren, a former director of medical services at the ministry of health. Until 2001, when the government – which was keen to boost its population size – decided to prioritise maternal health.

“[Waiting homes] were an approach that made sense,” said Dr Yadamsuren. “But when we reintroduced them nationwide, we really focused on strategy – the referral system, the criteria for who should use them, the funding mechanisms, and so on.”

This formalised approach included sending all women with high-risk pregnancies to give birth in provincial hospitals, which are better equipped and able to perform caesareans.

Khaliun Lkhamsuren in the maternal waiting room at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Khaliun Lkhamsuren is one of those expectant mothers. From a village roughly 90 miles west of Murun, the 34-year-old came to the hospital’s waiting home after a prenatal checkup found her baby was not only big, but in an awkward position. Midwives were concerned it might be a difficult delivery.

“I have no fear, because if things do go wrong I’m already in the hospital and the doctors are nearby,” Khaliun said, perched on the edge of a metal-framed bed. “It’s a very useful and convenient place for someone like me, who doesn’t have relatives to stay with in the provincial centre.”

Gansukh Dorj with his first daughter Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

She jokes that coming here is even “a bit of a break” – her husband has been left at home, in charge of their two young daughters.

At the other end of the province, Gansukh Dorj is doting on his third child, gently rocking her buggy back and forth to curb her tears. It’s his first daughter, and he can barely stop beaming.

“All I wanted was to have a girl,” the 40-year-old told the Telegraph, offering his visitors dried curd, milk tea and wrapped sweets before turning back to baby Gansuvd. “I think it will be different to raising boys, so at first I felt nervous, but now I’m getting used to it.”

Three months ago, his wife Narmanmdakh Battur gave birth in the nearest village health clinic, a four-hour drive on tough, unpaved roads from the picture-postcard valley where the nomadic family spend summer and autumn. The herders only have a motorbike, so a driver from the health centre picked them up in a 4x4 a week before Narmanmdakh’s due date.

The health team en route to house-calls in Khuvsgul Province, northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

From there, everything went smoothly until Dr Tsogbadrakh – the tireless obstetrician who also collected Otgonbayar – noticed the newborn had signs of jaundice. She asked them to stay at the waiting home for 10 days post-delivery, just in case.

“We wanted to monitor the baby there, because this is a very long way from the health centre in Renchinlkhumbe,” she said. “The waiting rooms are convenient before and also after delivery.”

But providing a space for women to stay close to doctors is only one pillar of Mongolia’s strategy to overcome distance. Health teams also reverse the journey to visit patients in their homes.

Dr Baasanjargal Tsogbadrakh and midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal, with the portable ultrasound device Credit : Simon Townsley

The Telegraph joined Dr Tsogbadrakh and her colleague, midwife Byambasuren Ulziijargal, on one of these trips, a 14-hour day driving across northern Khuvsgul to meet three families.

“In the winter it’s even harder,” said Ms Ulziijargal, as the 4x4 paused to inflate a slow puncture. “Many times we’ve been stuck in the snow, which in some places can be as deep as 120cm. And if it really doesn’t work, we would ride a horse or use a sleigh to get to the patients.”

Sometimes the healthcare workers, both mothers themselves, are on the road for two or three days, relying on their patients’ hospitality as they travel hundreds of miles to deliver vaccinations, health checks – and now, even baby scans.

Munkhzul Tseveedendev has her six-month scan inside her own home Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Renchinlkhumbe is one of 20 remote village clinics trialling portable ultrasounds, in a pilot scheme launched last year and funded by the Ministry of Health, UNFPA and the Luxembourg government. The devices, which cost around $8,800 (£6,500) per machine, look deceptively simple – just like a large laptop.

They’ve already had an impact, said Dr Tsogbadrakh, as she set up the ultrasound at the first stop of the day, an isolated log cabin on the banks of a small lake.

The health team check Munkhzul’s eight-month-old baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

It feels slightly surreal, a clash of domestic and medical: beside a vibrant orange chest full of trinkets and family photos, the ultrasound machine’s screen is filled with a moving black and white image, as Munkhzul Tseveedendev has her six-month scan inside her own home.

“It’s been great,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, gently moving the imaging wand across Munkhzul’s belly. “Before the portable ultrasound, we used to ask pregnant women to travel to the [village], but now we can take it out to them.

“It’s helping because one of our biggest challenges is when women delay coming to the clinic for checkups, and suddenly arrive when there’s already a problem,” she added later.

Midwife Byambasuren Ulziijarga checks baby Gansuvd in the family ger Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

While the health team is there, they also give Munkhzul’s eight-month-old baby a once over. She won’t stop blowing raspberries – an ominous sign in Mongolian culture.

“It means bad weather is coming,” said the midwife Ms Ulziijargal. She laughs, but the clouds soon turned grey, threatening snow but instead spitting rain as we arrived at Gansukh and Narmanmdakh’s ger hours later – their daughter is due a three-month health check.

“It’s very impactful to have them coming here, as it’s very difficult for us to reach Renchinlkhumbe,” said Gansukh, watching closely as Ms Ulziijargal notes down his daughter’s weight, heartbeat and breathing. She had a slight cold, so vaccinations were postponed, but little Gansuvd is otherwise growing well.

Baasgaa Badamdorj, 31, sits outside his home in Renchinlkhumbe while his wife is visited by the maternal health team Credit : Simon Townsley

“The medical services have got much better [since my second sons were born],” added Gansukh, referring to his teenage boys. “I think the quality of check ups has got much better.”

For Dr Tsedmaa Baatar, a gynaecologist and programme analyst at UN Population Fund (UNFPA) Mongolia, this is a fundamental point: while waiting homes offer critical infrastructure, and portable ultrasounds an innovative new tool to boost access, much of Mongolia’s success rests on improved expertise.

“We’ve really worked on the maternal complications, on how to deal with haemorrhage, eclampsia, sepsis etc,” said Dr Baatar, in the UN agency’s office in central Ulaanbaatar, the country’s gridlocked capital.

Otgontuya Nasanbayar, left, and Byambajargal Naidan, right, with their one-month-old baby in their family's ger following a visit from the maternal health team Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I used to work in the National Center for Maternal and Child Health here, and 25 years ago all complicated cases from all over Mongolia would be transferred to Ulaanbaatar,” she said. “But now the local hospitals in rural settings have the capacity to provide high quality services, which is a huge change… and maternal complications have decreased dramatically.”

This is not just down to better training. Mongolia has also set up a telemedicine network which connects specialists with healthcare workers across the country.

“A classic telemedicine scheme is between the doctor and patient, but ours is to improve expert knowledge at local hospitals,” said Dr Baatar. “Our aim was not to introduce this fancy telemedicine department. We are simply using the internet… to allow for joint decision making for complicated cases.

Dorjkhand Nyamdorj, 27, with her three day old baby at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Mongolia is a huge, sparsely populated country and sometimes delivering a quality healthcare service is a real challenge, so the government is trying to use technology as much as possible,” she added. “But we also know that technology alone is not a solution, we need well-trained, committed healthcare workers.”

Here, Mongolia is still falling short.

As it stands, the country is not on track to meet ambitious targets to reduce maternal mortality to around 15 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. Part of this is because of new risks – rising rates of noncommunicable diseases, as well as social issues including domestic violence and substance abuse, are increasingly affecting maternal health.

Seven day old Yaruu-Egshig is treated for jaundice at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But staffing is also a stumbling block, said Dr Baatar. While World Health Organization data shows the number of midwives rose from 612 in 2002 to 1,169 in 2024, this is still well below international standards.

According to analysis in the European Journal of Midwifery, the average midwife’s workload in Mongolia is roughly three times higher than the global average. The strain is even more acute in remote regions: research published in the Journal of Global Health found Ulaanbaatar has 3.96 physicians per 1,000 residents, compared to just 1.39 in Khuvsgul.

The issue is on the agenda. Supported by UNFPA, the government launched a strategy in July 2025 to boost the number of people training as midwives, improve their training, and give them greater autonomy so they can ease the burden on obstetricians and gynaecologists. There are roughly 600 in the country, said Dr Baatar – also not enough.

“We’ve made substantial progress over the past two decades,” said Mr Enkhbayar, the health minister. “However, recent maternal mortality figures are a reminder that these gains cannot be taken for granted.”

A traditional ger in northern Mongolia Credit : Simon Townsley

Back in Khuvsgul, the sun is just rising above the snow-capped mountains as Dr Tsogbadrakh and Ms Ulziijargal make yet another house call – to a ger roughly half an hour outside the village, where Ariunbolor Ganbayar is in the final trimester of her pregnancy.

It’s a rapid turnaround for the healthcare workers: the pair got home from their 14-hour day at around 10pm the night before, only to be called in the middle of the night when another woman from the village went into labour. They delivered the baby without complications at around 4am – and neither of them complain that they’ve only had two hours’ sleep.

Renchinlkhumbe, Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It is a lifestyle, not only a job,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, carefully sipping strong coffee from a flask as the 4x4 bounced the dusty steppe. “For example, in the last 14 days I’ve been all the time on the road – I was in the city for training, then I collected [Otgonbayar] for the emergency c-section, then I was on the road to treat people. My kids complain I’m sometimes very absent at home.

“Sometimes it is hard,” added Dr Tsogbadrakh, who’s been Renchinlkhumbe clinic’s obstetrician for eight years. “But the thing I love about my work is that moment when you safely deliver the baby, and you get to see the mother and the baby meet for the first time.

“It’s the beginning of a new human life.”

Otgontuya Nasanbayar, left, and Byambajargal Naidan, right, with their one-month-old baby in their family's ger following a visit from the maternal health team Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I used to work in the National Center for Maternal and Child Health here, and 25 years ago all complicated cases from all over Mongolia would be transferred to Ulaanbaatar,” she said. “But now the local hospitals in rural settings have the capacity to provide high quality services, which is a huge change… and maternal complications have decreased dramatically.”

This is not just down to better training. Mongolia has also set up a telemedicine network which connects specialists with healthcare workers across the country.

“A classic telemedicine scheme is between the doctor and patient, but ours is to improve expert knowledge at local hospitals,” said Dr Baatar. “Our aim was not to introduce this fancy telemedicine department. We are simply using the internet… to allow for joint decision making for complicated cases.

Dorjkhand Nyamdorj, 27, with her three day old baby at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Mongolia is a huge, sparsely populated country and sometimes delivering a quality healthcare service is a real challenge, so the government is trying to use technology as much as possible,” she added. “But we also know that technology alone is not a solution, we need well-trained, committed healthcare workers.”

Here, Mongolia is still falling short.

As it stands, the country is not on track to meet ambitious targets to reduce maternal mortality to around 15 deaths per 100,000 live births by 2030. Part of this is because of new risks – rising rates of noncommunicable diseases, as well as social issues including domestic violence and substance abuse, are increasingly affecting maternal health.

Seven day old Yaruu-Egshig is treated for jaundice at Murun provincial hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But staffing is also a stumbling block, said Dr Baatar. While World Health Organization data shows the number of midwives rose from 612 in 2002 to 1,169 in 2024, this is still well below international standards.

According to analysis in the European Journal of Midwifery, the average midwife’s workload in Mongolia is roughly three times higher than the global average. The strain is even more acute in remote regions: research published in the Journal of Global Health found Ulaanbaatar has 3.96 physicians per 1,000 residents, compared to just 1.39 in Khuvsgul.

The issue is on the agenda. Supported by UNFPA, the government launched a strategy in July 2025 to boost the number of people training as midwives, improve their training, and give them greater autonomy so they can ease the burden on obstetricians and gynaecologists. There are roughly 600 in the country, said Dr Baatar – also not enough.

“We’ve made substantial progress over the past two decades,” said Mr Enkhbayar, the health minister. “However, recent maternal mortality figures are a reminder that these gains cannot be taken for granted.”

A traditional ger in northern Mongolia Credit : Simon Townsley

Back in Khuvsgul, the sun is just rising above the snow-capped mountains as Dr Tsogbadrakh and Ms Ulziijargal make yet another house call – to a ger roughly half an hour outside the village, where Ariunbolor Ganbayar is in the final trimester of her pregnancy.

It’s a rapid turnaround for the healthcare workers: the pair got home from their 14-hour day at around 10pm the night before, only to be called in the middle of the night when another woman from the village went into labour. They delivered the baby without complications at around 4am – and neither of them complain that they’ve only had two hours’ sleep.

Renchinlkhumbe, Khuvsgul Province in northern Mongolia Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It is a lifestyle, not only a job,” said Dr Tsogbadrakh, carefully sipping strong coffee from a flask as the 4x4 bounced the dusty steppe. “For example, in the last 14 days I’ve been all the time on the road – I was in the city for training, then I collected [Otgonbayar] for the emergency c-section, then I was on the road to treat people. My kids complain I’m sometimes very absent at home.

“Sometimes it is hard,” added Dr Tsogbadrakh, who’s been Renchinlkhumbe clinic’s obstetrician for eight years. “But the thing I love about my work is that moment when you safely deliver the baby, and you get to see the mother and the baby meet for the first time.

“It’s the beginning of a new human life.”

Sports.content:
We have a busy day’s racing on Saturday with action from Doncaster, Southwell and Uttoxeter, live on Sky Sports Racing...

3.25 Doncaster - Last year's winner Castle Cove faces Nobody Knows

A typically competitive Virgin Bet November Handicap sees last year's winner Castle Cove and ante-post favourite Nobody Knows headline a field of 23.

William Haggas' Castle Cove has not been seen since landing this pot under Jason Hart last season and rates a fascinating runner under new pilot Cieren Fallon. Up eight pounds from last year's ready success, he must be considered if fit enough on this return.

Nobody Knows has been at the head of the betting for this contest since Monday and Richard Hughes has booked the services of Ryan Moore. The three-year-old caught the eye when staying on to finish fifth at York last month and is expected to step forward again over this extra yardage.

Stablemates Circus Of Rome and Duraji have each-way claims on the best of their form, while Alfred Wincham is another to note. He won by an eased down eight lengths at York on his last outing and must defy a 13-pound higher mark.

Coul Angel and Montassib feature among a field of 21 sprinters for this Listed Virgin Bet Every Saturday Money Back Wentworth Stakes.

Coul Angel arrives on a hat-trick having scored in handicap company at the Curragh and York the last twice. He is now five pounds higher as he heads into Listed company for the first time.

Montassib has not been successful since winning the Haydock Sprint Cup in 2024 but has not been disgraced this season and was fifth in this race last year.

Sports.title: Lampard: VAR didn't do its job
Sports.content:
Coventry boss Frank Lampard says VAR 'didn't do its job' in his side's defeat to Everton as three reviews controversially went against his side.

Two penalty appeals and a possible handball for Everton's second goal were all reviewed by VAR officials Timothy Wood and Gary Beswick, but nothing was given. They were also not awarded on-field by referee Stuart Attwell.

Coventry opened the scoring after the two penalty appeals, but were ultimately beaten 3-1 on Merseyside on Friday Night Football.

Lampard told Sky Sports: "I hate to sound like a moaner. It's a football match and if you win the game, that can happen here. I've worked here and know the momentum swings in the game.

"I'm not trying to talk about the circumstances of the actual football, but when big decisions change games, they absolutely do. It's disappointing. VAR is there for that and it didn't do its job."

Here, we breaks down each incident and what the pundits, managers and players had to say...

Tarkowski avoids punishment for elbow and hair pull

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Should Tarkowski have seen red for a hair pull during Everton's Premier League match against Coventry

Towards the end of the first half, James Tarkowski rose to defend a high ball into the box. As he did, he caught Ethan Pinnock with an elbow, before also appearing to pull the hair of Caleb Yirenkyi.

VAR did look at the incident, especially the elbow, but nothing was given in terms of a card or a penalty.

There was no communication from the Premier League Match Centre on if the hair pull was reviewed, but there was new guidance from the Premier League this summer, which says: "A red card will be issued when there is a clear and deliberate action to pull an opponent's hair with excessive force and/or brutality.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player FREE TO WATCH: Highlights from Everton’s match against Coventry in the Premier League

"A yellow card will be issued if the action is deemed to be without excessive force and/or brutality.

"Referees will enhance recognition of clear holding actions that have a clear material impact, and/or non-footballing holding actions with no place on the football pitch. This includes penalising defenders where they are clearly only focused on opponents and making a holding action that is impactful on the attacker's ability to play or challenge for the ball."

Lampard: I thought the rules were clear

"The first-half decision on Tarkowski got checked. Seeing it back, he pulls on Caleb's hair while competing with Ethan.

"I thought the rules were clear. I know they've changed the rules so it's no red card, I get that too. But he's pulling on his hair and [Yirenkyi] can't get his momentum to jump. I think it's a foul and a penalty and they decided no."

What did the pundits say?

Sky Sports' Jamie Redknapp on Friday Night Football: "Yirenkyi goes up, Tarkowski gets hold of his hair. He yanks it down. Is it excessive force? Probably not, but he pulls his hair, stopping any elevation. It's a definite penalty for me.

"Yirenkyi knows he has his hair pulled. It's unusual for Tarkowski to do. It's not the best piece of defending that's for sure... It's a foul. It's not a red card anymore but it's definitely a foul."

Lee Hendrie on Sky Sports co-commentary: "There's a clear pull... Tarkowski is in the heart of this. There's an elbow, which isn't a problem, but the hair pull will raise awareness.

"You can clearly see he's utilising the hair. It's a tight one. VAR have completely not looked at it or felt the need to look at it."

Moyes: We want the right result, but we've had decisions go against us Everton boss David Moyes to Sky Sports on whether he is bothered by Coventry's calls:



“I’m bothered because we want it [the result] to be right, but we’ve had a few decisions recently where we don’t think have gone our way.



"There was one possibly at Newcastle but there was one at Man City last season in a league game which was hugely important for us regarding getting into Europe.



"Sometimes they go for you, sometimes they don’t. If they were going against me, I’d be complaining a bit more.”

Mykolenko clip on Awoniyi not given

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Coventry denied a penalty by VAR after Mykolenko foul deemed as outside the box

At the start of the second half, Taiwo Awoniyi drove into the box with Vitalii Mykolenko behind him. There was some contact from behind which sent the striker down.

Referee Stuart Attwell said no penalty, while the VAR review deemed the contact to be outside the box.

Lampard: I can't believe it's not given

"I thought the one on Taiwo running through - it's a clear foul that the referee doesn't give in-game. I can't believe that because it's clear. Maybe he waited for VAR because it was on the borderline.

"But as I see it, Taiwo's foot is entering the box and his knee and the back of his knee is on the line of the box, which is a penalty."

"It's a definite penalty and it's rubbish from the VAR. It's a poor decision. It's a definite foul, they rush it too quickly, and his foot's on the line.

Sports.title: WTA chair apologises to Pegula after 'diva' comment broadcast
Sports.content:
Audio recording on practice courts will be deactivated at the WTA Finals after private comments made by Jessica Pegula about Mirra Andreeva were picked up, with the governing body's chair apologising to the American for the "regrettable" incident.

US player Pegula describing Russian teenager Andreeva as "a diva" while conversing with coach Mark Knowles during a practice session were heard on a YouTube livestream at Indian Wells, the venue for the WTA Tour season-ending event from November 8-15.

The WTA shouldered the blame for failing to properly inform players about active microphones, with chair Valerie Camillo saying there was "a lack of advanced notice and clear signage" as she confirmed audio will now be switched off for practice sessions.

Image: Pegula hopes the incident allows players to push for more privacy

Camillo added: "I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles. What happened was regrettable and unacceptable.

"Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction.

"As a member ​organisation, one of the primary responsibilities of the WTA is to protect ​players whenever possible. The players deserve better and we will continue to work to raise the bar for the WTA."

Image: Andreeva won the French Open this year, beating Maja Chwalińska in the final

Pegula: Let's keep pushing for more privacy

Pegula, who was also heard saying French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and that her coach, former Wimbledon winner, Conchita Martinez, encouraged her player's behaviour, addressed the incident on ESPN on Friday.

The world No 5 said: "Obviously I had no idea and was not informed that audio was being recorded. But it is what it is.

"I think it's something that we have fought a lot over the last couple years as there's a lot more surveillance, audio and, I guess, access to the players at tournaments than there has been in the past.

"I know for broadcasting that it's great for fans, but I think we've seen a couple incidents now throughout the year, the last couple of years really, where it seems highly unnecessary.

"I think [this will] definitely reignite the topic. Hopefully we can use this incident to keep pushing for more player privacy."

Image: Coco Gauff had called for more privacy back in January

Two-time Grand Slam champion Coco Gauff - in Pegula's group at the WTA Finals, alongside Linda Noskova and world No 1 Elena Rybakina - called for more privacy in January after cameras caught her smashing her racket following defeat to Elina Svitolina at the Australian Open quarter-finals in Melbourne.

Sports.title: Fritz misses out on ATP Finals after squandering chance to beat Alcaraz
Sports.content:
Taylor Fritz missed out on claiming the last spot at the ATP Finals in Turin later this month after squandering two match points in his Paris Masters quarter-final defeat to Carlos Alcaraz.

Fritz would have reached the end-of-season event in Italy at Rafael Jodar's expense had he beaten Alcaraz to make the last four.

He looked poised to do that after twice finding himself a point from victory in the second set, once on his opponent's serve at 5-3 up and then on his own with the score at 5-4.

However, Alcaraz rallied during a high-quality match to triumph 6-7 (10-12) 7-5 6-3 and ensure he will be joined by compatriot Jodar at the ATP Finals from November 15-22, live on Sky Sports.

Qualifiers for ATP Finals Alexander Zverev

Carlos Alcaraz

Ben Shelton

Daniil Medvedev

Arthur Fils

Flavio Cobolli

Frances Tiafoe

Rafael Jodar

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Paris Masters as Ben Shelton advanced to the semi-finals and ended opponent Tommy Paul's hopes of qualifying for the ATP Finals in Turin

Tommy Paul's three-set defeat to fellow American Ben Shelton earlier in the day - US Open finalist Shelton prevailing 6-4 4-6 6-3 - had ended his hopes of reaching the ATP Finals, with countryman Frances Tiafoe's place subsequently secured.

Fritz was looking to become the third US representative in this year's Turin showpiece, after Shelton and Tiafoe, but squandered a golden opportunity to get there and also defeat Alcaraz for just the second time in eight attempts.

Image: Fritz's heart-breaking defeat to Alcaraz confirmed Rafael Jodar's place in the ATP Finals later this month

The 29-year-old won the first set after a lengthy tie-break and then broke Alcaraz to open up a 4-3 lead in the second set, before saving a break point to make that 5-3.

Alcaraz had already qualified for the ATP Finals - an event he is yet to win in three previous tries - alongside world No 1 Alexander Zverev, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Shelton and Tiafoe.

Home hopes in Turin will rest on Cobolli, with Jannik Sinner - who on Friday announced a split with coach Darren Cahill after five years - ending his campaign early due to a knee problem that has sidelined him since winning Wimbledon in July.

Image: Spain's Rafael Jodar will make his ATP Finals debut in Turin

Alcaraz will face Casper Ruud in the semi-finals in Paris after the Norwegian saw off Portugal's Nuno Borges 7-6 (7-5) 6-4, with Shelton meeting home player Luca Van Assche, who overcame Australian qualifier - and Novak Djokovic's conqueror - Rinky Hijikata 6-4 6-7 (4-7) 7-5.

Should we get an Alcaraz-Shelton final in France, it would be a repeat of their five-set epic in the US Open quarter-finals, a match Shelton won in a final-set tie-break at Flushing Meadows.

Alcaraz said after fighting back against Fritz: "I tried not to let myself down in those difficult moments - to stay strong mentally.

"We played incredible tennis, both of us, and I used the energy of the people to give them what they wanted to watch. To entertain them."

Sports.title: Khawaja: Entire Australia team knew about ball-tampering scandal
Sports.content:
Former Australia opener Usman Khawaja has claimed that the side's entire dressing room knew about the ball-tampering incident in Cape Town in 2018.

That declaration, made by Khawaja in the Sydney Morning Herald ahead of the release of his book 'Sabr', is at odds with Cricket Australia's assertion that only Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were aware of the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa eight years ago.

Khawaja, who retired from international duty after Australia's 4-1 Ashes thrashing of England last winter, said: "It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us."

Image: Australia's Steve Smith was removed as captain after the ball-tampering scandal eight years ago

Captain-at-the-time Smith, Bancroft and Warner, who was found to have been the architect of the 'Sandpapergate' plot, all received bans after the incident, with Smith and Warner suspended for one year and Bancroft handed a nine-month sanction.

Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement in 2021 insisting they had no idea about the ball-tampering.

That came after Bancroft - who had aimed to conceal the sandpaper down his trousers during the Test in question - replied "I think it's probably self-explanatory" when asked in a newspaper interview whether the bowling attack knew about the scandal.

Cummins, Starc and Hazlewood have all been rested from this month's white-ball series at home to England while Lyon is not in the limited-overs set-up, so the quartet may not be quizzed on Khawaja's claims just yet.

Image: Josh Hazlewood, Nathan Lyon, Mitchell Starc and Pat Cummins issued a joint statement in 2021 denying knowledge of the scandal

Khawaja: I thought the truth would have come out by now

Khawaja wrote in his book that ball-tampering plans were first discussed in the second Test of the 2018 series in Port Elizabeth, now Gqeberha.

He continued: "In an ideal world, I don't want to do this.

"I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now.

"Maybe I thought Davey [Warner] would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more.

Cricket Australia's response to Khawaja claims A Cricket Australia statement read: "There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa. "During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. "All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

"At the end of the day, I think it's the right thing to do, particularly for those three guys. And I think most of the guys in the team, at some level, will be relieved we can finally move on.

"Even in the change rooms when I was talking to them after the game. I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on. We have to take it as a team'.

"I was always of that stance. Obviously, it didn't work that way, and those three guys got crucified.

"I've seen Davey over the last eight years just get nailed bad over and over again. It's taken a big man not to say anything and just to stay quiet. He's just copped it and copped it and copped it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player In 2018 footage emerged of Australia opener Cameron Bancroft using a foreign object to alter the condition of the ball against South Africa

"I've always felt like there's more to life than just cricket, and these guys, in some respect, deserve that justice. And it just doesn't feel like anyone's going to give it to them."

Reflecting on the first chats about ball-tampering, which led to sandpaper being seen as an "effective agent", Khawaja said: "It was at this point Smith essentially threw his hands in the air and said he didn't want to know."

The left-hander also expressed his surprise that he was never asked to give evidence despite playing in the Cape Town Test and sitting next to Bancroft in the dressing room.

'Australia found humility after Sandpapergate'

Khawaja scored over 6,000 runs for Australia's Test team in 88 matches between 2011 and 2026, notching 16 hundreds and 28 fifties with a best of 232 in Sri Lanka in January 2025.

He feels good came out of 'Sandpapergate' in that the side found "humility" in the aftermath.

Image: Khawaja believes Australia found 'humility' in the wake of 'Sandpapergate'

Khawaja added: "The best things come out of the worst times. I genuinely believe, for the Australian cricket team, the best thing that came out of Sandpaper is we found humility again.

"JL [Justin Langer] came in as coach and he was honestly probably the best coach we could've had at that time. He put humility back in the Australian cricket team. It was just lovely to see. It was beautiful.

"I really enjoyed it. I really enjoyed seeing where the Australian team went from that point onwards and obviously Cummins, who ended up becoming captain, was a part of that process and journey."

Speaking ahead of Australia's recent Test series in South Africa, which they lost 2-1, Cummins said he had given Khawaja his blessing to revisit the past after taking a phone call from his ex-team-mate.

"(I said) tell your story. It's fine," he said.

"It's obviously a long time ago and all the investigations, everything, was done back then. We answered every question a million times. It was dealt with. All I can say is that as a group, we have moved on."

Sports.title: Keenan notches hat-trick as Ireland blow Argentina away
Sports.content:
Hugo Keenan scored a hat-trick as Ireland notched six tries in a big Nations Championship bonus-point win over Argentina

Hugo Keenan notched a hat-trick as Ireland blew Argentina away in Dublin to secure a statement 42-12 Nations Championship victory.

On a night of big positives for Andy Farrell's charges, they scored six tries through full-back Keenan's three, hooker Dan Sheehan, fly-half Sam Prendergast and replacement front row Ronan Kelleher.

Argentina scored two tries through wing Mateo Carreras, and actually landed the opener in the Test, but by 55 minutes the contest was over, with the visitors totally outplayed.

Ireland 42-12 Argentina - Score summary Ireland - Tries: Keenan (15,30,50), Sheehan (25), Prendergast (42), Kelleher (55). Cons: Prendergast (15,26,30,42,51), Frawley (56). Argentina - Tries: M Carreras (10,46). Cons: Albornoz (46).

Indiscipline also proved a thorn for the Pumas again as centre Justo Piccardo and replacement lock Efraín Elias were shown costly yellow cards, with a vibrant Ireland needing little invitation to attack and score points.

A typically cagey and physical beginning to the fixture saw the visitors strike for the opening try in the 10th minute - wing Carreras claiming an inch-perfect Tomás Albornoz kick-pass over the head of final defender Craig Casey in a wonderful piece of playmaking skill.

Mateo Carreras soared in the air to collect an inch-perfect Tomás Albornoz kick-pass for the opening try

The Irish response came within five minutes, though, as a Casey-led counter-ruck earned territory, before a scintillating backline move saw Robert Baloucoune arc round and make great yards at pace, Mack Hansen offload inside brilliantly, and Keenan collect to finish.

Prendergast added the conversion for an early lead after Albornoz had earlier failed off the tee, while three superb Irish turnovers soon earned them the chance to strike again.

Ireland responded quickly through Keenan's first after sharp work from Rob Baloucoune and Mack Hansen

First, flanker Nick Timoney exquisitely won a breakdown penalty by his own try-line to quell a Pumas surge. Then, Tadhg Beirne got up to steal an Argentina lineout, while Timoney came up with the breakdown goods again soon after - this time on the halfway line.

When Ireland kicked to touch and into 22, an intricate move off a lineout saw Sheehan play a blind inside ball for Timoney to charge forward. The Ulster flanker was stopped just short, but quick Casey service saw Sheehan fly over for a 14-5 lead.

Ireland captain Dan Sheehan got over for their second try at the Aviva Stadium

Five minutes later, Ireland had their third try through Keenan again. Ryan Baird won another lineout steal to instigate the attack, with Ireland's full-back then doing marvellously well to battle and bounce his way over past a number of Argentina defenders.

Keenan wrestled his way over past a number of defenders for his second and Ireland's third try of the first half

When Prendergast converted, the Irish lead stood at 21-5, and worse looked likely to follow when Pumas centre Piccardo was sin-binned for giving away a cynical penalty in not being back 10 metres off a Sheehan quick-tap penalty.

Argentina centre Justo Piccardo was sent to the sin-bin during the first half

Ireland failed to add a fourth score before the break, however, as Sheehan was illegally halted in the corner by replacement Leonel Oviedo - referee Luke Pearce just about decreeing penalty-only was sufficient.

Argentina were fortunate to avoid the concession of a penalty try before half-time for an illegal tackle on Sheehan

Ireland put it behind them to score their bonus-point clinching fourth try less than two minutes into the second half, with Prendergast throwing a dummy bought by Marcos Kremer and racing in from deep.

Sam Prendergast celebrates his try early in the second half, as Ireland restarted strongly

The Pumas replied with their second try four minutes later, when centre Santiago Chocobares made the key break and Carreras powered his way over past Keenan, but Ireland then kicked on to another level.

The tireless Beirne won a trademark breakdown penalty deep in the Argentina half to earn the platform, with quick hands from Tadhg Furlong, Joe McCarthy and then Baird giving Keenan the space to dive over for his third.

Keenan completed his hat-trick in the 50th minute, wrapping up the game as a contest at that stage

With Baird continuing to cause havoc at the Argentina lineout with steals, the Pumas were soon back down to 14 players when the TMO showed images of Elias catching Keenan high in a shoulder-to-head tackle.

From the very next lineout, Ireland constructed a tight maul which drove forward at pace and was finished by Kelleher for their sixth try of the night.

Replacement Ciaran Frawley's conversion brought Ireland to their eventual 42-12 score, and head coach Farrell will be irked somewhat they failed to add more points from what was left in the Test.

Ireland added a sixth try through a dominant rolling maul, scored by Ronan Kelleher

Hansen showed some sensational skill and came close to both creating and scoring tries in what remained, but Kelleher's lineout performance was the central reason behind the home side failing to score more tries - the replacement coughing up a host of possession at the set-piece.

Farrell 'delighted' with win but warns: 'We have to be more ruthless'

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell said post-match:

"First and foremost, delighted to get the win and a good win at that. Six tries to two says a lot.

"Delighted to get the season off with a big win but I think the first game, we will learn a lot from that. It's a good place to be.

"We started really well in terms of being really clinical, we got into the 22 and scored two tries. We were dominant in that territory, which is what you want at this level.

"If you look at Hugo Keenan, Ryan Baird and Andrew Porter, lads who have not played international rugby in a while who have stepped up, Mack Hansen is another one, so I'm delighted for them.

"How we can be a bit more ruthless [is a lesson to take], because that's the team we want to be."

Ireland head coach Andy Farrell praised his side's efforts, but warns they must be more 'ruthless'

Keenan: Still a lot of work for us to do and get better at

Ireland's player of the match, Hugo Keenan said:

"You miss it. It's been 21 months since I've been here [Aviva Stadium] in green and it's been tough watching on.

"A bit like the rest of the lads, I'm just delighted to be out here and wanting to make this brilliant crowd proud and do them justice.

"I was at the end of three good plays, they were walk-ins to be honest, I'll take any.

"We got a bonus point playing against a really tough Argentina side. To beat them by 30 points and not play to our full potential is exciting because there is a lot to work on and get better at.

"We know every point counts. It's three tough games. We need to put ourselves in the best position and worry about what we can control."

Beirne: We were very good in patches

Ireland's Tadhg Beirne said post-match:

"I think we were very good in patches, and some of the tries we scored were proper team tries.

"We'll be walking away from that game thinking we could have got a lot more out of it. There were some good parts for sure, but there's certainly a lot of parts we could have been better.

"It's a great starting point for us, we know we need to keep improving. Fiji will be a challenge, we know they like to throw the ball about, and South Africa after that, but all eyes on Fiji. We need to keep improving the performance."

What's next?

For Ireland, they next face Fiji in their second Nations Championship Test of the autumn at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin on Saturday, November 14 (8.10pm kick-off).

Ireland's Nations Championship fixtures and results Australia 31-33 Ireland July 4 Japan 20-36 Ireland July 11 New Zealand 40-21 Ireland July 18 Ireland 42-12 Argentina November 6 Ireland vs Fiji Saturday, November 14 (8.10pm) Ireland vs South Africa Saturday, November 21 (4.40pm)

Argentina travel to face Italy in Genoa for their next Test, also on Saturday November 14 (11.40am kick-off GMT).

Sports.title: Leclerc plans 'significant' car changes after tough day for Ferrari
Sports.content:
Charles Leclerc says he will make "significant" setup changes to his car after "one of the worst feelings" in practice at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

Leclerc was seven tenths off pace-setter Kimi Antonelli in second practice and Lewis Hamilton was nearly half a second behind as Ferrari trailed Mercedes, McLaren and Red Bull on Friday.

It was a contrast to their recent pace with Ferrari claiming a podium position in the last four races but Leclerc is hoping they can turn that around in final practice on Saturday at 2.30pm and qualifying at 6pm, live on Sky Sports F1.

"FP2 was very tricky. Actually, if anything, one of the worst feeling I've had this year in the car, so there's plenty to work on, and it didn't feel quite right," said Leclerc.

"I've got some ideas. We'll change the car quite significantly, and we'll see how it goes. I hope we can do a step forward because even though I missed FP1, I don't think there was much performance in that.

"It's just the raw pace wasn't great."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc says he's 'settled' feud with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton after their clash in last week's Mexico City GP

Hamilton struggled to generate tyre temperature throughout the day, something which could be a big issue throughout the weekend as rain is forecast for Saturday afternoon during qualifying, and Sunday will be very cold at just 15C.

"It was a challenging day. The track is very bumpy and slippery, which made it difficult to get the tyres into the right window," said Hamilton.

"FP1 was okay overall, but FP2 proved more difficult. We've gathered plenty of useful data, so we'll work through that with the team tonight to understand where we can improve the car ahead of qualifying."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur answers questions about Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc after their incident in Mexico

Leclerc: Most special thing ever to become a father

Leclerc arrived late to Brazil after his wife Alexandra gave birth to a baby girl named Bianca on Wednesday.

The 29-year-old becomes the fifth Formula 1 driver on the current grid to be a father after Max Verstappen, Fernando Alonso, Nico Hulkenberg and Sergio Perez.

"It's definitely the most special thing ever," he said.

"You kind of expect it because I've always wanted to be a young dad, and obviously with Alex we felt like it was the right time, and it's a very, very special moment. Definitely a week I'll forever remember for all the positive reasons.

"Of course, there's been other things going on as well. But for me, this week was all about Bianca, and it's been it's been incredible."
