Sports.title: Nottingham Forest’s historic goal drought at home is part of longstanding problem
Sports.content:
Nottingham Forest and Schalke are yet to score at home in 2026-27. The former are one of only five teams in the history of the English top flight to have failed to score in their first four home league matches. Three of the preceding four also drew a blank in game five, which will be deflating news for Oliver Glasner with Manchester City heading to the City Ground on Saturday looking for a win after consecutive league defeats. Forest’s expected goals total implies they should have scored but a flaw in their data shows a reason why.

They also failed to find the net in a Carabao Cup home game with Leeds, meaning they have amassed 70 shots in all competitions without giving the home fans a goal to celebrate. As extreme as this situation has become, Forest scored only two goals more than the lowest home scorers in the Premier League last season (Burnley), drawing a blank on nine occasions. This is a longstanding issue.

The dishonour of scoring the fewest home goals in Europe’s big five leagues in modern times belongs to Dijon, who bagged eight in 19 Ligue 1 games in 2020-21. Fulham went one goal better in the same season to claim the Premier League’s wooden spoon for home scoring. Both scored three across their first four games, showing the unlikely depths to which Forest’s attack has sunk at the City Ground.

With expected goals a frequent element of post-match analysis, it can be easy to overlook that shots are independent of each other. One is not more likely to be converted when those that preceded it were missed, even though the team’s xG total ticks upward. A side that produced one expected goal through 100 shots valued at 0.01 xG would be far from guaranteed to score.

This reality lies at the heart of Forest’s home woes. Their 62 league shots have been worth 3.58 expected goals. It may feel reasonable to assume they deserve three goals. But only two of the efforts were deemed by Opta to be big chances, only five more had a better than one-in-10 probability of being converted and more than two-thirds were valued at 0.06 xG or less. Only against Coventry did they muster at least one expected goal in total, needing 24 attempts to register 1.09 xG.

Forest’s chance quality is so poor because many of their efforts are struck from long range. They have taken 50.3% of their City Ground shots from outside the box, at least 6% more than any Premier League team did on their respective patch in any of the past five seasons.

Glasner’s side are having to do this because they are struggling to get the ball into the penalty area. Again, this is a problem that predates the Austrian’s appointment. Forest were below the league average of 36.6% for their home pass accuracy into the box in 2025-26 (33.3%) and have sunk lower this season (29.6%). Cross accuracy is not the most instructive metric because the most dangerous deliveries can evade teammates if they are not anticipating them. Nonetheless, Forest’s home data paints the same picture as with their passing; below league average (26.6%) for completion rate last season (21.7%) and worse again in 2026-27 (19.0%).

Having to shoot from distance has helped make them chronically unable to put shots on target. Forest have done this only nine times in the league at the City Ground, giving them a shot accuracy rate of 14.5%. It is unsurprising to see Schalke on 18.8% given they are equally goal-shy. The least accurate home side across the past 10 seasons of football in Europe’s big five leagues are the Parma class of 2025-26. Even they managed to put 23.7% of their shots on target when taking last place in a sample of 974 team season examples.

If Forest don’t score against City, their next opportunity will come against a Chelsea side that have recently tightened up. No English top flight side have failed to score in their first six home games but Forest setting this unwanted record looks distinctly possible.

Sports.title: Cape Verde captain Ryan Mendes cleared of rape allegation as woman charged with false statement
Sports.content:
New Zealand police have dismissed a rape allegation against Cape Verde football captain Ryan Mendes and have charged the accuser with making a false statement.

Detective inspector Scott Beard said Friday the claim that a sexual assault occurred at a central Auckland hotel in March had not been substantiated.

A 40-year-old woman has been charged under New Zealand’s Crimes Act with making a false statement. She is expected to appear in court next week.

“A decision to prosecute in these circumstances is not taken lightly and follows months of investigative work by our Adult Sexual Assault Team,” Beard said.

The incident was alleged to have occurred hours after Cape Verde played Chile in a friendly match in Auckland, won 4-2 by Chile.

Mendes’ lawyer, Karl Trotter, said the allegation resulted in his client facing intense international media speculation.

Cape Verde qualified for the 2026 World Cup and the subject of the alleged assault arose at almost every media conference Mendes attended.

“Mr Mendes was thrilled to finally be able to get this behind him and he regards it as a complete vindication,” Karl Trotter told the New Zealand Herald newspaper.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It is to be hoped that this recent turn of events, clearing Mr Mendes of the allegation of rape, attracts the same level of media attention as the original reporting.”

The 36-year-old Mendes is Cape Verde’s most capped player, having made 103 appearances since his debut in 2010. He currently plays for RS Berkane in Morocco.

Sports.title: Why it's all gone wrong for Charlton: JAMES SHARPE reveals the summer failures, a player's mysterious disappearance and murmurs of yet another sale as Nathan Jones' side teeter on the brink
Sports.content:
Fear is creeping back in at the Valley. Charlton’s defeat by Bolton on Tuesday night, their fourth on the bounce, was greeted with the cacophony of boos it deserved.

Eleven games without a win and teetering above the Championship relegation zone. A fanbase that has been down this long and treacherous road before, and sure as hell doesn’t want to tread it again.

Certainly not when they thought those dark days were, at last, behind them. Only 10 weeks ago, Charlton sat top of the table after victory over Preston completed a hat-trick of early season wins, including a famous triumph in front of a record Championship attendance of 62,264 at West Ham.

It was a false dawn. For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards.

Charlton looked destined for relegation to League Two for the first time in their history when Jones took over in February 2024. They went 14 games unbeaten and survived. After spending eight of the previous nine seasons in the third tier, he took them up via the play-offs at the next time of asking and, last season, kept them in the Championship.

For a club that had endured so much instability, a period of normality and steady progression was on the cards. Jones is Charlton’s ninth managerial appointment since June 2016. Only now, the wonder is how much longer this can go on before nine becomes 10.

Fear is creeping back in at the Valley with Charlton 11 games without a win and teetering on the brink of the Championship relegation zone

For the first time under Nathan Jones, the ship has stalled and, for now, is going backwards

‘If I hadn’t done what I’ve done at this football club, it would have been an easier decision for them (the owners),’ Jones told South London Sport this week. ‘I have to win football games. Win games or you don’t survive.’

His next chance is against ninth-placed Sheffield United this Saturday afternoon. Jones insists he maintains a strong relationship with the Charlton board. The new chief executive Ben Mansford – formerly of Leeds, Blackpool and Barnsley and who ended the club’s spell of 19 months without one – twice tried to hire Jones at his previous clubs. Jones is understood still to have the backing of his players.

Perhaps it’s not best to let him know that both Alan Pardew and Chris Powell lost their jobs after defeats by the Blades.

‘We've spent a lot of time in League One recently and I think there is a kind of head-in-hands worry at the moment: please let's not go back there again,’ Heather McKinlay, chair of the Charlton Athletic Supporters' Trust tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘At the moment, it feels more like duty than fun. I think we have become a little bit worn down because we've been through the mill so much with the changes of ownership and the shenanigans over the near 20 years since we were in the Premier League.’

They have been through the mill, much of the difficulties driven by those in charge. Former owner Roland Duchatelet, who still owns the Valley and the training ground, once accused fans of wanting the club to fail. Charlton’s fans responded to his comments and mismanagement by carrying a red coffin to the Valley followed by a crowd of mourners in a mock funeral protest against his ownership.

They lobbed hundreds of plastic pigs on the pitch for one game, beach balls to halt another, and sent a black cab to Belgium as a ’Taxi for Roland’.

Within weeks of Duchatelet selling Charlton to businessmen Tahnoon Nimer and Matt Southall for £1, the two new men were embroiled in a bitter public row. Nimer accused Southall of using club money to fund his own lifestyle, which he denied, including renting a £150,000-a-year flat in London and giving a fleet of Range Rovers to his associates. Charlton fans occupied the boardroom in protest. Thomas Sandgaard, the next owner, was arrested by the FBI this year and charged with fraud. He denies any wrongdoing.

The highly impressive win away to West Ham in August now appears to have been a false dawn

Jones is Charlton's ninth manager in the last 10 years - but how long can he keep this up?

‘Charlton fans are a proactive lot,’ adds McKinlay. ‘If they feel they can make a difference, they’ll do something. I don’t feel we can do anything right now other than cheer them on. I think the ownership want the club to succeed. The manager wants the club to succeed. The players want the club to succeed. There's not really a baddie in this.’

As one club insider put it this week, it’s nice, in a strange way, that football is the main issue for once and not what’s going on off the field.

There is still a sense of that, mind. The current ownership group known as Global Football Partners is made up of seven shareholders, each with more than five per cent, but it remains unclear who is the driving force. Sources suggest some are more willing than others to put their money in with murmurings that the club is once again up for sale. Charlton insist they are merely looking for more investment to help drive the club forward.

Poor recruitment has not helped matters either. All the talk in the summer was about ‘evolving’ from a team that could get out of League One, then stay in the Championship, to one that could compete.

The club, however, spent a net total of just £1.5million this summer. They failed to find the right winger they needed, as a deal for Crystal Palace winger Jesurun Rak-Sakyi collapsed late on. Instead they signed teenager Junior Nkeng, who hasn’t played a single minute. A lack of creative midfielder is glaring too.

As for those who did arrive, Millenic Alli infuriated supporters in the defeat by Bolton when he headed the ball blindly into no man’s land during stoppage time with the team desperately searching for an equaliser. Nathaniel Chalobah arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He showed his class at the start of the season, got injured, returned and is now injured again.

That’s not to mention the bizarre mystery surrounding midfielder Timothy Ouma. The Kenya international, on loan from Slavia Prague, went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since. Ouma, who has not featured in a single matchday squad since the break, has previous for this, having also failed to return after international duty while on loan at Lech Poznan.

When Jones was asked about it a few weeks ago, he responded by saying: ‘We will address those rumours when they become relevant. Anything we need to put out, we will put out.’

Kenyan midfielder Timothy Ouma went off to play for his country during the recent break and has not been seen since

Nathaniel Chalobah (right) arrived as a free agent from Sheffield Wednesday with a reputation for being injury prone. He got injured, returned and is now injured again

Charlton remain tight-lipped on whether Ouma is still absent, though one insider admitted they still hadn’t seen him since the players returned from international duty. The Kenyan FA did not respond to requests for clarification.

It makes the decision to part ways with club captain Greg Docherty in the summer look even more misguided, with this a team lacking in leadership. Jones has been left to throw all the pieces up in the air and see where they land with constant changes to the team and the line-up. Selection and formation roulette, as some are calling it.

The Welshman is not everyone’s cup of tea, frequently mocked for his David Brent style, but there’s still a belief, not least from himself, that he can turn things around. ‘He’s a maverick, but he’s our maverick,’ laughs McKinlay.

Time is running out, though, because if Charlton cannot find their way again, the alternative is already too unnerving to think about.

Sports.title: RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: Why box-office Bryson DeChambeau MUST use a little-known loophole to join the European Tour - and not become an irrelevant YouTuber doing tricks for clicks
Sports.content:
RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: Why box-office Bryson DeChambeau MUST use a little-known loophole to join the European Tour - and not become an irrelevant YouTuber doing tricks for clicks

Riath Al-Samarrai Chief Sports Feature Writer

First, LIV Golf ran out of money. Then it ran out of time. Bryson DeChambeau is sufficiently wealthy that his own future won’t provide an exact replica of their car crash, but his career does hinge on a race against the clock.

It’s ticking fast towards November 15, which is a deadline of some significance. To explain why that is, you’ll have to indulge a small trip into the minutiae of the DP World Tour’s membership regulations.

That’s a complicated journey. But it leads to a fascinating place and the situation is pivotal, as DeChambeau is currently homeless – he has no competitive outlet for his golf now that LIV is dead and what he does next is crucial if he is to avoid becoming an irrelevance.

It has been clear for some time that the PGA Tour are in no rush to send a lifeboat in his direction – he rejected one at the start of this year and my sources suggest it is unlikely he will be presented with another sweetheart deal to go back.

If he is to return to those American fairways, he would have to serve a 12-month suspension in exile and earn his way back on another tour, just like Patrick Reed has done. Maybe the folk Stateside are feeling less vindictive now that LIV has perished, but as of today, I’m told the boat remains docked.

That leaves DeChambeau two prime choices: honour his threat to become a full-time YouTube golfer, which would be colossally stupid if he wishes to remain competitive between majors, or join the DP World Tour.

Bryson DeChambeau has no competitive outlet for his golf now that LIV is dead...

...but his 2024 US Open win opens the door for a spot on the DP World Tour - if he acts fast

I was discussing this with prominent figures on the DP World Tour on Thursday afternoon and reported the detail that evening – they quite fancy having DeChambeau around. He is a peacock of colour, flair and contradictions and controversies; two years ago, almost to the day, he was called to the stage by Donald Trump during his victory speech at the presidential election.

In short, he is box-office, and a very good golfer. Would the DP World Tour want him? Of course they bloody well do.

And this is where the November 15 deadline comes in, because DeChambeau is eligible to take up membership but would need to act fast. That traces to an offshoot of his win at the 2024 US Open, when Rory McIlroy missed a tiddler and DeChambeau claimed his second major.

That victory meant he could have five years on the DP circuit if he fancied, but back then, as LIV Golf’s foremost evangelist and personal confidant to the Saudi moneyman Yasir Al-Rumayyan, it won’t have even registered on his radar.

Now, it is ostensibly his best option, and most sensible, but those regulations exist with a twist: as per my reporting on Thursday, every year that has passed without DeChambeau triggering the membership has seen a further 12 months deducted from the back end of his eligibility.

In other words, the two years he spent not caring has cost him four, leaving only the 2027 season available to him. And to play in 2027 on the DP World Tour, he needs to commit by the close of business on November 15. So there it is – complex but urgent and of great importance.

I dearly hope he takes up that option, because golf is vastly more interesting with DeChambeau in it.

Ask many of his rivals and the view tends to be that he can be a bit of a prat, but valuable to their ecosystem. McIlroy, for one, has been clear in his feelings – when DeChambeau was caught up in a cheating storm at the Open last summer, McIlroy was pretty scathing and added he 'wasn’t particularly fond of him’.

DeChambeau was caught up in a cheating storm at the Open last summer when he was accused of improving his lie

Ask many of his rivals and the view tends to be that he can be a bit of a prat - but one that helps golf's ecosystem

Perhaps, in turn, DeChambeau might have enjoyed a different story on Thursday, shortly before his money tree was fed into the wood chipper. That involved McIlroy receiving a two-stroke penalty for improving his lie at a DP World Tour event in Abu Dhabi.

Now imagine if they had been playing side-by-side. And then think over the possibilities at the microphone.

That’s a conversation about the value of villains. I’ve written about it before in this space – one of the consequences of LIV was that it stripped the traditional tours of their most colourful individuals. The prime benefit to LIV’s demise will come from having them back.

If the PGA Tour are smart, they will send out the rescue party and finesse a few rules to get DeChambeau back and quickly. If they don’t, the DP World Tour might just snag a ratings-winner when their finances badly need one. But that is contingent on DeChambeau embracing logic.

As something of a mad scientist, he could talk all day about why he floats his golf balls in an Epsom salt and water solution (he is suspicious of manufacturing flaws in the dimples and likes to measure gravitational imbalances). He could also explain why fire ants present such a health threat that he once invoked USGA Rule 16.2.a for free relief on the ‘dangerous animal’ clause.

But he is also sufficiently irrational that at the height of his tantrum at The Open, he threatened to call Trump if the rules officials refused to back down.

That was one of the most absurd stories I’ve written in the past 12 months, stranger than ‘Penis-gate’ at the Winter Olympic ski-jumping.

But that’s what DeChambeau brings and there isn’t a sporting administrator on the planet who wouldn’t want a piece. Naturally, the videos of him launching wedge shots over his home and onto a back-garden green a few years back drew more views than footage of Scottie Scheffler playing the best golf since Tiger Woods.

Whether that same mind can now be trusted to make a reasonable decision is open to debate. But it would be a hideous loss to all parties if he chooses a path committed to putting Epsom-soaked golf balls down staircases for clicks.

It would be a hideous loss to all parties if DeChambeau focuses on being a YouTube golfer doing tricks for clicks

If the PGA Tour are smart, they will send out the rescue party and finesse a few rules to get DeChambeau back and quickly

PALMER FAILING TO SHOW TUCHEL HE CARES

A video has resurfaced since Jobe Bellingham was called up to join his brother Jude in Thomas Tuchel’s England squad. It shows him performing an impressive party piece – he can name, in reverse order, every winner of the Champions League/European Cup dating back to 1955.

If trivia were in any way relevant to England selection, Angus ‘Statto’ Loughran would have more caps than Harry Kane and Peter Shilton combined, but there is something heartwarming about a player who shows the depths of his obsession.

Indirectly, that footage made me think of Cole Palmer, who swerved the last international break with a minor injury and has been ignored for the latest gathering. If he’s fussed, he hasn’t made it known, which is part of his schtick.

Of course, there’s no imperative for Palmer to prove he can name the Steaua Bucharest side of 1986, but his biggest test is to show Tuchel he cares. Currently, you’d have to say he’s failing.

Cole Palmer (right) swerved the last international break and has been ignored by Thomas Tuchel for this one. If he’s fussed, he hasn’t made it known, which is part of his schtick

POLLOCK TREADING A FINE LINE

Henry Pollock will be the cover star of Tatler’s December issue. On Sunday, he will serve as cover from the bench for England’s game against Australia at Twickenham.

Aged 21 and loaded with both talent and charisma, he has his pick of audiences, but it’s a fine line that he’s choosing to walk.

With one sporting misstep, he will make life very easy for his many critics.

Sports.title: Derided Thierno Barry is no longer a source of frustration as star fires Everton to victory over Coventry on another big night for David Moyes amid Jack Grealish drama
Sports.content:
Derided Thierno Barry is no longer a source of frustration as star fires Everton to victory over Coventry on another big night for David Moyes amid Jack Grealish drama

Maybe Everton should request to play under the lights every week. It certainly seems to push David Moyes' team to new heights.

Following hot on the heels of consecutive night victories over Newcastle United, Friday's 3-1 win against Coventry City was a reminder of why, under Moyes, there is renewed sense of optimism at Everton.

Up to fifth, above Liverpool, and in a Carabao Cup quarter-final at Fleetwood, it could prove to be a special season.

This always felt like a big task for Frank Lampard, back at Everton for the first time since his sacking in 2023.

Popular as the ex-manager may be, there's no room for sentiment, certainly not from Moyes on a night he took charge of his 592nd game, drawing level with Harry Catterick for managing the most games in the club's history.

He'll set it outright after the international break against Brentford and Keith Andrews, who was 21 when Moyes first took up the reins at Everton.

Thierno Barry (right) now has 10 goals this season after being widely derided in his first season on Merseyside

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall had been left out of the England squad in the morning, but refused to let it spoil his night

His side started impressively, fashioning three shots in the opening 10 minutes, before losing all momentum and allowing Coventry into proceedings.

It took going 1-0 down, to a soft Yann Gboho goal, for the hosts to come alive. Thierno Barry, so often the source of frustration last season, was magnificent and all but won the game with a five-minute brace in the second half.

The striker didn't score his first goal until December last season. This campaign, he's reached 10 before the second international break. Moyes joked post-match that Erling Haaland should watch his back in the Golden Boot race is starting to feel less absurd. Barry now sits joint second in the charts.

Both goals against Coventry came via back post-duels. The first he confidently headed past Carl Rushworth, before bundling in a second five minutes later.

The disgruntled home fans booed the team off at half-time, yet were jubilantly cheering and signing after Barry's brace. The Frenchman danced on the pitch at full-time and was serenaded by the South Stand.

'I don't see loads of young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League,' said Moyes.

'He's come in and has settled in a bit more. His language and communication is better and obviously he's worked to get himself into the positions to score.'

Barry wasn't the only Everton goalscorer, of course. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was not one of the three Everton players named in Thomas Tuchel's England squad on Friday - only Arsenal had more representatives.

MATCH FACTS EVERTON (4-2-3-1): Pickford 5; Rohl 5 (O'Brien 73min, 6), Tarkowski 5, Branthwaite 6 (Keane 89), Mykolenko 6; Armstrong 6 (Hackney 73, 6), Garner 6; Dibling 5 (Johnson 73, 5), DEWSBURY-HALL 8, George 5 (Alcaraz 90); Barry 8. Scorers: Barry 56, 61 Dewsbury-Hall 81. Booked: Branthwaite. Manager: David Moyes 6. COVENTRY CITY (4-2-3-1): Rushworth 4; van Ewijk 5, Mfuni 6, Pinnock 6, Dasilva 6; Yirenkyi 6, Torp 6 (Grimes 86); Sakamoto 5 (Tchaouna 86), Rudoni 5 (Hamer 86), Gboho 6 (Thomas-Asante 73, 5); Awoniyi 5 (Cherif 87). Scorer: Gboho 52. Booked: Yirenkyi. Manager: Frank Lampard 5. Referee: Stuart Attwell 6. Attendance: 52,395.

But the midfielder sent a pointed message to the Three Lions' boss with a superb showing that was capped with a late powerful goal to end the contest.

'It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie,' Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports after the game. 'It's a massive dream to play for my country. I know I was close.

'Yeah, sad, but really proud of myself and how I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up. I've got the mentality. I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens.'

'He's desperate to play for England,' added Moyes. 'You never know if England get a couple of injuries, or anything changes.'

What ended as a comfortable win could have been a different outcome had Jame Tarkowski been punished for a hair pull on Caleb Yirenkyi, or if Vitalii Mykolenko's tussle with Taiwo Awoniyi in the box had been deemed a foul.

Both were checked and cleared by VAR, as was a handball claim in the build-up to Barry's second goal.

'Tarky pulls on Caleb's hair, they [VAR] are saying it's not enough of a pull,' said an aggrieved Lampard afterwards. 'That's a hard area to be in. What is hair pull and what's not?

'I think Taiwo, on the edge of the box was a penalty. I feel there's a penalty by the time Myko's knee is in the back of Taiwo's knee on the line of the box.

'Then the Barry one is handball. He flicks it in [with the hand] with the final touch. Nothing went for us tonight.'

Sports.title: French tennis star Arthur Fils shows class at Paris Masters as he consoles ball girl who was in tears after being accidentally hit in the face by Taylor Fritz's serve
Sports.content:
French tennis star Arthur Fils shows class at Paris Masters as he consoles ball girl who was in tears after being accidentally hit in the face by Taylor Fritz's serve

French tennis star Arthur Fils showed his class and compassion by taking care of a ball girl, who was in tears after being struck in the face.

Fils' opponent, Taylor Fritz, served the ball and it went out before ricocheting wildly off the back of the court during their Paris Masters clash and then striking the ball girl in the face.

It was an unpleasant moment and brought the youngster to tears but Fils, 22, immediately recognised she was hurt.

He strolled over and interrupted his rhythm to console the shaken ball girl and escorted her off court to receive medical attention.

The home crowd loved the gesture from their chivalrous countryman and offered warm applause for his act of generosity.

Fritz also looked concerned about the accidental incident and approached the net to check on the girl.

Arthur Fils comforting a ball girl after she accidentally got hit by a ball 🥺



​She burst into tears, and the Frenchman immediately walked over to make sure she was okay ❤️ pic.twitter.com/mTbF9lv1xw — Kalshi Tennis (@KalshiTen) November 5, 2026

Arthur Fils showed his concern for the tearful ball girl who had been accidentally struck

Ball boys and girls are often in the firing line of rapid serves and occasionally find themselves on the receiving end of an impact.

At the 2020 Australian Open, Rafael Nadal smashed a forehand into the ball girl standing by the umpire's chair by mistake.

The Spaniard gave her an apologetic hug and later handed her his headband from the match as a further gesture of contrition.

Fritz went on to beat Fils 6-3, 6-4 in a comfortable win and did not have to face a single break point in the entire match.

He went through and set up a clash against Carlos Alcaraz, where bizarrely there was another incident with a ball girl. This time the injury came from a fall while running back to the corner.

Photographers and other staff came to help her up and both players also checked on her. 'I think the ball girl twisted her ankle or something,' commentator Daniela Hantuchova said.

'Obviously just twisted her ankle. Bless her. Just going to be a little bit of a delay while she gets the treatment that she needs. I think she’s alright.'

She was then replaced by another ball girl while receiving treatment and whisked away off court. Alcaraz came out on top in three sets to progress to the semi-finals.

Sports.title: How Spurs turned their season around: Fiery three-hour meeting before Man United clash, the star who has lit a spark in struggling side and why Rodrigo Bentancur's red card was a key moment
Sports.content:
How Spurs turned their season around: Fiery three-hour meeting before Man United clash, the star who has lit a spark in struggling side and why Rodrigo Bentancur's red card was a key moment

Choose your Tottenham turning point. The training break in Marbella perhaps. The first win of the season against Coventry, the return of James Maddison, or a rare and emotional victory at Chelsea, only second time in 36 years.

Roberto De Zerbi, the man who has turned the tanker on the pitch, goes instinctively to a heated team meeting before the Manchester United game. It lasted for three hours, from 8pm to 11pm in the team hotel in Manchester city centre.

De Zerbi detected more fire and passion in the meeting room that day and realised change was in the air. He enjoyed hearing home truths exchanged among teammates and between them and his staff members.

'In normal meetings you speak about tactics and mentality,' said De Zerbi. 'In that meeting there was something different. If you are honest in the meeting and you remove the mask and explain your weaknesses a teammate can help you in a difficult moment.

'I believe in people, in relationships, in connections. I don't believe in robots. I don't believe you can come here, put on the shirt and go on the pitch. I believe in the right atmosphere. I love it when I see my players come together to help each other, coming to the stadium even when not selected in the squad. It's crucial.

'Sometimes you can fight but fight for the good of the club not for yourself. Not egoist players but he team, before everything.'

Spurs have won their last three matches having turned the corner under Roberto De Zerbi

Manchester United was the first fixture after the last international break. Spurs were bottom of the Premier League.

They played well at Old Trafford without capitalising, then went behind and had Rodrigo Bentancur sent off for butting Luke Shaw before summoning a fight back, with Dominic Solanke heading in a late equaliser from a cross by Sandro Tonali, the £100million midfielder who finished the game playing at left back.

It provided a spark. Spurs won the next three.

Red mist and serendipity

The impact of Bentancur's ban was amplified by Lucas Bergvall's knee injury in the same game. Neither have played since, although Bentancur is available again at Leeds, and De Zerbi reflects positively on the Uruguayan's rush of blood.

'Very important,' said the Spurs boss. 'I don't know if without that red card the reaction would have been like this, but the reaction was good because sometimes we are afraid to show more passion.

'I like people to say Tottenham played well but I want people to say Tottenham played with passion. That they were strong and helped each other on the pitch. That they had hot blood inside. That they played for the club and the fans. My dream is to hear people talk like this.'

Without Bentancur and Bergvall, De Zerbi flexed into a 352 formation against Coventry. Maddison started his first game for nearly 18 months and Spurs won for the first time this season, then disappeared on secretive training break for four nights in Marbella.

They were back in a familiar 4231 shape against Chelsea with Mateus Fernandes starting for the first time since he had been hooked at half time against Aston Villa and criticised by De Zerbi.

Fernandes was the best player on the pitch and clicked with Tonali and the pair excelled again against Crystal Palace.

For all the best laid plans, some good things can happen by chance.

Rodrigo Bentancur's red card in the draw with Man United has proved a key moment for Spurs

Patience with new signings

Back in August, in the aftermath of a 2-0 defeat by Newcastle in the first home game of this season, Tonali stood near the dressing rooms in conversation with club owners Vivienne Lewis and her son-in-law Nick Beucher.

Tonali was disconsolate. The new Spurs regime had invested a club record fee to sign him at the behest of De Zerbi but he was sluggish, miles from his best and had just been given the runaround by Nico Gonzalez, the player bought to replace him for half the price.

His body language was apologetic, and the owners appeared keen to offer some words of encouragement as they bid farewells and took a lift to the corporate suites in the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Two months on, the Italian has hit his stride. He has been dominant in the last two games. Sharper in mind, more decisive and quicker across the ground. Reading play, breaking things down, covering the miles. He looks like an elite midfielder.

'To play well, Tonali has to run and to work on the pitch,' said De Zerbi before hinting at more to come from Fernandes. 'Mateus is showing 50-60 per cent of his potential,' said the Spurs boss.

Injured players return

For all the rhetoric about unity, the return of Maddison has reset the creativity levels. His presence lifted the crowd and had a similar effect on his teammates. Possession is more secure. His quality on the ball gives others time to organise and with him Spurs look a lot more like scoring a goal. Passes fizz around at a brisker tempo and he carries threat from around the fringes of the penalty box. The goal he swept into the top corner to open the scoring against Coventry was exquisite.

Sandro Tonali has become a vital player for De Zerbi after a mixed start to his Tottenham career

Mo Kudus is back and Dejan Kulusevski's return after so long lifted morale. Less obvious is the return of Dominic Solanke, a genuine centre forward who can operate with his back to goal and bring others into play. Solanke has helped the team gel even if his goal return remains disappointing and De Zerbi admits he and Omar Marmoush are suffering low confidence.

And an emerging star...

After being criticised for ignoring the club's academy talent, De Zerbi has tried to integrate Luca Williams-Barnett. He cannot talk about togetherness if he refuses to engage with one significant arm of the club. Williams-Barnett made his Premier League debut as a sub against Palace. De Zerbi claimed he thought about starting him at Chelsea and urged the 18-year-old attacking midfielder to learn from those around him.

'The young player has to remove all social media and stay focused on improvement,' said De Zerbi. 'They have to follow the older teammates with more experience and work hard. Expectation and hype is normal. He can become a top player and has to get used to strong pressure and high expectation.'

Win at Leeds on Saturday and Spurs will go into another international break in touch with the top five. It has been quite a turnaround and chief executive Vinai Venkatesham popped up on a podcast this week talking about ambitions to win the Premier League title.

'Great to hear,' said De Zerbi. 'The first thing for people in this club is to be ambitious but to be ambitious you have to show the right mentality every day, game by game because words are not enough.

'What Vinai, the Lewis family and Johan Lange are doing is something special. In the last two seasons you can see they are changing a lot of things in this club. For me as coach, my staff and the players, we have to show we have the self to stay in this club.

'With the right behaviour, the right mentality, to be angry every day and to make a result. This is the best thing to do from our side.'

Sports.title: Some are calling this 'Tuchel 2.0' and his latest squad does feel like that. Here's why England think a tilt at the European Championship is within reach, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Some are calling this 'Tuchel 2.0' and his latest squad does feel like that. Here's why England think a tilt at the European Championship is within reach, writes IAN LADYMAN

One of Thomas Tuchel’s favourite analogies when it comes to the development of his England team is that of a train leaving a station with only the chosen few on it. As time moves on, the bodies lying on the tracks are growing greater in number.

Consider this statistic. Of the 26 players who travelled to the World Cup in America 13 are not in the squad chosen by England manager Tuchel for next week’s Nations League games against Croatia and Spain. And that does not include Cole Palmer and Phil Foden who, after missing out in the summer, were expected by many of us to have forced a way back in by now.

Tuchel’s latest selection has been affected by injuries, of course. But more significant is that the experienced German believes he is now starting to see an England team and squad develop in a way and in a direction that even he hadn’t envisaged once Argentina ended his World Cup hopes in that dismal Atlanta semi-final in July.

Different feelings, different style of play and, to a degree, different players.

Some are calling this ‘Tuchel 2.0’ and it does feel a little bit like that. The start of the second phase of Tuchel’s tenure, the start of the road towards a tilt at another trophy, the European Championships of 2028.

Having admitted to some worry ahead of the four-game international break FIFA saddled us all with last month, Tuchel sat down yesterday looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself.

Tuchel sat down with the media looking and sounding like a man once again certain of himself

The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham — Jude’s younger brother (right) — was the headline act but there were other messages written within

Certain enough of a direct, quick, athletic style of play that helped England to two wins over Czech Republic and one – by seven goals – against Croatia in Rijeka. And certain that a dependence on players like Jordan Henderson, Dan Burn and John Stones for what we may politely call ‘squad culture management’ lies now in the past.

All of this may crash down in Madrid next Sunday. Spain have already beaten Tuchel’s England once – at Wembley in late September – and a repeat this month would ask familiar questions about England against the really good teams.

But for now, Tuchel is confident enough to claim that he has found his path.

‘We said at some point we need to take the next step, to build on what we have, to get better and to improve otherwise you’re just left behind,’ said Tuchel yesterday.

‘That’s how football works. You have been champion in one season but you need to improve, you need to bring in new players for competition, young players, new energy, fresh energy. It’s also the way, naturally, the national team goes.

‘We cannot be stuck in the same personnel and in the same style of play.

‘I agreed with you last month. I was the first to admit I was not 100 per cent happy with the pure level of football we played in the US. I saw a higher level in training [than on the field], I saw a higher level in glimpses.

‘We adjusted some things tactically, created some new positions and took the next steps.’

The Tuchel we sat down with in late September still wore the scars of the summer’s disappointment – and the criticism that came with it – rather visibly. It was the first time we had seen him like that in his two years in the job. He was tetchy and easily provoked. Call it the Argentina effect if you like.

Here, he appeared rather healed. Good results tend to do that for a manager and a little time helps too. If he believes his team has moved on then maybe he has also and he had to.

Certainly, his selection squad speaks to that. The inclusion of Jobe Bellingham – Jude’s younger brother – was the headline act but there were other messages written within.

Henderson and Burn are available but not included. So too Arsenal’s Noni Madueke, excluded to the benefit of the more direct Liverpool winger Rio Ngumoha.

‘We need runners who will go between the lines,’ said Tuchel. A clear indication, there, that too much of England’s summer wing play was too slow and too conservatively narrow.

Palmer, Foden and Kobbie Mainoo are also on the outside looking in once again and the case of the Manchester United midfielder is perhaps indicative of how Tuchel now operates.

Moved to apologise to him in front of the whole squad in July for his lack of minutes at the World Cup, Tuchel was determined Mainoo would play in the opening four games of the Nations League campaign.

‘I was desperate to give him the minutes and desperate to include him in this new start,’ explained Tuchel.

‘But then he pulled out. He missed an excellent camp and also entered a difficult, difficult spell for himself.

‘Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise. So this is why he now suffers.’

We can talk about the whys and wherefores of that logic. If Mainoo was good enough in September then why is he not good enough now? How desperate could Tuchel really have been to play him that one withdrawal with injury closed the door for the next camp and opened it instead for Bellingham jnr?

This, though, is how Tuchel works. He is an adept tactician but he’s also a mood coach, someone who – after sobering club experiences at places like PSG, Chelsea and Bayern Munich – places huge emphasis on environments and gut feels and culture. If he feels something works, he doesn’t like to pick it apart without good reason.

This is why for example the growing voice and influence of Elliot Anderson has left Jordan Henderson suddenly surplus. Tuchel says the door is not closed on a player who will be 38 by the time the next Euros are played and he called him this week to say so. In Tuchel’s mind, though, England will now move without the veteran and others of his ilk.

‘I was concerned before the last camp that we missed the players who kept our standards,’ said Tuchel.

‘I was worried that we missed so many of them. But then this group found their own way and their own voices.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game changing duo of Palmer and Foden

‘I know what the others did. They built a platform on which these ones can build.’

Time will tell. To a degree, Spain will tell. Can England play the kind of higher tempo, front foot football we saw against Croatia and the Czechs against the world and European champions next Sunday? They embarrassed us when we didn’t have the ball at Wembley.

It’s also reasonable to ask why our head coach can’t find room in his squad – if not his team – for the game-changing duo of Palmer and Foden. England lacked good substitutes at the World Cup. There was too much like for like.

England need to win in order for such decisions to be vindicated and Tuchel knows that.

Asked yesterday if he felt as invigorated as he looked he said he did. ‘The last camp gave me a lot of energy, gave me a lot of extra belief,’ he said.

‘It gave me a lot of optimism to not compromise on the way England teams should play. Be physical but also step up in the pure level of performances.’

It’s certainly time for this now. The summer only served to expose English shortcomings. Tuchel’s train must arrive in Madrid next weekend, not only with fresh personnel but also new ideas clearly apparent.

Sports.title: Now go after the rest of the cheating Aussies: Usman Khawaja's explosive claims bring more shame onto a team who were cowardly as well as complicit - they must surely be punished and captain Pat Cummins cannot escape, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Now go after the rest of the cheating Aussies: Usman Khawaja's explosive claims bring more shame onto a team who were cowardly as well as complicit - they must surely be punished and captain Pat Cummins cannot escape, writes OLIVER HOLT

Usman Khawaja is adamant about it. ‘It was all of us,’ he writes in his soon-to-be-published autobiography. ‘Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us…If you read my story, if you read what I’m saying, I have numerous times said it’s us, the team. This is the team. It’s not Steve, Davey and Bangers. It’s all of us.’

His revelations about the Sandpapergate cheating scandal that rocked world cricket in 2018 and cast captain Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft as scapegoats will detonate another explosion under the Australia cricket team as they are about to head into an Ashes year. Those revelations will turn a dark episode in Australia’s cricket history even darker.

The three players’ admissions of their part in using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the Third Test of the series between South Africa and Australia at Newlands in Cape Town brought shame on the country.

A particularly tearful mea culpa from Smith at a subsequent press conference has been used to mock him and Australian masculinity ever since.

Each of the three players received bans from Test cricket for their part in the scandal but Khawaja’s revelations not only reopen the wounds of the grisly episode eight years after they thought they had banished it but also raise the possibility of Australia’s bowling attack being decimated before they fly to England for the Ashes series in the summer.

The significance of Khawaja’s revelations lies primarily in his allegations that Australia had experimented with the same ball-tampering tactics at the previous Test in Port Elizabeth but also in the fact that the majority of the team dodged responsibility for the cheating even though Khawaja says they were all complicit.

Cameron Bancroft (left), Steve Smith (right) and David Warner took the blame for Sandpapergate but Usman Khawaja has now revealed the whole team knew of the cheating

The rest of the team, pictured here in the Sandpapergate Test, must surely be punished

That second revelation strikes at the heart of the ethos of Australian cricket because it destroys the idea of ‘mateship’ within the ranks of the side.

What Khawaja is saying is that the majority of the team let three others take the fall when they should have stood together as one. They failed to do that. They let their mates swing.

One of those men who stood back and watched as Warner, Smith and Bancroft were thrown to the wolves was Pat Cummins, now the Australia captain. If what Khawaja says is true, then how can Cummins’ authority over the team remain? If what Khawaja says is true, then how can a man who did not stay true to the spirit of the Baggy Green retain the respect of the players he leads?

If what Khawaja says is true, then surely it will be incumbent on Cricket Australia to impose bans on the rest of the players in that Cape Town Test. Warner and Smith were both suspended from Test cricket for a year. The same sanction, presumably, may now be visited on the rest of the side.

Team sport, after all, ought to be about collective responsibility and that responsibility is something that those four bowlers, who still constitute the majority of the Australian attack now, dodged together.

They are very much in the line of fire now as Australian cricket stumbles into a new crisis.

Part of Khawaja’s motivation appears to be guilt that he did not stand up for his mates when he should have done.

He has watched, he writes in the autobiography, as Warner has ‘copped it’ over and over again for his part in the cheating and resolutely refused to implicate others. Warner, he suggests, has chosen secret honour. Others have not.

Khawaja (left) has decided to spill the beans in his soon-to-be-released autobiography and now serious questions must be asked of captain Pat Cummins (right)

But there will surely be wider repercussions for the Australian game now. In 2021, Australia’s bowlers in the Newlands Test – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon – released a statement in which they denied any knowledge of a foreign substance used to change the condition of the ball.

‘We feel compelled to put the key facts on the record again,’ the bowlers’ statement said.

‘We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands.

‘And to those who, despite the absence of evidence, insist that 'we must have known' about the use of a foreign substance simply because we are bowlers, we say this: The umpires during that Test match, Nigel Long and Richard Illingworth, both very respected and experienced umpires, inspected the ball after the images surfaced on the TV coverage and did not change it because there was no sign of damage.’

Those words will be picked over relentlessly in the next few weeks as Khawaja’s revelations are released in extracts in the Australian media.

Smith said he was left traumatised by the Sandpaper gate scandal in 2018 - pictured here with his father as he made his tearful public apology in Sydney

‘Same old Aussies, always cheating,’ is the common refrain of the Barmy Army during Ashes contests and it will be sung with renewed gusto now as one of the sport’s most infamous cheating scandals brings even more shame on Australia.

‘At the end of the day,’ Khawaja said, ‘I still think it’s the right thing to do for particularly those three guys (Warner, Smith and Bancroft). And I think most of the guys in the team, at some level, will be relieved that we can finally move on.’

It is a nice idea but the reality is that Australian cricket has been plunged into a new world of pain.

Sports.title: Bayern Munich's £400,000-a-week 'risk' on Harry Kane: Dietmar Hamann reveals doubts about Ballon d'Or winner - and claims no English team would have matched mega contract offer
Sports.content:
Bayern Munich are taking a major 'risk' giving Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane a bumper new deal, according to former midfielder Didi Hamann. Kane, 33, and Bayern Munich have agreed on a two-year contract extension worth £400,000 per week which will make him the world's highest-paid English sportsman. But ex-Liverpool and Bayern man Hamann has suggested that this may prove to be a poor move given Kane's age and possible decline. 'Whether he'll still be scoring goals in the coming years, we'll see. He's 33 years old and will be 36 when the contract expires. There's obviously a certain risk involved,' Champions League winner Hamann told Sky Germany. Hamann then went on to justify his bizarre comments by saying: 'He didn't play well for England at the European Championship two years ago, and he had problems in the last two knockout matches at the World Cup.' The ex-Germany international also suggested that staying at Bayern was the best deal Kane was going to get at this stage in his career, saying: 'I don't think there were any major suitors from England. Harry Kane has signed a two-year-long contract extension with Bayern but Didi Hamann is not convinced this is the right move for the Bavarians Speaking with Sky Germany Dietmar Hamann expressed concerns over his old side offering Kane such a large deal 'They would have taken him for 20 or 30 million, but Bayern would probably have wanted at least half or three-quarters back this summer of the 100 million euros they had to pay Tottenham for Kane in 2023. 'I don't think anyone would have paid that. That's why the contract extension is something they probably couldn't have done any differently.' Hamann is arguably taking a harsh view on Kane's new deal considering how the Englishman has performed since arriving in Germany. In three seasons at the Allianz he has 102 Bundesliga goals in as many games as well as 28 assists, winning the Bundesliga Golden Boot every year since his arrival. The Englishman's goals have fired Bayern to two back-to-back Bundesliga titles and a DFB-Pokal triumph. But clearly all of this is not enough for Hamann who has previously critiqued Kane's performances in Germany saying that last season his role in Kompany's Bayern side was 'unacceptable.' In his Sky Germany column the former defensive midfielder wrote: 'I don't know if Kompany is happy that Harry Kane is no longer playing exclusively as a striker. 'It's not acceptable to me that Kane is winning balls in his own penalty area, because that's not his job at all.'
