World.title: Fani-Kayode rejects senior counsel of Nigeria title
World.content:
Nigeria’s High Commissioner to South Africa, Femi Fani-Kayode, on Friday, disassociated himself from the designation of Senior Counsel of Nigeria (SCN), known as Blue Silk, that the Nigerian Law Society (NLS) conferred on him.

According to a press statement signed by his special assistant on media, Lizzy Okoji, Mr Fani-Kayode said he “did not personally authorise or approve the acceptance of the said designation and hereby formally disassociates himself from the purported conferment.”

He explained that he sent a representative to the NLS event for official engagements in honour of the society’s invitation.

Mr Fani-Kayode, a lawyer, described his representative’s acceptance of the designation as an “unfortunate administrative misjudgement” and did not reflect his endorsement or convictions.

The NLS, which gained attention in recent years with its posturing as a rival to the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) and introduction of the controversial Blue Silk title in 2025, reportedly conferred the title on Mr Fani-Kayode and four other lawyers.

The other recipients were Seyi Tinubu, Olufunmilayo Osifuye, Ihudiebube Chukwumdi and Alabi Adigun. The conferment reportedly took place on Thursday at the society’s 2026 Annual General Conference held in Utako, Abuja.

Mr Fani-Kayode, a former aviation minister, cast doubts on the legal status of the NLS.

He said, with his 41 years of professional experience as a legal practitioner, he would not “undermine the integrity of the legal profession, or bring the profession into disrepute.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“It is particularly pertinent to note that the purported conferment raises serious questions regarding its legal and professional implications, particularly in view of the statutory framework regulating the legal profession in Nigeria and relevant judicial pronouncements concerning the conferment of professional ranks outside the established legal framework.”

He urged the public to disregard any misrepresentation and reaffirmed his commitment to “the rule of law, professional ethics, and the dignity of the legal profession.”

The conferment of the designation of blue silk has been the subject of controversy in Nigeria.

In November 2025, the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) addressed concerns over the actions of Tonye Jaja, who was promoting the creation of the “privileged rank” or “Blue Silk” for legal practitioners.

According to the NBA, his action was inconsistent with the legal profession’s regulatory framework, misleading and misrepresented institutional structures.

On 12 February, the Legal Practitioners’ Privileges Committee (LPPC), a body saddled with the conferment of the rank of the Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), warned lawyers against using the designation ‘Blue Silk’ and stressed that the title is not recognised in the Nigerian legal profession.

In May, the Federal High Court in Abuja dismissed a suit seeking to introduce the rank of ‘Blue Silk’ for legal practitioners in Nigeria as an alternative to the rank of SAN.

World.title: Friday Sermon: Stop mocking President Tinubu’s Umrah Ibadah in the name of politics!, By Murtadha Gusau
World.content:
In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

All praise belongs to Allah, the Lord of all worlds, Who sees the hidden secrets of the chest and records every word uttered by the tongue. We send peace and blessings upon the Master of Prophets, Muhammad (Peace be upon him), who warned his Ummah against the destructive nature of the tongue and the violation of sacred symbols.

Dear brothers and sisters! President Bola Ahmed Tinubu performed the Ibadah of Umrah, the lesser Hajj in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, in late October 2026.

During the Umrah trip, President Tinubu and members of his delegation had the rare honour of entering inside the Noble Ka’abah to pray, following a privilege extended by King Salman Bin Abdulaziz Al Saud and Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman.

The Nigerian delegation included selected Muslim governors, led by Nigeria Governors’ Forum Chairman AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara State, National Security Advisor Nuhu Ribadu, industrialist Abdul Samad Rabiu, as well as various ministers and government officials.

During the spiritual exercise, President Tinubu prayed for lasting peace, national unity, security, economic progress, and stability in Nigeria. He also urged Nigerians to embrace national diversity as a source of strength.

President Tinubu subsequently departed Saudi Arabia after concluding the visit.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Dear servants of Allah! Know that this world is a fleeting shadow, and politics is but a shifting game played within its temporary borders. Leaders rise and fall, nations shift, and political allegiances evolve. Yet, there remain certain constants that a Muslim believer must never compromise: the sanctity of acts of worship, the reverence due to the rituals of Allah, and the absolute danger of letting political animosity corrupt the spiritual heart.

A dangerous trend has crept into our discourses—where the sacred is weaponised for worldly rivalries, and the spiritual journeys of individuals are subjected to the mockery of the public square. Specifically, we observe the tongues of many targeting the Umrah, the lesser pilgrimage of our leaders, including President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. This sermon is a clarion call, a solemn warning, and a heart-softening admonition to those who let political fervor blind them to spiritual boundaries: To Be careful!

The first and most critical reality to understand is that the Ibadah of Umrah is not a political rally; it is a sacred response to a divine invitation. When a human being—regardless of their political office, their shortcomings, or your personal opinion of their governance—puts on the white sheets of Ihram, cries out “Labbaikallahummah Labbaik”, Here I am, O Allah, at Your service, and circumambulates the Ka’abah, they are engaging in a foundational ritual of Islam.

Allah Almighty states clearly in the Noble Qur’an:

“That is so. And whoever honours the symbols of Allah – indeed, it is from the piety of hearts.” [Qur’an, 22:32]

Conversely, treating these symbols with flippancy or using them as punchlines for political memes borders on a spiritual catastrophe. When you mock a Muslim believer’s presence at the Ka’abah, are you mocking the man, or are you trivialising the place? Are you criticising his policies, or are you scoffing at the act of a servant standing before his Master, Allah?

The tongue is a small organ, but its harvest can drag a person face-down into the fire. Regulate your political speech so that it does not spill over into cosmic arrogance.

Human nature often tempts us to judge the intentions of others, especially those we dislike. In politics, it is easy to dismiss a leader’s pilgrimage as “PR,” “photo-ops,” or “hypocrisy.”

Let us recall the profound ascetic teaching from the life of the Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) and his companions. During a battle, Usamah Bin Zaid (may Allah be pleased with him) faced an enemy soldier who had killed many Muslim believers. Just as Usamah raised his sword to strike him, the man cried out, “La ilaha illallah”, There is no god but Allah. Usamah, believing the man only said it to save his life, struck him down anyway.

When news of this reached the Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him), his face changed with grief and anger. He turned to Usamah and repeatedly asked:

“Did you split open his heart to see whether he said it sincerely or not?” [Sahih Muslim]

If the Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) rebuked a beloved companion for questioning the shahadah and testimony of an active enemy on the battlefield, what gives any commentator, any blogger, any politician, or any citizen the right to peer into the heart of a pilgrim in Makkah and declare his worship invalid? Remember, you do not own the keys to acceptance; Allah Almighty does.

Political dissatisfaction is a right, and holding leaders accountable is a civic and Islamic duty. Islam encourages speaking truth to power and demanding justice. However, when political frustration mutates into blind hatred, it darkens the intellect and ruins spiritual discernment.

Allah the Most High warns the Muslim believers. He says:

“O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.” [Qur’an, 5:8]

Psychologically, when you mock someone’s prayers or pilgrimage, you are training your mind to view them as sub-human or entirely devoid of good. This is a deception of Iblis, the Satan. A person can be a flawed leader, make economic policies that cause hardship, or govern in a way you deeply disagree with—yet still have a spark of faith that drives them to tears in front of the Ka’abah.

Do not let your political stance rob you of your spiritual objectivity. If a leader goes to seek guidance, forgiveness, or strength at the House of Allah, the mature response of a Muslim believer is to pray that they find it—because a guided, righteous leader benefits the entire nation, while a broken leader leaves everyone vulnerable.

Consider this a final, moving narrative for the soul. The classical scholars of Islam—the ascetics and the righteous—used to fear talking about the sins or spiritual states of others because of a terrifying spiritual law: What you mock in your brother, Allah may test you with before you die.

Imam Ibn al-Qayyim wrote that criticising others for their spiritual vulnerabilities or mocking their relationship with Allah is a sign of self-righteousness. When you look at a leader’s Umrah and sneer, you are implicitly saying, “My worship is pure, but his is fake.” This arrogance destroys your own good deeds.

Imagine standing on the Day of Judgment. You expect to see your prayers, your charity, and your fasts. Instead, you find your scale empty because your good deeds were transferred to the politician you mocked. You handed over your eternal capital in exchange for a few likes, posts, retweets, or laughs in a political WhatsApp group. What a miserable bankruptcy!

Respected brothers and sisters! Let us draw a firm, unbreakable line between political critique and spiritual transgression.

● Critique policies? Yes.

● Demand accountability? Yes.

● Express frustration over governance? Yes.

● Mock the sacred acts of worship, judge intentions, or ridicule a human being standing at the House of Allah? Never.

Turn your tongues away from the sacred boundaries of worship. Protect your own scales of justice. If you see a leader at the Ka’abah, let your heart-softening reminder be:

“Ya Allah, if he is seeking Your face, guide him to justice for the sake of the millions he leads. And if he is lacking, reform his heart, for the reform of the leader is the reform of the Ummah.”

Fellow Nigerians! In recent times, a deeply troubling affliction has manifested within our public discourse—an ailment born of political rivalry that has breached the boundaries of faith. We have witnessed individuals, driven by political differences, resorting to mockery, sarcasm, and ridicule regarding the acts of worship performed by others. Specifically, the spectacle of turning the sacred journey of Umrah—undertaken by leaders, including President Bola Ahmed Tinubu—into a jest for political scoring is a dangerous transgression that requires an immediate, heart-softening warning.

Politics is a worldly endeavour, a sphere of governance, debate, policy, and critique. Critique policies as you wish. Demand accountability as you must. But when you cross the threshold of secular criticism to mock a Muslim believer standing before their Lord in the Haram of Makkah, wallahi you are no longer playing politics. You are playing with your hereafter, your Akhirah!

Allah, the Exalted, issues a severe warning in the Glorious Qur’an regarding those who turn signs of faith or devotion into objects of ridicule. He says:

“If you ask them, they will surely say, ‘We were only conversing and playing.’ Say, ‘Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?’ Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief.” [Qur’an, 9:65-66]

The Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) taught us that a person’s heart is a sanctuary known only to the Creator. When a Muslim believer puts on the Ihram, declares “Labbaikallahummah Labbaik,” and circumambulates the Ka’abah, they are answering the call of Prophet Ibrahim (AS). They are standing as a beggar at the door of the Almighty Allah. To reduce that profound spiritual submission into a meme, a punchline, or a weapon of political warfare is to display a terrifying lack of Taqwa and Allah-consciousness.

Remember the words of the Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him):

“A Muslim is the brother of a Muslim. He does not wrong him, he does not fail him, and he does not humiliate him. Piety is here”—and he pointed to his chest three times—”It is enough evil for a man to humiliate his Muslim brother.” [Sahih Muslim]

Consider the spiritual psychological cost of your actions. When you mock an act of worship, you cultivate a disease of arrogance within your own chest. You convince yourself that your political alignment makes you spiritually superior, or that your disdain for an earthly leader gives you the right to judge their standing before Allah. This is the very arrogance that led Iblis to destruction.

Let the history of our righteous predecessors serve as a moving narrative and an ascetic teaching. They would tremble at the thought of speaking ill of another person’s secret worship. They understood that a leader’s account is with Allah, and a servant’s devotion is private. If you believe a leader is falling short, the Prophetic remedy is sincere supplication and Du’a for their guidance and rectification, not public ridicule of their prayers.

Dear Muslim believers! This is a clarion call par-excellence to purify your hearts. The digital age and the political coliseum have desensitised us. We post, tweet, and share without weighing the weight of our words on the Day of Judgment.

Imagine standing on the Day of Resurrection, a day when every hidden deed is brought to light, and discovering that your good deeds have been transferred to the account of the very politician you despised—all because your tongue and your fingers could not refrain from mocking their pilgrimage. Is a transient political victory worth your eternal ruin?

Turn back to Allah in sincere repentance. Remove the poison of political malice from your spiritual practice. Let us critique with civility, hold to account with justice, but guard the sacred boundaries of Islam with absolute reverence.

Dear brothers and sisters! The Ka’abah is the absolute anchor of the human spirit, a terrestrial mirror of the celestial realm, and the immutable center around which the Muslim believer’s life must revolve. It is not merely a structure of granite and silk; it is the physical manifestation of divine oneness (Tauhid) and the ultimate focal point of human devotion.

When you stand before the Ka’abah, you do not merely look at a building; you stand at the intersection of heaven and earth. Islamic scholars of the heart remind us that the Ka’abah is positioned directly beneath the Baitul-Ma’mur, the most Frequented House in the seventh heaven, where seventy thousand angels circumambulate daily, never to return. When you perform Tawaf, your steps synchronise with the cosmic worship of the angelic host. You become part of a celestial symphony of praise that has echoed since the dawn of creation.

Five times a day, over two billion human beings turn their faces toward this single point on Earth. This is not an empty ritual; it is a psychological anchor. No matter how fractured, chaotic, or confusing your day has been, the moment you turn toward the Qiblah, you are choosing order over chaos. You are uniting your heart with millions of Muslim believers across time and space. The Ka’abah is our ultimate anchor of unity—a reminder that despite our different languages, cultures, and flaws, we share one heartbeat, one direction, and one Destination.

While the Ka’abah holds an unparalleled, sacred status, the Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) looked at it and delivered a profound truth that should shake every soul. He said:

“How great you are and how great is your sanctity! Yet, the sanctity of a Muslim believer is even greater in the sight of Allah than you.” [Sunan Ibn Majah]

This is the ultimate Islamic insight: The Ka’abah was built to direct the human heart to Allah, but the human heart itself is the vessel that holds Iman (faith). To disrespect, oppress, or break the heart of a fellow Muslim believer is a greater violation than tearing down the stones of the Ka’abah. We must honour the House of Allah, but we must also honour the servants of Allah.

Stop living a life without a center. If your life feels scattered, it is because you have placed your desires, your anxieties, or your worldly career at the core of your existence.

Reset your spiritual compass. Let your daily prayers be your personal Tawaf around the commands of Allah. Turn your face, your heart, and your ambitions toward the King of Kings, Allah. Just as the Ka’abah stands firm, unmoving amidst the millions who rush around it, let your faith remain unshakable amidst the turbulent storms of this life.

Dear servants of Allah! Know that the minor pilgrimage, the Umrah, is not a vacation. It is not a tourism of sight, but a migration of the soul. It is a divine invitation issued by the King of kings, Allah, to those He chooses to forgive.

When you intend Umrah, you enter the state of Ihram. You strip away the garments of status, wealth, and ego. You shroud yourself in two simple pieces of white cloth, stepping out of the world and into the rehearsal of your own resurrection. You stand equal to millions, declaring with your body and your breath that you own nothing, and that Allah Almighty owns everything.

The position of Umrah in Islam is the position of an absolute spiritual erasure. The Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) declared that:

“Alternate between Hajj and Umrah, for they remove poverty and sins just as the bellows remove impurities from iron, gold, and silver.”

And he said:

“An Umrah to another Umrah is an expiation for whatever sins occur between them.”

Umrah is the ultimate weapon of the Muslim believer against despair. When the weight of the world crushes your chest, when your sins feel like mountains, and when your heart feels hardened by the illusions of this temporary life, Umrah is the divine reset button. It is the place where tears do not represent weakness, but the washing away of a heavy past.

Think of the Tawaf. You circumambulate the Ka’abah—the visual center of your entire earthly existence. Seven times you orbit the house of Allah, aligning the beating of your heart with the axis of Islamic monotheism. Every step is a heartbeat. Every circle is a declaration that Allah is the center of your universe, your thoughts, your family, and your destiny.

Think of the Sa’yi. You run between Safa and Marwa, retracing the desperate, unyielding trust of Hajar. It is the ultimate psychological and physical manifestation of Tawakkul, the reliance on Allah Almighty. You run in the valley of your struggles, crying out to the Heavens, knowing that when the means of this world fail you, the Lord of the heavens will cause Zamzam to gush forth from beneath your feet.

You arrive burdened. You leave unburdened. You arrive captive to your desires. You leave emancipated. When you shave or trim your hair at the completion of your rites, you are shedding the final remnants of your old self. You step out of the Haram as a newborn soul, clothed in mercy, enveloped in peace, and armed with an unbreakable connection to your Creator, Allah.

Do not delay the call. If your wealth allows and your body is able, answer the invitation of your Lord. Let your tears flow upon the sacred gravel. Let your voice rise with the Talbiyah: “Labbaikallahummah Labbaik—Here I am, O Allah, here I am!”

And finally, know that, mocking the religion of Allah is not a casual slip of the tongue; it is a profound spiritual catastrophe that instantly nullifies faith. In an era where sacred symbols such as Umrah are reduced to punchlines and divine decrees are bartered for social validation, the Muslim believer must confront a sobering reality: treating Islam as a jest is a definitive exit from its fold.

The Creator of the cosmos has established boundaries that are absolute. The verses of Allah, His names, the character of His Messenger (Peace be upon him), and the pillars of His law are the bedrock of human existence. When these are mocked, it signals a deeper, terrifying pathology—the death of Taqwa and Allah-consciousness, and the total absence of reverence in the heart.

The gravity of this sin is perfectly illustrated in an incident during the Campaign of Tabuk. A group of individuals, sitting in a gathering, casually remarked about the reciters of the Noble Qur’an. They said:

“We have not seen anyone like these reciters of ours—they have the biggest appetites, the most untruthful tongues, and are the most cowardly in the face of the enemy.”

A companion, recognising the poison in these words, immediately called them out as hypocrites and reported the matter. The men rushed to the Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) as he was mounting his camel, clutching at his stirrups, pleading:

“O Messenger of Allah, we were only talking idly and jesting to pass the time on the journey!”

The divine response was immediate, terrifying, and eternal. Allah the Most High says:

“And if you ask them, they will surely say, ‘We were only conversing and playing.’ Say, ‘Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?’ Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief.” [Qur’an, 9:65–66]

Notice the psychological reality: they did not intend to wage war against Islam; they intended to make a joke. Yet Allah did not accept their excuse of “casual humour.” Idolising entertainment over the Almighty strips away the garment of Iman.

The Prophet Muhammad (Peace be upon him) warned us of this exact psychological desensitisation. He said:

“A servant may speak a word entirely half-heartedly, not realising its gravity, and because of it, he plummets into the Fire of Hell further than the distance between the East and the West.” [Al-Bukhari]

To protect your soul from this spiritual erosion, you must actively implement three boundaries:

1.⁠ ⁠Guard Your Tongue and Screen

Treat the Sunnah, the Umrah, the Ka’abah, the Hijab, the Beard, the Prayer, and the Islamic scholars with absolute sanctity. If a joke compromises these, it is toxic.

2.⁠ ⁠The Power of Departure

If you sit in a gathering—online or offline—where Islam is ridiculed, walk away. Remaining silent is complicity. Allah Almighty says:

“…do not sit with them until they enter into another conversation. Indeed, you would then be like them.” [Qur’an, 4:140]

3.⁠ ⁠Renew Your Awe

Constantly study the Majesty of Allah. The more you know Him, the more impossible it becomes to ever laugh at a joke made at His expense.

● The Bottom Line

Do not trade the eternal honour of being a servant of Allah for a cheap laugh. Protect your reverence, safeguard your tongue, and hold fast to the sacred.

May Allah open the doors to His Sacred House for every longing heart, cleanse us of our shortcomings, and accept from us our worship.

Ya Allah! Rectify our leaders and rectify our followers. Purify our hearts from hypocrisy, arrogance, and malice. Guide our tongues to speak only what is true and pleasing to You. Protect us from mocking Your signs and Your worship.

May Allah purify our hearts from rancour, safeguard our tongues from arrogance, and grant us the wisdom to balance our worldly concerns with our eternal obligations. Ameen.

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds. May the peace, blessings and salutations of Allah be upon our noble Messenger, Muhammad, and upon his family, his Companions and his true followers.

Murtadha Muhammad Gusau is the Chief Imam of Nagazi-Uvete Jumu’ah and the late Alhaji Abdur-Rahman Okene’s Mosques, Okene, Kogi State, Nigeria. He can be reached via: [email protected] or +2348038289761 or +2348024192217.

World.title: Nigeria, eight other African countries record 67 yellow fever cases, 18 deaths — WHO
World.content:
Nigeria and eight other African countries recorded 67 confirmed yellow fever cases, including 18 deaths, between January and October 2026, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO).

The affected countries are Burkina Faso, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, Nigeria and Togo.

In a Disease Outbreak News report published on 6 November 2026, the WHO said yellow fever transmission continues across its African Region, with recent outbreak activity concentrated in parts of West Africa, including communities close to international borders.

Nigeria recorded four confirmed cases, including one death, during the reporting period, while Cameroon reported nine cases and one death.

Côte d’Ivoire recorded the highest number of confirmed cases, with 30 infections and 10 deaths, followed by Burkina Faso, which reported 15 cases and three deaths.

Ghana recorded four cases and three deaths, while Liberia reported one laboratory-confirmed case. The Central African Republic recorded two cases, while Guinea and Togo reported one case each. No deaths were recorded among confirmed cases in the latter three countries.

The WHO noted that the figures reflect the latest information available as of 12 October 2026. It said the detection of cases in the nine countries indicates increased transmission across parts of West Africa.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Factors driving transmission

The WHO identified frequent cross-border movement, uneven vaccination coverage and environmental conditions that favour the spread of infected mosquitoes as factors increasing the risk of further transmission.

“Occupational and environmental exposures, including work in or near forested areas, mining activities, and other outdoor occupations, are important risk factors for yellow fever infection,” it noted.

“Frequent cross-border population movement, the presence of competent mosquito vectors, and uneven vaccination coverage increase the risk of further transmission and geographic spread.”

According to the WHO, cross-border movement for trade, farming, livestock, and mining could contribute to the spread of the virus between affected and neighbouring countries.

The WHO said affected countries, with support from the organisation and other partners, are strengthening disease surveillance, investigating cases, conducting laboratory tests and intensifying efforts to identify infections.

Other measures include community engagement, risk communication and vaccination activities in affected and high-risk areas.

Regional risk

The WHO said it assessed the overall public health risk associated with the yellow fever situation as moderate across the African Region on 27 October, while the global risk remains low.

It considered continued transmission and additional cases in the region likely, citing existing immunity gaps, challenges with surveillance and laboratory testing, insecurity, limited resources and difficulties accessing some affected communities.

The organisation warned that introducing the virus into densely populated urban and peri-urban areas with low vaccination coverage could trigger larger outbreaks and put additional pressure on public health response systems.

“Unvaccinated populations are at highest risk, particularly rural and forest-edge communities, mobile and cross-border populations and people who work in forested areas, agriculture or mining,” it added.

Vaccination remains key

Yellow fever is an acute viral disease transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. It can cause fever, headache, body aches, nausea, vomiting and weakness.

According to the WHO, about 15 per cent of infected people develop severe illness, which may involve recurrent high fever, jaundice, bleeding, shock and organ failure.

“Approximately half of patients who enter this severe phase die within seven to 10 days,” it noted.

The WHO said no specific antiviral treatment is routinely recommended, and clinical management is largely supportive.

It identified vaccination as the most effective preventive measure, noting that a single dose provides lifelong protection.

The WHO urged at-risk countries to maintain high vaccination coverage through routine immunisation and preventive or outbreak-response campaigns, particularly in communities with identified immunity gaps.

It also called for stronger surveillance, timely laboratory testing, mosquito control and public awareness of symptoms and prevention measures.

The organisation advised international travellers aged nine months and above visiting areas at risk of yellow fever transmission to receive vaccination.

World.title: Anambra will deliver over 50% of 2027 votes to Tinubu — Soludo
World.content:
File: Gov Charles Soludo of Anambra State and President Bola Tinubu.

By Vincent Ujumadu

Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, has promised to deliver at least 50 percent of the state’s votes to President Bola Tinubu, the presidential candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC), in the 2027 general elections.

Read Also: Tinubu to Nigerians: ‘I promise better future’

The governor made the declaration during the flag off of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) 2027 campaign at Ekwueme Square, Awka.

According to him, APGA has no presidential candidate for the 2027 general election and would, therefore, adopt President Tinubu as its preferred candidate.

“Today, we adopt the APC presidential candidate, Bola Ahmed Tinubu as our candidate,” he declared, noting that the president had demonstrated love and concern for the Igbo people, particularly the people of Anambra State.

The governor recalled that the President had appointed several Anambra indigenes to strategic positions in Lagos State during his tenure as governor.

He also recalled that APGA had adopted the presidential candidate of the ruling party in previous elections, noting that the party’s decision to support Tinubu in 2027 was a continuation of that political arrangement that had been in existence.

He lamented that Anambra State recorded fewer than 5,000 votes for Tinubu in the 2023 presidential election, yet the President has continued to address some of the challenges confronting the state and the South-East region.

He urged the Anambra electorate to support Tinubu in the 2027 election, arguing that doing so would give the state and the South-East a stronger opportunity to engage with the Federal Government and negotiate for their development.

“We need to vote for him in order to sit with the government at the centre and negotiate for the development of the South-East and Anambra State”, he declared.

World.title: Tinubu’s reforms need time to deliver, 2nd term will consolidate gains — Aguda
World.content:
Oluwole Aguda is a businessman, consultant on electoral mat- ters and political affairs, and a former governorship aspirant in Kogi State, under the African Action Con- gress (AAC) in 2019. In this interview, he examines President Bola Tinubu’s reform agenda, the steps the President must take to secure electoral support in the North ahead of the 2027 general election, and the political implications of the lingering face-off between Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma and his predecessor, Senator Rochas Okoro- cha, over the Imo West senatorial ticket.

Excerpts:

Given the hardship caused by fuel subsidy removal, naira devaluation and other economic policies, what tangible improvements in Nigerians’ living conditions can President Tinubu point to as justification for seeking a second term?

A fair assessment requires us to examine the immediate challenges confronting the economy and the long-term benefits expected from the reforms. Nigeria’s economy was bleeding, and stopping that haemorrhage was necessary to give the country a chance of recovery.

Ending fuel subsidy addressed an avenue for corruption and the unsustainable drain on public resources. NELFUND had disbursed over N300 billion to over 1.5m students across 319 tertiary institutions as at October 2026.

However, I would not suggest that these developments have largely translated into improved living conditions for most Nigerians. That remains the administration’s biggest challenge. The cost of food, transportation, housing, healthcare and other essentials continues to put enormous pressure on households.

Economic recovery must ultimately be measured by whether people can afford necessities, businesses can employ more workers and incomes can support a reasonable standard of living. The President’s case for another term should not rest solely on the courage to introduce reforms. It must also depend on translating them into better purchasing power, employment, productivity and social welfare. Reforms require time, but Nigerians enduring difficult adjustments must see a credible pathway to relief.

How would you assess the Tinubu administration’s performance, and what justifies giving it another four years?

There is intention coupled with execution across different sectoral interventions. While execution has been a challenge, progressive steps have been made. Investment in our military is important to sustaining a motivated Army, Navy and Air Force in the war against terrorism. The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway also promises to reduce travel time and transportation costs between the South-West and South-South.

One foundational challenge to national growth has been the lack of continuity in government policies, including those that could have delivered long-term benefits if sustained. Policy reversals have been the bane of our collective development. Any purposeful course must be entrenched long enough for its benefits to have an impact. Calls to restore fuel subsidy must be weighed against the implications for public finances and the country’s ability to fund infrastructure and social services. Are we going to reverse foreign exchange unification and return to the wasteful, corruption-ridden defence of the naira? How can we free resources for development and generations yet unborn? Having endured this much, Nigeria should not abandon necessary reforms without carefully evaluating their outcomes. I concede that the pace and distribution of benefits may not satisfy Nigerians, but the overall direction is not without merit.

Undertaking progressive reforms despite resistance and a decades-long preference for the path of least resistance represents a rare leadership opportunity.

A second term could consolidate the reforms and improve implementation. State police could strengthen security man- agement; naira stability could attract foreign investment, while improved oil exploration and production should raise output. The administration must demonstrate measurable progress in these areas.

How does the President address allegations that federal appointments have disproportionately favoured his Yoruba kinsmen and political associates at the expense of the constitutional principle of federal character?

Allegations of ethnic favouritism should not be dismissed, but neither should they be accepted without ev- idence. Federal appointments across ministries, departments, agencies and public institutions should be examined to establish whether they comply with the constitutional principle of federal character. Section 14(3) of the 1999 Constitution provides for government composition and public affairs to reflect Nigeria’s federal character and prevent the predominance of persons from a few states or ethnic groups. Every administration has an obligation to respect this safeguard for national inclusion.

I believe Nigeria has highly competent people across all ethnic groups and regions. Attending a unity college reinforced my conviction that intelligence and capacity are not exclusive to any group. Appointments to sensitive national positions must go beyond rewarding political loyalty or personal relationships. Associates may be qualified, but the government must demonstrate regard for competence, geographical balance and inclusion.

Appointment records should be as- sessed objectively, while the Federal Character Commission must monitor compliance and publish its findings. Nigerians must see fairness reflected in government.

What concrete achievements can Tinubu present to northern voters amid continuing concerns about insecurity, economic hardship and political representation?

Northern Nigerians, like citizens elsewhere, have the right to decide where to place their political support. Insecurity remains serious, particularly in communities affected by banditry, kidnapping, terrorism and displacement. These problems disrupt farming, trade, education and other economic activities. There are efforts to improve security and infrastructure. The Kaduna-Zaria-Kano dual carriage-way is nearing completion, the Soko-to-Badagry Superhighway is under construction, and other roads across northern Nigeria are receiving attention. Northern states also have more resources for capital projects than in previous years.

But the President must go beyond presenting road projects and increased allocations as evidence of performance. People in the North want to know whether farmers can return safely to their farms, children can attend school without fear of abduction, displaced families can return home and young people can find employment. The administration must show how its reforms benefit northern farmers, traders and small businesses.

Voters will judge the President by improvements in security, opportunity and quality of life.

The ruling party has attracted politically significant defectors because its leaders have created an environment that makes it attractive to politicians. That does not necessarily mean those joining share its ideals or are committed to a common manifesto. In my opinion, political survival is a major motivation.

Politicians gravitate towards what they perceive as political certainty rather than remain in an uncertain environment. How the President’s team translates that into electoral advantage is up to them. Every party has a responsibility to protect its interests, defend its base and seek new territory. If government machinery or unfair practices are not responsible for weakening opposition par- ties, political realignments and defec- tions are normal features of democratic competition.

However, the growing concentration of political influence in one party reminds us of the importance of a credible opposition. Democracy is strengthened when parties compete on ideas, programmes and performance, not when opposition parties are weakened through abuse of state power.

World.title: US offers $20m reward for info on ‘Iran’s nuclear program’: CENTCOM
World.content:
Iranians stand beneath an anti-US billboard depicting US President Donald Trump during a rally in Tehran’s Enqelab Square on November 4, 2026. Photo by ATTA KENARE / AFP.

Washington is offering a $20 million reward “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear program, the US military said Friday, as President Donald Trump reiterated Tehran wants to make a deal to end the war.

Read Also: Iran warns of wider war if US attacks after Trump election rout

A State Department program, Rewards for Justice, “is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community,” US Central Command said on X.

The program was established in 1984 under the State Department’s national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests.

In its statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran’s “lack of compliance with the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges.

It gave no specific parameters on what information would yield a $20 million reward.

Trump has repeatedly said US forces have effectively obliterated Iran’s nuclear program.

“If we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today,” Trump said Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida. “If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East.”

But the president also said Iran – which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war – is eager to end the conflict.

“We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” he said.

Diplomatic efforts by mediators have been in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting.

And on Tuesday Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue.

Earlier this week Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility.

Vanguard News

World.title: Trump: Lesson for Nigeria, by Stephanie Shaakaa
World.content:
File: U.S. President Donald Trump Photo: Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images/AFP.

Donald Trump wanted the November 3 midterm elections to be about him. He said so repeatedly, urging Americans to vote as though his name were on the ballot. He wanted a Republican victory to demonstrate that his presidency still commanded popular support and that his influence over American politics remained firmly intact.

Well, Americans took him seriously. Perhaps more seriously than he expected.

Democrats have won control of both chambers of the United States Congress, delivering a major electoral setback to Trump and his Republican Party. Yet, as the results became clear, Trump reached for an explanation that seemed to contradict his own campaign message. In a post on his Truth Social platform, he declared: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

The irony is difficult to miss. He had spent weeks asking Americans to treat the election as a verdict on his presidency. When the verdict went against him, he suddenly appeared to be distancing himself from it. He wanted the political benefits of making the election about him without accepting the consequences when voters delivered an unfavourable answer.

For readers in Nigeria, it is worth explaining what America calls midterm elections and why they matter.

In the United States, a president is elected for a four-year term, but congressional elections take place every two years. This means that halfway into a president’s tenure, Americans return to the polls to elect members of the legislature. These elections are called midterms because they take place in the middle of a presidential term.

Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 seats in the House are contested every two years, while senators serve six-year terms, with approximately one-third of the 100 Senate seats contested every two years.

Midterm elections do not determine who becomes president. The sitting president remains in office. Instead, voters decide which party controls Congress and, by extension, how much support or opposition the president will face in the legislature

This gives Americans an opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with a president’s performance without waiting another four years. They can strengthen the president’s party in Congress or hand control to the opposition, making it considerably more difficult for the president to advance his legislative agenda.

That is precisely what has happened to Trump.

American presidents often benefit from what is known as the coattail effect. When a president is popular, candidates from the same party can benefit from that popularity. His political strength becomes an advantage for others seeking elective office. But when a president becomes unpopular, the effect can work in reverse. Candidates associated with his administration may find themselves paying the price for public dissatisfaction with his leadership. In political terms, this is sometimes described as negative or reverse coattails.

Trump’s decision to place himself at the centre of the midterm campaign made this effect particularly consequential. Instead of allowing individual Republican candidates to make their own cases to voters, he encouraged Americans to judge them through the prism of his presidency. He effectively turned hundreds of congressional contests into a national assessment of his administration.

And voters had reasons to be dissatisfied. The cost of living, inflation, rising fuel prices, economic anxiety and concerns about his administration’s policies, including the war with Iran, featured prominently in the political atmosphere surrounding the election. The Associated Press’s voter analysis identified frustration over high costs and the direction of the administration among the forces behind the Republican setback. Not every voter necessarily shared the same grievance, but the cumulative dissatisfaction proved politically damaging.

The scale of the Democratic victories was particularly striking in traditionally Republican territory. Texas provided one of the clearest illustrations. For decades, the state had been one of the Republican Party’s most dependable strongholds. Yet Democrat James Talarico defeated Trump-backed Ken Paxton in the Senate contest, becoming the first Democrat elected to a Texas Senate seat since 1988. In the gubernatorial race, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Greg Abbott, ending Republican control of the governorship.

These were not merely victories for individual candidates. They challenged the assumption that established Republican strongholds were beyond the reach of Democratic competition. One election does not permanently change a state’s political identity, but it can expose the vulnerability of a party that has grown accustomed to treating certain constituencies as guaranteed territory.

The election also produced historic breakthroughs in American political representation. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of an American state. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the United States Senate. Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the Senate. Meanwhile, Hakeem Jeffries is positioned to become the first Black Speaker of the House if formally elected by the incoming Democratic majority. These achievements extend beyond party victories; they represent significant milestones in the country’s political history.

But beyond the personalities and historic milestones, the institutional consequences are substantial.

With Democrats controlling both chambers, Trump will face a Congress less willing to accommodate his agenda. The new majority can obstruct legislation, scrutinise government spending, investigate the administration and subject presidential appointments requiring congressional approval to greater scrutiny. Control of the Senate is particularly important because of its role in confirming federal judges and senior government officials.

Trump remains president and retains his constitutional powers, including the power to veto legislation. A Democratic Congress cannot simply remove him from office or take over the executive branch. But the political environment in which he must govern has changed considerably. The final two years of his presidency will be more complicated, and his administration will have to contend with an opposition that now controls the legislative machinery.

The results also raise questions about the future of the Republican Party. Trump’s endorsement has long been a powerful instrument in Republican politics. Candidates have sought his support, elected officials have adjusted their positions to accommodate his preferences, and the party has increasingly organised itself around his political identity. But when candidates associated with a president begin losing elections on a significant scale, an uncomfortable question emerges: is his influence still an electoral advantage, or has it become a liability?

The answer will matter as Republicans consider their political direction beyond Trump’s second term and the road to the 2028 presidential election.

None of this means that Democrats have secured a permanent realignment of American politics. Nor does it automatically determine who will win the next presidential election. Midterm results are not a crystal ball. They reflect the political mood at a particular moment, and voters can change their minds again. The Democratic Party must also demonstrate that winning control of Congress can translate into meaningful improvements in people’s lives. Defeating an unpopular administration and earning lasting public confidence are two different challenges.

There is, however, a lesson here for political leaders everywhere, including in Nigeria.

Elections are not always about the candidates whose names appear on the ballot. Sometimes, voters use the choices available to them to pass judgment on the person already occupying the highest office. A president may not be contesting, but his record, policies and conduct can still become the central issue in an election. Political power does not insulate an incumbent from electoral accountability, even when his name is nowhere on the ballot.

Trump invited Americans to make the midterm elections a referendum on his presidency. They did. When the result went against him, he insisted that his absence from the ballot was the problem.

But he cannot have it both ways.

He wanted the credit if Republicans won. He cannot so easily disown the verdict because they lost. The slingshot has turned in the opposite direction. Trump asked Americans to vote as though he were on the ballot. They did something more consequential: they voted on the presidency he was already exercising.

He asked for a political endorsement and received an electoral verdict.

World.title: From open pavilion to nation of orderlies: Is Zik’s ‘fear-free’ Nigeria still possible?
World.content:
.What a 1960 inauguration says about fear in today’s corridors of power

By Omeiza Ajayi

Nearly 66 years after Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe was sworn in as Nigeria’s first African Governor-General, the footage of that day – which has again recently gone viral – raises an uncomfortable question: why did a leader who held the highest office in the land need no retinue of security details standing behind him, while today every minister, and even some local government supervisors, cannot move without a swarm of details?

The inauguration took place on November 16, 1960, at Tafawa Balewa Square, barely six weeks after independence. It was also Zik’s 56th birthday.

The narrator of the newsreel set the scene plainly. “At the steps of the pavilion stand the Prime Minister and the Lord Chief Justice, symbolising the people and the law, on what is surely one of the most important occasions in the history of the country.”

No armed escort looms in the frame. No aide hovers at the shoulder of the man the crowd was chanting for. “Zik! Zik!” rang around the square as he arrived, and the vast stands, in the narrator’s words, were “hushed.”

Today the picture is reversed. In Abuja and in the state capitals, orderlies trail ministers into halls and offices. The situation is so bad that some security personnel actually enter into very enclosed spaces or rooms with their AK47 rifles in clear breach of security protocol. At the local government level, some unelected supervisory councillors have been known to move with armed vigilance team members or hunters, sometimes to intimidate the very people they were appointed to serve.

The easy explanation is insecurity, and it is not a false flag. Banditry, kidnapping and insurgency have made parts of the country dangerous, and no leader can be faulted for fearing for his life.

But the leaders of other nations also face threats. Behind the American president or a British prime minister stand trained protective officers, assigned to a defined danger. They do not crowd every public official, from the cabinet room to the ward office, with men whose chief duty is to announce importance. It is not uncommon in Nigeria to see security details standing and blocking a television camera.

That leaves the harder question. Are Nigeria’s leaders afraid of the general state of the country, or have they become afraid of their own people?

Zik, standing in the open that November morning, appeared to have settled that question for himself. He began his address with these words: “It is with humility, mingled with joy, that I thank this grand concourse of patriots and friends of Nigeria for congregating here today on the occasion of my inauguration as the first African Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of the Federation of Nigeria.”

He titled the speech “Respect for Human Dignity,” and he made no secret of what he feared for Nigeria. It was not assassins. It was division. “I appeal to all our leaders, far and near, to forget the wounds which were inflicted in cause of our internecine altercations. The love of our country should outweigh the love of our petty selves”, he said.

He named his rivals one by one, among them Alhaji Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto, and Chief Obafemi Awolowo, and invited them into what he called “this herculean task of national reconstruction.” A man who expects to be harmed by his rivals does not call them to his side before a crowd of thousands.

His vision was explicit. “Let us bind the nation’s wound, and let us heal the breaches of the past, so that in forging our nation, there shall emerge on this continent a hate-free, fear-free, and grief-free people.”

Fear-free was the promise. Sixty-six years on, the country has more roads, more universities and more money than that crowd could have imagined, yet fear now sits in the offices meant to dispel it. It sits with the minister who cannot cross a lobby unescorted, and with the local government chief who needs hunters to face his own community. It also sits with the citizen who cannot get near either of them. Nigeria’s innocence has long been defiled by rapists who sodomized her without protection. Today, we have a multitude of prostitue followership. The problem cuts both ways – a deceptive leadership and an ignorant followership.

Much of what Zik said that day still holds. “Nigerians believe passionately in the fundamental human rights,” he declared, and he warned that “we must jealously guard our freedom with our lives, if need be.” The words read today less like history than like an assignment left unfinished

What has changed is the distance between the governed and those who govern. In 1960, the footage shows a leader and a people with nothing between them. In 2026, the orderly has become the thing between them, a badge of rank as much as a shield.

Whether Nigeria can return to the open pavilion depends on whether its leaders can once again be trusted by the people, and can trust them in return. Security is a necessity, but it cannot replace that trust.

Zik believed the country could be “hate-free, fear-free, and grief-free.” The film of that November morning still plays, and it still asks of every leader who passes a crowd with armed men at his back: “The love of our country should outweigh the love of our petty selves.”

World.title: Daddy Showkey: Vanguard Award will be the biggest of my lifetime
World.content:
By Clifford Ndujihe & Benjamin Njoku

Chief John Odafe Asiemo, 57, popularly known as Daddy Showkey, is a household name in Nigerian music scene. He is the creator of ‘Galala’ music, which sound helped define Nigeria’s street music in the 90s.

Read Also: Nostalgia, glitz as icons reunite for Daddy Showkey’s 50th anniversary celebration

Daddy Showkey is a nominee for Vanguard Newspaper’s 2026 Entertainment Icon of the year award.

Speaking with ululation after being presented with the letter of nomination, on Tuesday at his Lagos residence, he said: “They say a prophet is not recognised by his own people. But I am a prophet who is being recognised by the people who built me. This is the greatest awards I have ever received in my life because it is coming from Vanguard. Vanguard is the first newspaper in Nigeria that wrote about me, when I was nothing. This is Vanguard, and I cherish it a lot.

“Apart from that, Vanguard played a big role in pushing me to the limelight.

“So, a recognition award coming from Vanguard, I must cherish it. It is like my own people saying it is high time. Sometimes, when I see Vanguard giving people awards, I always say in my mind, when is it going to be my turn?

“Now, it is my turn to receive the award and I am very grateful.”

Reminiscing on his early days, Daddy Showkey, who celebrated 50 years on the stage recently, continued: “For years, I kept coming to Vanguard head office, but I never met the publisher, Uncle Sam, in person.

After my secondary education, I hit the streets. From childhood, I had made up my mind to follow music.

At 13, in 1983, I started following Danladi Bako of NTA. I was always at his office on Lagos Island. He would give me a voucher to go and eat, and made me comfortable in his office.

My first song, “Big Belle”, was released in 1990 in Nawfia, Njikoka, Enugu-Ukwu, Anambra State.

I cannot forget the late Amadi Ogbonna(former Vanguard Entertainment Editor). He was one of the earliest journalists to write about me and played a huge role in my career. Before Ogbonnaya wrote about me, we used to walk from Kirikiri to Olodi areas, passing Vanguard. I remember saying one day while walking past Vanguard ‘this newspaper will one day write about me.’ It came to pass when Ogbonnaya wrote about me for the first time.

The second was Smart Irewudo, a former Champion Newspaper reporter, now based in the United States.

Before I started recording, during the June 12 crisis, I led Ajegunle boys who blocked roads and extorted money from motorists. Smart took my picture and published it in the Daily Champion. In his mind, he thought he had done me a great favour. He didn’t know the police would come after me.

Luckily, one of the policemen from Area F showed my picture to Amadi Ogbonna. He recognised me immediately and called me. When I showed up, Ogbonna took me to the police station and told them I wasn’t a bad boy, they should release me and focus on arresting real criminals.

That same week in 1999, Dr Obiefula Nwankwo offered to record my songs. On the day I signed as his artiste, Amadi Ogbonna and Smart Irewudo accompanied me. After signing the deal, we ended up at the Vanguard Canal. That’s where we celebrated it.

Ogbonna kept encouraging me, supporting my career financially and otherwise.

If Vanguard decides to honour me today, I would say I merit it. It is Vanguard honouring their own, recognising their own pikin. And it will be the biggest award I will ever receive in my lifetime.”

Vanguard News

World.title: Police rescue 10 stolen children in Abia
World.content:
Inspector General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu

By Steve Oko

UMUAHIA—The Abia State Police Command has arrested suspects linked to the October 17 attack on Uratta Divisional Police Headquarters, rescued 10 stolen children and recovered 15 firearms and 30 stolen vehicles in a major security crackdown across the state.

The Command also disclosed that it arrested 109 suspects, comprising 89 males and 20 females, in connection with 211 criminal cases recorded between September 11, 2026 and November 6, 2026.

Commissioner of Police, CP Wilfred Afolabi, who disclosed this on Friday while presenting the Command’s operational scorecard, said the arrests followed intelligence-driven operations and collaboration with other security agencies.

On the Uratta police station attack, Afolabi said investigations had led to the arrest of some of the suspected attackers, with one of them allegedly confessing to leading the gang that carried out the assault.

He said investigations were ongoing to track down other accomplices and establish the full circumstances surrounding the attack.

In a related security operation, operatives of the Anti-Kidnapping Unit raided a location at Ubakala, Umuahia South Local Government Area, on October 25, arresting a suspect identified as Osita.

The police reportedly recovered two locally fabricated guns, 16 live cartridges and four expended cartridges from the suspect.

Another suspect, 30-year-old suspect, was subsequently arrested for allegedly supplying ammunition illegally. Both suspects have been charged to court, according to the CP.

On child trafficking, Afolabi said police operatives rescued 10 children during the period under review and reunited them with their families.

He specifically disclosed that two suspects, including a 38-year-old , were arrested on October 11 over the alleged stealing of two children, seven-year-old Chiamaka Chikeze and nine-month-old Goodluck Chikeze.

The children were reportedly recovered and handed back to their parents, while the suspects were charged to court.

The police boss also announced the arrest of a five-man vehicle theft syndicate, aged 43, and 40.

A Toyota Corolla with registration number ROU 9338J was recovered from the suspects, who have also been charged to court.

In another operation, two suspected cultists, aged 27, and 25, were arrested on October 31 for allegedly dispossessing students of Abia State University, Uturu, of their mobile phones and other valuables at gunpoint.

A locally fabricated firearm was recovered from them.

The CP said one of the suspects had confessed to belonging to the Black Axe Confraternity, adding that efforts were ongoing to apprehend other members of the gang.

World.title: ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment
World.content:
By Omeiza Ajayi

The All Progressives Congress APC has told the Senator David Mark-led faction of the African Democratic Congress ADC to go sort out its internal mess and quit its “senseless rants” after a Federal High Court judgment sacked the faction’s leadership.

Read Also: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate?

In a statement Friday in Abuja, the APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, said the ruling party had no hand in the case. “To be clear, APC is neither a party nor an interlocutor in the matter. Nothing about the case has anything to do with the APC. And the APC has absolutely no role in the party’s judicial quagmire,” he said.

The judgment, delivered on Thursday by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, sacked the David Mark-led leadership of the ADC. It also nullified all official acts of that leadership, including its primary election processes and outcomes, like the presidential candidacy of former vice president Atiku Abubakar.

Morka said the case was brought by ADC national officers against the faction now removed from office, describing the suit as “a notorious case initiated by leaders of ADC against pirate leaders of ADC.”

He accused Mark and his associates of taking over the party “to satisfy Atiku Abubakar’s quixotic presidential ambition.” According to him, “it didn’t matter to them that their hostile takeover of that party was in flagrant violation of the rule of law and ADC’s internal democracy, as a court of competent jurisdiction has now declared.”

The APC spokesman also accused the ADC of reacting to court decisions according to whether they favour it. “Every time a court decides against the Senator David Mark-led factional African Democratic Congress, they accuse the All Progressives Congress of collusion and deprecate the judiciary. Every time a court decides in their favour, they hail the rule of law and extol the judiciary,” he said.

He added that the faction’s attitude showed “no iota of regard for the authority and independence of the judiciary, an indispensable pillar of any democracy.”

On Thursday’s ruling, Morka said it “was procured by their own lawlessness and demonstrates the vibrancy of the rule of law and independence of the judiciary in Nigeria.”

He said the ADC leaders “take no responsibility or accountability for the self-inflicted injury that the court only judicially certified.”

World.title: Tinubu, Shettima Fire Salvos at Obi, Atiku, Take 2027 Re-election Battle to South-south
World.content:
President approves establishment of Ibom deep sea port

Yilwatda, Yari: APC won’t rig elections to retain power in 2027

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

President Bola Tinubu and Vice-President Kashim Shettima yesterday launched blistering attacks on the presidential candidates of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi and that of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Atiku Abubakar, taking the All Progressives Congress’ (APC) 2027 re-election campaign to the South-south and challenging the opposition figures over their leadership records and political accomplishments.



The President is expected to take his campaign to Rivers State today.

While Tinubu questioned Obi’s capacity to provide the leadership required to tackle Nigeria’s challenges, citing his record as Anambra State Governor, Shettima challenged Atiku to account for the political structures, successors and enduring institutions he had built during his decades in public life.



The President, who spoke during a state visit and APC presidential rally in Akwa Ibom State, also approved the establishment of the Ibom Deep Sea Port, describing it as a major catalyst for economic development and prosperity in the state and the South-South region.

Governor Umo Eno had, in his welcome address at the APC presidential rally at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium, Uyo, appealed to the President to approve the project, assuring him that the people of Akwa Ibom would remain grateful if the request was granted.

“Your request for the Ibom Deep Sea Port is hereby approved. The Ibom Deep Sea Port will bring associated economic value and economic development to the people, just as the governor has said,” the President stated.



Tinubu commended Eno for his strides in infrastructure development and human capital investment, noting that he had promptly approved the upgrade of Victor Attah International Airport following the governor’s request.

He acknowledged the benefits of visionary leadership and continuity in governance, saying no societal challenge was insurmountable with focused and determined leadership.



He also urged those seeking elective positions to serve their people with sincerity and commitment.

“There is no reason why Akwa Ibom cannot leverage the value of its palm trees and agricultural produce. There is no reason that we cannot create skills development — skills that are enduring and everlasting. When your governor requested international status for the airport, I did not hesitate; I approved it. Now, as you do for one, you do for the other,” Tinubu added.

The President urged youths at the rally to remain focused and assess the credibility, track record and determination of politicians seeking their votes in the January 2027 general election.



“You, the youth—do you have your PVCs? That is the weapon with which you can defeat tyranny and reject those deceiving you. The weapon you have is the PVC.

“I don’t have to enumerate what I’ve done for you. I’ve committed my remaining years to struggling for democracy, freedom, authenticity, development, and progress. But you have heard details from one of our best friends—you’ve heard from Senator Adams Oshiomhole.

“Have you seen development or not? You have seen progress. Your universities are no longer on strike. Economic value is being added to your lives. Governor Eno, thank you for working so hard for the love of your people,” he stated.

On the forthcoming election, Tinubu described the January 16, 2027 poll as consequential, saying it would determine the direction of the country.



“This coming election on January 16, 2027, is consequential. It will define the direction of this country. When I took office, 27 out of 36 governors in this country were unable to meet salary obligations, let alone pensions and gratuities. Today, I stand before you to say we are out of that dark tunnel.

“I can beat my chest and say we are out of the greatest despair—the dark journey of uncertainty and possible bankruptcy,” he said.

The President criticised Obi, accusing the former Anambra State governor of failing to demonstrate the leadership required to confront major environmental challenges during his tenure.



Drawing a comparison between erosion problems in Anambra and the threat posed by the Atlantic Ocean to Lagos, Tinubu said effective leadership required courage and the determination to tackle difficult problems.

“In Anambra State, he could not confront erosion. I, Bola Tinubu, confronted the Atlantic Ocean,” he said.

He faulted Obi’s record compared with Eno’s efforts to tackle erosion and other infrastructure challenges in Akwa Ibom, arguing that political leadership should be measured by the willingness to confront problems rather than avoid them.



Tinubu also questioned Obi’s movement across political parties, asking whether the inability to manage political differences and maintain relationships demonstrated the qualities required for national leadership.

“Is that a leadership trait? Is that a leadership character?” he asked.

The President subsequently commended Senate President Godswill Akpabio for his leadership of the National Assembly, describing him as “a round peg in a round hole”.



Speaking during the commissioning of the new Victor Attah International Airport terminal, Tinubu acknowledged Akpabio’s management of the legislature and the support the National Assembly had given his administration.

“I recognise our host governor, Pastor Umo Eno and other members of the National Assembly here present, but let me single out our very able and respected Senate President who has navigated the affairs of the parliament very effectively,” he said.

Tinubu also described his visit to Akwa Ibom as a homecoming, recalling his time as a Mobil auditor in the state.

“I worked here as a Mobil Auditor. We built Ibeno, developed Eket and I never knew I would be the President of Nigeria one day. We did what we needed to do,” he said.



He again commended Eno for his performance, describing him as a man of conscience, commitment and vision.

“Governor Eno is a great man of conscience, commitment and visionary. When your request for the upgrade of the airport got to my desk, I didn’t hesitate because of your track record of performance,” the President said.

Earlier, Shettima challenged Atiku to demonstrate the enduring political institutions and successors he had produced during his decades in public life.



He argued that political experience should be assessed by tangible accomplishments, the development of successors and the ability to sustain political structures, rather than the length of time spent occupying public offices.

“The presidency is not a retirement benefit for long years in politics. It is a responsibility that must be earned through ideas, competence, organisation, public confidence and demonstrable results,” Shettima declared.



He questioned Atiku’s political influence in Adamawa State, challenging him to identify governors and deputy governors he had nurtured who remained committed to his current political ambition.

Shettima maintained that a presidential candidate seeking to unite Nigeria should demonstrate the ability to reconcile competing interests within his immediate political constituency.

“Charity, they say, begins at home. It does not end there, certainly. But what does not take root at home can hardly be expected to flourish elsewhere,” he said.



The Vice President also raised questions about businesses associated with Atiku, including Gotel Communications, Adamawa Plastics and Adama Beverages, saying their performance deserved scrutiny because the former Vice President had repeatedly presented his entrepreneurial experience as a qualification for managing Nigeria’s economy.

He contrasted Atiku’s political record with Tinubu’s leadership of Lagos State, where former governors Babatunde Fashola and Akinwunmi Ambode, alongside incumbent Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, had continued to identify with the President’s political structure.

“The question is no longer how long you have been in politics; it is what your years in politics have built, whom you have raised and what has endured,” he said.



Shettima also criticised Obi, accusing him of squandering the political goodwill he previously enjoyed through what he described as falsehoods and misleading statistics.

“Peter Obi has clearly messed up and squandered away his goodwill. He no longer excites when he speaks these days. He only draws suspicions,” he said.



On his part, Akpabio commended the six South-South governors for their developmental strides and support for the APC, assuring them that the National Assembly had provided a strong foundation for Tinubu to complete the structures he had laid.

He also thanked the President for approving the establishment of a Federal University of Agriculture, a Federal University of Technology and a Police Academy in Akwa Ibom State, reiterating that the South-South states stood firmly with the APC.

Akpabio’s remarks came as he praised the President’s leadership and the cooperation between the executive and legislative arms of government.



Also speaking, APC National Chairman, Yilwatda, maintained that the ruling party would not need electoral manipulation to secure Tinubu’s re-election, citing the administration’s achievements and the party’s expanding political structures.

“We don’t need to rig. We don’t need to add one vote to Mr President. He can win squarely,” he declared.

Yilwatda said Tinubu received more than 10 million votes durig the party’s presidential primary, exceeding the votes he secured in the 2023 general election.



He also cited the APC’s numerical strength among governors, federal lawmakers, state legislators and local government chairmen as evidence of its organisational capacity.

The National Chairman defended Tinubu’s economic reforms, highlighting investments in infrastructure, education, consumer credit, student loans and support for small businesses.



He said the administration’s policies were positioning Nigeria towards the President’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy by 2030.

Yilwatda particularly commended the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and Calabar-Itu-Ikot Ekpene road projects, saying they would improve transportation, reduce logistics costs and strengthen trade across the region.

Similarly, Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, insisted that the ruling party would not manipulate the 2027 election, maintaining that Tinubu’s achievements were sufficient to earn him another mandate.

“We are not going to rig the election, but Nigerians are going to vote for Asiwaju Bola Tinubu because he has laid the foundation for a better Nigeria,” he said.



Yari set a target of at least 1.6 million votes for Tinubu in Akwa Ibom, challenging the party’s leadership to mobilise eligible voters.

He also challenged opposition politicians over complaints about hunger and unemployment, arguing that the government had introduced programmes to support farmers, small businesses, market women and job creation.

“What programme do you have in place that is better than what Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu has today?

“In terms of unemployment, what do you have in place that Asiwaju has not put in place that you are going to present to Nigerians?” he asked.



Speaking on behalf of the Nigeria Governors Forum and the South-South governors, Bayelsa State Governor, Douye Diri, applauded Tinubu for the ongoing construction of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway and the establishment of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), among other legacy projects.

He also commended Eno for the massive turnout of supporters at the stadium.

“The Coastal Highway is a masterpiece. No President, living or dead, ever conceived it. All six governors of the South-South are solidly behind you. Carry go,” Diri assured the President.



At a reception in his honour at the 70-hectare Arise Palm Resort, Eno told Tinubu that he felt fulfilled by the approval of the Ibom Deep Sea Port project.

President-General of the Akwa Ibom Council of Traditional Rulers and Chancellor of Akwa Ibom State University, His Eminence Dr Ntenyin Solomon Etuk, expressed pride in identifying with the administration and prayed for the President’s success in his second-term bid.

Upon arrival in the state, Tinubu inaugurated the new Victor Attah International Airport terminal building, Ring Road 3, linking Idoro Road to Ikot Ekpene Road through Uyo and Ibiono Ibom, and the Arise Palm Resort.

World.title: Atiku: Nothing Will Keep Me Off 2027 Ballot, ADC Heads to Appeal Court
World.content:
*Former VP tells Tinubu: You can’t use courts to escape Nigerians’ verdict

*ADC seeks stay of execution, warns INEC against pre-empting appeal*Go and sort out your internal problems, APC fires back

*Heaven will not fall if Atiku is not on ballot, says Keyamo

*Coalition describes judgment as dangerous escalation

Chuks Okocha, Alex Enumah and Adedayo Akinwale in Abuja

As political intrigues gather momentum ahead of the 2027 general election, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar yesterday declared that nothing would stop him from contesting, insisting that he would be on the ballot.

The declaration came as the African Democratic Congress (ADC) appealed the judgment of the Federal High Court, Abuja, which nullified the party’s congresses and sacked the National Executive Committee led by Senator David Mark. The judgment delivered by Justice Peter Lifu, recognised an aggrieved party chieftain and former National Deputy Chairman of the ADC, Nafiu Bala Gombe, as the authentic leader of the party. Justice Lifu had, in the judgment delivered on Thursday, nullified all actions taken by the Mark-led executive, declaring them unlawful, unconstitutional, illegal, null and void. The judge held that the Mark-led executive emerged through an unlawful process and should not be recognised by INEC.



Furthermore, the Mark-led ADC in its appeal, warned the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) against taking any action that could pre-empt the outcome of its appeal.

While the ADC accused the All Progressives Congress (APC) of allegedly trying to destabilise the opposition party, the ruling party denied involvement in its internal crisis and urged it to resolve its problems.

The Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Festus Keyamo, said heaven would not fall if Atiku did not appear on the ballot in the 2027 general election.
