Guadalupe Taddei resigned as president of the INE last week after it came to light that lucrative contracts were awarded to electoral materials companies linked to a businessman with whom she had a close personal relationship. Taddei and that businessman, José Alfredo Hernández Casillas, are reportedly among 25 people who have been added to the Finance Ministry’s Blocked Persons List and who will be investigated by the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

On Friday morning, Sheinbaum asserted that corruption in the INE also occurred when Lorenzo Córdova was president of the institute between 2014 and 2023.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were the president’s remarks about the murder of a Cuernavaca city councilman. Gabriel Rivas Ríos, a Morena party member, was killed on Wednesday in Cuernavaca, capital of the state of Morelos.

Sheinbaum: ‘The INE needs to be cleaned up’

Sheinbaum asserted that corruption in INE’s rewarding of electoral materials contracts predates the 2023-2026 tenure of Taddei as the institute’s president.

Corruption occurred “during the entire period of Lorenzo Córdova,” she said.

“And probably before as well,” Sheinbaum added. “The audit will have to determine that.”

Sheinbaum noted that Córdova and other INE officials participated in various protests against an electoral reform proposal during the presidency of Andrés Manuel López Obrador. She recalled that the slogan of the protests was “El INE no se toca,’ or “Don’t touch the INE.”

“The INE has to be cleaned up. Maybe they said ‘don’t touch the INE’ in order to hang on to this whole electoral mafia that was built with them,” she said.

“The National Electoral Institute is an institute that must guarantee the will of the people, that must guarantee clean elections,” Sheinbaum added.

“In its operation, it must guarantee … transparency and republican austerity,” she said.

Sheinbaum laments murder of Cuernavaca councilman

Asked about the murder of Rivas, Sheinbaum said she knew him and described him as an environmental activist.

She described his murder as “sad and infuriating” and conveyed her condolences to his family and colleagues.

Sheinbaum said that when she heard about the homicide, she requested that the federal Security Cabinet “dedicate time and effort” to supporting the Morelos Attorney General’s Office in its investigation into the crime.

“It was a direct homicide. Some people on a motorbike shot him directly,” she said.

“There is no doubt it was a homicide that was ordered and carried out specifically against him,” Sheinbaum said.

She noted that Rivas had recently been critical of a real estate development in Cuernavaca that could cause “environmental problems.” She was referring to the Alto Verde residential project, whose construction was proposed on a site called La Cazahuatera.

The land where La Cazahuatera is located is “considered one of the last remnants of lowland deciduous forest within the urban area” of Cuernavaca, the news outlet Infobae reported.

In addition to contributing to efforts to solve Rivas’ murder, Sheinbaum said her administration would also work with Morelos Governor Margarita González Saravia “to see what can be done with this [real estate] development that he was fighting against.”

After a reporter noted that many environmental activists have been murdered or attacked in Mexico, Sheinbaum said that a lot of them now have government protection.

“They’ve approached us [to ask for protection],” she said, adding that government protection helps to “avoid” attacks on activists.

Sheinbaum said that Rivas hadn’t requested protection from the federal government.

“That doesn’t mean that we don’t condemn the homicide,” she added.

Sheinbaum explains her absence at Ibero-American Summit in Spain

Sheinbaum told reporters that she decided not to go to this week’s Ibero-American Summit in Madrid as she will travel to China for the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ summit later this month. She said visiting Spain as well as China would mean spending more time outside Mexico than she would like.

Sheinbaum said she advised Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez and King Felipe VI of her decision not to travel to Madrid.

“I wrote a letter to them … because they were the ones that invited me,” she said.

Sheinbaum noted that Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco represented her at the Ibero-American Summit, a gathering of leaders and officials from Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries.

She said she would seek a call with Sánchez to discuss the outcomes of the summit.

Mexico’s Foreign Ministry said in a statement that “the summit’s four agreements match Mexico’s priorities: care systems, academic mobility, disaster protection, and artificial intelligence that serves people.”

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Bucking expectations, Banxico lowers the interest rate, despite some inflation concerns
World.content:
Mexico’s central bank (Banxico) lowered its benchmark interest rate 25 basis points to 6.25%, surprising analysts, who as recently as this week expected the rate to remain unchanged.

In a split vote, the three bank governors supporting the reduction argued that there are no perceived demand pressures in the economy and that the degree of monetary restriction implemented is still in effect.

In a statement, Banxico adjudged that the disinflationary process has continued, indicating that, “given the prevailing slack conditions, the pass-through of exchange rate movements to prices would be limited.”

In what is viewed as guidance for future actions, the statement added that “going forward, the Governing Board believes that maintaining the rate for an extended period at the level achieved will support the convergence of inflation to its target and will be appropriate to meet external macroeconomic challenges.”

At the same time that Banxico reduced the interest rate, it raised its headline inflation forecast for the fourth quarter from 3.5% to 3.7%, acknowledging that risks remain tilted to the upside.

“This is mainly due to higher-than-anticipated levels for non-core inflation,” the statement said.

The bank also incorporated an upward adjustment to its estimate of core inflation for the last quarter, from 3.6% predicted in September to the 3.7% they now anticipate.

Although the economy continued to expand in the third-quarter, Banxico believes that “slack conditions are still expected throughout the forecast horizon, and downside risks to economic activity persist.”

Still, Banxico maintains that inflation will reach its target — 3% with a tolerance range of plus or minus 1 percentage point (2% to 4%) — by the fourth quarter of next year.

Banxico’s economic research identified four upside risks to its inflation forecasts: the persistence of core inflation; further depreciation of the peso; disruptions from trade policies or an inflationary impact from geopolitical conflicts; and, climate-related effects and unspecified cost pressures.

Looking ahead, the Governing Board said that maintaining the rate at its current level for an extended period “will support the convergence of inflation to its target and will be appropriate to address external macroeconomic challenges.”

Thursday’s surprise decision — 30 of the 36 institutions consulted by Citi expected the rate to remain unchanged — impacted the currency exchange market immediately.

The reduction pushed the dollar as high as 18.96 pesos during the day, although it later moderated its advance and closed at 18.7499. The peso lost 18.3 centavos, or 0.99%, compared to Wednesday’s close.

With reports from El Economista and El Financiero

World.title: My grandmother spent her life caring for others. Finding care for her changed my direction
World.content:
My grandmother Ene spent decades working as a hospital nurse. She cared for thousands of people she had never met before, then came home and looked after her own family. When my grandfather was struggling with Parkinson’s disease, she nursed him too.

To me, she was simply the best grandmother imaginable. Caring for people was part of her working life, but it was also how I knew her as a wife, mother and grandmother.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by RetireMexico.com (@retiremexico.official)

When she needed care for herself in her final years, I wanted to find somewhere that reflected that. Somewhere she would receive personal attention and feel comfortable living.

The options fell short. The places available felt like hospitals, lacked the personal care I had hoped for and were very expensive. I kept wishing there was somewhere better for her. She had given so much, and I struggled with how little of that seemed to be reflected in the choices available to her.

Ene died in the winter of 2025. Her experience stayed with me and eventually became part of the reason I started RetireMexico.

Making a home in Puerto Vallarta

Before settling in Mexico, I had spent years traveling. Home often depended on where the next flight took me. In 2021, I settled in Puerto Vallarta.

I have worked in marketing and sales since 2013. Along the way, I founded Spring Hub, a coworking space in Tallinn, Estonia, and Vivian Agency, the marketing agency I still run.

Those projects gave me experience building businesses. My grandmother’s final years brought me to a subject I understood much more personally. I had been a family member trying to find care for someone I loved, struggling to find an option that felt right.

When aging loved ones refuse help

Alejandra Arenas, who now co-leads RetireMexico with me, came to this work through experiences of her own.

Alejandra was born and raised in Puerto Vallarta. As a child, she watched her great-aunt live with dementia over six years of summer visits. Her great-aunt had been a pianist. Eventually, as Alejandra described it, she was “just pressing keys.”

Her great-uncle Armando cared for his wife around the clock without outside help.

Later, while in high school, Alejandra volunteered at a senior home on the outskirts of Puerto Vallarta. She helped organize movie nights and art activities. The residents received physical care, but some felt their families had set them aside.

“A home can meet every physical need and still fail the person living in it,” she told me.

Then there was Jim, her mother’s closest friend in Puerto Vallarta. An American who had lived there for more than 25 years, he developed cancer and later dementia. By then, he had no family or old friends left, only his cat.

Jim refused nearly all help, even as strangers began taking advantage of him. Alejandra and her mother became his caregivers, learning as they went how to protect him and manage the responsibilities that came with his declining health. They cared for him until he died in 2019.

For Alejandra, that experience raised a question that sits at the heart of our work. How do you help someone accept support while respecting the independence they still have?

“Finding the right care is only half of it,” she said. “The other half is finding the right moment, and helping someone still largely independent make that move without feeling erased.”

Finding a path forward

My grandmother’s experience and Alejandra’s years of caregiving were different, but they gave us plenty to talk about. We both knew how difficult these decisions could become when someone you loved needed help.

We began building RetireMexico as a free directory of senior living communities in Mexico, gathering information and checking the details with the homes themselves.

The work involves practical questions about staffing, rooms, costs and the care a residence can provide. Our own experiences also keep us asking about daily life. Who notices when a resident is withdrawn? What happens when someone refuses help? Will the person moving in have a say in how they live?

I still wish I could have found a better place for Ene. I cannot change the choices available to her then. But her experience continues to shape the questions I ask on behalf of other families.

Enelin Toneva is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Iceland Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
ICELAND · POLITICS

Key Facts Government Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, a centre-left Social Democrat, leads a coalition in office since 21 December 2024.

Parliament The coalition holds 36 of the 63 seats in the Althing, Iceland’s parliament.

EU vote On 29 August 2026 voters rejected restarting EU membership talks, 52.8% to 47.2%, in an advisory referendum.

US ties Iceland and the US held their annual Strategic Dialogue, a security and diplomacy meeting, on 2 and 3 November 2026.

Next election It is due in late 2028, four years after the last vote.

Iceland is run by a centre-left, three-party coalition under Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir, and in August voters told it not to restart talks on joining the European Union. The country matters to Americans because it hosts Keflavík Air Base, a former US base beside its main international airport that NATO and US forces use under a 1951 defence agreement.

This guide names who holds power in Reykjavík and what the August vote changed. It is part of our Europe politics coverage.

Iceland Politics: Who Holds Power

Iceland is a parliamentary republic in which the president is head of state and the prime minister runs the government. President Halla Tómasdóttir holds a largely ceremonial office, while the prime minister and cabinet make most decisions.

Kristrún Frostadóttir, 38, an economist, has led the Social Democratic Alliance, a centre-left party, since 2022. She became prime minister on 21 December 2024.

Her coalition also includes Viðreisn (Liberal Reform), a pro-EU liberal party, and the People’s Party, a populist party focused on pensions and welfare, led by Inga Sæland. Together the three hold 36 of the 63 seats in the Althing.

The Opposition and the 2024 Election

Iceland last voted on 30 November 2024, with turnout of 80.2%. The Social Democratic Alliance won 15 seats on 20.8% of the vote, just ahead of the centre-right Independence Party with 14 seats on 19.4%.

Viðreisn won 11 seats, the People’s Party 10, the Centre Party, a conservative populist party, 8 and the Progressive Party 5. The Centre Party and the Progressive Party, together with the Independence Party, make up the opposition.

The Independence Party, the senior partner in the previous government, is now chaired by Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir. The Progressive Party, a rural centrist party, chose Lilja Alfreðsdóttir as its chair in February 2026.

Why the EU Vote Matters

On 29 August 2026 Icelanders voted on whether to restart talks on joining the European Union. The No side won by 118,047 votes to 105,338, or 52.8% to 47.2%, on turnout of 82.6%, according to the National Electoral Commission and the foreign ministry.

The vote was advisory, not binding, and the government has said it will not resume membership talks during its term, which runs to 2028. It has not said whether it will ask parliament to withdraw Iceland’s 2009 EU application.

Both Reykjavík constituencies voted Yes and the other four voted No, which shows how divided the country is. Iceland therefore stays outside the EU but inside the European Economic Area, the pact that gives it access to the EU single market.

Foreign Policy Beyond the EU

On 11 March 2026 Iceland filed a declaration of intervention in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice, the UN’s main court. The government announced it on 12 March, alongside the Netherlands.

On 8 September Iceland and 11 other countries said they would pursue restrictions on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Their statement cited a housing tender in the E1 area, a contested West Bank site near Jerusalem.

Security and the United States

Iceland has no army, relies on NATO, the Western military alliance it co-founded in 1949, and has a 1951 defence agreement with the United States. That agreement lets US forces use Keflavík Air Base.

Iceland and the United States held their annual Strategic Dialogue in Reykjavík on 2 and 3 November 2026, according to a joint statement published by the Icelandic government. It marked 75 years of defence cooperation and followed a visit by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The statement lists NATO deterrence, Arctic cooperation, domain awareness (watching the seas and skies) and critical infrastructure among the topics.

What It Means for US Readers

Nothing in the referendum result or the Strategic Dialogue statement points to a change in Iceland’s ties with NATO or the 1951 US agreement. Keflavík and Arctic security cooperation therefore continue as before.

Staying outside the EU leaves Iceland’s trade arrangements unchanged, with market access through the European Economic Area. Politics rarely affects visitors, since Iceland is in the Schengen area, Europe’s passport-free travel zone, and Americans can stay up to 90 days in any 180 without a visa.

What Is Not Known

No current poll has been confirmed since the referendum, so how voters would split today is unclear. The next election is not due until late 2028.

It is not yet clear whether the government will ask parliament to withdraw Iceland’s 2009 EU application. It has said only that it will not resume membership talks this term.

We did not check the full cabinet list against the government’s own site. Readers who need ministers beyond those named here should consult the ministries’ pages.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Iceland’s prime minister?

Kristrún Frostadóttir of the Social Democratic Alliance has been prime minister since 21 December 2024. She leads a coalition with Viðreisn and the People’s Party.

How many seats does the governing coalition hold?

The three governing parties hold 36 of the 63 seats in the Althing. They are the Social Democratic Alliance with 15, Viðreisn with 11 and the People’s Party with 10.

What did Icelanders decide on the EU?

On 29 August 2026 voters rejected restarting EU membership talks, 52.8% to 47.2%. The vote was advisory, and the government said it will not resume talks this term.

When is Iceland’s next election?

It is due in late 2028, four years after the last vote. No earlier date has been confirmed.

Does the United States have a base in Iceland?

US forces left Keflavík in 2006, but a 1951 defence agreement still lets them use Keflavík Air Base. Iceland has no army of its own.

Latin America woke on 7 November angry and unsettled, with Paraguay’s fallen president in custody and the rest of the region counting the cost of money that is getting more expensive to trust.

Apartment towers lit at night in São Paulo. (File photo)

The Continent’s Mood Today

The loudest story on Saturday’s front pages, from São Paulo to Mexico City, was a former head of state detained in his own home. Paraguay’s Santiago Peña lost his job on Friday and his freedom within hours.

Elsewhere the feeling was quieter but related: prices, rates and public finances are squeezing households. Brazil’s services index fell to 44.5, Chile’s inflation reached 4.5% and Mexican car dealers fear a 2027 tax squeeze.

Paraguay – Anger, and a Country Waiting for Its Money

On 3 November the central bank put ueno, a digital bank with about 3 million customers, into resolution. Its solvency index had fallen below half the required minimum, only five days after a US$100 million capital plan was announced.

On Friday the Senate removed Peña, the second Paraguayan president impeached after Fernando Lugo in 2012. Peña had offered to resign, but the Senate rejected the offer.

Brazil – Gloom in the Services Sector

Brazil’s services index sat at 44.5 and overall business activity at 44.4, both below the 50 line that marks growth. For households and employers, that is the feeling of an economy holding its breath.

September factory output fell 2.5% from a year earlier (0.8% from August), a reminder that weak demand reaches the shop floor as well as the shops.

Mexico – Cheaper Money, Heavier Worries

Banxico, Mexico’s central bank, cut its rate to 6.25%, welcome news for borrowers. Yet cheaper money does not remove worries about the cost of living.

The national car dealers’ association AMDA says a cap on tax deductions planned for 2027 could threaten about 1,000 dealerships and 70,000 jobs, according to Mexican business daily Expansión.

Chile – Prices Up, Blockade Over

Annual inflation rose to 4.5% on fuel costs. Many households feel the pump price before they read any statistic.

In the port city of San Antonio, independent truckers ended a blockade of port-side depots on Friday. They signed a deal with cargo companies, brokered by the government.

Argentina – Patience Wearing Thin, Not Broken

Argentines are weighing an economy where jobs and prices still decide the mood. President Javier Milei‘s approval stood near 38% in AtlasIntel’s September poll, which suggests voters are tired but not yet ready to leave him.

The closure of tyre maker FATE, announced in February with about 920 jobs, shows how a factory shutdown can drag on.

Colombia – Fear of the Bill Coming Due

Goldman Sachs, the US bank, sees a high risk that the government’s fiscal plan slips and expects Congress to water it down. The government’s answer, the EfectIVA scheme, would refund VAT by income, but it is planned for 2028 and depends on Congress passing the government’s rescue law.

Security news cut both ways: troops killed William Andrés Daza Guetio, known as Pincher, a commander of a FARC dissident group, near Jamundí in the south-west.

The Shared Mood

The common feeling is distrust of whoever holds the money, whether a bank in Asunción, a ministry in Bogotá or a central bank in Mexico City. Paraguay made that feeling visible on Friday.

People across the region are asking the same plain question: who is looking after my savings, and who answers if it goes wrong?For the numbers behind the mood, see our daily Latin America market reports.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was Santiago Peña removed as president of Paraguay?

The Senate removed him on 6 November after the collapse of ueno bank, which had about 3 million customers.

Who is Paraguay’s new president?

Pedro Alliana, 52, was sworn in on 6 November and serves until August 2028.

Are ueno savers protected?

Savers are covered up to about US$38,000 each. The treatment of ueno’s US$350 million in dollar bonds is unresolved.

01 A split tape with a nervous undertone

Wall Street ended with two different stories. The Nasdaq Composite rose 1.09% to 24,579, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.46% to 51,286.

The S&P 500 gained 0.31% to 7,377. Investors favoured technology growth over the Dow’s older industrial names.

The VIX fell 9.01% to 25.64. That is still a reading that signals real unease beneath the rally.

Bonds and currencies sent a firmer message. The US 10-year Treasury yield rose 0.58% to 4.867%, and the dollar index gained 0.72% to 102.279.

Gold slipped 0.49% to $4,066/oz. Higher yields and a stronger dollar normally cost bullion buyers.

The trigger was the US jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October against a forecast of 65,000, and unemployment fell to 4.1% from 4.2%.

Strong hiring cuts the odds of quick US rate cuts, which explains the firmer yield and dollar. The University of Michigan survey of households showed year-ahead inflation expectations easing to 4.3% from 4.7%.

02 Expensive money, and Brazil feels it first

A higher yield and a stronger dollar on the same day tell a simple story. Markets are pricing money that stays costly for longer.

A 10-year yield at 4.867% lifts borrowing costs for US companies and homebuyers. It also pulls capital away from emerging markets.

Brazil sits right in that line of fire. On 4 November the central bank held the Selic at 13.75%, ending five straight quarter-point cuts, and the vote was unanimous.

Inflation gave the board little room. Consumer prices rose 4.58% in the 12 months to September, according to IBGE, Brazil’s statistics agency, above the 4.5% ceiling of the tolerance band around the 3% target.

A dollar index up 0.72% adds pressure on the real. A weaker real raises import prices and makes cuts harder to defend.

Prediction market Polymarket gave 89.0% odds to no change at the 9 December meeting. It gave 5.7% to a quarter-point cut, as of 6 November, 11 pm ET.

03 Diesel draws and a quiet Asian bid for bills

The US Energy Information Administration reported commercial crude stocks of 409.8 million barrels for the week ending 30 October, down 0.9 million. Gasoline stocks fell 0.2 million to 209.0 million barrels (source: eia.gov, Weekly Petroleum Status Report).

The bigger signal is in distillates. Stocks fell 3.6 million barrels to 99.3 million, which points to tight diesel supply.

Diesel drives freight and farm costs. Brazil imports part of its diesel, so a tight market feeds straight into its inflation debate.

In Japan, the 3-month bill auction cleared at 1.241, against 1.271 previously. A lower yield signals steady demand for short-term paper.

Euro area retail sales fell 0.7% in September, far worse than the 0.1% fall economists expected (source: Eurostat, the EU statistics office). Brazil’s balance of trade showed a surplus of US$9.3 billion in October, a record-sized month for trade flows at US$66.3 billion (source: MDIC, Brazil’s trade ministry).

China’s foreign exchange reserves were due on 7 November, with a consensus of 3.4 trillion US dollars, unchanged. Japan follows on Sunday night at 23:50 Lisbon time, with the previous reading at 1178.4.

What happened Gunmen opened fire on Guatemalan lawmaker Julio Portillo’s convoy in Río Hondo, in Zacapa province, on Friday 6 November.

Who died Three people died: Guatemala’s Interior Ministry says three police officers; local reports say two officers and a bodyguard.

The lawmaker Portillo survived and is in stable condition, the ministry says; firefighters said he was not shot.

What next Prosecutors of the Public Ministry lead the case; no suspect or motive was announced by Friday night.

Gunmen ambushed a Guatemalan congressman’s convoy in front of a police station on Friday. Three people died, and the lawmaker survived.

The convoy carried Julio Portillo, an opposition member of Congress for the eastern province of Zacapa. The attack came at kilometre 137 of the Atlantic Highway in Río Hondo, a town on the main road from Guatemala City to the Caribbean port of Puerto Barrios.

What We Know So Far

Guatemala’s Interior Ministry said three officers of the National Civil Police, the national force, died while repelling a “direct attack” on the lawmaker. It said the agents acted to defend his life, and that he was receiving care at a health centre.

Local reporting from the scene describes the victims differently: two officers who rode a motorcycle and one of Portillo’s own bodyguards. We cannot yet say which description is right, but every account agrees on three dead.

Municipal firefighters in Río Hondo said Portillo was unhurt and was taken to a medical facility. Later local reports say fragments from bullets that hit his windscreen reached him, but that he was not shot, while one wire report called him wounded and the ministry said only that he was in stable condition.

The ministry said the Public Ministry, Guatemala’s prosecution service, will lead the investigation. By late Friday no motive, suspect or arrest had been announced.

Who Is Julio Portillo?

Portillo won his seat in 2023 for Cabal, a centre-right party, and holds it for the 2024–2028 term. Cabal expelled him in April 2025, after mayors in Zacapa accused him of demanding illegal commissions.

In June 2025 prosecutors asked to lift his legal immunity over such allegations, and we have seen no conviction. On 31 October he joined the National Unity of Hope (UNE), the party of former first lady Sandra Torres.

Torres has run for president three times and is expected to try again in the 2027 election.

Why Zacapa Keeps Making Headlines

Zacapa is regarded as a strategic corridor for international drug trafficking and organised crime. At the end of September a shooting in the town of Huité killed eight people.

The Army blamed a territorial dispute between criminal groups, and the government opened an investigation into the Army’s own conduct. Last week the US Embassy rebuked a Zacapa mayor’s party over a lavish celebration, as we reported.

Friday’s attack puts the same province back at the centre of the security debate before voters choose a president, lawmakers and mayors next year.

What It Means for US Readers

Guatemala is a transit route for drugs bound for the United States and the home country of one of the largest migrant groups in the US. Violence in the east tests how far the government of President Bernardo Arévalo, a reformist elected in 2023, controls its own territory.

The loser is public confidence in that control, and a clear winner is hard to name. An arrest, or a public statement from prosecutors naming a motive, would show whether this was a political attack or organised crime settling scores.

Until then, expect pressure on Congress and the Interior Ministry for answers in the coming days. Any such move would matter to US officials who work with Guatemala on security and migration.

What Is Not Known

We do not know who fired, why, or how many of the dead were officers and how many were bodyguards. We also do not know how seriously, if at all, Portillo was hurt.

It is also unclear whether the lawmaker was the intended target. We will update this report when prosecutors or the ministry release more details.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to Julio Portillo?

He survived. Firefighters said he was unhurt, he was not shot, and Guatemala’s Interior Ministry said he was in stable condition.

Who died in the Zacapa attack?

Three people died. The Interior Ministry says all three were police officers, while local reports say two officers and one bodyguard.

World.title: Costa Rica Removes Don Pepe Figueres Monument After Protest Vandalism
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Ministry of Culture and Youth removed the bronze monument to former President José Figueres Ferrer from San José’s Plaza de la Democracia on Friday morning, less than four weeks before the country marks the anniversary of the army abolition Figueres declared in 1948.

Culture Minister Jorge Rodríguez Vives ordered the temporary removal after the sculpture was defaced during demonstrations in recent weeks. A crew from the state power company CNFL lifted the figures by crane, and the pieces were taken to the National Museum’s José Fabio Góngora facility in Pavas, where specialists will clean and restore them.

Rodríguez described the decision as difficult but necessary to protect the ensemble from further damage. He acknowledged freedom of expression and peaceful protest as pillars of Costa Rican democracy but said exercising those rights cannot come at the expense of the nation’s heritage.

The minister said he expects those responsible to cover the cost of restoration, subject to the findings of the competent authorities, adding that damage to national heritage should not go without consequences. He also said the figures will not return to the plaza until there are guarantees they will not be vandalized again. The ministry characterized the removal as a temporary conservation measure, not a surrender of public space to vandalism.

The National Museum, which administers the plaza, has filed criminal complaints with the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) and the San José prosecutor’s office. According to the museum’s preliminary technical assessment, the latest incident left graffiti, spray paint and scratches on the bronze figures themselves, whereas damage in October mainly affected the monument’s base.

The museum has warned it cannot guarantee a full return to the sculpture’s original condition, because the paint penetrated surfaces already worn by age. Specialists expect the work to take several weeks. Rodríguez put the cost of the initial cleaning alone at about 1 million colones (roughly $2,000). The ministry said the total cost will be determined once its technical and economic assessment is complete, and it has not announced a date for the monument’s return.

The damage occurred during protests against budget cuts to public education and university funding. The most recent incident followed a student demonstration in the plaza on the night of Monday, Nov. 2. María Ortega Zamora, president of the student federation at the State Distance University (UNED), said four hooded people dressed in black arrived around 1 a.m. and began defacing the monument. She denied that students were responsible.

The removal drew a sharp response from the National Liberation Party (PLN), which Figueres founded in 1951. Álvaro Ramírez, head of the PLN’s legislative caucus, likened the move to a dictator’s playbook, writing on social media that it erased memory, disrespected history and removed symbols of the country’s democracy.

Ramírez argued that a nation’s historical memory cannot be treated as an obstacle and that defending it is part of defending democracy. He said the PLN will demand that the restored statues be returned to the Plaza de la Democracia as testimony to Costa Rica’s history.

The dispute adds to tensions between President Laura Fernández’s administration and opposition parties, including the PLN, as the education budget protests continue. The ensemble, by Costa Rican sculptor Marisel Jiménez Rittner, was unveiled on April 28, 1998. Its four bronze elements depict Figueres, a girl with a violin symbolizing culture, a boy with a book representing education, and a sledgehammer recalling the abolition of the army.

This is not the first time the monument has left the plaza. It was moved to the National Museum’s gardens in 2008 during a renovation of the square, and its original sledgehammer had been stolen. After restoration by museum specialists and the sculptor, it was reinstalled in December 2016, when the space was renamed Plaza de la Democracia y de la Abolición del Ejército.

The plaza sits beside the National Museum, the former Bellavista barracks where Figueres declared the army abolished on Dec. 1, 1948. Army Abolition Day commemorations have traditionally included a floral offering at the monument, and it remains unclear whether the figures will be back in place for this year’s ceremony.

Figueres, popularly known as Don Pepe, led Costa Rica three times and remains one of the defining figures of its modern history, closely tied to the institutions, social reforms and unarmed democracy that shaped the country’s identity.

World.title: A Proposed 15% Tax Would Reach Costa Rica Residents’ Foreign Dividends and Interest
World.content:
Costa Rica residents who earn interest, dividends, rent or capital gains outside the country would pay a 15% tax on that income under a bill the government has sent to the Legislative Assembly, a change tax specialists say would break with the country’s long-standing territorial tax system.

The bill, presented by the Finance Ministry on Sept. 22, would tax five types of passive income earned abroad by Costa Rican tax residents: interest, dividends, royalties, rent and capital gains. It would apply to individuals as well as companies, trusts, investment funds and other structures that are tax residents in Costa Rica.

The proposal sets no minimum threshold. Daniel Pelecano, director of tax and legal services at Grant Thornton, said that means small and large investors would be taxed on the same terms. Costa Rica has generally taxed income based on where it is generated rather than where the earner lives. A 2023 reform, Law 10.381, taxed some foreign passive income, but only for certain entities in multinational groups that failed to meet economic-substance requirements.

The new bill would repeal those limits and make tax residency the deciding factor for passive income. It keeps the territorial rule for active income, such as earnings from work or a business. In the bill’s statement of reasons, the Finance Ministry argues that the 2023 rules reached very few taxpayers. It also says residents receiving the same foreign dividends or interest are treated differently depending on whether they belong to a multinational group.

The ministry says the bill takes into account tax already paid or withheld abroad in order to avoid double taxation. Tax specialists say the mechanism works as a deduction rather than a direct credit, with the foreign tax subtracted from the income before Costa Rica applies its own rate.

Tax lawyer Gabriel Zamora Baudrit illustrated the effect with $100 in US dividends that have already had $30 withheld. Costa Rica would apply its 15% rate to the remaining $70, collecting $10.50 and bringing the combined tax burden to 40.5%. Under a direct credit capped at the Costa Rican amount, the $30 already paid would exceed Costa Rica’s $15 charge, leaving nothing more to pay. Zamora said the bill’s formula falls short of that standard and amounts to a new tax on residents’ foreign passive income, not simply a 15% rate.

Companies that already pay corporate income tax would follow a different route. Rather than paying the flat 15%, they would add the foreign passive income to their taxable profits, which are taxed at rates of up to 30%. Marianela Masís, director of tax and legal services at PwC Costa Rica, said the bill is not a full worldwide income tax because it is limited to certain passive income. She said those most affected would be tax residents who now receive passive income from abroad and fall outside the special regime for multinational groups.

Specialists said retirees who live on returns from investments abroad could fall within the bill’s scope. How pension funds would be treated remains one of several open questions, along with the double-taxation formula, the lack of a threshold and how far the exception to territoriality should reach.

Central Bank President Róger Madrigal said in October that the tax could discourage residents from investing abroad, depending on how foreign tax rates compare with local ones. He said dollars brought back into the country would only affect the exchange rate if they were converted into colones and that the local financial system was deep enough to absorb any inflow.

The bill has only begun its passage through the Assembly, and its text could change. Tax specialists say it would need 38 votes if lawmakers classify it as a new tax, or 29 if it is treated as a reform of existing law. The Finance Ministry has not published an estimate of how much the tax would raise. The proposal comes as the government confronts a revenue shortfall that has already forced cuts across the 2027 budget.

World.title: Local Elections Drove Costa Rica’s CPTPP Reversal, Sources Say
World.content:
Concerns about the 2028 municipal elections helped drive Costa Rica’s decision to abandon its bid to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), according to four people linked to the accession process who spoke to local reporters on condition of anonymity. The government has not responded to their accounts.

President Laura Fernández announced on Oct. 28 that she would shelve the accession and dismissed Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos the same day. The previous administration of Rodrigo Chaves had announced, days before the current government took office, that it had concluded negotiations on the substantive terms of Costa Rica’s entry.

The CPTPP has been in force since 2018 and has 12 members: Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Brunei, Chile, Mexico, Canada, Peru, Vietnam, Singapore, Malaysia and the United Kingdom.

The sources’ accounts center on an Oct. 9 meeting at Casa Presidencial, where the president and Chaves, now Minister of Finance and of the Presidency, convened 46 organizations to review the agreement. One attendee said about 40 municipalities in agricultural areas, along with other business groups, opposed the deal.

That attendee said pushing ahead could have jeopardized those municipalities’ ties to the ruling Pueblo Soberano party. Attendees said Chaves defended the agreement at the meeting on free-market grounds. At the same meeting, the president asked Trejos to organize working groups with productive sectors and set Nov. 23 as the deadline to decide whether to sign the accession protocol, according to the sources. Some of them described the meeting as a formality, arguing the decision had already been made.

Agricultural groups protested outside Casa Presidencial on Oct. 9, and several organizations marched against the agreement on Nov. 3. Chaves publicly backed the reversal on Oct. 29. In a government video, he said he fully supported the president’s decision and noted that he had authorized the Foreign Trade Ministry to begin negotiations, citing access to a market of about 600 million consumers.

The sources also described friction over how the deal was handled. One said the government’s new approach included criticism of the way the Foreign Trade Ministry negotiated and of its failure to share information with business chambers. Trejos reportedly sought permission from the bloc’s 12 members to make the negotiated protocol public. According to the sources, that permission was not granted, and the text has not been released.

Costa Rica already has trade agreements with six CPTPP members: Mexico, Canada, Peru, Chile, Singapore and the United Kingdom. One source said the main additional benefit of membership would have been access to the Japanese market. The Presidency had not answered questions about the accounts submitted by local reporters on Nov. 3. The government has not publicly explained the reasons for the reversal beyond the president’s Oct. 28 announcement.

The bloc’s ministerial meeting in Vietnam, scheduled for Nov. 23 to 27, would have been Costa Rica’s first as a participant. With the accession shelved, the country’s existing bilateral agreements remain its main framework for trade with the Asia-Pacific region.

World.title: Your $1,000 Now Buys 46,810 Fewer Colones Than in January
World.content:
The US dollar slipped again in Costa Rica this week, leaving anyone who earns in dollars and spends in colones with noticeably less buying power than at the start of the year. The average rate on Monex, the Central Bank’s wholesale foreign exchange market, closed at 450.26 colones on Thursday, Nov. 5, according to Central Bank data. That was down from 453.81 on Oct. 26 and the lowest daily average since at least that date.

The Central Bank’s reference rate for Friday, Nov. 6, stood at 453.34 colones to sell dollars and 448.27 to buy them. A day earlier, the reference rate was 454.41 to sell and 449.63 to buy. The longer view shows the scale of the shift. On Jan. 2, the Monex average was 497.07 colones, which means Thursday’s close was 46.81 colones lower, a drop of about 9.4% since the start of 2026.

In practical terms, $1,000 converted at the Monex average on Jan. 2 would have brought 497,070 colones. At Thursday’s average, the same amount brings 450,260 colones, a difference of 46,810 colones, or about $104 at current rates. The decline cuts both ways. People paid in dollars and spending in colones, from exporters and tourism businesses to retirees receiving pensions from abroad, lose purchasing power as the rate falls, while households that earn colones and owe dollar-denominated rent or loans pay less to cover them.

The weak dollar has already squeezed some sectors that sell to foreigners, including medical tourism, where revenue measured in colones has fallen. The Monex average first dropped below 450 colones on July 17, when it reached 449.95, at the time the lowest level since the market opened in 2006. The Central Bank described the Costa Rica’s dollar surplus as extraordinary earlier this year and has bought dollars in the market to limit sharper falls.

The broader picture is one of abundant dollars, with the Costa Rica’s dollar supply hitting a record two decades after the end of scheduled devaluations. Monex is the wholesale market where banks and other authorized institutions trade dollars with one another, so its average does not match the price at a bank window. Banks and exchange houses set their own buying and selling prices around the Central Bank’s reference rate, which is published every business day.

World.title: 5,000 Shareholders, No Dividends and a Court Order for Hospital CIMA’s Top Executive
World.content:
A civil court in San José has ordered Clifton Neal Orme, the legal representative of Hospital CIMA, to appear in person and testify in a case brought by minority shareholders who say they have spent years trying to recover their investment in one of Costa Rica’s best-known private hospitals.

The order, issued Oct. 20 by the Second Collegiate Civil Court of First Instance is part of a pre-trial evidence proceeding. That type of proceeding gathers testimony and documents before a full lawsuit is filed, and the court has made no finding of wrongdoing. Neal must personally answer the shareholders’ questions as a party to the case and identify and produce any documents put to him.

He must also present an account of his administration, including a detailed list of the company’s assets and liabilities for 2025. The company, registered as Hospital San José S.A., must hand over a certified copy of the minutes of its Feb. 23, 2026, shareholders’ meeting and its financial statements for 2025.

The court warned that if Neal fails to appear without justification, refuses to answer or responds evasively, it may apply article 42.2 of the Civil Procedure Code. Under certain conditions, that provision allows a judge to treat the facts raised in the questioning as true. A hearing set for Oct. 29 was called off because the court had not yet appointed an English interpreter for Neal, who does not speak Spanish. The hospital must deposit 92,660 colones (about $204) to cover four hours of interpretation, and the court will set a new date once the case file is ready.

The proceeding was filed by shareholder Francisco Castro, who holds 17,336 shares. Panacea JSG S.A., a company represented by 79-year-old investor José Jop, joined as an interested party with 528,748 shares, or about 1.91% of the hospital’s capital.

The court rejected the shareholders’ request for a court-appointed expert to audit the company. Their combined stake of about 1.92% falls short of the 10% that article 26 of the Commercial Code requires for that measure, the court ruled, though it granted their other requests for financial and corporate records. Hospital CIMA’s legal representation said the company will comply with whatever the court requires of it through the proper legal channels. Because the matter is ongoing, it said it would not comment on specific proceedings or on the documents requested.

The case is the latest chapter in a long-running dispute between the hospital and its small investors. Sebastián Vargas, the attorney representing Jop, has said the company has more than 5,000 individual and corporate shareholders, some of whom say they have gone more than two decades without a dividend or a way to sell their stakes.

According to audited financial statements cited in local press reports, the company posted cumulative losses of more than 16.9 billion colones (about $37 million at current exchange rates) between 2019 and 2024. Hospital San José S.A. also appears among the large taxpayers that reported losses or zero taxable income to the Finance Ministry for four consecutive fiscal years, from 2021 through 2024.

The same statements show the balance owed to the hospital by International Hospital Corporation (IHC), a Dallas, Texas-based company related to the controlling shareholder, rose from $11.9 million in 2023 to $13.3 million in 2024. IHC designed and built the hospital, which opened in Escazú in 2000 and has long served the country’s medical tourism market.

Only one minority shareholder is known to have won a case against the hospital. In 2023, a court granted physician Manfred Freer the right to withdraw from the company and be paid for his shares, plus dividends, interest and costs, after finding the hospital had recorded profits in two consecutive periods without distributing them. The Supreme Court’s First Chamber upheld that ruling on April 10, 2025.

During that case, the hospital argued that withholding profits reflected a shareholder agreement to reinvest in its operations and maintain quality of care. A court-ordered appraisal later valued each of Freer’s shares at $6.32, against the $1 per share the hospital had maintained. The dispute has also reached the criminal courts. In December 2025, the hospital and Neal filed a criminal complaint for alleged extortion against Jop and Vargas after Jop raised options for recovering his money, including going to the press.

The Pavas Criminal Court dismissed that complaint, and the Specialized Criminal Court for Organized Crime upheld the dismissal on Sept. 30, 2026. Public registry records list Neal as vice president of Hospital San José S.A. and Gary Brent Wood as its president. No new date has been set for Neal’s testimony. Evidence gathered in pre-trial proceedings of this kind is typically used to decide whether to file a full civil lawsuit.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV Departs for First Latin America Journey to Uruguay Argentina and Peru
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV leaves Rome on Friday, November 6, 2026, for a twelve-day apostolic journey to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. The Holy See Press Office published the full itinerary in September and reconfirmed it this week, with no changes. The trip marks the first Latin America visit of his pontificate. It covers three countries and ten cities, with roughly a dozen flights, nine public Masses, seven cathedral visits and two stadium prayer vigils. Matteo Bruni, director of the Holy See Press Office, said the Pope is enthusiastic about the journey and that the program remains intact.

In Uruguay, from November 6 to 8, Leo XIV visits Montevideo, Paysandú and Florida. The motto is “I bring you news of great joy.” He arrives at Carrasco International Airport in the afternoon of November 6, holds a welcome ceremony at Plaza Independencia, meets authorities and the diplomatic corps, and visits President Yamandú Orsi. He celebrates vespers at the Metropolitan Cathedral.

The next day he flies to Paysandú for Mass, returns to Montevideo for a meeting in the Casavalle neighborhood and a session with the education community at the Catholic University of Uruguay, then leads a prayer vigil at Centenario Stadium. On November 8 he celebrates Mass at the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three in Florida before flying to Buenos Aires.

Argentina receives him from November 8 to 11. The motto is “Welcome everyone. Go and proclaim.” He arrives at Aeroparque Jorge Newbery, visits the monument to General José de San Martín, holds a welcome ceremony at Casa Rosada and meets President Javier Milei.

The program includes a visit to the Pequeño Cottolengo Don Orione in Claypole, Mass at the Monumento de los Españoles, a meeting with workers at the Catholic University of Argentina, an interreligious gathering, vespers with bishops and synodal teams at the Metropolitan Cathedral, a flight to Córdoba for Mass and a clergy meeting, a youth vigil back in Buenos Aires, a visit to the federal prison complex and Mass at the Basilica of Our Lady of Luján.

This is the first papal visit to Argentina since St. John Paul II in 1987. Argentina is the homeland of the late Pope Francis. Peru is the longest and most personal stage, from November 11 to 17. The motto is “Let us open our hearts.” Leo XIV arrives at Callao Air Base, holds a welcome ceremony at the Government Palace and meets the president. He visits Lima, Chiclayo, Cusco and Pucallpa.

Events include meetings with Peruvian bishops, a public gathering on challenges facing the country, a youth vigil at the National Stadium, Mass near Pimentel, a private visit to the San Óscar A. Romero Chapel, a university meeting, a helicopter flight to Santa Cruz de Succhabamba for Mass, a rite of coronation of the Immaculate Virgin in Chiclayo’s cathedral, a prayer at Saqsaywaman in Cusco, a meeting with Amazonian missionaries and peoples in Pucallpa, Mass there, a visit to a shelter for abandoned elderly people in Lima, and a final Mass at Las Palmas Air Base before departure on November 16. He returns to Rome on November 17.

The Holy See Press Office stated that the Pope remains clinically fit for travel after surgery on October 13, 2026, at Gemelli Hospital. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung after intraoperative examination confirmed lung adenocarcinoma. Doctors reported a successful operation with no complications and normal recovery. Bruni confirmed the program is unchanged.

Robert Francis Prevost, born September 14, 1955, in Chicago, is the first Augustinian and first American-born pope. He spent about two decades in Peru as a missionary, seminary formator and bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. He holds Peruvian citizenship. The Vatican described the Peru segment as a homecoming that allows him to return to places and communities that shaped his ministry.

The overall program emphasizes encounter, attention to the vulnerable, meetings with young people, workers, prisoners and victims of clerical sexual abuse, and the witness of local saints and blessed. The journey begins with the November 6 flight from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport. The Holy See Press Office has released the complete schedule of times and venues.

World.title: Costa Rica’s First Direct Flight From Poland Lands in Guanacaste
World.content:
Costa Rica now has its first direct air link with Poland. A LOT Polish Airlines Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner from Katowice landed at Guanacaste Airport in Liberia at about 2:40 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 5, opening a weekly charter service that runs through Dec. 17.

Costa Rican tourism officials put the number of passengers on board at 251, which matches the aircraft’s seating capacity, along with 11 crew members. Figures released in Poland put the number of passengers who left Katowice at 233. Passengers and crew were greeted at the airport, formally Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport, with folk music, dancing and welcome gifts.

The flights are charters sold by Rainbow Tours, one of Poland’s largest tour operators, and will operate every Thursday. The trip takes about 13 hours and spares travelers a change of planes at another European or North American hub. Piotr Burwicz, vice president of Rainbow Tours, said the route widens the long-haul holiday options available to Polish travelers, pointing to Costa Rica’s beaches, natural richness and opportunities for active tourism.

Poland is still a small market for Costa Rica, but it is growing. According to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT), 5,367 Polish visitors arrived by air between January and September 2026, up 20% from the same period last year. Over those nine months, the country received 335,586 European visitors by air.

Until now, few Polish travelers have used Guanacaste as their entry point. Of the 8,837 Polish tourists who visited Costa Rica in 2025, only 524 arrived through the Liberia airport, according to ICT figures released when the route was announced in February. ICT Executive President Marcos V. Borges said the new connection strengthens Costa Rica’s tourism ties with Europe and creates more opportunities to bring visitors to Guanacaste and nearby areas.

The flight comes as the airport continues to grow and add nonstop routes. Passenger traffic rose 10% year over year between January and September 2026, according to figures released by the terminal. The airport sits within easy reach of Tamarindo, Playa Flamingo, the Papagayo Peninsula and several national parks.

For Guanacaste, the route is another step toward visitor markets beyond the United States and Canada, which have long supplied most of the region’s tourists. Although the Polish service is scheduled only through mid-December, it brings a new stream of European customers to hotels, tour operators, restaurants and transport companies in the northwest as the high season begins.

World.title: Every Big Mac Sold in Costa Rica on Nov. 13 Goes to Charity
World.content:
It is not often that a Big Mac is the virtuous choice. On Friday, Nov. 13, McDonald’s restaurants across Costa Rica will hold Gran Día, an annual fundraiser in which all proceeds from every Big Mac sold go to charity. For one day a year, a double stack of beef and special sauce qualifies as philanthropy, and ordering two is practically a moral obligation.

This year Arcos Dorados, which operates the chain in Costa Rica, has set a goal of 75,000 Big Macs at its 81 restaurants nationwide. Last year’s edition sold 68,353 sandwiches and raised about 180 million colones, or roughly $398,000. The money is divided equally between two programs. Half goes to Casa Ronald McDonald, which houses families whose children are being treated at the Hospital Nacional de Niños in San José.

The house gives each family a room for as long as treatment lasts, along with four meals a day, psychological support, social work services and other activities during their stay. It also works with the Ministry of Public Education so that brothers and sisters of hospitalized children can keep up with school.

Most of the families come from rural and remote areas, and for them that support can last for months. Some have stayed more than a year. The house served more than 1,000 families in 2025, and in the first half of 2026 it had already welcomed 482 families and served more than 30,000 meals. According to the foundation, Gran Día accounts for roughly half of what the house raises from the private sector each year.

One of those families is that of Zoé Victoria Hernández, a 7-year-old from Santa Rosa de Turrialba who has undergone 16 surgeries for congenital conditions. Her family first turned to the house while her mother was still pregnant and has been connected to it for more than seven years.

The other half of the proceeds goes to YouthCan!, a program run by Aldeas Infantiles SOS that prepares young people between 15 and 24 for the workforce through career guidance, job skills training and first work placements. Since 2017, more than 3,900 young people have completed its training and 880 have gained their first work experience. Gran Día covers about 90 percent of the program’s funding.

Among its participants are siblings Saray and Josué Carvajal. Saray now studies business administration at the University of Costa Rica, while Josué is pursuing a technical degree in criminology and has completed an internship. There are two ways to take part. Customers can buy a Big Mac at any McDonald’s on Nov. 13, including through AutoMac or the McDonald’s app.

Coupons are also on sale now at restaurants, through AutoMac and in the app for anyone who wants to contribute ahead of time. Restaurants will host special activities with guest personalities throughout the day. Nutritionists may want to look away. For everyone else, it is a rare chance to do some good without giving up anything at all, except perhaps the salad you were planning to have.

Most charity drives ask you to sacrifice something. This one just asks you to order lunch.

World.title: Gov’t, Opposition agree to meet Monday after Parliament ruckus
World.content:
This combination photo shows Leader of Opposition Business Phillip Paulwell and House Speaker Juliet Holness

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Opposition Leader of Government Business Phillip Paulwell has agreed to meet with Government representatives on Monday, following Tuesday’s heated confrontation in the House of Representatives, which involved exchanges of profanity and allegations of misconduct.

Responding to an invitation from House Speaker Juliet Holness, Paulwell welcomed the proposed meeting but expressed concern and disappointment over the tone of her letter.

Citing what he described as deep-rooted distrust in Parliament, Paulwell said it could only be overcome if everyone recognises the essential role the Opposition plays in preserving democracy.

“Our role in holding the Government to account and ensuring transparency must be strengthened, not weakened,” Paulwell noted.

He criticised the Speaker’s approach to Parliament, accusing her of contributing to division in the House and being partial to the Jamaica Labour Party Government, citing Tuesday’s conflict as an example.

“When the stakes are highest, you have used the powers of the Speaker to secure the partisan interests of the Government, and that is absolutely antithetical to the principles and traditions of your office. The most recent glaring example of this was last Tuesday, when you entertained and sought to give effect to a motion brought by the House leader to abruptly and peremptorily shut down the debate on the Opposition’s censure motion against the Government, despite the interests of the minority clearly requiring that motion to be fully debated and then closed in the normal way,” he said.

READ: Tensions flare as Phillips, McKenzie clash in Parliament

Paulwell expressed hope that Monday’s meeting would be “a frank and constructive dialogue among equals, and not an occasion for admonishment”.

He maintained that it could ultimately be necessary to involve the prime minister and the leader of the Opposition or even an independent mediator or wider group of stakeholders to secure a lasting resolution.

World.title: JLP scales down annual conference
World.content:
Jamaica Labour Party Deputy Leader Desmond McKenzie (right) speaks during a press conference at the party’s headquarters on Belmont Road in Kingston on Friday, November 6, 2026 as party Chairman Robert Montague (centre) and Deputy General Secretary Dr Andrew Wheatley (left) listen.

For the second consecutive year, the Jamaica Labour Party will forgo its customary mass public conference, after cancelling last year’s staging in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, and instead hold a delegates-only meeting in Montego Bay on Sunday, November 15.

Deputy Leader Desmond McKenzie announced on Friday, during a press conference at the JLP’s headquarters, that the 2026 annual conference will be held at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in Rose Hall, St James, with approximately 6,000 delegates expected to attend.

The decision means there will be no usual large-scale public rally, as the party seeks to show solidarity with Jamaicans still struggling in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, particularly in western Jamaica.

McKenzie said the party’s leadership had recommended a business-focused conference, a proposal which was approved by the party’s Central Executive.

The meeting will begin at approximately 10 am and will address internal party matters, including the election of the party leader and deputy leaders.

Former Member of Parliament and Deputy Leader JC Hutchinson will not be seeking re-election, while St James Central MP Heroy Clarke has been nominated to replace him, with his nomination to be ratified at the conference.

Prime Minister and party leader Dr Andrew Holness is scheduled to deliver the main address at approximately 1:30 pm. His address will be open to the media and broadcast live, but the party’s other business will take place behind closed doors.

JLP Deputy General Secretary Dr Andrew Wheatley said the party expects to hold a grand public session next year.

World.title: Brown, Hall called up to Reggae Boyz squad for Mexico quarterfinal clash
World.content:
Jamaica's forward #16 Warner Brown celebrates after scoring a goal during the 2026 FIFA World Cup Concacaf qualifier football match between Jamaica and Guatemala at the Independence Park stadium in Kingston on June 10, 2025. (Photo: AFP)

Mount Pleasant striker Warner Brown and Tottenham midfielder Tyrese Hall are among the players called up by Reggae Boyz coach Rudolph Speid for their quarterfinals clash against Concacaf giants Mexico in the Nations League next week.

Brown has not played for the Boyz since the failed 2026 World Cup qualifying campaign while Hall last suited up during the 2026 Unity Cup.

Rotherham United right back Denzel Hall is the only newcomer, while Colarado Springs Switchback striker Khori Bennett, Louisville City FC midfielder Kevon lambert and Tampa Bay Rowdies goalkeeper Jahmali Waite have also earned recalls.

Jamaica will host the first leg at the National Stadium on November 14, before travelling to Mexico on November 17 for the second leg.

The other quarter-final matchups will see USA take on Haiti, Canada battling Guatemala, and Curacao taking on Panama.

The winners will not only book their spot in the Nations League Finals in March but the Concacaf Gold Cup next summer.
