Andre Blake (captain), Jahmali Waite, Amal Knight

Defenders

Ronaldo Webster, Christopher Ainsworth, Joel Latibeaudiere, Kyle Ming, Richard King, Damion Lowe, Miguel Freckleton, Denzel Hall

Midfielders

Kevon Lambert, Courtney Clarke, Karoy Anderson, Dwight Merrick, Tyrese Hall, Brandon Cover

Forwards

Warner Brown, Javon East, Renaldo Cephas, Tyreece Campbell, Kaheim Dixon, Khori Bennett

World.title: Bleeding billions
World.content:
In this file photo rescue crew and civilians are at a fatal crash scene in rural Jamaica.

THE Island Traffic Authority (ITA) has estimated the economic cost of road fatalities in Jamaica for 2025 was US$72 million (approximately $11.5 billion).

The estimate factors in the number of crash victims, their age at the time they died in a fatal crash, and their projected earnings if they had lived to retirement age.

According to the annual crash report, released this week by the ITA, the US$72 million was an increase of approximately US$4 million when compared to 2024 based on an increase in the number of lives lost last year.

“This underscores that road safety is not only a public health issue but also a critical economic concern,” the ITA said.

The report notes that 374 people lost their lives in 325 fatal crashes in 2025, a two per cent increase in fatalities and a three per cent increase in fatal crashes when compared to 2024.

Despite the increase, the ITA remains optimistic that things are trending in the right direction.

“Although the road-related deaths were slightly higher in 2025, it marks the second-consecutive year in which fatalities fell below the 400 mark,” said the authority

“The reduction signifies a noteworthy stride toward national and global road safety targets, and offers an opportunity for reflection, recalibration, and momentum-building,” the ITA added.

It noted that Jamaica‘s goal is to meet the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety (2020-2030) target, which is to reduce the tally of road fatalities that occurred in 2020 by half.

“Jamaica‘s current progress towards this target is a reduction of 14 per cent. To meet the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety (2020-2030) target Jamaica‘s road fatalities on average must be reduced by 8.3 per cent per annum,” said the ITA.

The report shows that St Catherine was the deadliest parish for road users in 2025 with 65 deaths.

St Ann came next with 36, followed by St Elizabeth with 34, St James 32, and Westmoreland 31.

St Andrew recorded 29 fatalities during the year, Clarendon had 26, Hanover and St Mary had 22 each.

They are followed by Trelawny and Manchester, which each recorded 20 deaths. The three safest parishes for road users last year were Portland with nine deaths, St Thomas with 11, and Kingston with 17.

As to what is driving the high number of crashes and fatalities, the ITA stated that “the majority of traffic crashes are rooted in driver behaviour, with excessive speed remaining the most dominant cause”.

Last year 114 fatal crashes were attributed to speeding — continuing a trend over the last six years. This was followed by failure to keep to the correct traffic lane with 68 crashes; pedestrians walking or standing in the road led to 26 crashes; turning to the right without due care saw 13 crashes; and overtaking improperly on the offside resulted in 31 crashes.

“These leading causes suggest a combination of aggressive driving and poor road discipline,” said the ITA, as it pointed out that the category “Others” represents the combined total of various other causes of road fatalities, accounting for 122 deaths in 2025.

The ITA said understanding the demographic composition and timing of fatal road crashes is crucial for developing targeted, equitable, and impactful road safety policies.

The data from 2020 to 2025 reveal persistent and concerning patterns regarding gender and age.

Worryingly, road traffic fatalities continue to be overwhelmingly male-dominated. In 2025, males accounted for 85 per cent of all traffic deaths (318 of 374), while females accounted for 15 per cent.

“The data reinforces that, while road safety strategies must address the general population, men — especially younger and middle-aged males — should be a primary focus for targeted road safety initiatives,” said ITA.

The data also pointed to age-based analysis which reveals another layer of vulnerability.

In 2025, the 25-29 and 30-34 age groups recorded 48 deaths each, accounting for 26 per cent of the total number of fatalities.

“Individuals aged 20-60 years constitute the core of Jamaica’s workforce [and accounted] for 223 fatalities in 2025, representing a substantial economic loss to the country in terms of productivity and labour force capacity,” the ITA noted.

Meanwhile, the elderly, aged 60 and above, recorded 71 deaths, an 82 per cent increase compared to 2024.

The ITA said understanding when fatal crashes are most likely to occur is critical for effective road safety planning.

It said the analysis of crash distribution across time — by month and day of the week — and road user category provide patterns that can point to potential behavioural and temporal risk factors.

Over the past five years, the first quarter of the year (January to March) has consistently recorded high fatality numbers. However, in 2025, the third quarter reported the highest number of fatalities (106 deaths).

The traditionally high-risk, mid-year months — July and August — saw a resurgence in 2025, with July recording the highest total crashes for the year (39 deaths). November recorded the least number of deaths in 2025 (24).

In terms of day of the week, the data show that weekends remain disproportionately dangerous.

The ITA said Saturdays and Sundays consistently record the highest number of crashes and fatalities. In 2025, Sundays recorded 58 crashes and 74 deaths, while Saturdays accounted for 52 crashes and 64 deaths.

“These figures reflect persistent risks associated with weekend travel, which is typically characterised by leisure driving, night-time events, increased alcohol consumption, and higher traffic volumes and more varied traffic patterns associated with non-work activities,” added the ITA.

Christmas Day emerged as the most dangerous holiday over the six-year period, recording the highest number of fatal crashes (17) and fatalities (19).

This is followed by New Year’s Day (13 deaths) and Independence Day (12 deaths).

“The data indicate that festive holidays tend to be associated with increased road traffic fatalities, likely due to higher traffic volumes, longer travel distances, and celebratory activities,” the ITA noted.

World.title: Detective recounts gun find
World.content:
The Supreme Court in downtown Kingston where 25 alleged members of the Tesha Miller-led faction of the Klansman Gang are being tried.

A Clarendon police detective testified Thursday that he discovered two firearms hidden in a vehicle driven by former Jamaica Urban Transit Company (JUTC) bus driver Charles McLeary, one of 25 men on trial for crimes allegedly committed by the reputed Tesha Miller faction of the Klansman Gang.

That motor vehicle, a 2011 Honda Stream, was one of two seized by investigators after the takedown of five alleged members of the gang on Friday, June 26, 2020.

According to prosecutors, the accused — Bjourn Thomas, Sharn Gilzene, Conroy Cadogan, McLeary, and Kemar Francis — “knowingly facilitated the commission of a serious offence to wit the murder of Jermaine Jones and Allen Cameron” in John’s Hall, Clarendon, that same day. They were taken into custody following a highway chase.

The detective sergeant, testifying during the ongoing trial which has been unfolding in the Home Circuit Division of the Supreme Court in downtown Kingston, told the court that he went to the May Pen Police Station on Sunday, June 28, where he was introduced to McLeary, who was then 40 years old and a resident of Portmore, St Catherine; and Thomas, who was unemployed and a resident of Spanish Town.

He said after being introduced to the two, he went to the two motor vehicles

— which had been sealed with evidence tape

— that were parked on the compound accompanied by three other cops and the two accused. According to the cop, who said he only searched one of the two cars, under the direct gaze of McLeary and the others, after partially detaching the glove compartment of the vehicle and looking further into the cavity of the dashboard in a section of the air conditioner’s air filter, he saw “what looked like the base of a magazine and a pistol with a grip”.

The sleuth said he “shouted out ‘Find!’” when he made the discovery and pointed to where he observed the objects. He said after ensuring that McLeary not only saw but verbalised what was found, two forensic scene of crime investigators who were present photographed the silver and black 9mm Beretta pistol with the magazine affixed and packaged it. He told the court, under further questioning by the prosecutor marshalling the evidence, that in continuing his search he checked the gear lever section of the car by removing an area closer to the flooring of the vehicle and observed what looked like the pistol grip of a firearm.

He said the weapon, which was removed, shown to McLeary, and photographed by the forensic crime scene experts, turned out to be a black Smith & Wesson Springfield .40 calibre pistol with a magazine affixed. That pistol, he said, along with ammunition, was also packaged. The cop said, a further search of the vehicle turned up a pair of shoes in the trunk which McLeary claimed as his.

Asked by the prosecutor eliciting the evidence if he would be able to identify McLeary again if he saw him, the detective sergeant answered confidently in the affirmative. He was only allowed to do so, however, after the docks were reshuffled in his absence following a request from McLeary’s attorney Javed Grant.

Interestingly, 15 of the 17 accused who were in the main dock held their heads down from the moment the lawman entered and throughout his entire testimony, only sitting upright after trial judge Justice Dale Palmer instructed that they do so for the identification.

The lawman, who returned to the courtroom following the reshuffle, despite several intense moments spent looking at the 25 accused row by row, incorrectly identified the accused Shawn Pottinger as McLeary, sending a ripple of murmurs across the room. The Crown, at that point, indicated that it had no further questions for the cop but would be recalling him in relation to items it intends to tender.

Following the failed identification, Grant, in cross-examining the cop, accused him of lying about his observation of the serial number on one of the pistols. According to the cop, he had not touched the firearm but based on his proximity to the scenes of crime officer who retrieved it, had been able to view the number.

“I am suggesting to you that you are lying when you say you observed the serial number while the forensic officers handled it,” Grant challenged.

“I totally reject that suggestion,” the cop shot back.

The 25 accused — the second faction of the gang to now be tried by the courts — are to answer to 16 offences allegedly committed over the span of five years between August 2017 and November 2022, according to the case being built by the Crown.

In the matter which began in February this year, the prosecution in unveiling what it said was the “anatomy” of the gang, said it would be leading evidence to show that members acted as drivers, among them Thomas and Francis, along with the accused Dwayne Frater, and Travis Drummond. It said it would establish that McLeary was linked by employment and by role in the criminal organisation.

World.title: Shenseea finds freedom in growth
World.content:
Shenseea’s latest EP, Catalyst, will be released on Friday, November 5.

“I feel like it’s better to be judged than not experience something at all,” said international recording artiste Shenseea.

For her, those words represent more than a change in perspective. They capture a personal turning point, one that required her to confront the things she had kept buried. It is this willingness to let go, to embrace the uncomfortable, and allow listeners access to a more unguarded side of her, that gives her latest EP, Catalyst, its emotional centre.

The eight-track project, which will be released today, Friday, November 6, finds the artiste reflecting on how far she has travelled, while making room for the woman she is still becoming.

Rather than abandoning the sounds and personality that first endeared her to audiences, Shenseea sees the release as an opportunity to reconnect with those foundations while moving confidently into another phase of her career.

At the heart of that journey is Vulnerability, a deeply personal offering that she describes as one of the most creatively fulfilling songs she has recorded.

“Vulnerability is the one song I really felt like I was putting it all out there on, for sure. It’s definitely in my top five of most creative songs ever, because it’s my most vulnerable song. Of all the records that I’ve put out, you’ve never heard me sing like that before, or say the stuff that I’m saying. It came straight from the heart,” she told the Jamaica Observer’s Splash.

For an artiste accustomed to commanding attention through her confident delivery and larger-than-life performances, allowing that level of emotional exposure was not necessarily an easy decision. However, she had reached a point at which keeping her thoughts and experiences to herself was beginning to take a toll on her creativity. There were things she wanted to communicate to her audience, experiences she wanted to put into context, and parts of her story she felt had remained misunderstood. Yet, in trying to keep those feelings contained, she was inadvertently creating a barrier between herself and the music.

“I had so much on my mind, so much I wanted to say to the people, letting them know what went down, giving them behind-the-scenes of why things are happening, and why I am how I am. I was holding it in and mi just couldn’t focus creatively. It was draining the life out of me. I couldn’t get to put it in my music and I couldn’t have fun with the music because I was so bothered personally,” she explained.

Eventually, she realised that the freedom she needed could only come from laying it all out on a track.

“I had to put it out there just to clear up myself and, honestly, ever since I released that track I feel so liberated and free,” she said.

The response from listeners further affirmed her decision, with many recognising the significance of seeing an otherwise guarded side of the artiste.

“I think people really took from it that, ‘Wow, she really let it all out,’ and that’s what it was made for,” she added.

That sense of liberation is central to the thinking behind Catalyst, whose title reflects Shenseea’s recognition that meaningful growth cannot be rushed.

Looking back at the earlier stages of her career, she acknowledges that her ambition sometimes made her eager to reach the destination without fully appreciating the experiences required to get there. Knowing the heights she wanted to achieve, she admits that she sometimes overlooked the importance of the journey itself.

“Earlier on in my career, there is a lesson I learnt. It’s that you cannot change from point A to Z without going through the rest of the alphabet, and I feel like I took that leap,” she said. “Being young and in the industry and knowing where I wanted to go, it was like I didn’t remember that I couldn’t do it all at once. That’s what helped me to make Catalyst, because I felt like I needed to take those steps that I felt like I stepped over.

“I felt like I missed some steps and Catalyst is me trying to make the smoothest transition into a new phase without changing me entirely,” she added.

It is a perspective that speaks to an artiste who is increasingly comfortable with the idea that evolution does not require abandoning one’s identity. Having explored different sounds and audiences throughout her career, Shenseea is now interested in bringing the different chapters of her musical journey into conversation with each other.

“The version of me that you’re getting on this EP is the Shenyeng Anthem mixed with Lighter Shenseea. Mi feel like it’s going to show where I’m coming from, you’ll feel the nostalgia. It’s also going to show where we are currently, and where we’re headed,” she said.

That connection to her beginnings is particularly important as she reflects on her personal growth; personally and artistically.

“Everything that I have said to myself that this is how I see myself in the future at this age, doing this, singing this, at this level, I am doing it right now,” she said. “So every other thing that I wanna accomplish is literally just for young Shenseea before the artistry begun. Just me listening to the music and deciding I wanted to become an international superstar. I am very proud of myself.”

The journey, however, has not been without its difficult moments. Shenseea acknowledged experiencing a period of depression that was unfamiliar to her and left her questioning herself in ways she had not previously experienced. With the help of God, and those around her, she said she was able to navigate that chapter and arrive at a place of greater contentment.

“This is how I felt when I just started out and this is why this project is so important to me. I feel like I’m starting over, but phase two,” she explained.

That renewed outlook has also influenced her relationship with music itself. While the pursuit of international recognition and industry accolades formed part of the ambition that propelled her forward, she is now placing greater emphasis on the simple pleasure of creating.

“I really had to bring back some stuff that makes me feel like I have to go hard, and that includes doing music for the love and not just for a submission or accolades. The music I am doing now is because I literally have fun doing them, I am in love with them, and I want to share them with the world,” she said.

The shift comes alongside another chapter in her professional journey, following a change in management as she continues to navigate the demands of an international career. For Shenseea, the transition is another reminder that growth sometimes requires accepting that certain people and circumstances are only meant to accompany you for a portion of the journey.

“I feel like nothing happens before its time, and one thing I had to sit with is that not everyone who started the journey with you, is meant to finish it with you,” she told Splash. “Stuff happens along the way and you can either decide to be like this is it, or you choose something or someone who will help you carry on your journey further. I feel like everything is just God. His timing is so impeccable, and I can’t argue with that. I have the drive in me to keep going and that’s what I’m going to do.”

Catalyst is now available for streaming across all digital platforms.

World.title: Kemtek means business
World.content:
Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang (second right) congratulates Kemtek Development and Construction Limited Chairman and Managing Director Dr Sylvester Tulloch following the official opening of the company’s new corporate headquarters on Constant Spring Road, on Wednesday. Sharing the moment are Tulloch’s sons and fellow Kemtek directors, Garwin (left) and Karl.

AFTER nearly four decades concentrating on residential housing, family-owned Kemtek Development and Construction Limited has made its first investment in commercial real estate, completing a 90,000-square-foot corporate complex along Constant Spring Road, St Andrew in a move that broadens its property business beyond the sale of homes.

The development at 147–149 Constant Spring Road — officially opened on Wednesday evening — combines Kemtek’s new corporate headquarters with five of the six floors intended for leasing, positioning the company to earn rental income alongside revenues from its long-standing residential development operations.

The investment represents a significant departure for the Tulloch family business, which has spent the past 37 years developing housing communities across Jamaica and is currently undertaking five gated developments comprising approximately 2,500 housing solutions in Greater Bernard Lodge, St Catherine.

Kemtek has not disclosed how much it spent on the commercial complex, which has been six years in the making since the company acquired the property in 2020. However, the development marks an expansion of its property interests as it puts its experience in residential construction to work in the commercial market.

Chairman and Managing Director Dr Sylvester Tulloch, who founded the company in 1989, described the project as a new stage in Kemtek’s development.

“For 37 years, Kemtek has been associated primarily with residential development. Today, this building demonstrates that the knowledge, expertise, and experience we have accrued over those years can also be applied to commercial property development,” he told guests at Wednesday’s opening.

The move also marks a striking progression for a company that once operated from just 600 square feet of rented premises on Balmoral Avenue in Kingston. Its new building represents 150 times that space, reflecting the growth of a business that has delivered thousands of homes and progressively expanded its operations over the decades.

Director Garwin Tulloch, reflecting on the company’s journey during the ceremony, recalled its progression from the Balmoral Avenue office to an 800-square-foot location at another commercial complex, before expanding further to accommodate its administrative and legal operations.

“This transition has been remarkable. From 600 square feet of rented space to where we are today,” he said, recalling visits to the original office as a schoolboy and the responsibilities he now carries in the family enterprise.

While the company has not disclosed the financing structure for its latest investment, Garwin acknowledged Jamaica National as a financing partner and National Commercial Bank for its support during the company’s early days. The current project involved several local contractors and suppliers, with Karl Tulloch, who oversees administration and special projects, playing a central role in coordinating the development.

Kemtek’s move into commercial real estate comes against the background of a residential portfolio that has expanded considerably since its first development in St Catherine in 1989. The company has delivered more than 3,000 housing solutions across its North Coast developments, including projects in Drax Hall, St Ann, while its ongoing Greater Bernard Lodge programme represents another substantial commitment to the housing market.

The company’s origins, however, were considerably more modest than its current development pipeline suggests.

The elder Tulloch, who previously spent 10 years in teaching and another decade in development banking, established Kemtek on June 15, 1989, with the ambition of providing quality homes at affordable prices. Its first project, undertaken with business partner Frank Otter, involved the acquisition of approximately 29 acres at Keystone, St Catherine, for $1 million.

Raising the equity for that acquisition required Tulloch to sell his personal vehicle for $350,000 and secure a further $150,000 loan from the then Mutual Security Bank. The partners subsequently sold 25 lots at $50,000 each to generate initial construction funds before obtaining a $12-million debenture loan from Jamaica National Building Society to advance the development.

The project was completed within three years, establishing the financial base for further expansion. Tulloch and his late wife, Julie, subsequently acquired full ownership of the business after buying out the original partner.

Kemtek went on to develop residential properties across several parishes, but its growth was tested during Jamaica’s financial crisis in the 1990s, when interest rates climbed to approximately 35 per cent and the company found itself carrying an $18-million loan against townhouses that were proving difficult to sell.

Rather than continue accumulating interest, Tulloch said he calculated the cost of six months’ interest payments and reduced the asking prices of the remaining units by an equivalent amount. Within six months, Kemtek had sold four units, repaid the outstanding loan and retained enough capital to acquire another property.

“That experience taught me an important lesson. Success in business is not simply about having good plans. It is about recognising when circumstances have changed and having the courage to change your strategy,” he said.

The business has since grown into a second-generation family enterprise, with Tulloch’s four sons occupying key management positions. Garwin oversees operations, Handel is responsible for technical services, Karl handles administration and special projects, while Romain leads human resources.

Their involvement has become an important part of Kemtek’s succession planning as the company seeks to preserve the business established by its founder while pursuing new areas of investment.

“For me, this represents something very important. It represents continuity, succession, and the opportunity to build an institution that will outlive its founders,” elder Tulloch said.

Wednesday’s opening attracted several senior government officials, including Deputy Prime Minister Dr Horace Chang, who delivered the keynote address, ministers Daryl Vaz and Dr Christopher Tufton, Minister of State Delano Seiveright, Opposition Member of Parliament Fitz Jackson and St Andrew Custos, Ian Forbes.

Chang praised the company’s contribution to Jamaica’s housing market and highlighted the role of developers in creating employment and supporting the development of safer communities. He also pointed to the importance of construction quality, particularly as the country continues its recovery from Hurricane Melissa.

During the ceremony, the elder Tulloch also announced the establishment of the Kemtek Foundation, which is expected to commence operations with $50 million in seed funding, increasing eventually to $100 million. The foundation will provide scholarships and educational grants, support early childhood institutions and assist vulnerable families.

World.title: WE’VE GOT THIS!
World.content:
Head coach Sasher-Gaye Henry-Wright (second left) instructs Jamaica’s senior Sunshine Girls during a practice match against an All-Star Mixed Team at National Indoor Sports Centre on December 5, 2025. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

JAMAICA Netball Head Coach Sasher-Gaye Henry-Wright says the return of senior players, led by co-captain Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard, has lifted spirits in the camp as the Sunshine Girls prepare for the four-match Horizon Series against England Roses.

The series represents the final scheduled major assignment for the Sunshine Girls before the 2027 Netball World Cup.

The team leaves for England on November 14, ahead of the first two encounters at the Copper Box Arena in London on November 21 and 22. The series then returns home for the final two matches at the National Indoor Sports Centre (NISC) in St Andrew on December 5 and 6.

Contested in honour of netball icons Jamaica’s Molly Rhone and England’s Jean Hornsby, the Horizon Series has quickly developed into a keen rivalry since its inception in 2024.

The inaugural series produced a classic, with Jamaica claiming a 2-1 victory after one match was tied, underlining the evenly matched nature of the two sides.

Last year, England ran out 2-0 winners after both matches in Jamaica were cancelled due to the devastating passage of Hurricane Melissa in October 2025, leaving unfinished business between the teams.

This year’s renewal carries added significance, coming on the back of a historic campaign for the Sunshine Girls, who captured a silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games.

And Henry-Wright says excitement is building.

“I mean, we’re excited that we have a lot of our senior players back. This is our last preparation. We’re actually picking up our preparation for World Cup next year. So it’s good to have most of your players in. It’s a great feeling,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“Training is going well, so far. We’re really trying to intensify as much as we can in terms of physical preparation and also in terms of tactical preparation. I mean, there are still areas that we really need to work on. You know, we still don’t have all the combinations, but, you know, sometimes when you don’t have it, it’s good that girls have to work without certain areas to keep a little bit more discipline.

“But we are quite excited that we have most of our players. So we have six players that are away that will join the squad, we have two in England and four in Australia and we have a week to prepare so it’s going to be hard work that is one disadvantage that we have to join so late but despite that we’re really trying to ramp up mental preparation, physical preparation and all the other preparations that we can,” Henry-Wright added.

The biggest boost, she said, is the return of Fowler-Nembhard from maternity leave.

“We’re just happy to have back Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard. I think you know she’s just coming out of maternity leave. You know nothing to prove and we’re just hoping that she will lead from the front as one of our captains. She’s always carrying the team, being disciplined leading from the front so the expectation is the same and I know she’s excited to rejoin so we just can’t wait to reunite with her,” Henry-Wright said.

Jamaica enter the series ranked number four in the world, one spot behind England at number three, and Henry-Wright expects a high-intensity battle for the trophy.

“We are very excited about our Commonwealth performance. It comes down to how hard we play and how steady and focused we keep so it’s a high intensity game. England is a very good component. They are number three in the world. We are ranked number four. They have the last tournament and they will be coming hard to maintain that. We also want to take back that trophy. It comes down to how disciplined our girls are, how well they will improve and take care of that ball. Try to get a lot of defensive plays so that they can keep attacking the game. We’re looking forward to a very intense and fierce competition from our rivals,” she said.

With six overseas-based players joining late, Henry-Wright admitted the short preparation window will be demanding, but said the squad is used to each other and will hit the ground running once together.

“I mean, we just have to start as we get there, you know, in terms of our preparation. As soon as we meet, we get together and we’ll start our preparation in terms of our court work and whatever team building and bonding activities we do, we’ll definitely do whatever mental preparation we need to do, we will definitely do to get them ready. And they are used to each other. I mean, they have not played. I mean, some of them might play with Janelle for the first time because I know Brie would be playing with her for the first time. So it’s going to be interesting and it’s something that will is going to be new to us so you know it’s just good that we can get that connection in the attack going,” Henry-Wright explained.

Despite the challenges, she insisted the mood in camp is high.

“The spirit is high, I think as we get closer I think the girls are even more excited and you know mean more you know going a little bit harder and harder for each training session I think we’re building nicely so it’s just the time that we will just meet together continue preparing ensuring that they stay healthy and, you know, giving all the good recoveries that we can and for them to really execute and keep practising and building for each training session,” she said.

World.title: Ein Spaziergang mit Bodo Ramelow
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Share via email

Die Welt spielt verrückt, doch im Präsidium des Bundestages herrscht überraschende Einigkeit. Bundestagsvizepräsident Bodo Ramelow (Die Linke) gibt im Gespräch mit Gordon Repinski einen seltenen Einblick in die überparteiliche Zusammenarbeit, auch bei Nachtschichten. Dabei wird deutlich, mit welcher Strategie das Gremium den Provokationen der AfD begegnet.

In seiner eigenen Partei brodelt es derweil gewaltig. Ramelow findet deutliche Worte zur Antisemitismus-Debatte innerhalb der Linken und kritisiert das taktische Lavieren einzelner Abgeordneter. Warum er trotzdem eine Gesinnungsprüfung ablehnt, aber klare rote Linien beim Existenzrecht Israels zieht, offenbart die tiefe Zerrissenheit seiner Partei.

Zudem verrät er, warum die Wahrnehmung der Linken im Bundestag derzeit auch von der Gruppe der „Silberlocken“ abhängt, wie sich die Silberlocken regelmäßig absprechen und warum er sich trotz aller Krisen nicht verrückt machen lässt.

Mit den Linken, aber auch der SPD und den Grünen beschäftigt sich auch der neue Podcast von POLITICO und WELT. In „Inside Links“ geht es jede Woche darum, wie in Deutschland womöglich eine neue linke Mehrheit entsteht, zu welchem Preis und wer künftig dabei möglicherweise am Regierungstisch sitzen könnte. „Inside Links“ gibt es auf den Podcast-Plattformen zu hören und zu sehen, unter anderem auch hier.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

Für alle Hauptstadt-Profis: Der Berlin Playbook-Newsletter bietet jeden Morgen die wichtigsten Themen und Einordnungen. Jetzt kostenlos abonnieren.

World.title: Merz’s conservatives poised to nominate Germany’s first woman president
World.content:
President of the Bavarian parliament Ilse Aigner arrives at the Christian Social Union party congress in Munich, on Oct. 23, 2026. | Alexandra Beier/AFP via Getty Images

BERLIN — Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner is set to become Germany’s next president, making her the country’s first woman to hold the office, according to two senior conservatives with knowledge of the matter.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s conservative bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) will nominate Aigner to succeed outgoing German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the officials told BILD, which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network. Both officials were granted anonymity to discuss internal party matters freely. Aigner’s nomination will officially be announced Monday, according to the officials.

Aigner, who previously served as agriculture minister under former German Chancellor Angela Merkel from 2008 to 2013, is currently president of the Bavarian State Parliament. She is also a member of the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

World.title: Trump’s ‘big, beautiful’ European security plan isn’t convincing Europe
World.content:
The latest U.S. proposal underscores growing anxiety around Trump’s fresh rapprochement with Russia as he ramps up pressure on Ukraine and his administration attempts to revive long-stalled talks to end Moscow’s full-scale war against Kyiv.

POLITICO spoke to 12 NATO diplomats, EU envoys and European government officials, all of whom were granted anonymity to speak freely on the sensitive issue. NATO allies were not briefed about the American plans in advance, according to three alliance diplomats, and many remain skeptical of the idea.

U.S. President Donald Trump late Thursday talked of a “big, beautiful agreement,” after meeting with Putin’s envoy Kirill Dmitriev, adding: “It’s going to involve more than Ukraine, and I could even say it might involve all of Europe.”

“Our objective is to develop practical arrangements that address the security concerns of all sides, reduce the risk of future conflict, and create a more stable and predictable security environment,” Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner added soon after.

Kushner said the arrangement would have five goals: “Permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.”

“It is a bit obscure what Kushner meant,” said one NATO diplomat. “The general sentiment in Europe is that any discussion with Russia on the future architecture at the moment will just be used by Moscow to legitimize their arguments ... it will not fly with the European allies.”

World.title: Wave of bomb threats target Irish media outlets and more European flights
World.content:
“We have expected a rise in hybrid threats to Ireland because of our hosting of the EU presidency, and the EPC meeting will be by far the biggest set-piece event of that presidency, so one must presume it’s no coincidence that we’re experiencing this spike in hybrid activity now,” the Irish official said.

The Irish government said the threats against media outlets were probably part of a European-wide pattern of threats that have targeted dozens of airlines this week, including Irish carriers Ryanair and Aer Lingus. Hackers also targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in at least seven European countries.

“It is not known yet who is responsible for these threats, whether it is individuals or a centralized or coordinated effort,” the Irish government said in a statement. “However, these threats come on the heels of the ongoing disruption to aviation around Europe caused by similar threats, and it seems likely that this is a coordinated campaign of disruption.”

Bomb threats also targeted at least 18 European flights Friday, after at least 22 the day before, raising concerns that the hoaxes may be part of a coordinated campaign to disrupt air traffic.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares told Spanish public broadcaster TVE on Friday that the bomb threats affecting flights could be “an attempt at hybrid aggression and war in some psychological way.” He added that “it cannot be a coincidence that so many identical events occur with the same modus operandi throughout Europe.”

Luis Gallego, CEO of airline group IAG, said: “It is clear that what they [the perpetrators] are looking for is to create chaos and disruption in the different airports.”

World.title: Spain and the Netherlands battle over ECB presidency
World.content:
Exiting European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde gives a press conference in Frankfurt am Main, Germany, on Oct. 29, 2026. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images

Pablo Hernández de Cos and Klaas Knot are in the hunt for the top job after Christine Lagarde’s exit.

BRUSSELS — The Netherlands and Spain on Friday submitted candidates to succeed Christine Lagarde, who steps down as president of the European Central Bank on Feb. 7.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, a former president of the Dutch central bank, were the only candidates to emerge after the 5 p.m. deadline, as expected.

Their candidacies are part of a larger game of musical chairs that includes France and Germany, as Europe’s four economic powerhouses negotiate how to secure their seats on the ECB’s executive board.

World.title: ‘I don’t know if it reassured or worried them’: European envoys quiz Le Pen over lunch
World.content:
The group of ambassadors from the eight countries that share a border with metropolitan France — Germany, Spain, Belgium, Italy, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Monaco and Andorra — already met with conservative presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau in September. They are planning to host meetings with the other presidential hopefuls, including far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, at their respective embassies in the coming months.

“I don’t know if it reassured or worried them,” said an adviser to Marine Le Pen who accompanied her to the lunch. “What is sure is that they can now report back to their capitals what the National Rally wants to do,” the adviser added.

Le Pen was mainly questioned about her plans to downsize the EU and on bilateral issues, as well as U.S. President Donald Trump after his seismic defeat in the midterm elections.

While in the past, the National Rally has been supportive of Trump, the party has progressively distanced itself from the U.S. president. The National Rally’s Jordan Bardella on Wednesday said his party was not affected by the result and suggested that Trump’s popularity was undermined by the war in the Middle East and its economic consequences.



Le Pen has also been campaigning for a harsher approach on migration, which would involve stricter checks at the borders, potentially impacting countries whose envoys she met on Wednesday. All of them, apart from Andorra and Monaco, are part of the Schengen free-movement area.

“There is a general interest on what would her stance be on the key issues of mutual interest and cooperation on which we are working with France,” said one diplomat from a participating country.

“It was a very frank exchange. She told them what she says everywhere and she was able to elaborate on a number of topics a little more at length than she would do on TV,” the same adviser said, adding that Le Pen regularly meets ambassadors.

Back in December, Le Pen and her No. 2 Jordan Bardella also met with U.S. ambassador Charles Kushner. The far-right leaders are also preparing the ground for a possible election win by meeting top French business executives.

Marcelo Wesfreid and Nicolas Camut contributed to this report.

World.title: Election favorite says Spain should quit as World Cup co-host if Morocco stages the final
World.content:
Feijóo noted that the 2030 World Cup was originally a Spanish-Portuguese bid, until Morocco was invited at a later stage. Despite that chronology, Moroccan officials have been pushing vigorously to stage the final, which is the world’s most prestigious sports event.

Rafael Louzán, Spain’s football chief, told POLITICO in June that he was confident either Madrid or Barcelona would host the final, despite Morocco pouring vast amounts of cash into football infrastructure.

Tensions have flared between the two countries in recent months. Spanish political parties this summer accused Morocco of stoking a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, after 80,000 people surged into the city in late July.

A Sigma Dos poll for El Mundo following the Ceuta crisis found that 84.4% of Spaniards opposed Spain continuing to co-host the World Cup with Morocco.

Leftist party Sumar, the Socialists’ junior coalition partner, said this summer that the World Cup “cannot be shared with a country that uses desperate people for its own geostrategic interests.”

The left-wing party tabled a resolution in parliament that far-right Vox backed in an unusual convergence. The text never made it to a vote because parliament was dissolved ahead of the snap election.

World.title: EU prosecutors open second fraud probe into Spanish high-speed rail
World.content:
The EPPO did not clarify what investigators are looking for or whether any money was misspent, and no findings have been made public. It added that no further details would be released at this stage.

A first probe, opened in March after the Adamuz crash that killed 46 people, covered EU funds for track maintenance on the same line. There has been no public update on its progress.

The EU’s Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas expressed deep concern at a press briefing on Wednesday over two serious accidents in Spain within a year, calling them “very worrying” and “definitely not something we want to see.” He noted that Spain had reached out to the EU’s railway agency, ERA, to assist with the ongoing national investigation.

Two senior Spanish officials have already stepped down following the Urda crash. Puente resigned Tuesday, calling his decision “a matter of political dignity,” while Adif President Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña quit Wednesday, less than 24 hours later.

Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo is running the Transport Ministry until the Nov. 29 election. The crash took place just weeks before the vote, with Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialists already trailing in the polls and facing further political fallout over the tragedy.

World.title: ‘Brief burst of intense heat’ could give hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades a second life
World.content:
Wind energy has been described as one of the “cheapest and most scalable solutions” to the climate crisis – but its boom is creating growing concern.

 

Turbines dotted across Europe and its waters are engineered to withstand some of the harshest conditions, from intense UV radiation to strong wind gusts, extreme temperatures and even lightning strikes.

While around 85 to 90 per cent of a wind turbine’s total mass can be recycled, the durability of the blades makes it difficult for the remaining elements to be reprocessed.

Wind turbine blades are clogging up Europe’s landfills

As a result, many turbine blades end up in landfill sites once they are decommissioned, typically after 20 years of service, or are incinerated.

Annual decommissioned blade waste in Europe is projected to increase from 20,000 tonnes in 2025 to 55,000 tonnes by 2030 as older fleets reach their end-of-life.

WindEurope, the European wind industry association, introduced a voluntary industry-wide landfill ban that came into effect last year to tackle this.

The association is urging EU policymakers to enshrine the ban into formal legislation, arguing it would further accelerate the development of sustainable recycling technologies.

Wind turbines undergo flash joule heating

Researchers have recently discovered a new way to give hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades a second life – by subjecting them to a “brief burst of intense heat”.

The study, published in the science journal Chem Circularity, found so-called ‘flash joule heating’ can transform blades – often made from silica-containing fiberglass and carbon-rich polymer resin – into silicon carbide and graphene, two valuable materials for manufacturing.

Blades were heated to about 2,000°C in seconds; at such high temperatures, carbon can react with silica to form silicon carbide, a hard, heat-resistant material.

Carbon can also reorganise into graphene under these conditions, a material known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity.

The research team found that adding the broken-down blades to other materials before heating made the new material more useful for creating new rotor blades.

Just 0.3 per cent (by weight) of the recovered materials was able to make resin stiffer and stronger and improve its resistance to deformation by 27 per cent under tension and nine per cent when bent.

“The mixture of silicon carbide and graphene can be incorporated back into resins for new wind turbine blades, improving their mechanical and thermal properties,” says senior author and chemical and environmental engineer Bing Deng of Tsinghua University, China.

“That is more than recycling – it’s upcycling. We’re turning something that has little value into something that’s worth much more.”

World.title: Earn points, save cash: A basic guide to frequent-flyer programmes in Europe
World.content:
Unless you’re an actual frequent flyer, you probably don’t pay much attention to loyalty programmes.

 

And why would you? You might assume that if you’re not constantly racking up air miles, it’s not worth your time.

That’s where you’d be wrong, because it takes very little effort to set yourself up in a way that will earn you points in your sleep, all of which puts money back in your pocket the next time you go to book a flight.

Here’s everything you need to know about the main frequent-flyer programmes in Europe.

Back to basics: Why should I join a frequent-flyer programme?

There are two main reasons to join a frequent-flyer programme: Earning miles, which can be used to pay for things, and earning elite status, which gives you benefits like lounge access every time you fly.

Confusingly, the names for miles and tier status points vary from airline to airline.

As an example, passengers flying with Qatar Airways earn both Avios and Qpoints with every flight. Avios can be used to pay for flights or upgrades, while Qpoints help you move between privilege club membership tiers.

The lowest tier on Qatar Airways is burgundy – to reach silver, you need to earn 150 Qpoints within any 12-month period. For gold, it’s 300; for platinum, it’s 600.

As a silver member, benefits include 15kg extra baggage allowance, priority boarding, and lounge access. You also get a 25% tier bonus on eligible flights, which makes it easier to keep the status once you’ve initially earned it.

As you move up the tiers, the benefits improve.

By contrast, the Air France-KLM travel currency is simply called “Miles”, while experience points (XP) help with your status tier.

The lowest tier is explorer; to become a silver member, you need to earn 100 XP in a year; for gold, 180 XP; for ultimate, you need 900 XP.

You earn more miles per flight depending on what tier you are (meaning you can save more money), while some tiers also have free seat selection, lounge access and additional baggage.

Which frequent-flyer programme should I join?

The short answer to this is: You should probably join all of them.

I’m certainly not saying pull up a list of every single airline out there and methodically make your way through them. But every time you fly with a new carrier, you might as well sign up while booking the flight, particularly now many airlines are offering free on-board wifi to members.

The long answer is: You should pick one main airline, then try to fly mostly with them along with other carriers that are part of the same alliance.

This is because you’ll be able to transfer miles earned between different airlines, meaning miles you earned flying around Europe with British Airways could be used to get money off a flight to Tokyo with Japan Airlines, or to Sydney with Qantas. All three carriers are part of the oneworld Alliance.

Many airlines are part of alliances, which means you can use your miles with different carriers Skyteam

And why do airline alliances matter?

You could pick your main airline willy-nilly, but the easiest option will be to look at which airports are nearest to you and see if any of them are a home base for a full-service – not budget – carrier.

As an example, Amsterdam Schiphol is the home base for KLM. If you fly from this airport frequently, chances are you are already flying with them naturally as they will serve the most destinations from the Dutch capital.

By signing up to KLM’s Flying Blue frequent-flyer programme – which is also the same programme for Air France and Transavia – you’ll benefit from the SkyTeam airline alliance. This means you’ll be able to transfer points or miles gained from flying between carriers in the group.

In Europe, SkyTeam airlines include Air France, Air Europa, Scandinavian Airlines, TAROM and Virgin Atlantic, but the group also has carriers like Delta Air Lines and Aeroméxico in North America, plus Korean Air, China Airlines and Vietnam Airlines and Saudia in Asia.

If your nearest airport is Frankfurt or Munich, signing up for Lufthansa’s Miles & More scheme gives you access to the Star Alliance.

That alliance includes European carriers like Aegean Airlines, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, LOT Polish Airlines, TAP Air Portugal and Turkish Airlines, plus United Airlines, Air Canada and Copa Airlines in the Americas; Singapore Airlines, Air China, ANA and EVA Air in Asia; and Air New Zealand in Australasia.

Should your main airport be Madrid, then you’ll want to join the Iberia Club to access the oneworld Alliance.

European airlines signed up to the scheme include British Airways and Finnair; Asian carriers like Cathay Pacific, Japan Airlines, Qatar Airways and Malaysia Airlines; plus Qantas in Australasia.

Budget airlines like Ryanair, Wizz Air or easyJet aren’t typically members of airline alliances, nor do they have frequent flyer programmes in the traditional sense.

However, easyJet now offers “easyJet Plus” membership, which is a set annual fee that gives benefits like speedy boarding, a large cabin bag included on board, and free premium seat selection. Wizz Air has a “Discount Club”, which includes discounts on fares and on luggage after paying the annual fee.

Those who make it to a higher status tier with an airline might get free lounge access KLM

How to earn miles – without flying

The amount of miles you earn while flying depends on a number of factors, such as the seat class you flew in, your airline tier status, and either the length of the flight or its cost.

But it certainly isn’t the only way to earn – for many airlines, it’s not even how the majority of people do so. In 2015, American Airlines sold 58% of its miles to third parties, meaning just 42% were handed out through flight purchases.

Different airlines will have different partners, which you’ll be able to find on the relevant carrier’s website, but they typically cover travel-associated spending, like hotels, car rentals and tour operators. They may also cover retail brands.

Members of the Aer Lingus loyalty programme, AerClub, can earn Avios on Uber rides, by shopping at M&S, and ordering through Domino’s – you just need to make sure you’ve registered to collect Avios with the right partner.

Many hotel groups, such as Marriott Bonvoy or Accor, have partnerships with airline brands which mean points you earn during stays can be changed into miles, although the ratios may not necessarily be 1:1.

Throughout the year, hotels or airlines may run special promotions that increase the number of miles you earn for a set period of time.

While you may get an email about it in your inbox, you can also follow specialty blogs that are dedicated to maximising your loyalty points earning. These vary from country to country, but in the UK, there is Head for Points, while in Germany you can try Meilenjunkies.

These websites also go into detail about various co-branded credit or debit cards you can 

All I can say is that it’s a big commitment, and that you should fully read all of the terms and conditions before signing up for anything.

Other ways to earn tier status

Another reason airport alliances matter is that some carriers offer status matches.

Essentially, this means that if you have reached the silver or gold tier with one brand, you might be able to get the same with another without having to match the number of flights taken.

Virgin Atlantic offers status matches for all the SkyTeam alliance airlines. For silver status, you need to book one Virgin Atlantic flight in any cabin and share proof of status; for gold, you’ll need to share the same proof but make a premium or upper class booking.

Outside of the alliance, Virgin Atlantic will also match status on British Airways, Iberia and Lufthansa.

You can use your miles to upgrade to business class Lufthansa

How much are my miles worth, and what can I spend them on?

There’s no way to exchange airline miles for cash, so there’s no actual “worth” set in stone.

Points can be used to save money on flights, to pay for an upgrade, or to pay for the flight completely, although airlines will only have a set number of miles-only seats on each plane. You may also be able to use them at the airline partners where you can earn them, which we covered above.

When people talk about how much your airline miles are worth, this is how much money you are saving by using them divided by the number you have – so you may get more bang for your buck depending on what you use them for.

The blogs mentioned above will have various breakdowns for the different airline miles and recommendations for how to spend them, but of course, it’s up to you.

A few years back, I used my miles whenever I could to save money on flights, but nowadays, I prefer to save them up and upgrade to business class when I have enough.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 7th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: 'We have proven ourselves': UAE vows to remain reliable energy supplier to Europe
World.content:
The UAE will remain a reliable energy supplier to Europe and the world despite the regional crisis, Undersecretary of Energy and Petroleum Affairs Sharif Al Olama told Euronews.

 

Speaking at ADIPEC in Abu Dhabi, Al Olama said the UAE's oil exports continued throughout the crisis and that the country is using the experience to strengthen its energy infrastructure.

"I'm glad to say that we have proven ourselves during this crisis," he said.

Away from the cameras, conversations among the senior officials gathered at ADIPEC from across the world were dominated by the threat of renewed military strikes in the region amid the ongoing US-Iran war. Many had resigned themselves to their inevitability, while still hoping diplomacy could find a way forward.

Al Olama was candid about the pressure the sector has faced. "This is not a big secret. We are going through a crisis. The first few months were very difficult."

He credited the UAE's long-term decision to spread its energy mix across nuclear, renewables and fossil fuels, with hydrogen and other future fuels in development.

"To diversify the energy sources was the right decision to make and it has helped in terms of making sure that our systems continue to operate and the services were uninterrupted during the entire period of the crisis," Al Olama said.

He credited investment in diversified export routes for keeping oil moving to international customers, with further improvement expected "as time goes by".

"In the case of our oil exports, it has continued during the crisis."

Lessons from the period are now being built into facility design, the capacity under construction and the back-up held across the system. "We have learned a lot from the current crisis when it comes to the design of our facilities, when it comes the capacities that we are building, when it come to the redundancy in the systems itself."

On renewables, Al Olama said the UAE now has around 8.2 gigawatts of solar capacity, with plans to grow to 20 gigawatts and beyond.

"We are getting some of the cheapest kilowatt-hours that renewable energies can produce in the world here in the UAE and we're only expanding on that," he explained.

"So there are massive projects coming on their way over the next few years."

Planning for AI demand

The rapid growth of AI data centres, a recurring theme on the exhibition floor at ADIPEC, presents what he described as a global challenge for energy planners, and one Europe faces as it races to build its own AI capacity.

"The growth you're seeing is no longer even exponential. It's a vertical growth. That's massive," Al Olama said.

The UAE's answer starts with efficiency, he pointed out, citing cases where AI tools have cut power consumption at some data centres by 40%. Planning for expansion, cooling and the use of existing infrastructure follows.

"This is a challenge that we're living through, but we are planning properly for the future," Al Olama said.

Asked whether Europe could learn from the UAE, he framed it as a two-way exchange. "I think, to be honest, it's not about teaching, I think how governments interact. We learn from each other."

He said the UAE is looking at rating data centres for energy efficiency and climate neutrality, and is sharing practice with European governments. "I'm 100% sure there are excellent practices in Europe that we are actually exchanging views on with our counterparts in other governments."

Al Olama's message to Europe and the wider world was one of reliability and partnership, with the UAE committed to its energy transition.

"The UAE has and will remain a very reliable energy supplier," he said. "We believe in partnerships, in successful strategic partnerships that add value both at both ends."

The UAE plans to bring a series of large solar projects online over the next few years as it works towards net zero by 2050, the same deadline the EU has set for its own climate neutrality.

World.title: Are Europeans saving enough for retirement? Here is how much more they need to put aside
World.content:
Mandatory pensions are projected to fall short of the OECD’s retirement income target in 22 of the 30 European countries it studied.

 

In its Pensions Outlook 2026, the OECD estimates how much extra employees on average wages would need to save over a full career to retire on 70% of their gross pay.

Lithuania has the biggest gap as a share of earnings, at 20.7%, while Switzerland has the highest estimated monthly contribution, at more than €1,000 a month for men on average wages.

The OECD calls this the contribution gap. It is the extra share of earnings employees would need to put into a voluntary pension plan, on top of their mandatory contributions, to reach the target.

How much income people need in retirement depends partly on what they expect to spend. “There is no universal retirement income objective. Instead of using target replacement rates, one could use consumption benchmarks, which are target expenditure levels to reach specific lifestyles in retirement,” Stéphanie Payet, a policy analyst at the OECD, told Euronews Business.

The OECD calculates the contribution gaps, which vary from 0.4% in Turkey to 20.7% in Lithuania among male employees with average earnings. The rates are mostly the same for women. But in Poland and Hungary, the gap for women is 8.6 and 2.9 percentage points higher, respectively.

The gap is in double digits in many countries: Ireland (19.4%), Poland (17.3%), Croatia (15.7%), Slovenia (12.5%), Latvia (12.3%), Estonia (12.2%), Switzerland (12.1%), Germany (11.1%), Belgium (10.7%) and Iceland (10%).

“Where gaps are large, this means that people are often under-saved, and so they won’t have enough to have a good standard of living in retirement,” Professor Iain Clacher of the University of Leeds told Euronews Business.

Among other major economies, the gap is 9.1% in the UK and 6.2% in France.

It is smaller in Bulgaria (4.4%), Slovakia (3.9%) and Sweden (2.2%). Turkey has the smallest positive gap, at 0.4%.

In Austria, Denmark, Greece, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain, mandatory pensions are expected to meet the OECD’s retirement income target for men on average wages.

How much extra would workers need to save each month?

Euronews Business applied the OECD’s contribution rates to average gross wages in 2025. The same percentage can translate into very different amounts depending on what workers earn.

At 2025 average gross wages, the estimated extra contribution for men ranges from about €5 a month in Turkey to €1,084 in Switzerland.

The figure exceeds €500 a month in Ireland (€974), Iceland (€716), Germany (€617), Belgium (€556) and Norway (€532).

In the UK, a man on the average wage would need to save about €494 a month to reach the OECD benchmark. The figure is €238 in France, €64 in Slovakia, €68 in Bulgaria, €91 in Sweden, €111 in Romania, €129 in Hungary and €360 in Poland.

Even a relatively small monthly contribution can be a burden where wages are lower. Average gross monthly earnings in 2025 ranged from €1,549 in Turkey to €8,957 in Switzerland. They were €5,558 in Germany, €5,445 in the UK, €4,195 in Sweden, €3,830 in France, €2,078 in Poland and €1,772 in Hungary.

At those wage levels, a retirement income equal to 70% of earnings would be about €1,084 a month in Turkey and €6,270 in Switzerland.

Why do contribution gaps differ?

Payet said the differences are directly linked to how much income employees can expect from mandatory pensions. The replacement rate measures pension income as a share of a worker’s earnings before retirement.

“A lower replacement rate from the mandatory pension system means that you will need to contribute more on a voluntary basis to reach the target replacement rate,” she said.

Professor Traute Meyer of the University of Southampton linked Poland’s large pension contribution gap to state pension cuts after the transition from state socialism to a market economy. She linked Ireland’s large gap to the country’s traditionally low mandatory pensions as a liberal welfare state. She pointed to Sweden’s strong public pension mandates, rooted in social democratic governance, as a reason for its smaller gap.

“Low gaps may also mean only formal workers are protected, leaving many outside mandatory coverage (Turkey),” she said.

Purchasing power of money in retirement

Professor Lauri Leppik of Tallinn University said a small contribution gap tells us little about what a mandatory pension can buy in countries such as Turkey.

Clacher added that “The contribution gap alone does not give a clear picture as the other factor that is important is the purchasing power of money in retirement".

Pension income varies widely across Europe. In 2023, EU spending on old-age pensions averaged about €1,440 a month per beneficiary, according to Eurostat.

That figure covers people already receiving a pension, including those with shorter careers. The OECD benchmark is for employees entering the labour market who go on to complete a full career.

Retirement poverty

Meyer pointed to the risk of poverty in retirement.

“Research consistently shows that voluntary retirement saving is insufficient, especially among lower earners. People underestimate future needs, prioritise current demands, distrust private schemes or lack the means to save,” she told Euronews Business.

What could change before workers retire?

The contribution gap is a forward-looking measure. It does not tell us anything about current pensioners. “It is based on expected replacement rates for workers entering the labour force today, assuming the rules of the pension system will remain the same until these workers retire,” Payet said.

The projections include changes already written into law, including scheduled increases in retirement ages. Professor Marek Góra of the Warsaw School of Economics said further changes could affect how much workers need to save. In his view, higher retirement ages would reduce the need for extra savings, while lower replacement rates would increase it.

“As a result, the actual need for voluntary additional retirement savings is less clear-cut than the estimates suggest,” he said.

How does the contribution gap work?

Payet gave the example of an average earner whose mandatory pension is expected to replace 50% of their earnings. Under the assumptions in her example, putting about 9% of earnings into a defined contribution pension plan from age 22 until retirement would cover the remaining 20 percentage points.

Take a worker earning €3,000 a month just before retirement. The 70% target would give them a gross retirement income of €2,100 a month. If their mandatory pension paid €1,500 a month, the shortfall would be €600 a month.

At a wage of €3,000, a 9% contribution comes to €270 a month. The worker would save the same share of earnings throughout their career, so the amount in euros would be lower when they earned less. Under the assumptions in the example, those contributions and their investment returns would provide the extra €600 a month in retirement.

World.title: Polar vortex weakens weeks ahead of schedule, raising risk of cold spells
World.content:
Meteorologists are monitoring an unusually early weakening of the polar vortex, a vast circulation of cold air above the Arctic, raising the possibility of colder weather across parts of Europe, North America and Asia in the weeks ahead.

 

The disruption could increase the likelihood of colder spells across northern and central Europe, including parts of Scandinavia, the British Isles, Germany and Poland.

The phenomenon normally strengthens throughout autumn, reaching its peak around January before gradually weakening towards the end of winter. Major disruptions, which can allow Arctic air to move further south, typically occur between January and March.

This year, however, scientists have observed signs of disruption as early as November, an unprecedented development in modern meteorological records.

Professor Andrew Charlton-Perez, a meteorologist at the University of Reading, said in an expert commentary published by the university that scientists had never observed a sudden stratospheric warming so early in the season.

The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and extremely cold air circulating high above the Arctic. When it weakens or becomes displaced, the jet stream can become distorted, potentially allowing cold Arctic air to spill into lower latitudes.

Scientists assess potential impact on winter weather

Its effects can take several weeks to reach the lower atmosphere, where weather systems develop, and the eventual impact depends on the position of high- and low-pressure systems.

Scientists are also examining the possible influence of the strong El Niño developing in the Pacific, which can affect atmospheric circulation and contribute to disturbances in the polar vortex.

Related UN warns El Nino could be strongest on record as it urges world to prepare

Climate change has also been raised as a possible factor influencing some of the atmospheric processes involved, although no direct link to the current exceptionally early disruption has been established.

For now, meteorologists are continuing to monitor developments, with the coming weeks expected to provide a clearer indication of whether the disturbance will translate into significant changes in winter weather across the Northern Hemisphere.

World.title: From gastronomy to sports: What to discover in Spain's Region of Valencia
World.content:
The Region of Valencia has long been a popular destination, with tourists flocking to hot spots like Alicante and Benidorm.

 

But as travellers look to develop a deeper connection with the countries they visit, other destinations are starting to have their moment in the spotlight.

Speaking at World Travel Market in London, José Manuel Camarero Benitez, the regional vice-minister for tourism for the Region of Valencia, shared with Euronews Travel how they have avoided the overtourism problems that other areas of Spain are facing.

“It’s not just promoting tourism – we try to manage tourism,” Camarero said. “We are not aiming to promote the same places, and telling people to go do the same things at the same time.

“We try to attract people outside of the peak season. For example, even now in November, we have sunshine and temperatures above 20 degrees so you can enjoy diving, swimming and other activities.”

The tourism board is currently running a campaign entitled “could this be happiness?”, which encourages visitors to discover happiness in the small things, like feeling the sand between your toes or seeing the shimmer of the sea.

The province of Castellón is ready for its moment in the spotlight Jack Coble/Unsplash

Castellón: The next hot destination

The provinces of Alicante and Valencia are already well known and loved, but Camarero thinks it’s time for Castellón to shine.

“I always say Alicante has been our success for 60 years in the Valencia region, now Castellón will be the next success,” he added, noting that the city is particularly known for its gastronomy.

Offering a diversity of experiences, you can dig into langoustine in Vinaròs, hike through the Sierra de Irta mountainscape, see ancient cave art in Ares del Maestrat, and go canyoning in Montanejos.

A big year for sport

The region of Valencia is also preparing for a big year of sport in 2027.

Over the course of the year, Valencia city will host the Copa del Rey basketball tournament, the European Indoor Athletics Championships, SailGP, and the MotoGP Valencia Grand Prix, while Alicante will host the start of The Ocean Race.

For golf fans, Alicante will also host the IAGTO European Convention in May, and Camarero is encouraging players to come discover the region’s offerings.

“It’s the best opportunity to come to Alicante to see all 30 sites and discover not only golf as a sport, but golf as a lifestyle, with gastronomy, culture and the other things you can enjoy during your stay,” he said.

Sustainability as key

The region of Valencia has long prioritised sustainability, with Valencia serving as the European Green Capital in 2024.

That will continue in 2028, with Benidorm handed the European Green Leaf award, which is for cities with between 20,000 and 100,000 inhabitants, last month.

“Sustainability is not just a word for us, it’s both the present and the future,” Camarero said.

World.title: A trip to the Philippines offers hidden gems, slow food and colourful events
World.content:
An archipelago of more than 7,000 islands in Southeast Asia, the Philippines offers everything from coastline and tropical rainforests to volcanic peaks.

 

Speaking to Euronews Travel at World Travel Market in London, Marga Nograles, COO at Tourism Promotions Board Philippines, described the country as tropical, and one that welcomes visitors in every season.

There is an “authentic experience for every traveller” at any time of the year, Nograles said. “From December to May, we have whale watching activities, which can be done in four destinations around the Philippines. Around that time also, we [have] perfect island hopping experiences, [for travellers] visiting all our award-winning beach resorts.”

For adventure tourists, she recommended visiting Siargao Island from September to January for watersports when waves can reach as high as around nine feet.

“We have many surfers coming into the Philippines at that time,” she said. “That is also the best for canyoneering and doing the sardine run.”

The Ruins in Bacolod Tourism Promotions Board Philippines

Hidden gems in the Philippines

Beyond the capital, Manila, Nograles shared the Philippines’ must-visit destinations.

“Siquijor remains one of our hidden gems, with beautiful beaches, waterfalls, and rich local tradition,” she said.

The third smallest province across the country, Siquijor features white sand beaches, crystal clear waters and rich marine biodiversity. Visitors can enjoy kayaking, trekking and snorkelling in the Caticugan Marine Protected Area, among other popular activities to do on the island.

In Pampanga, Nograles recommended Clark for being an accessible getaway and an area that has a “rich history, exciting culinary culture, and growing leisure opportunities”.

She also spotlighted how Camiguin, an island home to 14 volcanoes, was listed among The New York Times’ 52 Places to Go in 2026, making it the only province in the Philippines to receive such international distinction.

“Its volcanic landscapes, waterfalls and natural springs make it a wonderful destination for nature and adventure,” she said.

The coastal country offers visitors no shortage of seafood dishes Avel Chuklanov/Unsplash

Food tourism: Where to eat in the Philippines

Nicknamed the “heart of the Philippines”, Iloilo City was named as a Creative City of Gastronomy in 2023 by UNESCO and is home to more than 300 restaurants.

"It's very interesting to come visit because their cuisine is heavily inspired by the culture and traditions of that city," Nograles said.

UNESCO recognises Iloilo for its culture of "fiesta" and tradition of festive banquets. Since 2021, the province has also held Timplada, an event that showcases local cuisine. This includes educational activities focused on Iloilo culinary heritage.

Bacolod, an urbanised city on the northwest coast of Negros Island, became the first international Slow Food Hub in Asia and the Pacific, according to the Slow Food Foundation.

“Bacolod City is a slow food hub in Asia and the centre for sustainable gastronomy,” said Nograles. “Negros Occidental also is the organic capital of the Philippines.”

She recommends visiting Carbin Reef in Negros Occidental. It’s a sandbar where visitors can sample "kinilaw", which is a traditional Filipino seafood dish where raw fish is marinated in vinegar, diced into cubes and accompanied with tomato, red onions, ginger and lemon zest.

MassKara Festival in Bacolod Sherwin Ballesteros/Tourism Promotions Board Philippines

Colourful celebrations of faith, flowers and harvest

Nograles told Euronews Travel that the country hosts more than 40,000 festivals each year. And there are three in particular that she highlights for travellers.

“First is the Sinulog, which is in Cebu in the Visayas,” she said. “Sinulog is a celebration of faith. In the Philippines, they celebrate the Señor Santo Niño (the Holy Child Jesus).

"During this time, the whole city stops because everyone is celebrating in the streets. They take out their boats. And everyone has their face painted. The energy is unlike any other.”

In the southern city of Davao, the Kadayawan Festival is a celebration of harvest. “There are different concerts, also street dancing,” she said. “[There are] also the freshest fruits around that time so, we also get a lot of visitors coming in – so it would be nice to come visit and try the fruits of the south of the Philippines.”

Further north of the archipelago is where the month-long Panagbenga Festival takes place. "That is a celebration of the flowers," she said. "So all kinds of flowers are in bloom up the mountains during that time."

World.title: US asks China to uphold Busan trade deal commitments
World.content:
The US urged Beijing to meet commitments from a 2025 accord — particularly on agricultural purchases and rare earths supply. China, meanwhile, expressed concern over the US' "economic, trade restrictive" measures.

Top officials of United States President Donald Trump's administration have called on China to "fully and immediately" implement its commitments under a 2025 trade agreement between the two nations, including on rare earth and other critical minerals.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Friday held a videoconference with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on the trade and economic relationship between Washington and Beijing, a statement from Greer's office said.

Greer "emphasized the critical importance of China taking concrete actions to fully implement its past commitments, particularly as they relate to agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals.” it added.

The US-China trade agreement
