World.title: The rise and fall of Russell Brand, shapeshifting sexual predator
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

His most recent, and current, incarnation is as a profound man of faith – an identity coincidentally adopted at the exact time he needed to appear without sin.

Or rather, performing as whatever version of Russell Brand was most useful to him at that moment. Feral TV host? Rock-star comic? Insatiable sex addict? Pseudo-intellectual? Unlikely family man? Political revolutionary? Conspiracy-peddling influencer?

Soon after that appearance he largely gave up acting for the next decade, embarking instead on an occasionally dazzling career performing as himself.

Billy was just a character, of course, but as a cocky, unkempt, oddly charismatic man-child with a knack for refusing to admit wrongdoing, he also served as a useful introduction to the man playing him. Brand would go on to make a garish reputation from those very traits – and adding a few more adult qualities as he grew older, too.

That was 1994. Brand was appearing as “Billy” in an episode of The Bill. At the time he was an aspiring actor who’d recently been expelled from the Italia Conti Academy of Theatre Arts for truancy and drug use. This was his first major screen role.

Many years ago, Russell Brand’s career in the public eye began with an arrest. He denied all charges, of course. “I was never there!” the then-teenager cried, as a policeman read him his rights. Brand flounced onto his unmade bed. “I can’t believe this is happening,” he sulked. “Well, it is,” came the response, “so get your brain in gear.”

Barbara was his biggest fan, and the original reason for what would become a desperate, insatiable need for attention and ego-stroking. “My mum thinks I’m an excellent swimmer,” he said in 2007, “simply because I’ve not yet drowned.”

“A trivial Greek tragedy” is how he used to describe his early life as an only child in Grays, Essex, and it was certainly tragic. As he tells it in his autobiography, My Booky Wook, he was an intense and awkward child, and so obsessed with his mother, Barbara, that he felt they should get married. His father, Ron, left when Brand was six months old, to be replaced by a macho stepdad called Colin, whom Brand hated.

On November 5, Brand was found guilty of three charges of sexual assault and one rape , following a three-week trial at Southwark Crown Court. He was told he was facing a lengthy custodial sentence and would be sentenced on Monday. After a lifetime of shapeshifting, even he won’t be able to slip out of this one.

Yet three decades on from The Bill, Brand, now 51, has been back in trouble with the law. Again, he denied everything. Again, he couldn’t believe it. But this time the arrest was all too real, the charges deeply serious, and the consequences career-finishing.

Today his current faith of choice is Christianity. In the past Brand has also had a Hindu wedding and identified as a Buddhist, so much so that he was once selected by the Dalai Lama to host a youth event.

Immediately he hired three prostitutes: two for him, one for his son. Years later Ron would comment when his son was charged with rape and sexual assault. “The Russell Brand vendetta,” he wrote on Facebook. “Like a man who owns an orchard being accused of stealing an apple.” He supported his son in court last month.

The teenage Brand developed bulimia, and found escapes in drugs, sex and self-harm. As a treat, Ron took him to Thailand when he was 16.

Ron, a “wheeler-dealer”, eventually came back on the scene; Brand later wrote that his father would invite him over to his house, then put porn on the television for him while he “diddled birds in the room next door”.

At 13, the agile mind his teacher identified found what it really needed: attention and adulation. A school production of Bugsy Malone, in which Brand, a portly boy, played “Fat Sam”, proved formative. “People laughed, and I felt this sudden rush of adrenaline surging through me. It was like a drug.”

“I was very unhappy,” Brand would later admit. “I didn’t get on with my stepdad at all. And I just remember feeling lonely and totally impotent – there was nothing I could do about my situation… I had to deal with feeling ordinary, dull, tedious and powerless by trying to subvert those ideas, being anarchic and dangerous.”

The family was poor, and Barbara had cancer three times. Brand, who was mostly a loner at school, was gifted but coy. As one perceptive school teacher wrote in a class report: “Russell is more able than he would have us think.”

At the peak of his three years on the drug he flourished as a wild child on MTV, where he established himself as a presenter who’d do and say anything. In one infamous segment he masturbated a male stranger in a public toilet – despite being, in his own words, “hysterically heterosexual”. His celebrity interviews generally involved him flirting relentlessly with his guests.

Taking heroin, he “felt enveloped in this womb of comfort”, he said. “And although I spent every day in this kind of heroin daze, it just seemed to make life much more manageable.”

After being expelled from Italia Conti, “the baton of self-harm was handed directly from eating disorder to narcotics abuse in a single, graceful movement”, as he put it in 2006. You name it, he snorted it, swallowed it or smoked it.

Like many in a new city, he decided to reinvent himself: growing his hair out, wearing flamboyant clothes, exaggerating his fey physical ticks and developing a florid, arcane manner of speaking. His memoir includes a photograph of him as a child, wearing fancy dress, his hand cocked on his hip. “This is the exact moment when I decided to act gay to attract girls. It took 15 years to produce results,” reads the caption.

In the same year as his Thailand trip, Brand left home, signed on at an extras agency and won a place at Italia Conti, necessitating a move to London.

Yet all those events, especially the Bin Laden stunt, would only end up adding to the Brand myth. In the early noughties, badly behaved rock stars were a dying breed. Brand was more than happy to loom into that gap, and became a permanent tabloid fixture as a result.

The model Kelly Brook had a similarly grim experience, recalling how Brand repeatedly asked to see glamour photos of her taken at age 15.

“He wouldn’t take no for an answer … He always goes that step too far. Never quite far enough to slap his face but usually too far. Throughout the whole interview he kept making shocking remarks that I can’t even repeat. Just uttering the words would make me blush.”

He was later rehired by MTV to present a chat show, and proved just as inappropriate. “He is completely crazy and a bit of a vile predator,” pop star Dannii Minogue recalled in 2006, shortly after experiencing the Brand treatment live on air.

His wildness would eventually cost him his job, when he arrived for work on the day after 9/11, high, dressed as Osama bin Laden and with his drug dealer in tow. He was due to interview Kylie Minogue. It was, he’d later say, probably “the worst time to do it, in many ways”. A few months earlier, inappropriate behaviour had resulted in him being kicked out of the Edinburgh Fringe, too.

Staff at MTV – especially female staff – saw all sides of him, before and after he quit drink and drugs in 2002. One complainant in Brand’s recent trial was a colleague from the time. According to her testimony, the two of them were friendly in the office until suddenly “his demeanour changed” and, during an alleged attack, Brand “turned into this wild-eyed maniac”.

With each passing year of that decade, his fame grew, his reputation added another layer of notoriety, and a man whose greatest addiction was fast becoming attention couldn’t get enough. But then, neither could commissioners and bookers. Updating his look again, he dyed and backcombed his hair, grew a beard, began liberally applying eyeliner, and built a uniform of skinny jeans, winklepickers, silk scarves and shirts unbuttoned to the navel.

He knew it was outmoded and knew it was startling.

A ‘star is born’

Paired with an undeniably quick wit, the whole effect was brilliant. After people started noticing him as a host on UK TV channel E4, he was invited to disturb more mainstream television. One was the BBC’s Friday Night with Jonathan Ross in 2006, which was later considered his “star is born” moment. Watching clips of it now, it’s difficult to tell who is more spellbound: the audience, his fellow guests, or Ross.

Russell Brand in 2009. Simon Schluter

Fleet Street was similarly charmed. He gave the tabloids plenty to talk about, while the broadsheets and colour supplements lined up to try and psychoanalyse this oddity. “He was charming, articulate, outrageous and very, very funny,” Piers Morgan wrote in a particularly revealing interview with Brand for GQ.

Almost all those interviews eventually fixated on sex. Brand was fond of it, you see. As a younger man he was put into rehab (“the winky nick”, as he put it) for sex addiction. Occasionally he confessed to associating sex with guilt – “afterwards a fog of guilt descends”, he wrote – but on the whole, he was more than happy to extol his priapic excesses.

“I love f---ing,” he told The Observer in 2017. “My house has a hot tub for damned good reasons, and none of them spiritual.” In his interview with Morgan he’s asked whether he’s slept with more than 1000 women. Brand is hurt that the suggested number is so low. In a “good week”, he said, he’d sleep with 20 women. “One in the morning, maybe two for lunch and three for tea. Then someone might stick around all night.”

When Morgan asked whether he was a “sexual predator”, Brand responded: “I resent the word ‘predator’. I like to think of myself as a conduit of natural forces. After all, the most natural thing in the world for people to do is f---, isn’t it? All you have to do is remove all the reasons why women don’t actually go through with it, like pride and reputation.”

Wherever he went, this reputation preceded him like a bad cologne, of course. Some women threw themselves at him but others conspired to never be in his presence. Jo Hemmings, a psychologist who has often worked on reality TV, recalls the culture on Big Brother.

“He worked on Big Brother’s Big Mouth and I was on Big Brother’s Little Brother, but some of the crew were the same and I know that the women – girls, as they were, really – felt uncomfortable being around him,” she says. “He got rather into their personal space and was pretty intense but, back in the day, people didn’t want to speak up about their concerns, other than preferring not to work on his show, for fear of losing their jobs or rocking the boat.”

Never idle, Brand had simultaneously launched a stop-start radio career, initially on indie-rock station XFM, until he was sacked for reading pornographic stories on air. He moved to BBC Radio 2, until he was taken off air from that, too, in what could have been the greatest scandal of his career, had he been anybody else.

His time as a BBC radio host was already studded with sackable moments. Like the time he called his newsreader “erotic” and told her, on air, that “we’re going to get under that desk and we’re going to unleash hell on your thighs”. Or the time he conducted a telephone interview with Jimmy Savile and promised he’d send his assistant to his flat, naked, to massage him.

The prank-call incident

Worse was to come. Late one night, Brand and Jonathan Ross thought it would be funny to call the then-78-year-old actor Andrew Sachs, who’d been due to appear on the show. Both Brand and Ross left messages on Sachs’ answering machine informing him that Brand had had sex with Sachs’ granddaughter, 23-year-old singer and erotic dancer Georgina Baillie. The backlash was swift and brutal, growing to such a tumult that even Gordon Brown, then the prime minister, joined in, calling it “clearly inappropriate and unacceptable behaviour”.

Jonathan Ross, left, and Russell Brand, right were sacked by the BBC in 2008 because they left lewd messages on the voicemail of Andrew Sachs. AP Photo/PA/file

“I was full of self-pity, self-hatred. I wasn’t eating,” Baillie said last week of the immediate aftermath. “I went back to using [drugs]. I turned to an eating disorder … It went on for weeks. I’m terrified to this day of newspapers, I can’t look at them.” She confirmed she received no apology from Brand or the BBC. Ross wrote her a letter she never saw.

Brand and Ross were suspended (with Brand then quitting before he could be fired), and the controller of Radio 2, Lesley Douglas, resigned. Again, though, Brand didn’t seem too fussed, instead enjoying the attention.

Perhaps the greatest rebuke in “Sachsgate”, as it became known, was delivered by former Telegraph editor Charles Moore, at the GQ Awards five years later. Brand, presenting, had shocked the audience by commenting that the night’s sponsors, Hugo Boss, had once made uniforms for the Nazi Party. Moore, newly awarded “writer of the year”, chose his target and didn’t miss.

“I was very interested when Russell Brand chose to praise the stylishness of the Nazis,” Moore told the room. “Because, of course, that fits with the fact that when they persecuted the Sachs family in the 1930s, Andrew Sachs, who was only young, then fled to this country. He was then persecuted by Russell Brand and Jonathan Ross in their disgusting phone call.” The room broke into thunderous applause.

“What I’ve learnt – to my cost – on several occasions in my life, is that people will put up with all manner of bad behaviour so long as you’re giving them what they want,” Brand once mused. “But the minute you’re not, you’re f---ed. They’ll wipe their hands of you without a second glance.”

The many rebrands

Russell Brand in a scene from Arthur. AP

To say that Sachsgate damaged Brand’s career would be to misunderstand how rarely a fly landed on him during the first four decades of his life.

He was moving far too fast, building a CV that took in comedy, radio presenting, TV and, increasingly, Hollywood films (including 2008’s Forgetting Sarah Marshall, in which he largely played himself; Rock of Ages, in which he largely played himself; and the remake of Arthur, in which … you get the idea).

By 2011 he had also married American pop star Katy Perry at the height of her career. Their wedding, a closely guarded traditional Hindu ceremony, took place at a luxury resort in Rajasthan, India, with the bride and groom sitting atop elephants.

Russell Brand and Katy Perry were married for 14 months before divorcing in 2011.

Their marriage lasted for 14 months. In an interview in 2013, Perry, who would call Brand “very controlling” and “really hurtful”, told Vogue: “I haven’t heard from him since he texted me saying he was divorcing me [on] December 31, 2011.”

Brand returned to Britain from Los Angeles and reinvented himself as a political revolutionary. His next stand-up tour, Messiah Complex, was about Che Guevara, Gandhi, Malcolm X and Jesus. He wrote a book, Revolution, which advocated non-voting. Johnny Rotten of the Sex Pistols called that “the most idiotic thing I’ve ever heard”.

In 2014, the same year he topped a YouGov poll asking which celebrity had the most negative influence on public debate, he launched a YouTube show, The Trews, in which Brand quickly made his first forays into conspiracy theories, including claiming the US government might be behind 9/11.

When Ed Miliband, the then Labour leader, appeared on The Trews in a desperate attempt to woo Brand’s politically disaffected fans before the 2015 general election, he was widely mocked. Brand, reversing on his earlier policy regarding the democratic process, endorsed Miliband. Despite leading an unpopular coalition government, the Conservatives won a majority.

Brand ended The Trews in 2015, soon shapeshifting again into a reformed figure who wished to marry and have children. He reunited with a former girlfriend, Laura Gallacher, and they wed in Henley-on-Thames in 2017. They have three children: Mabel, 10, Peggy, eight, and Herb, three.

Russell Brand and wife Laura Brand arrive at Southwark Crown Court in October. AP

From their Oxfordshire base he set about turning himself into a guru, initially via podcasts and his YouTube channel. Slowly but surely he accrued a fierce online following, while simultaneously presenting as a wholesome family man. In an interview, he praised the MeToo movement as a “really positive change”. He also appeared on The Great British Bake Off, baking a vagina made from biscuits as his showstopper.

Journalists were still being charmed. “He was just very engaging,” admits one female writer, who interviewed him during this period. “You rack your brain now, thinking: ‘How could I have got someone so wrong?’ But I found him perfectly lovely, to the point where I’d say he was one of my favourite interviews because he was so engaged in the chat.”

At the end of the 2010s YouTube was largely where Brand made his home. The British public had long grown bored of his act; TV commissioners knew better than to take a risk on him; politicians considered him repellent to voters; even fellow celebrities started to call him out.

But broadcasting from his Oxfordshire home was easy and lucrative: the more sensational his takes on current affairs and politics, the more his audience grew. By 2022 he had 6 million subscribers, many of them die-hard acolytes from either extreme of the political spectrum, plus a growing number attracted to Brand as a quasi-religious figure. And he would need their support: the following year, an investigation by The Times, The Sunday Times and Channel 4’s Dispatches accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a period spanning seven years and during the height of his fame.

Loading

Brand tried to get ahead of the story, posting a video titled “So, This Is Happening” – a two-minute pre-denial in which he “absolutely” refuted the allegations. Brand’s army mobilised in the comments.

“We’re with you, Russell,” wrote one, yielding 4000 “likes”. “I’ve been wondering how long it would be until they tried to pull this card,” another read, beside a crying emoji. “I’m with you all the way, Russell. They did it to Assange. They tried it with Bernie Sanders. They did it to Corbyn. They’ll try it with anyone they find a threat,” lamented a third.

As his reputation tanked further, Brand found God, enlisting Bear Grylls to baptise him in the River Thames. The timing of his conversion was considered suspicious, and never more than when Piers Morgan challenged him to find a particular Bible verse, live on air.

For what felt like an hour, Brand silently leafed through the good book, failing to find what he was looking for. He continued to carry a Bible everywhere, including to court in recent weeks.

After his baptism he moved his family to Florida, where his tendency towards conspiracy theories and support for the MAGA movement meant he was welcomed with, if not open arms, then certainly a curious handshake. There, his broadcasting took on a religious nature. He and Laura would read from the Bible and light candles; he’d present himself, Messianic hair in full flow, in front of stained-glass windows.

In reality, the ongoing legal battles meant his finances had dwindled. In recent months he’s been selling, QVC-style, “magical amulets” that he claims protect people from Wi-Fi and “other evil energies”, as well as the odd nutritional powder.

His circle has shrunk, as well, to a small handful of trusted friends, including Jake Smith, his American manager and producer, and Joe McCann, a former boxer who often accompanies Brand to church. Along with Laura and, on one occasion, her father, former golfer Bernard Gallacher, both have attended court with Brand in recent weeks. McCann, easily spotted by his top-knot and tattoos, served as Brand’s bodyguard as he stalked into court, usually muttering that he feels blessed.

Brand always needed to be looked at, always wished to be followed. He once published a children’s book retelling The Pied Piper of Hamelin, the old tale about a mysterious figure whose flute enchants the naive.

“I think the Pied Piper is such an interesting figure,” Brand said at the time. “When you think about [it], it’s weird what he did, taking them children away, and it makes you ask questions. Why did he do it? Is that OK? Why did it happen?”

The eventual book, Russell Brand’s Trickster Tales: The Pied Piper of Hamelin, was published in 2014. The titular figure was depicted as a tall, slender man with a nest of long, knotted black hair. “More than anything else,” Brand said, “I’m the trickster.”

The Pied Piper has finally been caught. But can anyone silence him for good?

Additional reporting by Kimberley Bond

Telegraph, London

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491 or Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Dee-lighted: Melbourne storm back from 28 points down, Cats heartbroken in dying seconds
World.content:
AFLW finals SportAFLAFLW Dee-lighted: Melbourne storm back from 28 points down, Cats heartbroken in dying seconds Hannah Kennelly Updated November 7, 2026 — 4:53pm ,first published 3:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. With 18 seconds left on the clock at Ikon Park, Geelong star Chloe Scheer took a deep breath and lined up for a set shot, directly in front and about 20 metres from goal. After a dominant first half of Saturday’s qualifying final, the Cats coughed up a 28-point margin to a surging Melbourne to find themselves five points down in the dying minutes of the final quarter. Sheer joy: The Demons snatched the win. Getty Images An always-reliable Scheer took her shot as Melbourne defenders watched on helplessly – but it sailed wide for a point. Cue pandemonium from the euphoric Demons, who won the nail-biting game by four points, and devastation for the Cats in what will go down as one of the greatest AFLW finals in history.



It was a fourth-quarter masterclass from the Demons to snatch the lead and win 8.8 (56) to 8.4 (52), booking a preliminary final berth. Saturday’s highly anticipated match-up saw Cats coach Mick Stinear face his old Demons – a team he coached for 10 seasons. A gracious Stinear conceded Melbourne were the better team and said the Cats would rally around a disappointed Scheer. “The outcome of the game is not on her; that’s on us as a coaching team and a playing group to be more consistent,” he said post-match. “We shouldn’t have put ourselves in that position.”



Stinear praised Geelong’s pressure in the first half, but said the team lost their way in the third quarter and Melbourne “made us pay on turnover”. “I thought our pressure and effort and intent was really good for the whole game, but our method and ability to execute fundamentally lacked at critical times, and to their credit, they came over the top of us, and we nearly escaped with a win. “But I didn’t feel like we’d earned it with the second half we had.” Georgie Prespakis was sensational for the Cats on Saturday via Getty Images At half-time the Cats seemed to have the game locked away, boasting a 22-point margin. But the Demons found their groove, and a star turn from Alyssa Bannan helped them home.



Geelong should have been playing in front of a home crowd at GMHBA Stadium but had to settle for Ikon Park after a venue-booking clash with the AUSX Supercross Championship – a dirt-bike racing series. Editor's pick AFLW A Cat brought this Irish move to the AFLW. It’s made the AFL consider a rule change Due to the AFLW season structure and length, the Cats and Demons hadn’t faced each other in more than a year, with the Demons winning their round 12 clash back in 2025. Since then, both teams have experienced significant change, with Stinear departing for the Cats and Melbourne welcoming new coach Tom Wilson. There were nerves in the opening term, with both sides missing opportunities to convert. But Rebecca Webster’s long-range effort from 50 with a fortunate bounce gave the Cats the opening goal and steadied the ship.



A blistering second quarter from Georgie Prespakis, Scheer and Jacqueline Parry pushed the Cats further up the scoreboard and almost left the Demons goaless for the first half, but they were saved by a last-minute snap from Eliza McNamara. Momentum shifted in the third, with a goal from a 100-game Melbourne veteran Tyla Hanks followed by a brilliant running goal from Kate Hore. Suddenly, there were holes in the Cats’ defence and the Demons pounced. Melbourne came roaring back into the contest and a second goal from Bannan cut the margin to just one point with less than eight minutes left. A thrilling few minutes followed and an extraordinary Paxy Paxman kicked truly to put the Demons in front. View post on X



Post-match, Wilson praised veteran Paxman and star Tayla Harris, who laid some sensational tackles in critical moments. Their teammate Tahlia Gillard joked her heart rate was still through the roof, well after the final siren. “There’s [so] much excitement, [that was] just such a team performance, and for some of those girls to get their first finals win, that’s pretty good one to experience,” she said. Both teams made it through with minimal injuries, with Cats star Nina Morrison briefly coming to the bench after a hard hit from Harris, but later returning to play. Demon Saraid Taylor – who has been nursing a calf injury for most of the season – also left the field after getting her leg trapped and twisted under her opponent, but also returned to play. In typical Melbourne weather, Ikon Park was hit by flashes of torrential rain followed by a 15-minute lightning delay and then patches of sunshine.



There’s a short break before the second qualifying final starts at 4.05pm at Ikon Park, with reigning premiers North Melbourne facing the Carlton. The Kangaroo juggernaut is eying a historic three-peat this year and have cruised through the season, but they aren’t invincible. Hawthorn defeated the Roos back in round six and Carlton came close earlier in the year. More to come Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Satisfying your bloodlust is one thing. What happened at the boxing on Friday night is another
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLWorld Boxing Satisfying your bloodlust is one thing. What happened at the boxing on Friday night is another Adrian Proszenko November 7, 2026 — 4:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I remember the first time I saw Nelson Asofa-Solomona shirtless. It was June 2018, in a Colorado hotel. Covering the ill-fated Denver rugby league Test between England and New Zealand, I was walking past the hotel swimming pool and caught sight of the biggest human I had seen. Loading I remember thinking to myself: this man, if so inclined, could inflict serious damage on anyone. And so it came to pass at Sydney’s TikTok Entertainment Centre on Friday night.



Sitting only a few metres away from the action – only the likes of Kangaroos World Cup stars Latrell Mitchell, Pat Carrigan, Harry Grant, Sam Walker, Lindsay Smith had a better vantage – Asofa-Solomona unleashed a series of unanswered right hands – including four vicious uppercuts – that ended the pugilistic career of Paul Gallen. At least two of the final blows were superfluous, delivered after Gallen’s porch lights had been turned off. Yet still they came, while Gallen was suspended between the ropes and the canvas. It was the job of Asofa-Solomona, and referee Chris Condon, to ensure they weren’t thrown. With much power comes much responsibility. Paul Gallen took more punishment than was required. Getty Images It was sickening to witness – even for punters who had paid the $70 pay-per-view fee to have their bloodlust sated, let alone those who had parted with even more cash to watch it ringside.



Not that Gallen was complaining. “I said to him, ‘Don’t worry, I would have done the same thing’,” Gallen told me on Saturday. Paul Gallen and Nelson Asofa-Solomona exchange punches. Getty Images “I’ve got no issue, no problem. He beat me fair and square.” And yet it wasn’t the evening’s most disturbing scene. It was the final bout on the card but Asofa-Solomona was in the mood to keep punching on. “Big Nasty” jumped out of the ring, made a beeline for a spectator, and cocked a huge right roundhouse punch that, mercifully, he aborted just in time. After whaling on a concussed Gallen, this is proof he can pull a punch at will.





Asofa-Solomona claimed he acted in defence of then-Storm teammate Suliasi Vunivalu. The NRL integrity unit took a dim view and suspended him for three Test matches and issued a suspended $15,000 fine. Nelson Asofa-Solomona after beating Paul Gallen. Getty Images Asofa-Solomona, first and foremost, is a footballer. He did not grow up in the ring and is still a relative novice, which is why I’m prepared to cut him some slack for the late blows on Gallen. Even if, momentarily, the lines between sanctioned violence and assault were blurred. However, his conduct outside the ring is a concern. If a punter did, in fact, make a racial slur, he should receive a long ban from boxing. If Asofa-Solomona isn’t careful, he may end up with one as well. World.title: Powerhouse Parramatta opening LIVE updates: Sydney’s new $915m cultural institution opens doors to the world
World.content:
This wasn’t how I expected my Saturday to go: I was coming down an escalator when I saw what appeared to be bits of the roof raining down on visitors.

An acoustic ceiling panel above the escalators on the ground level of the Powerhouse fell onto the grating. The grating stopped most of the debris falling but some still got through, hitting the ground and only narrowly missing people stepping off the escalator.

Part of the roof collapsed at Powerhouse Parramatta on opening day. Anthony Segaert

Staff rushed to shut down the escalators going up and down, forcing the still-strong crowds onto elevators, causing a momentary queue. The escalator momentarily reopened – then staff shut it again.

The Powerhouse tells us it was a “lightweight acoustic panel” that came loose.

One perk for visitors: Task Eternal, usually a paid exhibit, has been opened up for public access.

World.content:

A young couple bought an Edwardian in inner-city Prahran for $1,080,000, clinching it for $20,000 below its advertised reserve after it was passed in to them at auction. They were the sole bidders for the two-bedroom 10 Vail Street, in a tree-lined neighbourhood. Their single bid of $1,060,000 was $40,000 shy of the $1.1 million advertised reserve. The property was one of 612 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. Biggin Scott Stonnington agent Michael Tynan later negotiated with the pair, who increased their offer to $1,080,000. It was enough to close the deal.



The period home at 10 Vail Street passed in, but later sold to its sole bidders. JOE ARMAO Earlier, auctioneer James Burne asked for an opening bid, but onlookers played it cool. He launched with a vendor bid of $1,050,000, then paused for discussions. When he returned, the eventual buyers put forward a $1,060,000 bid, and the home was passed in. Two other prospective buyers had flagged their interest in the brick period house, which had decorative fireplaces, a courtyard and a shed, between Williams Road and Orrong Road. However, one didn’t attend the auction and the other sat it out. The courtyard at 10 Vail Street. Domain “It’s not turnkey, but if you put the work into it, you’ve got a really great home that’s only going to go up in value, especially when the market recovers,” Tynan said. “This one, people will regret not purchasing.”



Related Article Victoria residential property What life’s like in Melbourne’s most mortgage-stressed suburb now Tynan said homes not needing renovations, priced between $1 million and $3 million, were performing well in the current market. Interstate investors are also active, with their eye on older one- and two-bedroom apartments. “The yields are starting to get to 6 to 7 per cent for some of these apartments that are selling,” he said. In Fitzroy North, first home buyers kissed and hugged as the hammer fell in their favour, following a fast auction. They are renting around the corner and paid $1.78 million for the classic three-bedroom terrace at 168 Scotchmer Street, against its reserve of $1.67 million.



“They had come off a couple of losses, so it was good to finally win,” agent and auctioneer Mark Verrocchi of Nelson Alexander Fitzroy said. Five bidders – four first home buyers and one downsizer – registered for the auction, and all took part. “I think a lot of them were really hopeful,” Verrocchi said. “They saw the reserve, and they thought, ‘Geez, that’s incredible value for North Fitzroy’.” The auction opened with a bid of $1.6 million and quickly sailed past the reserve. Bidding persisted in speed and strength, mostly in rises of $5000 and $10,000, until Verrocchi closed the contest at $1.78 million.



An indoor outdoor living area at the Fitzroy North home. Domain The underbidders were also trying to buy their first property. One of their mothers stepped in and took over bidding in the closing stages. The buyers confided in Verrocchi afterwards that their final bid was their maximum. Related Article Interest rates How home owners are beating the latest rate hike The auction lasted about five minutes – just enough for the full array of Melbourne’s weather. “It started with sunshine and ended with torrential rain,” Verrocchi said.



He said bidders were attracted to the home’s proximity to the city, schools, trams and the Edinburgh Gardens. In Thomastown, a Sydney investor struck a $710,000 deal before the auctioneer could warm up their vocal cords, selling a 1970s property to an interstate buyer who is relocating to Melbourne and will make it her home. Three potential bidders turned up for the auction of 311 High Street, including a family representative of the buyer. The three-bedroom house on 555 square metres had a reserve of $700,000, a lavender sink and bath and a metal Hills Hoist in the garden.



Harcourts agent Kiara Comans spoke to the prospective buyers separately during the 30-minute open for inspection before the auction, and negotiations kicked off. The buyer’s representative offered $680,000, and after some back-and-forth, the vendor agreed to a sale price of $710,000. “It’s maybe not where we would have been 12 months ago, but it’s definitely a good result for the market that we’re in,” Comans said. The lavender-hued bathroom at 311 High Street. Domain Comans said the buyer was always serious, and made an offer before the home was even listed.



“The owner decided that they would be better off to go ahead with an auction, just to see what we could get for the property by putting it on the market,” she said. Property alerts are now available in The Age app. Turn them on to receive the latest market news and trends.

World.title: Rising Democratic star Jon Ossoff's reelection fuels presidential prospects
World.content:
Democrat Jon Ossoff's reelection this week to the US Senate in the southern state of Georgia will fuel speculation over a 2028 presidential run by one of the party's young rising stars.

While the 39-year-old has said that he has "zero interest in running for president," his victory in Georgia bolsters his status in the party two years before the next presidential vote.

NBC News and CBS News called the race in Ossoff's favour, as he fended off a challenge from Republican Mike Collins in a state that President Donald Trump won in 2024.

The victory does not mean the Democratic Party gained a seat in the 100-member Senate, but it was nevertheless good, early news for Democrats on a night that saw a wave of defeats for Republicans.

In a spirited appearance in Georgia's capital of Atlanta, Ossoff painted Democratic midterm election gains as a rebuke of "the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame duck President Donald J. Trump."

"Tonight, we've struck a necessary and undeniable blow on behalf of justice and progress," he told a jubilant crowd.

Some of his supporters, including 26-year-old nurse Gracie Surface, told AFP that she hopes he runs for president.

"We need him. We need some young blood," she said after casting her vote in Atlanta.

Ossoff, whose rolled-up shirt sleeves and youthful vibe make him a natural media star, has already drawn comparisons to former president Barack Obama, who appeared on the campaign trail to support him.

Ossoff has also captured attention by homing in on alleged corruption in the Trump administration and mocking the Republican president's behaviour.

His comments on Trump's loyal and omnipresent 35-year-old aide Natalie Harp, in particular, made headlines and drew Trump's ire over the summer.

US Senator Jon Ossoff, Democrat from Georgia, speaks during an election night party after winning reelection in the US midterm elections in Atlanta, Georgia on November 3, 2026. ERIK S. LESSER / AFP

White House anger

"The president sleeps through his meetings. He golfs and trades stocks. He doesn't want to do the job," Ossoff told a campaign rally in August.

"He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenceless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar," Ossoff added.

His comments thrust Harp further into the spotlight, setting the internet alight -- and angering the White House.

Trump has since dismissed Ossoff as a "Pee-wee Herman lookalike," while White House Communications Director Steven Cheung called the lawmaker "the biggest cuck loser in politics," using internet slang for a sexually submissive man.

Ossoff's supporters praise his authenticity and ability to transcend partisan divides to bring people together across party lines.

He shows the "sign of a true leader," said Catherine Urbain, who works in the healthcare sector.

ERIK S. LESSER / AFP

Obama comparisons

"When he speaks, I think of Barack Obama," said Mary, a canvasser in her 60s who did not give her last name.

"I think it's because he's empathetic. He's real," she said.

Obama, the first Black US president, remains hugely popular within the Democratic Party.

Others like Jan Callum, a 77-year-old retired teacher, said Ossoff is "very articulate" but added that it is difficult to compare between the politicians.

Still, Obama's travel to rally support for Ossoff has given further substance to a comparison earlier drawn by The New York Times.

Urbain reminisced on attending a rally for former Democratic nominee Kamala Harris two years ago when Ossoff took the stage.

"When I heard him speak then, I was like: 'This man is phenomenal. He's going to be president,'" she recalled.

"I feel he's authentic, he cares but also that he's not scared to stand up," she added. "I feel that he's one of the few that really doesn't let Trump get away."

Ossoff made a major political breakthrough in 2021, flipping a Republican-held Senate seat as he won a runoff election.

At 33, he became the youngest senator for that legislative term.

Previously, he was an aide to civil rights icon John Lewis, and before entering politics, he ran a documentary film production firm, focusing particularly on corruption.

World.title: MetService updates thunderstorm warning for Waikato, Waitakere, Franklin and Rodney
World.content:
Thunderstorms which have swept across the North Island this afternoon have caused flooding and a home's roof to collapse.

MetService has lifted both of its severe thunderstorm warnings.

Red warnings were in place north of Auckland and south of Hamilton, where thunderstorms were strongest this afternoon.

A yellow thunderstorm watch is still in place covering Auckland, Coromandel, and much of Waikato.

There are reports of a roof collapsing at a house in Wairau Valley and a flooded house in Totara Vale in Auckland after this afternoon's brief storm.

MetService rain radar at 5pm Saturday. Supplied / MetService

Fire and Emergency NZ said they had been called to "a couple" of weather-related calls across Auckland by 5.30pm, including a roof collapse and flooding inside a house.

Both were in Auckland's Wairau Valley on the North Shore, the spokesperson said, and one fire truck had been sent to each.

The severe thunderstorms are moving towards the southeast.

This billboard came down in strong winds in Grey Lynn, Auckland, overnight Friday. RNZ / Josie Campbell

Much of Auckland was drenched in heavy rain and hail late this afternoon.

In Auckland's Grey Lynn between Elgin and Northland streets, a billboard came down in strong winds. It knocked over fencing and was lying across the footpath and cycle lane and onto the road.

Lightning has also delayed the kick-off for the Auckland FC v Phoenix football derby.

Send your pictures and video of any storm damage in your area to iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Embedded content removed for printing https://x.com/MetService/status/2118881503732171197

In Blenheim, part of the roof outside the Cotton On store in Blenheim collapsed because of rain build up. No one was injured and the shop has reopened to customers.

Metservice meteorologist Devlin Linden said today's severe weather had struck the North Island and parts of the South.

"Quite a lot of activity along much of the western North Island, right the way from Auckland down to Taranaki and that western flank, but there is also a good amount of activity in other places around the country.

"These storms are convective storms and are driven by heat thoughout the day. It's expected they're likely to continue though to early this evening, when things start to cool down" says Mr Linden.

Overnight Friday, MetService recorded nearly 2000 lightning strikes throughout the top of the North Island, as well as heavy rainfall, with downpours reaching 33.5mm an hour in the Bay of Plenty.

About 1845 lightning strikes were recorded from midnight.

World.title: Union takes health authorities to court over forensic mental health unit understaffing
World.content:
The union representing mental health nurses at Auckland's secure forensic unit is taking health authorities to the Employment Relations Authority over what it calls understaffing that amounts to a "dangerous gamble".

The Public Service Association (PSA) represents mental health nurses, physiotherapists, social workers and security guards at the Mason Clinic and said as of late Septemebr there were 35 roles vacant, some since 2025.

National secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said that was in breach of two collective agreements which required Health New Zealand to fill the roles as soon as practically possible. She said its failure to do so was putting both staff and the public in danger.

Fleur Fitzsimons. Supplied

"The Mason Clinic cares for people with serious mental illness who have been charged with or convicted of serious offences. You cannot do that work safely with dozens of roles left empty."

Fitzsimons said the roles were not being filled because of a Government funding freeze.

"We've raised this repeatedly since March. Staff told us in July they were at breaking point. When we wrote again in September, Health NZ didn't reply until we chased it a month later."

She said short-staffing was putting pressure on nurses, psychologists and other staff.

"It is not limited to the Mason Clinic and the problem is being aggravated by internal transfers of staff to other mental health units creating vacancies that leave other units short staffed."

Health New Zealand operations director Brad Healey said it was "engaging" with the PSA.

"We are confident in the quality and safety of the care being delivered at the Mason Clinic and patient and staff safety is always our highest priority."

He said while there were vacancies, it was working to cover the roster through overtime and casual staff.

World.title: Darwin Howe jailed for Wainuiomata house shooting and other offences
World.content:
Darwin Howe held a military-style semi-automatic firearm and fired from a stolen car towards a house, peppering the living room with bullets.

Attached to the firearm was a high-capacity magazine containing at least 20 rounds of ammunition.

As glass flew around the Wellington living room, it struck a teenager sleeping in the lounge, leaving him with a cut above the eye. The incident lasted just 10 seconds.

Howe wanted to intimidate a man who lived at the Wainuiomata house whom he considered had a role in the death of his associate in a fatal crash at Bunnythorpe, near Palmerston North, days before.

But inside the address early that January morning last year, the man's partner and eight children were also sleeping.

"The effect on the occupants of the house must have been significant," Judge Bruce Davidson would later remark.

140 previous convictions

Howe's conviction history spans 16 years and includes 140 convictions, including more than 30 for driving while disqualified.

As Judge Davidson's sentencing notes from the Wellington District Court made clear, Howe also has a poor history of compliance.

Sentenced to home detention in 2024 for a spate of offending in mid-to-late-2023, it didn't take long for Howe to breach his conditions.

In February 2024, he accidentally shot himself in the leg, leading to a charge of possession of a firearm without a licence.

In July and September that year, Howe twice drove while disqualified. He also assaulted his partner, punching her in the throat and causing minor injuries.

He was associated with the theft and repainting of stolen cars and was seen with a stolen motorcycle. In October, he burgled a house in Wellington.

Just before Christmas 2024, police searched Howe's house during a bail breach, finding methamphetamine and cannabis.

In his sentencing indication, Judge Davidson noted that Howe's detailed plan to target the house involved stolen vehicles.

The judge noted the offending was planned and premeditated, inherently dangerous, and that actual danger and injury occurred.

Sentencing took place at the Wellington District Court. RNZ / Richard Tindiller

The judge also noted that both burglary charges were planned and premeditated and involved a confrontation with an occupant. The other offending, which spanned nearly a year, affected a large number of victims and occurred while he was on bail.

"I have no victim impact material before me, but it is self-evident that a large number of victims have been affected.

"This ranges from stress and inconvenience for victims whose motor vehicles had been taken, to the safety of other road users; to the occupants of a commercial and residential property and the occupants of the house shot at, including one victim who suffered actual injury," the judge said.

Crown prosecutor Sebastian Hartley sought an end sentence of between six and a half and seven years' jail, noting the Wainuiomata shooting was a "bad case justifying a starting point of five years' imprisonment".

But Howe's lawyer Alex Dye submitted that was too high and instead suggested an end sentence in the range of four and a half years was appropriate.

Taking into account Howe's guilty plea, Judge Davidson offered an end sentence of five years and three months.

At Howe's sentencing in June, the judge considered what additional sentencing discounts could be offered.

"You are now aged 34, and it is abundantly plain to me that you are, yet again, another product of a dysfunctional upbringing. The psychological report, in particular, makes that very clear."

But the judge also noted that while in custody, Howe had begun to show genuine insight into his offending and the necessary rehabilitative steps he needed to take, including moving to a different part of the country upon release, to get away from gang associations.

He had also attended restorative justice and apologised.

Howe was jailed for four years and three months for the shooting and a raft of other firearms, violence, property, drug and driving offences.

Co-offender sentenced

Last month, Howe's associate Sivaly Kadeth was sentenced for his role in the offending.

According to Judge Jan Kelly's sentencing indication, on New Year's Eve 2024, two cars were towed from the scene of a fatal crash near Bunnythorpe.

The Crown's case was that on January 3, Howe and Kadeth drove to Palmerston North, where they were captured on CCTV scoping out the premises of Crash Services.

At 5am that morning, a black Mazda was stolen from Palmerston North by unknown people.

A short time later, the pair reversed the car into a large roller door of Crash Services in an attempt to ram-raid the premises.

According to the summary of facts, either Kadeth or Howe tried to steal property from the car belonging to Howe's associate but fled when they realised there was someone in the building.

Kadeth was also found to have assisted in the execution of Howe's plan by helping him steal a car. He also met Howe after the shooting, and the two drove out of Wainuiomata together.

At sentencing, Judge Kelly noted that although Kadeth had a limited criminal history, these charges represented a notable escalation in the nature and seriousness of his offending.

Kadeth had a degree in commercial law and marketing and had held various roles but had been unemployed since 2024 when his role was disestablished.

He told probation he experienced a period of low mood and emotional distress and at the time of the offending he was struggling with methamphetamine use.

Now 44, probation had assessed his risk of harm should he reoffend in the same manner as high.

Judge Kelly said the aggravating factors included Kadeth's previous convictions for drugs, driving and theft.

In mitigation, she noted there was a causal nexus between Kadeth's drug use and the offending.

On charges of discharging a firearm to intimidate, a representative charge of unlawfully taking a motor vehicle and a charge of burglary, Kadeth was sentenced to 11 months' home detention.

The judge also ordered him to pay $500 to the insurer IAG and $400 in reparation.

*This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Lehmann says 'everyone' was ball tampering globally, denies Khawaja's sandpaper claims
World.content:
Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann claims ball tampering was once ever-present in international cricket, but denies Usman Khawaja's claim of widespread knowledge of the 2018 sandpaper plot.

Lehmann was the coach of the Test team during the Cape Town controversy, in which Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during the match.

Bancroft, captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner were all suspended in the wake of the incident, while Lehmann stood down from his post.

Khawaja's explosive Sandpapergate claim Usman Khawaja claims all staff and players knew that the Australian team was using sandpaper to tamper with the ball during the 2018 tour of South Africa.

In an interview with Nine newspapers on the eve of the release of his new book, Sabr, Khawaja claimed Cape Town was not the first time the Australian side had used sandpaper to tamper with the ball and that the plan had been known by "all of us".

"Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

Speaking to ABC Sport's Summer Grandstand, Lehmann denied personal knowledge of the use of sandpaper and said he does not think all members of the Australian camp would have known about it either.

Lehmann did claim though that up until that day, "everyone around the world" was ball tampering.

Loading...

"I don't think everyone would have known [about the use of sandpaper]. You do know ball tampering is going on because it's been happening for 150 years," Lehmann said.

"It's just how it's being done, and how you would know to that extent? That's an individual case by case, to be fair.

"I can only speak to what I know, and I know ball tampering was a big part of the game of cricket. Now it is obsolete.

"That doesn't make it right either, but that's the case, and we paid a heavy price for that."

Khawaja said he had suggested to the entire playing group after Bancroft had been caught that they take collective responsibility.

Lehmann, who is part of the ABC's cricket commentary team and has recently joined the ABC Cricket Podcast as a co-host, said he could not confirm or deny that discussion took place, as he was not present.

Darren Lehmann stood down as Australian coach after Cape Town. (AP: Halden Krog)

"I don't remember that. There were two change rooms obviously, and there were meetings going on everywhere. To be perfectly honest I was in meetings with Cricket Australia a lot," Lehmann said.

"That could have been the case, I don't know. I'm not saying yes or no to that one. There will be different points of view everywhere on this whole matter."

Lehmann also said he was not aware of an alleged conversation between Bancroft and a member of the coaching team, which Khawaja said was important in the formation of the sandpaper plan.

Earlier on Saturday, a Cricket Australia (CA) spokesperson said they remained comfortable with the initial findings of their investigation.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Lehmann said the 2018 incident left him in a "really dark place" and said the release of Khawaja's book and its explosive accusations has brought up "bad memories" for him, the players and their families.

"End of the day, Cricket Australia had their findings. It was a really tough week, two weeks, at that time going through the process and talking to all the relevant parties," he said.

"I was in a really dark place for a period of time where for four months I didn't leave my house.

"Eight years after the fact and trying to sell a book is a bit different. That's Usman's choice and that's the way he wants to go.

"For the families and the people involved, I feel for them right now because it's taking them back to a really bad place. It's been eight years. You get to a place where you move on, and I've moved on with my life."

Darren Lehmann said the Cape Town affair left him "in a dark place". (AP: Halden Krog)

Lehmann said Khawaja had not reached out to him in advance of these claims going public.

"For me it's a really touchy one mentally, more than anything else, and I know the boys will be feeling that as well.

"Could he have said this at the time? I suppose that's one of the things in the book. I mean, books are there to sell.

"He's spoken to Pat Cummins apparently and the players. I haven't spoken to Usman, he hasn't texted me or rang me. That's just the way it is."

In 2021, Australia's Test bowling quartet of Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon released a statement denying any knowledge of the ball-tampering plan.

Speaking to SA Grandstand on Saturday morning, former Australian fast bowler and current South Australia coach Ryan Harris said he thought it was "a bit disappointing" that it had taken Khawaja "eight years to say that".

"That's probably all I want to say on that. Like most people, I've been interested to hear what the book is going to say."

Jason Gillespie, another former Australian fast bowler, said he had always "found it a challenge to believe" only three players knew of the plan, but would not suggest everybody was across it and backed the testimony of the bowling group.

"This is what was interesting, the umpires at the time studied the ball and said they couldn't see any evidence of ball tampering. That's what I find fascinating.

"And that's what the bowlers have come out and said, the actual umpires looked at the ball and found no evidence … of ball tampering."

World.title: Triumph, tragedy and Alan Jones's drive to survive F1's deadliest era
World.content:
The motor racing world is mourning the death of Alan Jones, the 1980 Formula 1 world champion, who died on Thursday aged 80.

The Australian legend, a winner of 12 grands prix, leaves a huge legacy both on and off the track after a life dedicated to the sport.

As tributes flood in for Jones, and reflections of his tremendous career are written, his death has brought into focus the dangerous and deadly era of motorsport he competed in.

Jones raced and won in an era when the safety of drivers, marshals and spectators was not front of mind.

In an already dangerous sport, the period Jones raced in is often remembered much more for its tragedies than its triumphs.

And it was tragedies that had a major impact on Jones's career, right from the very beginning.

Jones begins F1 career at tragic Spanish Grand Prix

Alan Jones made his F1 debut at the 1975 Spanish Grand Prix, one of the darkest and most controversial F1 weekends in history.

Rolf Stommelen suffered serious leg injuries, while five spectators were killed when his car crossed the barrier. (Getty Images: Sutton Images/David Phipps)

There was drama from the start with fears barriers at the Montjuïc Circuit in Barcelona were not bolted in correctly.

Members of the Grand Prix Drivers Association went on strike before practice, but the race went ahead after alleged rumours that the Guardia Civil, Spanish law enforcement, would seize the cars, which were at the Montjuïc stadium.

Jones qualified 21st for Hesketh Racing, but would retire just three laps into the race after a collision.

But the horror of the day was still to come.

Race leader Rolf Stommelen went off the circuit on lap 26 due to a broken rear wing, with his Hill-Ford car crossing the barrier into the crowd.

Five spectators were killed and Stommelen was seriously injured. The race continued for another four laps it was called off.

The 1975 Spanish Grand Prix holds another slice of history, with Lella Lombardi becoming the first, and to this date, only female driver to score F1 world championship points after placing sixth.

Jones gets F1 drive after fatal accident

After falling out with Team Surtees at the end of the 1976 F1 season, Jones was out of the series for the start of 1977.

He would get his chance to return to F1 following a harrowing and tragic accident in South Africa.

Anthem mix-up fed Alan Jones legend Alan Jones's first F1 grand prix victory in 1977 was so out of the blue that he said the band played Happy Birthday to him instead of the national anthem, but is the story true?

Welshman Tom Pryce and a track marshal were killed in an incident that was indicative of the poor and unimaginably lacklustre safety measures of the day.

Renzo Zorzi, who drove for Shadow, suffered a fuel leak and pulled off to the side of the main straight at the Kyalami circuit.

A small fire broke out, leading to a pair of marshals running onto the track to extinguish the flame. One driver was able to swerve and avoid the marshals, but not Pryce, Zorzi's teammate.

Pryce was unsighted and drove at full speed into 19-year-old marshal Frederik Jansen van Vuuren, killing the teenager on impact.

Van Vuuren was carrying a massive fire extinguisher that hit Pryce in the helmet, killing the Welshman instantly.

Race winner Niki Lauda was preparing to celebrate on the podium, until a member of tyre manufacturer Goodyear was able to get to the Austrian and inform him of Pryce's death.

The horrific and needless deaths ultimately led to Jones being called into the Shadow team for the next race in the United States.

Later that year, Jones would claim a stunning maiden win in Austria, the only win Shadow ever achieved, which set him up for future glory in the years to come.

Jones 'turns down' Ferrari after double tragedy

From 1979 to 1981, Jones was at the peak of his powers.

Driving for Williams, he won 11 grands prix in those three years and claimed the 1980 world championship.

But things could have been much different had a potential move to Ferrari eventuated.

Ferrari had met Jones, telling him he was their second option if the famed Italian team could not sign Mario Andretti.

Ferrari missed out on Andretti, who went on to win the 1978 championship with Lotus, but the Scuderia instead signed Canadian Gilles Villeneuve.

Jones went on to sign with Williams, in what proved to be a formidable partnership.

But, as happened so often in motorsport, tragedy struck.

Ferrari suffered a pair of horrors in 1982, a year after Jones first retired from F1.

The remains of Gilles Villeneuve's destroyed Ferrari chassis, after his fatal crash in Belgium in which he was thrown from the car. (Getty Images: LAT Images)

Villeneuve died after a crash during qualifying for the Belgian Grand Prix, when he ran into the rear of a much slower car. Villeneuve's car launched into the air and he was thrown out as it crashed back to earth.

Didier Pironi suffered a similarly scary incident in Germany, suffering horrific leg fractures after running into the back of Alain Prost's unsighted Renault.

Jones claimed years later that Ferrari reached out to him to fill in for the final rounds of the 1982 season, but he took too long to reply and Ferrari chose another replacement.

F1 safety improves after Jones's retirement

In total, there were five drivers killed on F1 grand prix weekends during Jones's career.

Ayrton Senna, Roland Ratzenberger, and how the San Marino Grand Prix changed Formula 1 While the legendary Ayrton Senna took most of the spotlight, Roland Ratzenberger's legacy lives on through F1's safety innovations.

That does not include two drivers killed in F1 tests, as well as Australian Brian McGuire, who was killed at Brands Hatch in England in 1977 while driving an F1 car.

It was a horrifying era for Formula 1, but one that did improve in the years following Jones's retirement in 1986.

F1 went several years without a fatal incident, until a horrific weekend at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix when Ayrton Senna and Roland Ratzenberger died in separate crashes.

There has been just one fatality in F1 since, when Jules Bianchi went off the circuit at Suzuka in 2014 and collided with a crane that was recovering the beached car of Adrian Sutil.

Several safety measures have been put in place, both on the race car and in how marshals and recovery vehicles enter the racing circuit.

The Halo, a curved, wishbone-shaped structure, now sits above the driver and has played its part in protecting drivers in several incidents, including Romain Grosjean's fiery 2020 crash in Bahrain, Lewis Hamilton being trapped underneath the wheel of Max Verstappen's Red Bull during the 2021 Italian Grand Prix, and Guanyu Zhou's frightening crash at Silverstone in 2022.

World.title: Stricter regulation on the cards for controversial combat sports
World.content:
A NSW parliamentary inquiry has heard that controversial emerging combat sports, notorious for head-injury risks, are prepared to accept regulation, despite some medical experts calling for them to be blacklisted entirely.

NSW Sport Minister Steve Kamper referred activities like collision running, bare-knuckle boxing, and competitive slapping to a committee to investigate if they should be brought further under the control of the state's Combat Sport Authority (CSA).

On Friday, CSA chair Darren Kane told a hearing that the sports should be subject to stronger controls.

"These sports are dangerous, there's no way of hiding behind that … but rugby league's dangerous, and cricket's dangerous, thoroughbred racing is dangerous," he said.

"There's a very good reason why an ambulance follows every race around the inside of a racetrack, to make sure that they're on hand if a jockey falls off.

" It's a balancing act. "

Darren Kane says the sports should be subject to stronger controls. (Supplied: NSW parliament)

Under heavy scrutiny at the hearing was collision running — where two athletes run at each other and collide.

Neurologist Rowena Mobbs urged the committee to ban the sports being investigated, due to risks of brain injury like concussion, especially in collision running.

"I cannot see that it's a fundamental activity of a human to run at a brick wall, let alone a brick wall coming at you," Dr Mobbs said.

"I just can't see any sense in that."

Rowena Mobbs told the inquiry that the sports carry the risk of traumatic brain injury. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Organisers from the Run Nation Championship (RNC), a prominent collision running event, did not participate in the inquiry, nor did power slap organisers.

Mr Kane noted in his evidence that RNC had been working collaboratively with the CSA for an upcoming planned event in Sydney.

Boxing offshoot

The organisers of two fight groups gave evidence at the hearing — GTG Fight Club and Bare Knuckle Australia (BKA).

BKA spokesman Michael McConnell said there was reluctance in the community around regulation, but that it would be necessary to continue growing the sport.

"We can do this safely, and everyone can be looked after in the best way possible," he said.

" I think having these regulations is essential for this sport to not just survive but thrive and transcend and elevate to the next level. "

Michael McConnell hopes that any regulations are developed fairly and collaboratively. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

BKA said their bouts included vetted fighters, who were matched up by weight class and had their abilities assessed through gloved-up test fights.

The fighters were then paired up and fought without traditional boxing gloves.

BKA co-founder Randall Rayment said he was hesitant about regulation and wanted governments to "back off".

But he said he wanted the government to understand the positive outlet that bare-knuckle-style boxing could be for men who wanted a controlled environment to express themselves.

Harm minimisation

Organisers of the sports being examined have claimed the presence of medical staff at events was a harm-prevention strategy.

But in her evidence, Dr Mobbs refuted that argument.

"I state that no doctor on the sideline will be able to modify the risk of traumatic brain injury in either collision sports or power slap," she said.

" It is window dressing as far as prevention. "

'Do not try this at home': Controversial contact sport on the rise The Run Nation Championship will see two athletes run at each other, in a sport criticised for its head injury risks. Organisers argue the championship has been professionalised, and will grow to be as big as boxing.

In a written submission, the Australian Medical Association's (AMA) NSW branch said it did not endorse any of the sports in question, but it believed regulations were needed.

"Emerging activities typically magnify the most violent aspects of established sports, and thus present a significant public health concern," the AMA submission said.

"The NSW government should invest in evidence-based public education campaigns to increase awareness of the short-term and long-term health consequences of concussion, repetitive head impacts and traumatic brain injury associated with emerging combat sports and comparable activities."

Dr Mobbs and other medical bodies that made submissions agreed that education was crucial.

Social benefit

Sione Tongia and Stephen Gardiner have faced off in a BKA fight, but consider themselves close mates.

"I feel like at the end of the day, we're boxing; we just don't have gloves on," Mr Gardiner said.

Randall Rayment (centre), with fighters Sione Tongia (left) and Stephen Gardiner. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

Mr Tongia said he felt bare-knuckle events should remain to provide a place for young men to channel aggression and differences.

The fight club concept gaining traction in only unregulated Australian state The organiser of this fight club says it saves lives. But critics say it is putting young men at serious risk.

"I guarantee you that two people who have beef, after they fight each other, they feel good, they feel better," he said.

"When I fight, I don't fight for beef.

" I just fight because I feel like I better myself by doing it. "

The parliamentary committee will hand down its findings in a report by the end of 2026.

World.title: Aussie's heroic Paris Masters run ends at the hands of rising French star
World.content:
Rinky Hijikata has finally been awakened from his dream week at the Paris Masters as a new young French tennis hero ended the Australian's bid to reach his first big-time tennis semi-final.

For the third match running, Hijikata, who came from behind to defeat Novak Djokovic in the second round, battled back from a set down with some scintillating tennis as he quieted the home fans cheering for their new hope, Luca Van Assche.

But it was the 22-year-old Paris-based Van Assche, also playing in his first Masters 1000 quarter-final, who rose to new heights as he came from 2-0 down in the final set to prevail 6-4, 6-7 (4-7), 7-5 after a memorable two-and-three-quarter hour duel.

It meant the end of what felt like a major breakthrough week for the 25-year-old Sydneysider Hijikata, who looked early in that final set as if he was going to win his sixth match in seven days and become the first qualifier to reach the last-four at the Paris Masters in nine years.

Ultimately, he was defeated by a young player who said he felt inspired by the crowd as he struggled physically in the deciding set.

"The crowd were so important for me, supporting me so much in the tough moments, and that's why I played my best tennis," said Belgian-born Van Assche, who becomes the 12th Frenchman to make the semi-finals in Paris and will next tackle American Ben Shelton.

Hijikata's consolation will be to start next week as Australia's number two man behind Alex de Minaur as he enters the world's top-60.

Hijikata certainly continued with that fearless, aggressive streak in the second set tiebreak against Van Assche, maintaining his fine form by then earning an immediate break in the third set.

But Van Assche is one of the most highly regarded young talents in the game, and his defensive prowess helped him turn the tide in the final set with some extraordinary wall-like resilience that kept forcing Hijikata to play one shot too many.

Third seed Shelton, bombing down 19 aces, had earlier prevailed in an all-American match-up to reach the Paris semis for the first time, roaring to a 6-4, 4-6, 6-3 win that ended Tommy Paul's quiet late bid to qualify for the ATP Finals in Turin later in November.

The victory sealed qualification for the end-of-season men's championship for another US star, Frances Tiafoe, alongside world number one Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Shelton, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli and Arthur Fils.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
