World.title: Megan Schutt on ADHD, medication and what's changed since her diagnosis
World.content:
The fire in Megan Schutt's belly has driven her to unbelievable heights.

World Cup titles, Commonwealth Games gold, more than 300 wickets across all formats, and 14 years at the top of the game.

Loading Instagram content

An intimidating swing bowler, the 33-year-old has built a successful career on being an aggressive competitor. She is passionate and motivated by an "I'll show you" energy.

That fiery part of her personality comes in handy when on the cricket field, but less so off it.

Since receiving an ADHD diagnosis last year, Schutt has unlocked new insights about herself. The unique ways her brain works and rational explanations for her reactions.

"Cricket has been a great regulator for me," Schutt told ABC Sport.

"I've always been able to control myself on the field and then I'd come off and blow my fuse at spilling a cup of coke or something, so that was a real sign.

"Everything kind of clicked and made sense.

"I was quick to anger as a kid and never understood why that happened when I had a great childhood, happy parents.

"To be able to get my emotions in check has been a big change."

Beyond the rage, Schutt is learning to go easier on herself.

Megan has a daughter Rylee that she shares with ex-wife, Jess. (Getty: Hannah Peters)

"I set really high standards in a lot of areas and am realising they probably aren't achievable," she said.

"I'm getting older and the body wakes up sorer, so I've got to rest more.

"I find that hard, I feel guilty for it, I feel lazy.

"It's made me realise I need to not be so quick to judge myself or feel ashamed."

Seeing real change

Since she started taking ADHD medication, Schutt's Aussie teammates reckon she's more friendly.

"Darcie Brown and Georgia Wareham tell me that I'm a much nicer person when I'm on meds," she said.

Teammates have seen a change in Schutt's mood since she started taking medication. (Getty: Chris Hyde)

"They do make it easier to bat — I no longer have 1,400 shot selections in my head, of which I can only play three anyways — but other than that, I don't think my cricket has changed."

As an elite athlete regularly tested by anti-doping organisations, Schutt requires permission to take her medication with a therapeutic use exemption (TUE) from her doctor and psychologist.

It's a strict process that must be reviewed every 12 months or when her dose changes.

Having that clearance is vital, yet it doesn't bring Schutt complete peace of mind.

Two weeks ago, she was handed a two-match ban for failing to adhere to requirements around the use of prescription medication.

Megan Schutt says ADHD medication helps her with selecting a shot. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

This meant she missed the third T20 International against New Zealand and the opening match of the Women's Big Bash for the Adelaide Strikers.

Schutt returned to play on Thursday at Drummoyne Oval against the Brisbane Heat.

This interview was conducted in September, before the error, and there has been no indication whether the suspension is linked to Schutt's ADHD medication.

In a statement, a Cricket Australia spokesperson said:

"The circumstances of the breach are confidential, but Megan has expressed remorse and is aware of her obligations in this area."

Megan Schutt is back playing after a two-match suspension over prescription medication guidelines. (Getty Images/Cricket Australia: Jason McCawley)

"You do stress," Schutt said.

"I've been drug-tested a few times and I'm like, what if the TUE is inactive or we got our dosing wrong.

"I think you're targeted more being on amphetamines," she said.

Schutt believes the fear of accidentally testing positive for a prohibited substance could put others in her position off medicating.

"Some of the younger players won't take cold and flu," she said.

"You can't even have a protein shake from a cafe in case something is added to the powder.

"If someone cooks you something in their house and it's not approved, you could be done for.

"You've got to think twice, or it could be the end of your career."

As much as Schutt understands the importance of the process, she also gets frustrated about the extra hoops she has to jump through to take essential medicine to function.

Megan Schutt says she does stress about taking medication sometimes. (Getty: Matthew Lewis)

"At the end of the day, you are told a thousand times you are responsible for what you put in your body, but accidents happen," she said.

"What I struggle with is, if you have ADHD, it is obviously no longer a stimulant. I get a little bit angry about needing a TUE in the first place."

Navigating co-parenting and travel

Schutt has a five-year-old daughter, Rylee, with ex-wife Jess.

The pair separated last year and have been adjusting to co-parenting while navigating Rylee's autism and ADHD.

As her daughter started treatment, Schutt recognised her own triggers, which in turn led to her diagnosis.

It's been a tricky balance managing Rylee's appointments while playing professionally.

As a member of the national team, there is a lot of travel involved, and Cricket Australia's parental policies allow children and a carer to come along.

Loading Instagram content

Unfortunately, that hasn't been a viable option for Rylee.

"We had a lot of therapies back in the day — physio, OT, speech, dietitian — and there was no way I was going to pull her out of those routines just to have her on tour," Schutt said.

"It would have been too unsettling.

"It was easier for me to miss them, which was a hard one to wrap my head around because it's not what you picture when you have a child.

"Up until a year ago she preferred being held by myself or Jess anyway, so it really just made it impossible to bring her."

The marriage separation has also presented challenges to travel as Rylee has gotten older and potentially more ready, with it harder to bring along a designated carer.

There are also health and safety regulations that have got in the way.

"The system is not really set up for a single parent to take their kid, so it has been quite frustrating," Schutt said.

"I think the sport could maybe be a little more relaxed and aware of individual situations rather than having blanket rules for everyone."

Going out on a high

This has contributed to Schutt's decision to retire from ICC tournaments, going out on a high at the T20 World Cup as part of the wider squad that won the July final at Lord's.

The Australian team lifts the ICC Women's T20 World Cup trophy at Lord's in July. (Getty: Alex Davidson)

Schutt is still making an impact in the ODI format and was named Player of the Series against Bangladesh last month for taking 10 wickets overall and best figures of 4/16.

However, she's been in and out of the T20I team and hasn't played a Test since 2019.

"I've missed so much of Rylee's life and she's at an age where she can communicate that sadness and it hurts.

"At the back end of the World Cup she said, 'You're never coming back.'

"Every single session of FaceTime would be her asking, 'Are you on the plane yet?'

"It got to a point where me being away was doing more harm than good."

"The guilt is too much and spending more time on the bench makes me question why I'm away.

"Coming home to Adelaide brings a tear to my eye now. It's a realisation of where I want to be."

World.title: Connecting community through sport celebrated at Indigenous Sports Awards
World.content:
When Noongar and Martujarra man Nat Heath was young he was diagnosed with Guillian-Barre Syndrome, an autoimmune disease that attacks the nervous system and causes paralysis.

The diagnosis didn't set him back, but became one of his biggest motivators.

"Getting into triathlon, I just wanted to test my endurance, because the doctor said I would never have the same endurance after having the illness," he said.

After seeing what he achieved from his first triathlon, Heath went on to compete in six ironman events and won a championship in his age division.

"Which was amazing for myself, but there was just no other Black fellas doing the sport," he said.

"So I wanted to create a avenue where more mob could feel like they could participate in the sport of triathlon."

It inspired him to establish TriMob in 2020, an organisation that encourages mob to be physically active, through triathlons or marathons.

TriMob is a First Nations-led organisation encouraging Indigenous people to participate in triathlon. (Supplied: TriMob)

"Connecting community is a big piece of what we do, making sure our programs are culturally safe," Heath said.

"People feel a lot safer to come into our program just try it."

The organisation runs a "Mob the Marathon" program, to train participants from all over Australia to compete in the Sydney Marathon, now a World Major.

Talisha Godwin joined the program at the start of the year as a beginner, having little experience in training for or running a marathon.

"As a woman, as a mum, I just didn't think I couldn't do it," she said.

"I felt supported, I'd pushed so hard for myself to get there. I'd had days where I just couldn't do it, I was too tired, there was too much to do.

"But then one of the things one of the guys said in the group was, 'how can you show up one per cent today?'

"And that's a mantra I just said over and over and over again."

TriMob is a nominee for Team of the Year at the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Sports Awards. (Supplied: TriMob)

Godwin was amazed the community she was able to find in the program

"Showing up at the start line and finding the rest of the mob there in your group and starting together as a group and knowing it doesn't matter where we are on the race, on the track, we're all crossing the line together and supporting each other," she said.

Recognising First Nations excellence

TriMob is one of the nominees for Team of the Year at the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Sports Awards (NATSISAs).

The awards were established by late Aboriginal activist and former international soccer player Charles Perkins in 1986, to use sport as an example of bringing people from all backgrounds together.

It is now organised by former AFL player Nathan Lovett-Murray.

Nathan Lovett-Murray had a long AFL career with Essendon. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

"I recently just found out that my great grandfather, Pastor Sir Doug Nichols, used to host the event," he said.

"Now I'm hosting the event. So it's a bit of family history there and it's something that I'm really proud to be a part of."

As it grew in the 1990s, it showcased the best athletes from a range of sports, and at times became one of the only ways for the sporting contributions of mob to be recognised.

"Played with the Bombers for 10 years in the AFL and I wasn't able to attend the Sports Awards, but I did attend the Deadly Awards that used to be on," Lovett-Murray said.

"I actually won an award for football, so I remember going to those awards and loved seeing all the speeches of all the winners."

The NATSISAs serve as way for First Nations athletes to come together and find community with other mob from different sports.

Nathan Lovett-Murray was instrumental in reviving the NATSISAs after their 20-year hiatus. (ABC News)

This year's event will be held on Gadigal land at the Sydney Cricket Ground tonight, the first time the city has hosted the ceremony since 2001.

Before that it was on 20-year hiatus until 2023 and was brought back to be held in Brisbane and Melbourne.

Lovett-Murray hopes that in future more organisations and sponsors can get on board and support the growth of Indigenous athletes.

"Because when you support the Sports Awards, you're supporting First Nations sports all around the country," he said.

Cathy Freeman will be this year's keynote speaker, and categories include Lifetime Achievement award, Sportsperson of the Year, and National Trailblazer award.

World.title: Fine line between boxing and barbarism breached in 'frightening' KO
World.content:
The reaction from those watching the replays of Nelson Asofa-Solomona's sickening knockout of Paul Gallen speaks volumes.

Former Cronulla Sharks teammate of Gallen, Michael Ennis, looked desperately shaken as he admitted he found it hard to watch.

Tim Tszyu called it "frightening".

In real time, it was even worse.

"Oh jeez, oh no!" cried experienced caller Ben Damon on Main Event's commentary as the footage showed Asofa-Solomona's fist detonating onto Gallen's expressionless features.

"The last one was the worst one boys," Danny Green cried.

"That was the one he didn't need," he added, as Damon said, "that's no good," over the top of him.

"The last one was a bad one," Green reiterated.

"That's hard to watch," a shaken Damon summarised.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona crushed Paul Gallen inside the opening round. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

The fight only lasted two minutes and 56 seconds.

In that time, Asofa-Solomona both proved he was capable of taking another step in his quest to climb boxing's Penrose stairs, and similarly unsuitable to do so.

After a steady start, a thunderous right hand from Asofa-Solomona staggered the 45-year-old Gallen back towards the ropes.

Then another left-right combination put him right back against them.

Asofa-Solomona saw Gallen's head roll back, his arms flailing and glimpsed the opening for an upper cut.

He promptly delivered, landing a blow with such hideous force that Gallen was sent to the brink of unconsciousness.

A second upper cut unquestionably delivered him into that foul abyss.

Paul Gallen was left stricken on the canvas. (Supplied: No Limit Boxing)

But Asofa-Solomona wasn't done.

An unnecessary third grazed Gallen's granite chin as he sank to a seated position, his legs folded under him like a grotesquely discarded marionette.

Still, Asofa-Solomona wasn't done.

As referee Chris Condon threw himself between the fighters, a black-shirted angel of deliverance from the punishment Gallen had already endured for too long, Asofa-Solomona aimed another, sickening blow into the head of his stricken rival.

Few will understand this sanctimonious sermonising about such a despicable blow taking place amidst the wanton violence of a boxing bout.

This was boxing, wasn't it?

Hadn't Paulo Aokuso landed such a sweetly-timed left hand onto the head of Mobin Khahrazeh earlier in the night that it had observers positively purring?

Paulo Aokuso delivered a lauded statement KO in his bout. (No Limit)

Isn't it the point to knock your opponent out, to inflict such damage to a fellow human's brain that they lose consciousness in the pursuit of entertainment?

Yes, oddly enough, it is.

But even within the sanctioned barbarism of modern blood sports, there are rules in place to limit the hurt inflicted on a helpless opponent without being accused of hypocrisy.

It's there in almost every rule book you can care to find.

For example, the Australian National Boxing Federation:

55. Some fouls for which a referee may penalise or disqualify a boxer are: (a) Hitting an opponent who is down or is rising from a knockdown.

There can be caveats.

It took eight seconds from the first of those crushing Asofa-Solomona punches to land before referee Condon stopped the fight, but the four punishing upper cuts all came in the space of two-and-a-half horrific seconds.

It's barely enough time for anyone to react, not least a man who is on the charge and fighting for his future as a novice boxer.

But Gallen was clearly down.

Not only that, he was clearly out.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona delivered a devastating quartet of upper cuts. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Hundreds of boxers around the world have learned when enough is enough and to stop.

Hitting an unconscious opponent is beyond the pale, an unacceptable sin that breaches the unique brotherhood two fighters join when touching gloves with one another in the squared circle.

But Asofa-Solomona was clearly fired up.

His ill-advised leap into the crowd moments later proved that.

There is a caveat there, too.

Asofa-Solomona added context to his mad dash towards a punter in his post-fight press conference, telling reporters at the TikTok Entertainment Centre that he had been subject to a racist taunt.

Nelson Asofa-Solomona was heckled by someone in the crowd and lowered himself to challenge them directly. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

"Someone was doing an ape gesture. I stood on the ropes and it looked like someone threw something at me," he was reported as saying.

"If I had my time back, I would, because that's not on. But what that guy did to me, in terms of that gesture, is not on either.

"I'd just seen red."

Nobody should ever be subject to such foul, vindictive and uneducated slop and nobody should ever deign to suggest how someone should react if they are.

But his calamitous dash into the not-so-cheap seats added to the chaotic conclusion of the fight, meaning his indiscretion at its sickening conclusion was largely overlooked.

Asofa-Solomona proved to most onlookers that he has some skill in a ring on Friday night.

But the next time he delivers a knockout blow, he'd do well to stop before he risks inflicting any further damage.

World.title: Khawaja claims all players knew about Sandpapergate ball tampering
World.content:
All players and staff knew about the ball tampering during the infamous 2018 Cape Town Test, Usman Khawaja has told Nine newspapers ahead of the release of his book.

In an explosive claim in his new book Sabr, Khawaja says sandpaper was also used in the previous Test in Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.

"It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us," Khawaja told Nine newspapers.

"I don't want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now."

The claim is at odds with Cricket Australia's assertion that only Cameron Bancroft, Steve Smith and David Warner knew about the tactic. Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitch Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon also denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it.

Bancroft was banned for nine months after being caught using sandpaper on the ball during the third Test of the series in South Africa, while captain Smith and vice-captain Warner copped 12-month bans for their parts in the scheme.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith front the media after Bancroft was caught using sandpaper to tamper with the ball. (Gallo Images via Getty: Ashley Vlotman)

In the book, Khawaja claims that lighthearted discussions about the use of sandpaper at St George's Park in Gqeberha during the second Test led to Smith walking out of the rooms and saying that he didn't want to know about it.

He claims Bancroft then volunteered to use sandpaper in the first innings of that Test, where the ball swung significantly. He also said he sat next to Bancroft at Newlands in Cape Town during the third Test and saw who spoke to the young batter during the match that would see the Australian team caught out.

A Cricket Australia spokesperson said they remained comfortable with the initial findings of their investigation.

"There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case.

"All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process."

Khawaja said he was never interviewed by Cricket Australia about the incident. He also said the South Africa team were "far better" at working on the ball and that the Australians were "trying to keep up with them". Then South African captain Faf du Plessis had twice been sanctioned for ball tampering.

Khawaja has been promoting his book across various media outlets over the past weeks. However, the claims made in the ball-tampering chapters had been redacted until today. He said he had dedicated the chapter to Bancroft, Warner and Smith because he had seen how the saga had weighed on all three players.

Khawaja told ABC Radio National's Conversations program that revisiting the 2018 series for the book was particularly difficult.

Loading...

"Everyone in that team, one way or another, was affected and we still are affected by that to this day," he said.

"For me, writing that chapter was more about what I thought was the right thing to do. … I still struggle to talk about it in a lot of respects. There's no easy way to talk about what happened over there. There's no easy way to write about that period of Cricket Australia and that period of my life.

"It's just about telling my story. and what my feelings were particularly at that time and what I saw."

Khawaja said it was a culmination of seven years of playing with a "win at all costs" mentality that made the rest of the cricket world hate them.

He said that started after the 2011 Argus Review, which came in the wake of the team's first home Ashes series loss in 24 years, during which Khawaja made his Test debut as England won by an innings and 83 runs to complete a dominant 3-1 series victory.

"The way we were playing, we were disrespecting other players and I talked to other players in other teams I was friends with and they were just like 'yeah, we hate your boys'," he said.

Usman Khawaja reveals illness he kept secret his entire Test cricket career Cricket great Usman Khawaja could barely walk and thought he had a terminal illness when he was just starting out his Test career. He was soon diagnosed with a crippling disease, which he has kept secret for 17 years.

"This all manifested during that time with sandpaper, and no-one had our backs after that either because why would they? We just acted like idiots for the last seven years."

Khawaja's childhood coach and mentor, Bill Anderson, told Australian Story last month: "Usman actually tried to coerce them all to say 'we all knew what was going on' and some of them wouldn't buy into that. Ussie's view being, 'they're not going to sack us all'."

The 39-year-old told Conversations that if he could have his time over again, he would have stood his ground more resolutely.

The silver lining of the whole affair, Khawaja said, was that it forced the Australian men's team to have a long, hard look at its playing style.

"The best things come out of the worst times. I genuinely believe, for the Australian cricket team, the best thing that came out of Sandpaper is we found humility again," he said.

"JL [Justin Langer] came in as coach and he was honestly probably the best coach we could've had at that time. He put humility back in the Australian cricket team.

"It was just lovely to see. It was beautiful. I really enjoyed it. I really enjoyed seeing where the Australian team went from that point onwards and obviously Pat Cummins, who ended up becoming the captain, was a part of that process and journey."

Tech.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25 trillion, as rival Anthropic nears its IPO
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. That would make it one of the world’s most valuable companies, not long after raising $122 billion from investors in March at a valuation of $852 billion.

Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects.

OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. Earlier this year, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it’s holding off on its own IPO until it can make more confident claims about its models’ safety. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

Tech.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says.

Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new.

The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

Tech.title: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
Tech.content:
SpaceX has declared that it’s going to make Starlink Mobile a “major” mobile carrier. The Elon Musk-owned company has already deployed thousands of direct-to-cell satellites, but its next big challenge is building out its 5G network here on Earth.

As part of its plans to rival AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, SpaceX has inked a deal with Qualcomm, which will deploy its cellular technology across tens of thousands of 5G cell sites starting in 2027. SpaceX is also reportedly in talks to buy Boost Mobile, potentially allowing it to launch Starlink Mobile through the service. Another report suggests SpaceX may tap into 80,000 cell sites across the US to build out its network.

SpaceX’s big plans have garnered some reactions in the telecom industry. Tim Höttges, the CEO of T-Mobile’s parent company Deutsche Telekom, said he takes SpaceX’s plans “super serious” but that it could cost Musk more than $200 billion to pull off.

Tech.title: KPop Demon Hunters on 4K Blu-ray costs less than a month of Netflix Premium
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Buying the 4K Blu-ray disc version of KPop Demon Hunters was already going to be a wise idea for some people, especially those who primarily keep their $26.99 Netflix Premium subscription just to watch the hit animated flick in 4K. But at just $24.99 from Barnes and Noble and Amazon instead of its original $49.95 price, it’s easier than ever to recommend.

The Criterion Collection version of the film recently launched, and comes with a bunch of extras in a gorgeous set. In addition to the 4K digital master, complete with Dolby Vision HDR and Dolby Atmos sound, you also get two standard 1080p Blu-rays, one containing the film, and the other packed with special features (a full feature-length animatic, a making-of documentary, lyric videos, and more). It includes physical goodies, too, like collectible postcards, as well as an essay by Polygon alum Karen Han.

Kpop Demon Hunters was on my list of physical movies to buy, and this deal just turned it into a must-buy ahead of the holiday season.

Update, 4:50PM ET, November 6th: Previously, this deal was available for in-store pickup at Barnes and Noble, but it’s currently available online at both Barnes and Noble and Amazon.

Tech.title: All the latest updates on AI data centers
Tech.content:
Massive new data centers are the physical foundation for tech companies’ hopes and dreams for AI. But the rush to expand warehouses full of energy-hungry servers has also kicked up fights across the world over their impact on power grids, utility bills, nearby communities, and the environment.

Data centers were a major bipartisan issue ahead of the 2026 midterms, and voters largely opposed data center expansion at the polls. Tech giants like OpenAI and Amazon are promising to work more closely with local communities and cover their data center energy costs. But following the election, Democratic leaders are calling for further data center restrictions and slowdowns that the AI companies will have to grapple with.

Tech.title: Shure’s popular podcasting and streaming mic is almost $50 off
Tech.content:
is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

While the Shure Mv7 Plus is popular with streamers and podcasters, it’s equally good at impressing your friends and coworkers on meetings and Discord calls. It’s currently marked down to $255 at various retailers, including Amazon, Guitar Center, and directly from Shure. That’s almost $50 lower than its usual price, and just a few dollars off Amazon’s all-time low. Tech.title: Lame-duck Congress might actually do something: speed up energy projects
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A massive permitting bill that could help energy projects come online much quicker and potentially lower utility bills for Americans is advancing with bipartisan support. And while it could be a catalyst for lots of clean energy, it could also speed up polluting projects and limit oversight of new data centers.

With data centers demanding more electricity for AI, environmental advocates fear that developers could take advantage of the reforms to evade public scrutiny and rely more heavily on fossil fuels. The bill sacrifices caution for speed, limiting environmental reviews and preventing communities from stopping a project from moving forward by taking it to court.

“Whether it is permits to bulldoze wetlands, the fast-tracking of gas pipelines or general environmental review, with this legislation, data centers would not need to answer to the concerns of local communities,” Christy Goldfuss, executive director of the nonprofit Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), says in an email to The Verge. “People would be shocked to realize their representatives are rushing such a consequential decision.”

The bill sacrifices caution for speed

“They swung big with this bill. It’s a really good bipartisan compromise,” Xan Fishman, executive vice president of the Energy Program at the Bipartisan Policy Center, tells The Verge.

Four senators calling themselves the “four corners” — Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM) — introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) on September 30th. “If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” Whitehouse, a climate hawk, said in the press release.

The announcement simultaneously garnered support from climate and renewable energy groups, as well as fossil fuel interests. “Pass the frickin’ bill so we can start building things again,” the US Oil & Gas Association said in a statement.

The Senate could vote to move the bill forward as early as next week, teeing it up for potential passage before the end of the year, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman expects President Trump will want to sign the bill if the current Republican-controlled Congress acts, adding in an email that the White House has been “very involved” in negotiations. Newly empowered Democrats, however, could decide to drag out debate on the bill until next year in order to make fewer concessions to Republicans.

“Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control.”

If it becomes law, the bill would limit the reach of bedrock laws (stemming back to the 1970s environmental movement) that protect water resources and endangered species and give the public an opportunity to weigh in on large projects that might impact public health. Over the years, however, reviews that once took months at most might take several years or even decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. Fishman attributes the delays largely to lengthy legal battles. Now, agencies have to spend more time preparing for lawsuits as they consider permitting applications, Fishman says. That holds up development on all kinds of infrastructure projects, including cleaner energy alternatives to fossil fuels.

Fishman expects BAAJA to be very effective in amending outdated permitting rules that have become burdensome to projects across the board, even those that might ultimately have a net positive impact on the environment. “Sometimes, bureaucratic processes that are created with good intentions kind of spiral out of control,” he says. “You want to protect the environment, you want to protect people, but you want to get to a yes or no [on a permit application] in a reasonable amount of time and you don’t want to have this endless litigation cycle.”

The bill would set a 45-day deadline for a lead agency to issue a decision on a project after completing an environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). In many cases, NEPA review is the only opportunity for nearby residents to weigh in on large projects that involve the federal government. And it’s been a key tool for opponents to high-profile projects including the Dakota Access and Keystone XL pipelines. BAAJA narrows the scope of projects subject to NEPA, creating exclusions for transmission upgrades and certain pipeline expansions, to name a couple. Many projects receiving federal loans or grants or that have already been through a similar state environmental assessment would no longer trigger NEPA review.

The bill also sets a strict new 150-day limit for anyone to challenge a project in court over alleged violations of NEPA, the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, or National Historic Preservation Act. And BAAJA strips away a court’s ability to halt a project altogether even if it finds that a federal agency violated NEPA; it would simply force the agency to correct any issues.

The Clean Water Act allows the Army Corps of Engineers to issue general permits to projects that discharge dredged material into US waters as long as they’re deemed as having “minimal adverse environmental effects.” BAAJA could make it easier for large projects including data centers to qualify for those permits.

Some environmental groups are concerned that those general permits would take away public participation requirements for individual projects, especially when it comes to data centers that use a lot of water. The proposals in BAAJA amount to “rubber-stamping permits under the Clean Water Act” and “blocking interference from States and Tribes,” according to the environmental organization Earthjustice Action.

“It will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out.”

They’re also concerned that BAAJA aligns with the Trump administration’s push to deregulate industry and weaken environmental protections in order to swiftly build out more data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them. Data center energy demand has led to a surge of new gas projects in the US, and the bipartisan bill could help streamline reviews for new pipelines delivering fuel for data centers.

“One very big reason why passing BAAJA is such a high priority for the gas industry is it will enable fast delivery of gas to fuel the data center build-out,” Earthjustice Action President Abigail Dillen said in a Thursday blog. “BAAJA delivers a precision strike for developers of dirty data centers.”

Long pipeline delays slow data center development, according to energy research firm Wood Mackenzie. Permitting reform could benefit data center developers building out their own gas generation rather than relying solely on the grid, so-called “behind-the-meter” projects, by ending regulatory delays when it comes to connecting pipelines. Reforms would also speed grid-connected gas generation, Wood Mackenzie says in a recent news release.

“I don’t think we’re seeing it as this bill helping one type of technology over the other. I think it clears the way for all technologies to get onto the grid a little quicker,” Siddhant Warrier, research analyst for North American Power for Wood Mackenzie, tells The Verge.

Notably, the bill is supposed to protect bipartisan interests by preventing any single administration from attacking a particular project type — such as the Biden administration attempting to phase down oil and gas in the power sector or the Trump administration issuing stop work orders to wind farms. BAAJA aims to provide “project certainty” by barring federal agencies from canceling or suspending permits they’ve already approved in most cases. It even allows developers to take agencies to court for “disparate treatment” to sue for damages incurred from project delays.

“This part of the legislation could also lead to a slew of industry lawsuits that result in taxpayers paying billions of dollars to private industry,” the NRDC warns in its analysis of the bill. It could also prevent communities from challenging projects, including data centers, that wind up having unforeseen consequences for the environment and public health.

Despite those concerns, the NRDC and other advocacy groups are optimistic about the bill boosting renewable energy and enabling power grid upgrades needed to meet rising demand while keeping costs down.

BAAJA could shorten the time needed to build a new transmission line nearly in half — from 10 years or more to around five or six years, the NRDC estimates. Transmission lines that carry electricity across long distances — key to getting electrons to urban centers from far-flung solar and wind farms — are particularly tricky to build because of the patchwork of permitting processes they’re subject to across different jurisdictions.

Two separate reports project that the permitting bill would increase renewable energy capacity in the US and cut greenhouse gas emissions as a result. It also points to modest reductions in energy costs as a result of BAAJA passing compared to a baseline reflecting the status quo. The average annual cost of producing electricity would fall by as much as 7 percent by 2041, according to modeling by think tank Resources for the Future. Household electricity bills would lower by $50 to $78 per year by 2040, according to an analysis by research firm Rhodium Group. The White House put out its own analysis in October claiming that the average household could see their electricity bills fall by as much as $251 each year as a result of BAAJA.

One of the ways BAAJA aims to keep utility bills from rising is to force data center developers to pay more for transmission costs. Current law prevents utilities from charging them for costs stemming from both new builds and existing infrastructure, which inadvertently shifts costs to other customers to fill in the gap. The bipartisan bill mandates what’s called “and pricing” so that data centers and other large electricity customers would be on the hook to pay for both added and existing infrastructure.

The bill would also require utilities to disclose electricity sales to data centers. It would force large data center developers to make financial assurances to utilities before they break ground, as well as make them responsible for covering costs of new energy projects even if the data center shutters before the infrastructure is paid off.

Unfortunately, the bill may only solve part of the problem since utility rates reflect more than just transmission costs. Increasing electricity demand from the data center boom can still raise prices for fuel and gas turbines, for example. And the bill doesn’t address other issues that have sparked backlash against data centers, like noise and air pollution from generators on site.

Still, without permitting reform, gas and power prices would likely continue to climb as new energy projects keep hitting bottlenecks, according to Wood Mackenzie. Even environmental groups concerned about some of the provisions in BAAJA are holding out to see if Congress can amend the bill to strengthen environmental and consumer protections.

The bill has become a sort of Rorschach test for its backers, one expert speaking on background tells The Verge. They’re all optimistic that their energy source of choice, be it oil and gas or solar and wind, will ultimately come out on top — as long as it gets the green light to build.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI can create custom ‘spaces’ for the version of the app you need right now
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta will now allow you to build customized, app-like experiences within Muse. The new feature, called “spaces,” allows its AI assistant to build things like a shopping hub, school dashboard, music tracker, trivia game, and more, which you can interact with directly in the Muse app.

Meta says you can create a new space by describing it. If you connect an outside app to Muse — like Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable, Notion, and others Muse works with — the AI assistant will continuously pull information from them, allowing it to update pricing, dates, and other information in your space in the background. You can also interact with elements inside your spaces by checking things off, adding notes, and making edits.

Related Muse has a voice mode now

You can also change the placement of your spaces in the Muse app, too, as Meta lets you keep them in the sidebar, move them into your main tab, or schedule when you see them. “For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday,” Meta says.

Meta also announced that it’s bringing new “Active Memory” and “Active Focus” capabilities from its Muse Wonder AI model into the Muse app and its Meta AI chatbot. This will allow Muse to understand when past information becomes relevant during conversations, as well as make it better at working toward goals.

Meta is rolling out spaces to all Muse users. The company is also looking into ways to share your spaces with other users and collaborate with them.

Tech.title: Sequoia shutting down its Scouts program marks the end of an era
Tech.content:
Sequoia this week announced a broad overhaul in a memo posted to X, a move that includes closing its London office and shutting down its scout program. Observers warn that it would be a mistake to read too much into the London closure, since the British capital has a thriving AI scene. On the other hand, the decision to end scouts says more about where venture investing is headed.

That’s partly because 17 years ago, Sequoia pioneered the scouts model, in which select founders and operators write checks on the firm’s behalf. Amid increased competition for deal flow, many VC firms followed suit. But a consensus now seems to be emerging that the model has reached its limits in its current form.

Not everyone was sold on the model in the first place. “They pioneered the scout program but [to be honest] it never made sense to me!” VC Sheel Mohnot wrote on X this week. “The scouts themselves don’t really care that much about the investments, you can still miss (like they did with Uber), not sure what it gets you. I suspect other firms will shutter theirs too.” he added.

To be clear, Sequoia didn’t make a case against scouts in the memo. Instead, it framed its decision as part of a broader need for more focus. But its goal of “putting more energy behind fewer people and things” is likely to resonate with others who’ve questioned the ‘spray and pray’ approach to scouting.

Rival firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), for instance, rolled out a global scout network aimed at spotting opportunities in the U.S. and also in smaller European hubs. But a16z partner Gabriel Vasquez told TechCrunch earlier this year that the firm had revamped its program to double down “on the best people.”

Under this new approach, Vasquez explained, scouts get more resources but are also expected to be more active, such as by co-hosting dinners with the firm. “They get more budget, but we have reduced the number,” he said.

This also seems to indicate that it is VC firms that have been driving an overhaul of the model. For founders, being a scout is attractive: it brings them closer to firms they may want checks from someday, or even a partner role with, and being seen as someone who can write a check can raise their standing among other founders.

Some scouts will undoubtedly mourn the end of Sequoia’s program. Among them is Station F boss Roxanne Varza, who wrote on LinkedIn that she was “sad” to hear that the program was getting cut off, and “hope[d] that other funds [w]on’t follow suit.”

Varza, a former Sequoia scout from 2020 to 2025, told TechCrunch that she had no information beyond what has been shared publicly, but observed that becoming a scout had often been a stepping stone for aspiring investment managers.

“I cannot name all of the incredible scouts that have gone on to join or build funds, but there are quite a few. And the scout programs may have helped them get there — allowed them to build an investment track record, allowed them to build relationships with various funds directly, and more,” she wrote to TechCrunch.

According to Varza, the program’s impact went beyond the individual level, instead helping the entire ecosystem become more mature. “I believe they have helped to foster the investment culture and early-stage investment landscape that we now see in Europe, for example,” Varza said.

While others may agree with Varza about the role these programs have played, they may still have run their course for two reasons. First, seasoned operators may get more financial upside as angels. When it’s their own money, they get to keep the returns, too. Second, leading VC firms are now big and well-known enough that the best founders tend to come to them, so they worry less about missing deals, except at the very earliest stages or in niches and geographies where they have less reach.

Still, the pull of those early and niche deals is why scouts programs are much more likely to get revamped than to disappear entirely. “While Sequoia may be cutting the program, venture partner-style deals are likely to continue,” said Varza in her email to TechCrunch. “Scouts was just a way to scale the format. I don’t imagine Sequoia would end all forms of venture partners, but they are full of surprises.”

Tech.title: From the front row to the hot seat — what the midterms mean for Big Tech
Tech.content:
Right before the midterm elections, OpenAI hired Jessica Schumer, daughter of Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer. The company also said it would start calling its data centers “compute campuses.”

For the past two years, many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names have built closer ties with President Donald Trump and his administration. Several attended White House events, some companies scaled back diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and some executives donated millions to super PACs supporting his campaign and allied candidates. Administration policies also benefited the industry, including tax breaks, the pausing of some federal investigations, and looser AI regulation. Meanwhile, Meta faced lawsuits and billion-dollar fines, and OpenAI faced suits alleging its technology harmed users.

Now, with the midterms shifting the balance of power in Washington, those same companies are working to rebuild ties with Democrats, who have pledged to tighten oversight of AI. How far that gets them may depend less on image-polishing than on where the real fights are happening: in state capitols, in communities deciding whether to host data centers, and, as we’ve seen this past week, in the markets watching the AI boom.

J.B. Branch, director of federal AI governance and technology policy at Public Citizen, a nonprofit advocacy group that describes itself as nonpartisan, told me that the tech industry “realizes they have an optics problem.” He characterized moves like the Schumer hire and the rebranding as “PR washing.” He expects more of it, too, pointing to OpenAI’s partnership with the American Federation of Teachers, announced last year, as well as Anthropic’s newly launched Claude Corps and Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. “I would imagine more of that sort of investment in these corporate, private-public partnerships,” he said.

These initiatives didn’t spring up overnight. Meta and other tech companies reportedly began looking for ways to strengthen their ties to Democrats as Democratic gains in the midterms looked more likely. Reached for comment about the midterm elections’ impact on Meta, a company spokesperson pointed TechCrunch to remarks that Meta President Dina Powell McCormick made this week at WSJ Tech. “You have to work with the government that the American people elect,” McCormick had said. “I have seen it across the board that you have to be bipartisan, and you want to be, because you want buy-in on the things that you’re trying to do.”

Not everyone expects them to work. Alice Marwick, director of research at the tech policy nonprofit Data & Society, told me she expects Big Tech to try to pivot back toward the middle, “if not the left. But it’s a little too late,” she said. “Tech companies should be asking themselves how their products can make people’s lives better, because right now, it doesn’t seem like they are.”

If Democrats follow through on pledges to tighten oversight of AI and Big Tech, the industry could face a tougher environment. Data center moratoriums are gaining traction, and a wave of AI regulation bills awaits drafting. At the same event, Powell McCormick said Meta wants to show that communities welcoming its investments will see “an enormous amount of benefit,” while those that don’t want them “will of course have the right to stop them.”

Still, the next two years could bring political gridlock in Washington. Aryan Ranjan, founder of Baraza, a political campaign management software company, told me most action will likely happen at the state level, since states have already sued tech companies and passed regulations. “A coalition built on newer, working-class voters is likely to push Democrats to frame AI around electricity bills, data-center siting and jobs rather than abstract AI safety,” he said of what to expect at the federal level.

Last December, the Trump administration signed an executive order creating the AI Litigation Task Force, a federal group meant to challenge state AI laws. The administration has argued that U.S. AI companies “must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulations.” Many states have nonetheless passed their own laws, including measures on chatbots and deepfakes.

It also remains to be seen how President Trump will respond, including whether he’ll sign more AI executive orders or veto bills that could be seen as anti-AI. Clearly, voters want stronger guardrails around the technology.

In a statement to TechCrunch, a White House official said: “American leadership in super intelligence is essential for our national security, economic prosperity, and the quality of life of the American people. President Trump is committed to ensuring America continues to lead the world in super intelligence while protecting American consumers. As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.”

Branch argued that Trump’s political fortunes are now tied to the AI industry. On Wednesday, the day after the midterms, a trillion-dollar market sell-off spooked investors, some are whom are reportedly now reconsidering Anthropic’s reported trillion-dollar IPO. “There’s a very strong likelihood that there will be an AI bubble pop, and it’ll happen on Trump’s hands,” Branch said, predicting a possible market collapse. “Does he want to sink or swim along with the AI industry?”

For now, the rules companies face may vary by location. “For the next two years, a company’s AI rules may depend more on where it operates rather than on anything Washington passes,” Ranjan said.

Tech.title: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google
Tech.content:
Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.

Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.

Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.

Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, but it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.

The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.

Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.

The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.

Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.

Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members, including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.

Tech.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
Tech.content:
In Brief

OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.

In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market, with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

Tech.title: The Duo apps are coming, says Apple
Tech.content:
The early iPhone Duo reviews were a bit hard on Apple’s new foldable for the lack of Duo-optimized apps available at the time of launch. But Apple says things are changing quickly on the software front. The company on Friday announced there are now over 100,000 apps built for the Duo live on the App Store, and it’s seeing thousands more being added to the store every day.

The news was timed alongside the release of over a dozen more notable Duo-ready apps, including Microsoft Word and Outlook, Zoom, sports apps from the NBA and NHL, shopping apps like Etsy and LTK, productivity apps like Goodnotes and Extra, the Halide Mark III camera app, and others. These join the iPhone Duo-optimized apps that were already available, like Netflix, YouTube, Instagram, and WhatsApp.

Non-optimized apps are definitely less than ideal, as they come with a black bar on the side of the screen, which takes up valuable space. Sometimes, they hide important functions under an overflow menu.

Apple’s data seems to suggest that at least some iOS developers may have needed extra time to get their apps ready for its latest form factor. The company said that more than 2,000 app developers attended its over 50 in-person workshops that were hosted across 19 cities worldwide. Here, the developers could use the Duo and work on their apps with Apple’s support.

The Duo has also proven to be more popular than perhaps Apple had planned for, given its high price point. (It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model.) The device quickly sold out within hours of orders opening up, and now, Duo ship times have shifted into the next year. On its earnings call this week, Apple said it’s “hard to predict” when the Duo constraints leading to those delays will improve.

“It’s been wonderful to see how quickly developers have embraced iPhone Duo, and we’re grateful for their creativity and innovation,” said Susan Prescott, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Developer Relations, in a statement referring to the 100,000-app milestone. “The enthusiasm has been incredible, and we’re excited to see the pace of updates continue to accelerate as more and more apps optimize for iPhone Duo,” she added.

Other notable apps that have been updated for iOS 27 and optimized for the iPhone Duo include the following: Spotify, CBS, Tubi, BBC iPlayer (U.K.), Yahoo Fantasy Sports, Sportsnet (Canada), Facebook Messenger, Google Chat, ChatGPT, Grok Bot, Microsoft Copilot, Excel, PowerPoint, SAP Concur, monday.com, PDF Expert, Documents, iA Writer, Substack, The Washington Post, Yahoo News, FOX News, Kalshi, Yahoo Finance, Canva, Suno, Tinder, Google Translate, Strava, Alma, Withings, MyFitnessPal, Bevel, Transit, Citi Bike, ParkMobile, Viator, Tesla Robotaxi, Priceline, Kroger, Domino’s, Taco Bell, Untappd, The Weather Channel, FOX Weather, and RainViewer.

Not all these updates have yet to fully roll out, we should note.

Spotify, for instance, is still showing the black bar on the side, and the App Store doesn’t yet say an update is available on our review unit of the Duo. However, given that this list comes directly from Apple, we expect to see these updates soon.

Tech.title: Hundreds of Artex AI hacking tools found publicly exposed to the web
Tech.content:
Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post, cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September. Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October, which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”

Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.

The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

Tech.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent
Tech.content:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Image Credits:Meta

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice, which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot, which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry.

Tech.title: The Cybertruck’s Death Is Actually Great News for EVs
Tech.content:
Building smaller vehicles is, of course, one way to make EVs cheaper. With less weight to propel, you can rely on a smaller battery. And given that the battery pack is the most costly component of an EV, that can in turn help automakers offer more affordable vehicles at a time when the price of so many other consumer goods is skyrocketing. That includes the current crop of EVs: The average transaction price for a new model is now $55,800, according to Cox Automotive.

Going small—or smaller, anyway—also means making the most of a limited battery supply chain. The vast majority of Cybertruck drivers are doing the same thing with their vehicles as Hyundai Ioniq 5 drivers: getting groceries, commuting, and driving kids to soccer games. But a standard-range Ioniq 5 driver is doing it with a battery about half the size.

After President Donald Trump’s administration killed EV incentives last year, sales plummeted. The Iran War and rising gas prices have led to an uptick in interest, though sales still lag behind the global average. (Used hybrid sales have also picked up, reflecting the pain people have been feeling at the pump.) Even with a Democratic-controlled Congress, EV incentives coming back under Trump are about as likely as defense secretary Pete Hegseth putting pronouns in his email signature. But should Democrats take the White House in 2028, marking the culmination of Woke 2.0, support for would-be EV buyers becomes much more likely.

Automakers pivoting to smaller cars could be much better positioned to meet pent-up demand if that happens, while also lowering the risks of delivery delays.

Even Elon’s announcement killing the Cybertruck points to where the market is heading: He claims Tesla is ending production to make room for cranking out more Cybercabs. The battery size in those vehicles? Just 48 kilowatt-hours.

Additional reporting by Aarian Marshall.

Tech.title: How Stephen Miller Schemed His Way to the Top
Tech.content:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced that Stephen Miller, one of his most powerful and politically aggressive aides, would be his next White House chief of staff following disastrous results for Republicans in the midterm elections.

Miller, whose titles until now were deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser, has orchestrated the most polarizing policies of Trump’s second term—most notably a brutal crackdown on immigration that has claimed the lives of US citizens.

Trump made the change public in a statement on his Truth Social platform, writing that Miller would take over from Susie Wiles on Monday—less than a week after Republicans lost the House and Senate in a searing rebuke of Trump’s policy agenda.

In recent days, Trump has privately blamed Wiles for the worst Republican midterm performance in decades, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday, the sources say.

Trump broadly considered three candidates to replace Wiles, the sources say: special envoy Steve Witkoff, director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, and Miller.

But with the looming threat of congressional investigations starting next year, Trump settled on Miller, seemingly because of his zeal in defending the president and his deep loyalty. Miller has been with Trump since his first campaign and stood by him through his political exile in 2021.

Miller had made his interest in the job known inside the West Wing for weeks, ever since Wiles weathered a series of negative stories before the midterms that suggested her job was at risk, the sources say.

In recent months, Trump also started cutting Wiles out of certain decisions, which contributed to the sense among her detractors that she was on shaky ground, sources say. For instance, Trump reportedly hired Katie Zacharia as press secretary without consulting Wiles, though the White House pushed back on the claim.

With Wiles’ departure, White House aides were bracing for further personnel changes. Among other names, Wiles’ deputies James Blair, who put together the GOP midterm strategy, and Richard Walters are seen as vulnerable to being fired by Miller unless they resign first, sources say.

The changing of the guard is also likely to bring respite to defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has had a strained relationship with Wiles as of late but is seen as ideologically aligned with Miller, sources say.

Hegseth and Miller worked closely last year when the Trump administration began a campaign of strikes against boats around Venezuela. Miller, who also leads the Homeland Security Council within the White House, orchestrated the campaign through the Pentagon.

Wiles leaves the White House as arguably the most successful chief of staff to Trump, who infamously cycled through chiefs in his first term. By comparison, Wiles kept Trump’s confidence from the start of his second presidential campaign in 2021.

Still, Wiles weathered a number of challenges in recent months. She underwent a successful course of chemotherapy, but also faced accusations that her daughter had received lucrative contracts in part because of the family’s connection to the president. (The White House and Wiles’ daughter’s firm pushed back on these claims.)

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime,” Wiles wrote on X. “I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First.”

Tech.title: Free Chinese AI Models Are Getting Scary Good at Hacking
Tech.content:
Open-weight artificial intelligence models are now almost as capable of hacking into computer networks as the best closed ones, according to new research that heralds a much-anticipated turning point in the cybersecurity landscape.

Vals, a company that measures AI capabilities, set out to test how well different AI models could carry out complex, multi-step network instructions on mock corporate networks.

“The best frontier models, locked up inside the labs and available only through trusted access programs, are now starting to be matched by open models that anybody can download,” says Nikil Ravi, a researcher at Vals.

The company’s findings suggest that closed models no longer have a definitive edge in cyber skills, meaning recent efforts by frontier labs to limit access to their models, and thereby slow the proliferation of such capabilities, may potentially be moot.

The findings are also noteworthy given that the US frontier labs, particularly Anthropic, premised the limited release of new models—beginning with Claude Mythos Preview in April—on the idea that gated access would only buy time before advanced hacking capabilities were broadly available.

Tech.title: AI Companies Really, Really Want to Buy Your Work Files and Emails
Tech.content:
Lately a new kind of pitch has found its way into my inbox. “Not sure if you've heard,” writes someone named Nick, “but AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI are paying media companies such as Wired $350K to $1.8M as a one time fee for a copy of their old work records (documents, emails, slack messages, tickets, etc.) for training better models.”

Another email with a similar pitch (adding call transcripts to the list of desired information) raised the stakes to a possible $2 million. “Public data is exhausted, and the labs are spending over $45B on private data to build better models,” writes someone named Cora.

While I was aware that AI companies are buying expert data from various sources, there hasn’t been that much attention paid to it. But once I looked into it, I discovered that this business is way bigger than I suspected—and according to its practitioners, it could have as much impact on workers and society as the data centers that are dominating the news these days.

The companies that contacted me are part of an industry boom in data acquisition that’s been quietly buying the workflows of sizable companies and is still so hungry that it’s bleeding into our inboxes. A freelance writer recently wrote about her experience with a company called Handshake, which offered her $1,000 for her work on a single story. (She didn’t sell.) A representative from Handshake confirmed the offer to me: “We license professional documents across a lot of fields so the labs can test and train how models handle real knowledge work,” he said. “Journalism is one of those fields.” Handshake tells me that a big part of its business is buying graduate students’ papers and coursework.

An entrepreneur friend of mine tells me he’s been getting mail from multiple companies whose business is “helping startups wind down their companies," as one email from a company named Sunset explained it. “We handle the full process, scrubbing and anonymizing the data so the company people and any identifying details are stripped out, then brokering the deal with the labs.”

Those newer data acquisition startups are hoping to achieve the quick success of the dominant companies in the field, which themselves are only a few years old. Industry leaders Handshake, Micro1, and Mercor are snapping up databases as if it were a modern gold rush. The industry leader seems to be Mercor, founded in 2023; last year its three cofounders became billionaires at 22. Like all the companies, it claims to have partnerships with just about all the major AI labs. (The response from the companies themselves was more circumspect: Anthropic acknowledges that there’s a big market for data, but told me that it doesn’t buy workflow from live companies like WIRED. OpenAI didn’t come up with a response before publication.)

Tech.title: RIP Cybertruck. You Were Unloved, Unwanted, and Utterly Absurd
Tech.content:
Elon Musk, in a post on X, has officially called time on the Cybertruck, stating that “Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production.”

Produced for less than four years, the polarizing pickup is seemingly dying as it lived, with the news being greeted in a flurry of replies in praise of the EV as well as deriding it. James Star, claiming to be a Tesla employee, posted that it was “the saddest news! Cybertruck (was) the best car Tesla sold,” right next to a user called Captain Ford who simply replied to Musk with “Fuck that shitbox.”

Tesla has not responded to WIRED’s request for comment and clarification that the Cybertruck will no longer be made at all. The Cybertruck is exclusively made at Gigafactory Texas, as this is apparently the only Tesla facility equipped with the machinery required to manufacture the truck’s unique stainless steel body, which supposedly started to rust in some cases.

Despite whipping up a fevered number of reservations—allegedly more than a million according to Musk, who at the end of 2023 crowed that demand was “off the charts!”—the truck failed to sell, shifting less than 50,000 units in total by March last year.

EVWire cites Kelley Blue Book data suggesting that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks in the first three quarters of this year in the US, down 28 percent year-over-year, adding that Musk’s announcement post came about 80 minutes after Tesla raised US Cybertruck prices and paused new orders for the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD version.
